#### Abstract

Visual Grounding, also known as Referring Expression Comprehension and Phrase Grounding, aims to ground the specific region(s) within the image(s) based on the given expression text. This task simulates the common referential relationships between visual and linguistic modalities, enabling machines to develop human-like multimodal comprehension capabilities. Consequently, it has extensive applications in various domains. However, since 2021, visual grounding has witnessed significant advancements, with emerging new concepts such as grounded pre-training, grounding multimodal LLMs, generalized visual grounding, and giga-pixel grounding, which have brought numerous new challenges. In this survey, we first examine the developmental history of visual grounding and provide an overview of essential background knowledge, including fundamental concepts and evaluation metrics. We systematically track and summarize the advancements, and then meticulously define and organize the various settings to standardize future research and ensure a fair comparison. In the dataset section, we compile a comprehensive list of current relevant datasets, conduct a fair comparative analysis, and provide ultimate performance prediction to inspire the development of new standard benchmarks. Additionally, we delve into numerous applications and highlight several advanced topics. Finally, we outline the challenges confronting visual grounding and propose valuable directions for future research, which may serve as inspiration for subsequent researchers. By extracting common technical details, this survey encompasses the representative work in each subtopic over the past decade. To the best of our knowledge, this paper represents the most comprehensive overview currently available in the field of visual grounding. This survey is designed to be suitable for both beginners and experienced researchers, serving as an invaluable resource for understanding key concepts and tracking the latest research developments.

UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding with Generated Language Conditions Wenbin Tan1, 2, Jiawen Lin1, Yuan Xie3, Yachao Zhang1* , Yanyun Qu1* 1Key Laboratory of Multimedia Trusted Perception and Efficient Computing, Ministry of Education of China, School of Informatics, Xiamen University, Xiamen, China 2School of Big Data, Tongren University, Tongren, China 3School of Computer Science and Technology, East China Normal University, Shanghai, China wbtan@stu.xmu.edu.cn, yachaozhang@xmu.edu.cn, yyqu@xmu.edu.cn Abstract Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding (Zero-Shot 3DVG) aims to localize target objects in 3D scenes from natural lan-guage descriptions without relying on instance-wise de-scription annotations.
Existing methods rely on extra 2D images during inference and/or require multi-turn in-teractions with large language models (LLMs) or vision-language models (VLMs), which increase latency, compu-tational cost, and deployment complexity.
To overcome these limitations, we propose Unaided Zero-shot 3D Visual Grounding with generated language conditions (UZ3DVG), which is fed with 3D point clouds and textual descriptions only during inference and does not depend on external models. This is a new training paradigm: a VLM is em-ployed solely to produce object-wise descriptions (pseudo labels) and reasoning chains for training a lightweight 3DVG model with robust spatial reasoning. Specifically, the introduced Open-Vocabulary Multi-Source Spatial Annota-tion and Reasoning Chain Generator processes RGB-D im-ages or 3D-projected 2D images from open-world scenes to generate spatial pseudo-labels and reasoning chains for training. Then, we propose Reasoning Chain Distillation, which transfers reasoning knowledge extracted by a large teacher network to a lightweight student network. To rep-resent both global and local geometric relationships, the Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling (GeoSM) module is in-troduced to align textual reasoning with 3D spatial struc-tures.
Experiments show that UZ3DVG achieves SOTA zero-shot performance on ScanRefer and NR3D, with infer-ence speeds up to 7.69 FPS, approximately 38 times faster than SOTA methods.
The code is available at https: //github.com/tanwb/UZ3DVG.

1. Introduction 3D visual grounding (3DVG)[32, 40, 46, 51, 57] aims to lo-calize target objects in 3D scenes based on natural language descriptions. This task holds broad application potential in domains such as indoor robotic visual navigation[42], vir-tual reality (VR)[44], and augmented reality (AR)[7].
Existing 3DVG methods, such as EDA[45], MCLN[28], and TSP3D[10], primarily focus on the closed-set setting[2, 4, 15, 23, 34, 49, 50, 58]. Although these methods have achieved significant performance improvements, their train-This CVPR paper is the Open Access version, provided by the Computer Vision Foundation.
Except for this watermark, it is identical to the accepted version; the final published version of the proceedings is available on IEEE Xplore.
9547 ing heavily relies on large-scale human-annotated paired data (i.e., language descriptions and 3D objects) [2, 4]. This high annotation cost severely limits the generalization abil-ity and deployment of these models in novel scenes.
Recent studies explore zero-shot 3DVG [17, 19, 47, 51], including ZSVG3D [51] and SeeGround [17]. These meth-ods integrate large language models (LLMs) [25] or vision-language models (VLMs) [12] into the 3DVG inference pipeline, leveraging their semantic understanding and rea-soning capabilities.
However, they often call LLMs or VLMs during inference or perform multi-round interac-tions, as illustrated in Fig. 1, leading to high latency, com-putational overhead, increased costs, and deployment diffi-culties. Current zero-shot 3DVG methods typically run at less than the real-time threshold of 6 FPS [10].
To address these challenges in zero-shot 3DVG, we pro-pose Unaided Zero-shot 3D Visual Grounding with gen-erated language conditions (UZ3DVG). To the best of our knowledge, UZ3DVG is the first zero-shot 3DVG model that, during inference, uses only 3D point cloud inputs with-out 2D imagery or external LLMs/VLMs. Its core idea com-prises two components: (i) constructing high-quality 3D pseudo-labels, and (ii) supervising a lightweight model with pseudo-labels and reasoning chains generated by a VLM.
We design the Open-Vocabulary Multi-Source Spatial Annotation and Reasoning Chain Generator (MSAG-RC) to extract RGB images and depth information, enabling effec-tive transformation from 2D imagery to 3D spatial annota-tions. MSAG-RC uses open-vocabulary 2D detectors (e.g., Grounding DINO [20]) and segmentation models such as SAM2 [29] to obtain object masks and categories. By com-bining these with depth maps and camera parameters, the 2D segmentation results are back-projected into 3D space to recover object-scale information. The projected 3D data is encoded and fed into a VLM via prompt engineering to generate spatial pseudo-labels and reasoning chains, which serve as supervision to address the absence of spatial anno-tations and reasoning guidance in zero-shot training.
To transfer reasoning knowledge and logical structures within the chains to a compact model, we employ Reason-ing Chain Distillation (RCD). A large teacher network ex-tracts such knowledge from the generated chains and dis-tills it into a lightweight student network. Due to the multi-relational complexity of the chains, mapping target infor-mation to sparse point clouds remains challenging. To mit-igate this, we propose the Geometry-Aware Spatial Mod-eling (GeoSM) module, which encodes global context and local geometric relationships. GeoSM processes aligned vi-sual features to provide positional references at both levels, thereby enhancing the correspondence between textual rea-soning chains and 3D spatial structures.
Experimental results show that UZ3DVG achieves Acc@0.25/0.5 of 45.42%/41.08% on ScanRefer, surpassing SeeGround [17] by 1.32%/1.68%. On the more challeng-ing Multiple subset of ScanRefer, it achieves Acc@0.25/0.5 of 40.49%/36.33%, outperforming SeeGround [17] by 6.49%/6.33%.
The inference speed reaches 7.69 FPS, about 38 times faster than SeeGround’s 0.2 FPS. These re-sults confirm UZ3DVG’s robustness in complex scenes as well as its superior accuracy and efficiency.
In summary, our contributions are: • We propose a novel zero-shot 3DVG paradigm that, at in-ference, relies solely on 3D point clouds as input, without using 2D images or interacting with VLMs, and employs an efficient network, retaining high speed and flexible de-ployment.
• To address the gap between 2D foundation models and 3D pseudo labels, we design the MSAG-RC to embed multi-modal information from RGB and depth into 3D space, and leverage the zero-shot capability of a VLM to gener-ate spatial pseudo labels and reasoning chains. We further introduce Reasoning Chain Distillation (RCD) to allevi-ate the inherent shift between foundation model knowl-edge and 3D visual grounding.
• UZ3DVG achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the ScanRefer and NR3D, with an inference speed ap-proximately 38 times faster than that of existing methods.
2. Related Work 3D Visual Grounding. Most current 3DVG research[13, 18, 27, 28, 43, 46, 55] follows supervised paradigms, requir-ing large-scale manual 3D labels from densely annotated datasets such as ScanRefer[4] and ReferIt3D[2], which align language descriptions with target objects in 3D scenes.
Representative works[5, 6, 10] address challenges in-cluding text–point cloud alignment[33, 45], geometric fea-ture extraction[39, 40], and contextual cue modeling[57], using approaches such as Transformer-based attention[11, 57, 58], contrastive learning[1], graph-based relational modeling[9, 13, 36, 50], and text-guided voxel pruning[10], generally improving accuracy via manual 3D label supervi-sion. Weak supervision was also explored[54, 56], but not in 3D visual grounding.
However, reliance on manual annotation limits general-ization to unseen environments. To address this, we propose a zero-shot open-vocabulary 3DVG paradigm that uses au-tomatically generated 3D pseudo labels to enhance adapt-ability and robustness in diverse 3D scenes.

Figure 2. Overview of the UZ3DVG framework with training and inference phases. In training, MSAG-RC converts RGB-D images into spatial description pseudo-labels and reasoning chains to guide 3DVG model training, and RCD distills reasoning knowledge and logic from a teacher network to a lightweight student network head. Reasoning-enhanced text features are aligned with 3D backbone features (SpConv) and augmented via TSVDE, then processed by GeoSM to model global context and local geometry before the prediction head outputs localization results. During inference, only point clouds and text inputs are used, without MSAG-RC and RCD-teacher.
Ground [17], VLM-Grounder [47], and OpenEQA [24], which employ strategies like 3D-to-2D rendering, multi-view projection, and embodied-agent interaction.
Although effective, these methods rely on VLM-based inference, causing high latency and computational over-head. Our work aims to address these speed and deploy-ment challenges with UZ3DVG, which relies solely on 3D point clouds during inference, without VLM interaction.
3. Methodology 3.1. Overview To tackle slow inference, and deployment complexity caused by 2D reliance and multi-turn LLM/VLM inter-actions in zero-shot 3DVG, we introduce UZ3DVG. The network architecture, illustrated in Figure 2, consists of a training phase and an inference phase.
During the training phase, both branches operate simultaneously, be-ginning with RGB-depth images processed by the Open-Vocabulary Multi-Source Spatial Annotation and Reason-ing Chain Generator (MSAG-RC) to produce spatial de-scription pseudo-labels and corresponding reasoning chains for guiding the 3DVG model. To enhance spatial reason-ing ability and accelerate inference, these pseudo-labels and reasoning chains are first fed into a larger teacher net-work to extract reasoning knowledge and logic, which are then transferred to a lightweight student network through Reasoning Chain Distillation (RCD). The spatial descrip-tion pseudo-labels undergo feature extraction before enter-ing the student network, while the Text-Semantic-guided Visual Detail Enhancement (TSVDE) module samples and augments details related to textual semantics from low-level visual features to help the model locate representa-tions of reasoning logic. Following cross-modal text-visual alignment, the aligned visual features are passed to the Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling (GeoSM) module to ex-plicitly model global information and local geometric rela-tionships within the 3D scene, assisting the student model in reasoning and improving its localization performance.
Notably, the pseudo-labels, 3D information, and reasoning chains generated by MSAG-RC are used exclusively during training, whereas in the inference phase only the actual lo-calization descriptions and 3D point clouds are required to achieve 3D visual localization.
3.2. Multi-Source Annotation and Reasoning Chain To address annotation scarcity and insufficient structured reasoning supervision in zero-shot 3D localization, and to effectively bridge the representational gap between 2D im-age inputs and 3D spatial localization annotations, we pro-9549 pose the Open-Vocabulary Multi-Source Spatial Annota-tion and Reasoning Chain Generator (MSAG-RC). This ap-proach relies solely on 2D inputs obtained from RGB-depth images or projected 3D point clouds, enabling the joint gen-eration of 3D semantic labels and spatial reasoning chains without manual annotations.
Open-Vocabulary 3D Bounding Box Generation. Given an RGB-D video sequence, we uniformly sample frames at a fixed interval to obtain the i-th RGB image Ii ∈RH×W ×3 and its corresponding depth map Di ∈RH×W . We first ap-ply an open-vocabulary 2D object detector (e.g., Grounding DINO [20]) to predict coarse 2D bounding boxes b2D i,j ∈ R4. To obtain more accurate object boundaries, we further employ SAM2 [29] to convert each valid b2D i,j into a pixel-level segmentation mask: Mi,j = SAM2(Ii, b2D i,j ) ∈{0, 1}H×W .
(1) After filtering invalid or noisy depth values, the valid masked pixel set is defined as Ωi,j = {(u, v) | Mi,j[u, v] = 1, Di[u, v] ∈R}, (2) where R denotes the valid depth range after outlier removal.
For all valid pixels (u, v) ∈Ωi,j, the corresponding depth values are given by zi(u, v) = Di[u, v]. We back-project all such pixels into 3D with the depth intrinsic matrix Kd and camera pose T(i) c2w, and further transform them into the axis-aligned scene coordinate system with A: e Pi,j = A T(i) c2w �Di[u, v] K−1 d [u, v, 1]⊤ .
(3) An axis-aligned 3D pseudo box b3D i,j = [ci,j, si,j] ∈R6 is computed from the aligned point cloud extrema pmin i,j = min(e Pi,j) and pmax i,j = max(e Pi,j) as ci,j = pmax i,j + pmin i,j 2 , sraw i,j = pmax i,j −pmin i,j .
(4) Multi-Source Spatial Annotation. After obtaining object-level 3D geometry, we design a symbolic-logic-based spa-tial prompt constructor to transform geometric attributes into structured prompts for a VLM. For the j-th valid ob-ject in frame i, let its category be κi,j, its 3D pseudo box be b3D i,j = [ci,j, si,j], and its target-specific spatial context be Ci,j. Together with the annotated RGB image ˜ Ii,j, the VLM generates a natural language spatial description: di,j = VLM(˜ Ii,j; ci,j, si,j, κi,j, Ci,j), (5) where ˜ Ii,j is the RGB image with the target object high-lighted by a 2D bounding box and identifier, and di,j is a human readable room-level spatial description.
Reasoning Chain Generation. To produce structured su-pervision for lightweight model reasoning, we craft prompts that instruct the VLMs to emulate a robot localizing tar-gets from object relationships in the pseudo 3D scene. No-tably, this pseudo 3D scene is the same one used to generate di,j. After generating the description, the VLM is imme-diately prompted to produce the corresponding reasoning chain. The predefined template requires the reasoning chain to contain the structured components Anchor, References, and Reasoning. To further improve pseudo-label quality, prompt engineering requires the VLM to verify that Ri,j is consistent with di,j while correcting localization failures in both. After self-verification, the VLM returns: (di,j, Ri,j, γi,j) = G(˜ Ii,j, b3D i,j , κi,j, Ci,j), (6) where G denotes the prompt-constrained VLM generation function, Ri,j is the structured reasoning chain, and γi,j is the self-assigned confidence score; see Suppl. for details.
The final outputs are 3D spatial semantic labels, reason-ing chains, and confidence scores. The entire process is automated through prompt engineering, requiring no man-ual labeling and enabling 3D localization annotation from RGB-D sequences in open environments.
3.3. Reasoning Chain Distillation To efficiently transfer reasoning chain knowledge from the teacher model to the student model while maintaining fast inference speed, we design the Reasoning Chain Distilla-tion module (RCD). This module adopts a dual path distil-lation scheme, in which the teacher network simultaneously guides the student network with textual and visual features enhanced by reasoning chains. Under distillation loss con-straints, the reasoning logic embedded in the chain is inter-nalized into the student’s spatial reasoning capability.
RCD-Teacher.
The teacher network consists of three tightly connected layers: (i) reasoning chain parsing and encoding, (ii) noise filtering and feature enhancement, and (iii) cross-modal alignment and distillation output.
First, given a reasoning chain R and its corresponding open-vocabulary spatial annotation text features Tovsd, the teacher network begins by extracting the Anchor, Refer-ence, and Reasoning components from the structured rea-soning chain. These components are separately encoded by a frozen RoBERTa encoder [21] and yield the initial component-level representation Ctea chain, which constitutes the reasoning chain parsing and encoding stage.
This is followed by the noise filtering and feature en-hancement stage. To suppress noisy components while re-taining those semantically aligned with Tovsd, the teacher applies a quality gating mechanism to Ctea chain conditioned on the global text context, yielding the gated component repre-sentation Cfilt chain = Gate �Ctea chain, Tovsd  .
(7) To model logical dependencies among the gated compo-nents, we apply self-attention: Htea c = SAc(Cfilt chain). The 9550 resulting component features are first grounded to the orig-inal text features through cross-attention, and are then in-jected back into the textual stream through a cross-attention module followed by gated fusion, producing the enhanced textual representation Ttea fus.
Finally, in the cross-modal alignment and distillation output stage, the fused textual representation Ttea fus is aligned with teacher visual features Vtea, which are derived from the same source visual input as the student features, through three layers of bidirectional cross-modal attention. Specifi-cally, self-attention is first applied to both streams, followed by cross-attention: (Vtea out, Ttea out) = CA �SAv(Vtea), SAt(Ttea fus)  .
(8) The resulting aligned features (Vtea out, Ttea out) serve as the distillation targets for guiding the student network.
RCD-Student. Under the guidance of the teacher, the stu-dent network is designed to identify reasoning-relevant fea-tures in localization descriptions, extract the underlying rea-soning logic, and improve localization accuracy through a lightweight pseudo reasoning mechanism. It is structurally analogous to the teacher but has reduced capacity, compris-ing three stages: (i) pseudo reasoning signal generation, (ii) reasoning aware feature enhancement, and (iii) cross modal alignment.
Given the language spatial description features Tovsd, we apply masked global average pooling to obtain a global context: tstu pool = GAP(Tovsd). This pooled feature is fed into a lightweight query generator and an attention-based extractor to produce three pseudo reasoning components Rstu comp, which mimic the three components in the teacher reasoning chain, namely Anchor, Reference, and Reason-ing. These components are further aggregated into a global student reasoning representation Rstu.
To align the student representation with the teacher rep-resentation, we apply a reasoning distillation objective that enforces consistency at both the component and global lev-els, defined as Lr = Lcomp r + Lglobal r , (9) where Lcomp r and Lglobal r denote student-teacher alignment over the reasoning components and the aggregated global representations, respectively.
The student then enhances its textual representation by concatenating Rstu with Tovsd, transforming the fused fea-tures with an MLP, and injecting the result into the origi-nal textual stream with confidence weighted residual fusion.
The enhanced textual features are subsequently aligned with visual features through a lightweight bidirectional cross modal encoder with two layers, yielding Vstu out and Tstu out.
To transfer the teacher’s reasoning dynamics, we define reasoning gains as Gtea = Ttea out −Tovsd, Gstu = Tstu out −Tovsd, (10) and align them via Lg = Lcos + Lmse + Lmag, (11) where Lcos, Lmse, and Lmag respectively constrain gain di-rection, normalized gain magnitude, and overall enhance-ment strength.
Additionally, visual features are distilled with a foreground-background hybrid loss: Lv = Lfg(Vstu out, Vtea out) + Lbg(Vstu out, Vtea out), (12) where Lfg and Lbg denote foreground matching and back-ground matching, respectively.
Collectively, the above losses enable efficient reasoning chain distillation.
Text-Semantic-Guided Visual Detail Enhancement. To enrich visual features with fine-grained details from text-relevant regions and improve reasoning performance, we in-troduce the Text-Semantic-Guided Visual Detail Enhance-ment module (TSVDE). During upsampling, the module leverages textual semantics and reasoning-enhanced visual features to guide feature refinement. Specifically, it applies similarity-based sampling to emphasize regions closely aligned with textual semantics, thereby enhancing the fine-grained details required by the reasoning chain (see Suppl.
Sec. 1.1 for details).
3.4. Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling Reasoning chains often contain spatial predicates (e.g., “left of”, “above”) relying on geometric relationships. However, visual features from sparse convolutions (SpConv) lack ex-plicit spatial-relation modeling, which limits reasoning-to-visual mapping.
To address this limitation, we propose Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling (GeoSM) to integrate global and local ge-ometry. First, to capture the global 3D spatial context, we normalize the coordinates pi corresponding to the aligned visual features, following ideas from 3DGraphLLM [52], and compute absolute positional embeddings via sinusoidal encoding: ˆ pi = 2 · pi −pmin pmax −pmin + ε −1, (13) where pmin and pmax are point cloud bounds, and ε ensures stability. The encoded positions capture global layout cues, yielding the positional feature f pos i after linear projection.
For local geometry, we build K-nearest-neighbor neigh-borhoods. For each point pi, the relative displacement is defined as ∆pij = pj −pi. We aggregate neighbor fea-tures, concatenate them with ∆pij, and pass the combined representation through an MLP followed by a max pooling layer to obtain local relational feature f rel i .
Finally, concatenating f pos i and f rel i yields gi =  f pos i , f rel i  , which is then added back to the original vi-sual feature through a residual connection, thereby provid-ing comprehensive spatial context for reasoning.

4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup and Datasets To ensure fairness in comparative evaluation, we assess model accuracy on two widely used benchmark datasets: ScanRefer [4] and NR3D [2]. ScanRefer comprises 800 ScanNet scenes and a validation set of 9,508 natural lan-guage descriptions, each specifying a target object and its spatial context.
Results are reported separately for “Unique” and “Multiple” cases. To avoid data leakage, all RGB-D images in our experiments come from scenes dis-joint from those in the ScanRefer validation set. NR3D, a subset of ReferIt3D [2], contains 7,904 validation samples, with evaluation distinguishing “Easy” and “Hard”, and an-notations further labeling references as “View-Dependent” (Dep.) or “View-Independent” (Indep.).
Without loss of generality, in the MSAG-RC branch, we employ Qwen3-VL-Plus [3, 35] and Doubao-seed-1.6 [31] as VLMs. Details are provided in Suppl. Sec. S1.2. Dur-ing inference, for a fair comparison with ZSVG3D [51] and SeeGround [17] when using Mask3D [30], we use Mask3D [30] only for post hoc bounding box refinement; more details are provided in Suppl. Sec. S1.3. The ac-curacies of LERF [16] and OpenScene [26] are taken from ZSVG3D [51] and SeeGround [17], and their speeds are evaluated using the official code.

5. Conclusion In this paper, we present Unaided Zero-shot 3D Visual Grounding with generated language conditions (UZ3DVG), a paradigm that performs inference solely from 3D point clouds, removing dependence on 2D inputs and external LLMs/VLMs that cause high latency, heavy computation, and deployment difficulties. To address the gap between 2D foundation models and 3D pseudo labels, we design the MSAG-RC to embed multi-modal information from RGB and depth into 3D space, and leverage the zero-shot ca-pability of a VLM to generate spatial pseudo labels and reasoning chains. To further enhance reasoning, the RCD module distills chain knowledge into a student network in zero-shot settings. The GeoSM module captures global lay-outs and local geometric relations, thereby enhancing the correspondence between textual reasoning chains and 3D spatial structures, further improving localization accuracy.
Experiments show that UZ3DVG achieves SOTA on Scan-Refer and NR3D, runs at 7.69 FPS, and supports fully local-ized deployment, establishing a new paradigm for zero-shot 3DVG in open-world scenes.

args.summary:
**Summary of UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding with Generated Language Conditions**

This paper, presented at CVPR, introduces UZ3DVG, a novel zero-shot 3D visual grounding (3DVG) framework that localizes target objects in 3D scenes using natural language descriptions. Unlike existing zero-shot methods that rely on additional 2D images or multi-turn interactions with large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) during inference—causing high latency and computational cost—UZ3DVG is the first zero-shot 3DVG model that, during inference, uses only 3D point clouds and text, without 2D imagery or external LLM/VLM interaction.

**Key Components:**
- **MSAG-RC (Multi-Source Spatial Annotation and Reasoning Chain Generator):** Processes RGB-D images to generate 3D spatial pseudo-labels and reasoning chains, bridging the gap between 2D foundation models and 3D labels.
- **RCD (Reasoning Chain Distillation):** Transfers reasoning knowledge from a large teacher network to a lightweight student network, enabling efficient inference.
- **GeoSM (Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling):** Captures both global and local geometric relationships to align textual reasoning with 3D spatial structures.
- **TSVDE (Text-Semantic-Guided Visual Detail Enhancement):** Enriches visual features with fine-grained details from text-relevant regions.

**Key Results:**
- Achieves state-of-the-art on ScanRefer: Acc@0.25/0.5 of 45.42%/41.08% (beats SeeGround by 1.32%/1.68%).
- On the challenging "Multiple" subset of ScanRefer: Acc@0.25/0.5 of 40.49%/36.33% (beats SeeGround by 6.49%/6.33%).
- On NR3D: Overall accuracy of 46.5%, surpassing ZSVG3D by 7.5% and SeeGround by 0.4%.
- Inference speed: 7.69 FPS (approximately 38× faster than SeeGround's 0.2 FPS).

**Training Paradigm:** A VLM is used only during training to generate pseudo-labels and reasoning chains. The lightweight 3DVG model is trained using these generated annotations and does not require any external models during inference.

This repo is used for recording, tracking, and benchmarking several recent visual grounding methods to supplement our [Grounding Survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.20206).

### Links: [TPAMI](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11235566), [ArXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.20206), [《机器之心》中文解读](https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/I0SNcv9RypSV5Fp9sh4bLQ)

**Please leave a STAR ⭐ if you like this project!**

### 🔥 Add Your Paper in our Repo and Survey!

* If you find any work missing or have any suggestions (papers, implementations, and other resources), feel free to [pull requests](https://github.com/linhuixiao/Awesome-Visual-Grounding/pulls). We will add the missing papers to this repo as soon as possible.
* You are welcome to give us an issue or PR (pull request) for your visual grounding related works!
* **Note that:** Due to the huge paper in Arxiv, we are sorry to cover all in our survey. **You can directly present a PR into this repo** and we will record it for next version update of our survey.

### 🔥 New

* 🔥🔥🔥 **Our Grounding survey ([TPAMI](https://doi.org/10.1109/TPAMI.2025.3630635), [Arxiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.20206), [Project](https://github.com/linhuixiao/Awesome-Visual-Grounding)) has been accepted by TPAMI on October 30, 2025 !!!**
* 🔥 **We made our survey paper public and created this repository on** **December 28, 2024**.
* **Our advanced one-tower grounding work OneRef ([Paper](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=siPdcro6uD), [Code](https://github.com/linhuixiao/OneRef)) has been accepted by top conference NeurIPS 2024 in October 2024!**
* **Our advanced grounding work HiVG ([Paper](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=NMMyGy1kKZ), [Code](https://github.com/linhuixiao/HiVG)) has been accepted by top conference ACM MM 2024 in July 2024!**
* **Our grounding work CLIP-VG ([Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.08685), [Code](https://github.com/linhuixiao/CLIP-VG)) has been accepted by top journal TMM in September 2023!**

### 🔥 Highlight!!

* A comprehensive survey for Visual Grounding, including Referring Expression Comprehension and Phrase Grounding.
* It includes the newly concepts, such as Grounding Multi-modal LLMs, Generalized Visual Grounding, and VLP-based grounding transfer works.
* We list detailed results for the most representative works and give a fairer and clearer comparison of different approaches.
* We provide a list of future research insights.

# Introduction

**We are the first survey in the past five years to systematically track and summarize the development of visual grounding over the last decade.** By extracting common technical details, this review encompasses the most representative work in each subtopic.

**This survey is also currently the most comprehensive review in the field of visual grounding.** We aim for this article to serve as a valuable resource not only for beginners seeking an introduction to grounding but also for researchers with an established foundation, enabling them to navigate and stay up-to-date with the latest advancements.

args.summary:
This is a GitHub repository page for "Awesome-Visual-Grounding," a comprehensive survey on visual grounding accepted by TPAMI (IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence) in 2025. The repository is maintained by Linhui Xiao and colleagues, serving as a curated collection of research papers, methods, and benchmarks in visual grounding.

The survey covers the past decade of visual grounding research, including:
- **Main Tasks**: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) and Phrase Grounding
- **Settings Covered**: Fully supervised, weakly supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, zero-shot, multi-task, and generalized visual grounding
- **Method Categories**: Traditional CNN-based, Transformer-based, VLP-based, grounding-oriented pre-training, and Grounding Multimodal LLMs (GMLLMs)
- **Applications**: Grounded object detection, referring counting, remote sensing, medical visual grounding, 3D visual grounding, video object grounding, and robotic/multimodal agent applications

The repository includes extensive tables of research papers organized by category, each with year, venue, paper title, and code links. It also covers datasets and benchmarks (including the five classical datasets and newly curated scenarios), advanced topics (NLP structure parsing, spatial relations, modular grounding), and future research insights.

The authors have also published related works including OneRef (NeurIPS 2024), HiVG (ACM MM 2024), and CLIP-VG (TMM 2023). The repository states it is "the first survey in the past five years to systematically track and summarize the development of visual grounding over the last decade" and "currently the most comprehensive review in the field of visual grounding."

# Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models

###### Abstract

Visual grounding refers to the ability of a model to identify a region within some visual input that matches a textual description.
Consequently, a model equipped with visual grounding capabilities can target a wide range of applications in various domains, including referring expression comprehension, answering questions pertinent to fine-grained details in images or videos, captioning visual context by explicitly referring to entities, as well as low- and high-level control in simulated and real environments.
In this survey paper, we review representative works across the key areas of research on modern general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs). We first outline the importance of grounding in VLMs, then delineate the core components of the contemporary paradigm for developing grounded models, and examine their practical applications, including benchmarks and evaluation metrics for grounded multimodal generation. We also discuss the multifaceted interrelations among visual grounding, multimodal chain-of-thought, and reasoning in VLMs. Finally, we analyse the challenges inherent to visual grounding and suggest promising directions for future research.

*K*eywords Visual Grounding, Vision-Language Models, Multimodal Grounded Generation

## 1 Introduction

Visual grounding [li2etal025](#bib.bib1) represents a fundamental challenge in multimodal artificial intelligence, requiring systems to establish precise correspondences between natural language descriptions and specific regions or objects within visual scenes.
This capability is essential for enabling machines to comprehend and manipulate visual content through linguistic interaction, forming the cornerstone of human-computer interfaces that rely on natural language communication about visual information.
The field encompasses a diverse spectrum of tasks and applications, ranging from core problems such as referring expression comprehension ([kazemzadeh-etal-2014-referitgame](#bib.bib2); [he2023grec](#bib.bib3); [krishna2017visual](#bib.bib4)) and grounded captioning ([PontTuset\_eccv2020](#bib.bib5); [peng2023kosmos](#bib.bib6)) to complex applications including grounded visual question answering ([zhu2016visual7w](#bib.bib7); [lai2024lisa](#bib.bib8)), low- and high-level robotic control in interactive environments ([shridhar2020alfred](#bib.bib9); [jiang2022vima](#bib.bib10); [gao2023alexa](#bib.bib11)), and agents operating across web, mobile, and desktop environments ([cheng2024seeclick](#bib.bib12); [gou2025navigating](#bib.bib13)).

Visual grounding has evolved through several distinct paradigms. Early approaches combined Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) ([Mao\_2016\_CVPR](#bib.bib14); [Liu\_2017\_ICCV](#bib.bib15); [yu2016modeling](#bib.bib16)). These were followed by specialised transformer-based models emerging from multi-task vision language pre-training (VLP) ([kamath2021mdetr](#bib.bib17); [deng2021transvg](#bib.bib18); [chen2020uniter](#bib.bib19); [wang2022ofa](#bib.bib20); [cho2021unifying](#bib.bib21); [pantazopoulos-etal-2023-multitask](#bib.bib22)), and more recently by methods that leverage vision-language models (VLMs) ([youferret](#bib.bib23); [chen2023shikra](#bib.bib24); [bai2023qwen](#bib.bib25); [bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26)).
This progression toward grounded text generation has enabled multimodal models to establish intrinsic connections between linguistic expressions and corresponding visual elements, equipping machines with increasingly sophisticated fine-grained multimodal comprehension capabilities.

This survey primarily examines multimodal grounded generation in VLMs published from 2022 onward, while also incorporating key insights from foundational VLP models. The main contributions of this work are: (i) a comprehensive overview of grounding in VLMs, extending beyond the traditional focus on generalised Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) ([kazemzadeh2014referitgame](#bib.bib27)) to encompass underexplored research domains; (ii) an analysis of how core architectural components influence grounding capabilities, offering a perspective absent from prior surveys ([liang2024survey](#bib.bib28); [wu2023multimodal](#bib.bib29); [huang2023visual](#bib.bib30); [caffagni2024revolution](#bib.bib31)); (iii) a coverage of additional grounding-related tasks, such as grounded captioning, grounded visual question answering, and agents interacting with Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs); and (iv) a discussion of grounding as a component of multimodal reasoning, both as an intermediate step and as part of solution-level reasoning processes.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. [Section 2](#S2 "2 Preliminaries ‣ Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models") presents the essential background, including definitions and relevant research domains. [Section 3](#S3 "3 Developing Grounding Visual Language Models ‣ Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models") synthesises prior work on the development of VLMs with grounding capabilities. [Section 4](#S4 "4 Evaluations ‣ Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models") provides a comprehensive analysis of existing applications, datasets, and benchmarks, spanning image-level visual grounding to agents that interact with environments and web interfaces. Finally, [Section 5](#S5 "5 Challenges and Future Directions for Grounding VLM Research ‣ Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models") discusses the key components involved in developing grounded VLMs and examines the challenges and open questions facing the next generation of these models.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 What is Visual Grounding?

In earlier works, visual grounding, where a model is tasked with localising a specific region within a visual context that aligns with an input textual query ([xiao2024towards](#bib.bib32)), is often referred to as REC ([kazemzadeh2014referitgame](#bib.bib27)) or phrase localisation (PL) ([plummer2015flickr30k](#bib.bib33)), where the input query describes exactly one entity in an image. However, this definition is narrow and does not adequately encompass neighbouring fields such as grounded captioning, visual question answering grounded in visual elements, and interactive agent-based environments. In these settings, the textual query may take various forms, for instance, specifying a region of interest (e.g. describe the region with a concise caption), posing a question (e.g. which of these objects is used to cut items?), or giving an instruction (e.g. clean up old cookies from the Amazon store). Accordingly, we define visual grounding more broadly as the capability to precisely localise and identify specific objects, regions, or concepts within a visual context, conditioned on natural language descriptions or instructions, thereby bridging textual understanding and visual reasoning.

### 2.2 The Role of Grounding in Modern VLMs

Grounding in VLMs is essential not only for enabling fine-grained downstream applications, but also for establishing an interpretable link between predicted perceptions and actual localisation within the visual context. Although VLM outputs often imply an understanding of visual elements, grounding explicitly verifies whether the model can accurately identify and localise the relevant objects, regions, or concepts. This connection between language and precise visual evidence is critical for both transparency and reliability in multimodal reasoning. Prior research indicates that hallucination in VLMs arises from an excessive reliance on the language prior, with the dependence on the visual prompt diminishing as more tokens are generated ([favero2024multi](#bib.bib34); [goyal2017making](#bib.bib35); [wang2023evaluation](#bib.bib36); [frank-etal-2021-vision](#bib.bib37); [lin2023revisiting](#bib.bib38)). Without proper grounding, these models may generate plausible-sounding descriptions that do not correspond to actual visual content, resulting in unreliable outputs in critical applications. Grounding addresses this issue by ensuring that when a model describes an object or relationship, it can demonstrate its understanding by precisely identifying where that information appears in the visual input.

Consequently, VLMs without grounding capabilities often struggle to establish precise correspondences between textual descriptions and visual elements. This can result in responses that are semantically plausible but spatially inaccurate. Recent research ([youferret](#bib.bib23); [chen2023shikra](#bib.bib24)) suggests that grounding mitigates this issue by encouraging models to commit to specific spatial locations, thereby enhancing both the accuracy and interpretability of their visual understanding.
However, subsequent studies ([lin2023revisiting](#bib.bib38)) have shown that grounding objectives do not exhibit a causal relationship with reductions in object hallucinations, as quantified in visual question answering and image captioning tasks, indicating that further investigation is necessary. Nevertheless, the ability to precisely refer to regions that align with open-ended textual input remains an invaluable asset, enabling VLMs to support a wide range of downstream applications ([kazemzadeh-etal-2014-referitgame](#bib.bib2); [zhu2016visual7w](#bib.bib7); [zheng2024seeact](#bib.bib39); [wu2023webui](#bib.bib40)).

### 2.3 Representing Visual References

Visual grounding requires converting continuous spatial coordinates into formats that language models can process effectively.
Consequently, the design choice of representing regions plays a crucial role in model development. There are two broad categories for representing the bounding box: object-centric and pixel-level.

##### Object-centric

Object-centric methods present the model with region proposals, optionally accompanied by image-level features, and task the model with selecting the candidate proposal that satisfies the input textual query. In this framework, each individual object is processed separately by a vision component ([Girshick\_2015\_ICCV](#bib.bib41); [ren2015faster](#bib.bib42); [He\_2017\_ICCV](#bib.bib43); [reis2023real](#bib.bib44); [khanam2024yolov11](#bib.bib45)). Consequently, these methods offload visual perception to a unimodal expert and produce models that learn to match textual queries to one or more object candidates provided as inputs. The matching is typically implemented using sentinel tokens ([cho2021unifying](#bib.bib21); [pantazopoulos-etal-2023-multitask](#bib.bib22); [zhang2025gpt4roi](#bib.bib46)), where each sentinel token corresponds to the position of a bounding box in the sequence. Such a design offers interpretable object-level reasoning and a clean representation for detection and grounding tasks. However, it is constrained by predefined object categories, a lack of fine-grained spatial relationships, and the computational overhead from multi-stage processing. These limitations, combined with the flexibility and capacity of ViT-based encoders, have led to the prevalence of models that adopt a pixel-level approach.

##### Pixel-level

In pixel-level approaches, the image is divided into a grid of patches, typically using a vision transformer (ViT) ([zhai2023sigmoid](#bib.bib47); [radford2021learning](#bib.bib48); [tschannen2025siglip](#bib.bib49); [carion2020end](#bib.bib50); [zhang2021vinvl](#bib.bib51)) pretrained with contrastive objectives on image-text pairs.
The ViT ([dosovitskiyimage](#bib.bib52)) partitions the image into a fixed-size grid of patches (e.g. a patch may represent 14×1414\times 14, 16×1616\times 16, 32×3232\times 32 pixels), with each patch embedded as a visual token that encodes localised information.
Pixel-level visual regions are commonly represented in two ways: discretising the image into a grid with fixed-size bins or directly encoding coordinates as textual outputs. The choice between discretised and raw coordinate representations has significant implications for model performance and capability. Discretised coordinates involve rounding continuous coordinates to discrete levels ([wang2022ofa](#bib.bib20); [luunified2023](#bib.bib53); [yang2022unitab](#bib.bib54); [wang2023visionllm](#bib.bib55); [wanggit](#bib.bib56)), thereby reducing the vocabulary size while maintaining reasonable spatial precision.
The quantisation level, thus, serves as a critical hyperparameter, balancing accuracy, and computational efficiency. As an alternative, vector quantisation obtains patch representations from the latent space of an autoencoder, yielding a learned set of discrete visual tokens ([bigverdi2025perception](#bib.bib57)). In contrast, raw numeric tokens encode region coordinates directly as digit sequences, analogous to specifying a bounding box numerically such as ⟨142,67,298,134⟩\langle 142,67,298,134\rangle ([youferret](#bib.bib23); [chen2023shikra](#bib.bib24); [bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [wang2024cogvlm](#bib.bib58); [chen2024expanding](#bib.bib59)). While this method offers higher spatial precision, it requires the model to perform arithmetic and compositional reasoning over tokenised numbers, which poses a challenge for transformer architectures not inherently designed for numerical reasoning.

##### Object-centric vs Pixel-level

The representation of regions of interest is a key component of model design. While earlier methods were largely object-centric, contemporary vision-language models predominantly adopt pixel-level representations with vision transformer backbones. Accordingly, the remainder of this survey focuses on pixel-level approaches.

##### Discretised vs Raw coordinates

Recent work has investigated the choice between discretised and raw coordinate formats at the pixel-level, indicating that the raw-coordinate format may be advantageous over discretisation ([chen2023shikra](#bib.bib24)). However, an in-depth comparison between the two has yet to be conducted. A possible explanation for the observed advantage of the raw-coordinate format is that, during the development of the VLM, the model already acquires some knowledge of numerical order, likely as a result of pre-training the language backbone on text data. In contrast, the embeddings of discrete tokens are typically initialised from scratch, requiring the model to learn their meanings and mappings without any prior knowledge. Nevertheless, the raw-coordinate format results in shared representations for numerical characters, which may lead to ambiguity. For example, a general-purpose VLM capable of both visual grounding and visual question answering may assign the same learned representation to the token “33”, regardless of its visual or textual context. This phenomenon, often referred to as the modality gap ([NEURIPS2022\_702f4db7](#bib.bib60)), can significantly impact downstream performance.

##### Set-of-Marks

An alternative way of representing visual references in VLMs is through the use of a Set-of-Marks (SOM) ([yang2023set](#bib.bib61); [yang2023dawn](#bib.bib62); [wan2024contrastive](#bib.bib63); [yang2023fine](#bib.bib64); [lei2025scaffolding](#bib.bib65); [cai2024vip](#bib.bib66)).
This method follows a two-step process and it is particularly suitable to VLMs that are not equipped with grounding capabilities during training. In the first step, the image is partitioned into regions with off-the-shelf segmentation models ([ravi2024sam](#bib.bib67); [kirillov2023segment](#bib.bib68); [zou2023segment](#bib.bib69)). These regions are then labeled with a set of marks such as alphanumeric characters, symbols, masks, boxes, or colors. In the second step, the VLM performs visual grounding by leveraging the marks depicted in the image. It is worth noting that, while this approach can be effective, the performance of the VLM is strongly dependent on its Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and reading comprehension capabilities.

These representations underpin the grounding process, enabling models to align textual queries with corresponding visual regions. Framing grounding as a cross-modal retrieval objective provides a coherent perspective for understanding how these components contribute to effective multimodal reasoning.

### 2.4 Grounding as an In-Context Cross-Modal Retrieval Task

Visual grounding can be framed as an in-context multimodal retrieval task in modern VLMs ([pantazopoulos-etal-2024-shaking](#bib.bib70)).
Both tasks follow a similar pattern: given a context and a query, the model is required to locate and reference the relevant part of the context.

In standard text-based in-context retrieval ([rajpurkar-etal-2018-know](#bib.bib71)), the model receives a passage of text (the context) and a question (the query), and it is tasked with identifying and extracting the specific text span that answers the question. This grounding task follows the same structure but operates across modalities. The model receives visual patches as the context and a textual description as the query, and it aims to determine which visual region corresponds to the description.

The key distinction lies in the embedding spaces and the requirement for cross-modal mapping. In text-based retrieval, both input and output reside in the same semantic space (text tokens to text tokens). Visual grounding, by contrast, requires the model to bridge two distinct representation spaces. The model is required to understand the semantic content of the textual query, map that understanding onto the visual patch representations, and then translate the result back into textual coordinates or descriptions. Viewed from this perspective, the VLM performs a two-step process: first matching the textual query to the visual modality and then generating a textual response. Aligning text and visual representations remains the core difficulty of visual grounding, underscoring the need for effective cross-modal reasoning.

### 2.5 Research Domains

This section highlights key research domains where visual grounding is prevalent and outlines directions for more in-depth analysis in the subsequent sections. [Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In 2.4 Grounding as an In-Context Cross-Modal Retrieval Task ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models") illustrates input-output pairs from representative datasets across research domains related to visual grounding.

##### Referring Expression Comprehension (REC)

REC ([kazemzadeh-etal-2014-referitgame](#bib.bib2); [yu2016modeling](#bib.bib16); [nagaraja2016modeling](#bib.bib74)) requires the model to localise a specific region (i.e. a bounding box) within an image based on a given textual description. Similarly, Referring Expression Segmentation (RES) ([lai2024lisa](#bib.bib8)) tasks the model with identifying an image-level mask that satisfies the query. Both
REC and RES rely on the strong assumption that a sentence describes exactly one object within an image, an assumption that often does not hold in real-world scenarios. Consequently, earlier models struggled when handling expressions referring to multiple or novel visual entities. More recently, Generalised Referring Expression Comprehension (GREC) ([he2023grec](#bib.bib3)) and Generalised Referring Expression Segmentation (GRES) ([liu2023gres](#bib.bib75)) have been proposed, which involve grounding on one, multiple, or even no objects described by the textual input within an image.

##### Grounded Visual Question Answering (GVQA)

GVQA requires the model to link answers to questions based on fine-grained visual observations. In this setting, visual grounding is required at the answer-level, where the model either provides a region in the image corresponding to the answer of the input question ([zhu2016visual7w](#bib.bib7); [chen2022grounding](#bib.bib76); [gan2017vqs](#bib.bib77)), or outputs both a textual answer and the associated region ([vogel2025refchartqa](#bib.bib78)). Grounding may also be necessary for interpreting the question itself, particularly when the visual prompt refers to or points at specific objects in the scene ([mani2020point](#bib.bib79); [deitke2024molmo](#bib.bib80); [Aho:72](#bib.bib81)).

##### Grounded Captioning (GC)

Grounded captioning refers a model’s ability to generate captions that are explicitly anchored in visual regions. Existing work often produces multiple region-level descriptions ([krishna2017visual](#bib.bib4)), a setting commonly referred to as dense captioning. In contrast, other approaches generate more holistic captions that describe the entire image while embedding references to specific regions directly within the description ([peng2023kosmos](#bib.bib6); [gonzalez2021panoptic](#bib.bib82)). Some methods also produce visual traces that align words in the captions with corresponding regions in the image ([PontTuset\_eccv2020](#bib.bib5)). More recently, grounded captioning has been extended to conversational settings ([ma2024groma](#bib.bib83)), in which the model generates grounded responses within a dialogue.

##### Agents Interacting with Graphical User Interfaces

Grounding plays a crucial role in enabling interactive agents to perceive, reason about, and act within their environment.
In this context, the textual query is often formulated as an instruction (e.g. execute a database search for specific records, or update a spreadsheet with newly provided values) rather than a description of an object in the scene. The agent then predicts the correct sequence of actions that satisfies the instruction. Thus, grounding not only allows the agent to interact effectively with elements in the GUI [nguyen2025guiagentssurvey](#bib.bib84), but also plays a critical role in task success, as a single grounding error can cause the agent to stall and fail to complete the task.

##### Grounded Reasoning

Inspired by the recent advances in LLMs ([guo2025deepseek](#bib.bib85); [shao2024deepseekmath](#bib.bib86)), several approaches have adopted reinforcement learning to enhance multimodal reasoning capabilities by designing rule-based rewards tailored to specific downstream tasks ([kim2025robot](#bib.bib87); [wang2025pixelthink](#bib.bib88)). Since grounding provides a flexible medium with interpretable explanations, two promising avenues have emerged for grounded VLMs. First, grounding can be viewed as an intermediate reasoning step, where rewards are designed to align with the model’s reasoning trace ([fan2025grit](#bib.bib89)). Second, the model can be directly rewarded based on its grounding performance at the solution level, without imposing constraints on the intermediate reasoning process ([shen2025vlm](#bib.bib90)). This remains an active area of research with the potential to unlock new capabilities of modern VLMs across the previously discussed domains.

## 3 Developing Grounding Visual Language Models

This section provides an overview of the development of VLMs, with a focus on architectural design choices and training regimes that influence grounding performance. The overview first outlines general design and training components that affect downstream applications, with particular emphasis on grounding capabilities.

Early work demonstrated the potential of combining Large Language Models (LLMs) with pre-trained vision encoders across diverse multimodal tasks ([alayrac2022flamingo](#bib.bib91); [tsimpoukelli2021multimodal](#bib.bib92)). These studies motivated a paradigm shift away from complex multimodal architectures, explicit modality fusion, and specialised objectives ([chen2020uniter](#bib.bib19); [tan2019lxmert](#bib.bib93); [lu2019vilbert](#bib.bib94)), towards a simplified formulation, in which patch-based representations from a vision encoder are treated as token embeddings for input to a language model. [Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3 Developing Grounding Visual Language Models ‣ Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models") illustrates the architectural design of modern VLMs.

Most contemporary models ([bai2023qwen](#bib.bib25); [bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [yang2025qwen3](#bib.bib97); [laurenccon2024obelics](#bib.bib98); [laurenccon2024matters](#bib.bib99); [liu2024visual](#bib.bib100); [chen2023pali](#bib.bib101)) follow a common template comprising three components: a visual encoder ([zhai2023sigmoid](#bib.bib47); [radford2021learning](#bib.bib48); [fang2023eva](#bib.bib102); [groeneveld-etal-2024-olmo](#bib.bib103)), a connector module, and a language backbone ([touvron2023llama](#bib.bib104); [jiang2023mistral](#bib.bib105); [team2024gemma](#bib.bib106)). The connector aligns the visual and textual embedding spaces, typically through a linear projection, typically through a pooling mechanism to downsample the image sequence, or more advanced designs that incorporate standalone or interleaved transformer blocks within the language model. These architectural choices are discussed in more detail below. The vision encoder provides the language model with visual representations. Most approaches adopt CLIP-based architectures ([radford2021learning](#bib.bib48); [fang2023eva](#bib.bib102); [wortsman2022robust](#bib.bib126)), whose pretraining objective is the alignment between textual and visual embeddings. The language backbone is generally a transformer-based language model, although some studies ([pantazopoulos-etal-2024-shaking](#bib.bib70); [zhao2024cobra](#bib.bib127); [qiao2024vl](#bib.bib128)) have explored alternatives such as Mamba ([gu2023mamba](#bib.bib129)), a structured state-space model that matches or surpasses transformer performance in sequence modelling while offering improved inference efficiency and linear scaling with sequence length. To the best of our knowledge, grounding with a Mamba backbone has been explored in a limited number of studies; the findings in ([pantazopoulos-etal-2024-shaking](#bib.bib70)) indicate that transformer-based backbones perform significantly better on grounding tasks.

In addition, a connector module bridges the two modalities by matching their embedding dimensions. Most recent models adopt a simple projection mechanism ([chen2023shikra](#bib.bib24); [bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [li2024llava](#bib.bib130)). A common challenge arises because the number of visual patch embeddings often exceeds the number of textual tokens. This imbalance can increase training and inference times, especially in applications involving high-resolution images, videos, or large multimodal documents. One solution is to compress the visual sequence using a resampler component, which may take the form of average pooling ([zang2025contextual](#bib.bib118)), attention mechanisms before the language model([peng2023kosmos](#bib.bib6)), or multi-stage processes (e.g. ([laurenccon2024building](#bib.bib131))). Other designs ([alayrac2022flamingo](#bib.bib91); [dai2024instructblip](#bib.bib132); [zhao2023bubogpt](#bib.bib107)) interleave cross-attention modules within the language model itself.

Training VLMs is also a complex, resource-intensive task, with many open research questions regarding the contribution of individual components to downstream performance. Challenges related to reproducibility, proprietary weights, and inconsistent evaluation protocols complicate direct comparisons across models. Some studies ([fan2025grit](#bib.bib89); [shen2025vlm](#bib.bib90); [luo2025gui](#bib.bib133)) have further explored reinforcement learning as an additional training phase, motivated by advances in language modelling ([guo2025deepseek](#bib.bib85); [shao2024deepseekmath](#bib.bib86)).

In summary, the design, development, and training of VLMs constitute an intricate process. Recent work ([pantazopoulos-etal-2024-shaking](#bib.bib70); [laurenccon2024matters](#bib.bib99); [karamcheti2024prismatic](#bib.bib134)) has analysed the effects of individual components in the VLM architecture. The following sections examine these components in greater detail and assess their impact on grounding capabilities.

### 3.1 Vision Encoder

The most commonly employed visual encoders are based on pre-trained ViT models with a CLIP-based objective, which leverages the inherent alignment of CLIP embeddings ([radford2021learning](#bib.bib48); [fang2023eva](#bib.bib102)). The standard image-text contrastive objective aligns image and text embeddings for matching (positive) pairs while ensuring that unrelated (negative) pairs remain dissimilar in the embedding space. This is achieved through a batch-level, softmax-based contrastive loss applied twice to normalise pairwise image-text and text-image similarity scores.

Although effective, this approach has two notable limitations. First, the computation requires two separate steps to estimate image-to-text and text-to-image similarities. Second, the degree of alignment depends on the batch size, since larger batches can provide more negative pairs. These limitations are addressed in SigLIP ([zhai2023sigmoid](#bib.bib47); [tschannen2025siglip](#bib.bib49)), where the sigmoid loss eliminates the need for operations across the full batch, thereby reducing the requirement to distribute the loss and improving efficiency. Consequently, many subsequent VLMs ([laurenccon2024matters](#bib.bib99); [marafioti2025smolvlm](#bib.bib135); [laurenccon2024building](#bib.bib131)) adopt the SigLIP variation, although these models are not specifically designed for multimodal grounding applications. A side-by-side comparison for REC is presented in ([karamcheti2024prismatic](#bib.bib134)), showing that SigLIP slightly outperforms CLIP.

#### 3.1.1 Image Resolution

Recent research has demonstrated that providing high-resolution images to VLMs reduces hallucinations and enhances multimodal understanding, leading to improved performance on tasks requiring fine-grained details ([wang2022ofa](#bib.bib20); [bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [pantazopoulos-etal-2024-shaking](#bib.bib70); [liu2023improved](#bib.bib95); [li2024llava](#bib.bib130); [karamcheti2024prismatic](#bib.bib134); [zhang24next](#bib.bib109); [liu2024llavanext](#bib.bib136); [chenpali](#bib.bib137); [beyer2024paligemma](#bib.bib138); [steiner2024paligemma](#bib.bib139); [mckinzie2024mm1](#bib.bib140)).
However, most off-the-shelf vision encoders operate on low-resolution images and do not enforce a fixed square aspect ratio. This creates practical challenges: (i) models trained on smaller images must adapt to larger ones at inference; and (ii) the increased number of tokens leads to higher computational costs in both the visual encoder and the language model.
To address these issues, two broad categories of approaches have been proposed, aimed at ensuring that the language model receives high-quality visual representations.

##### Positional-Encoding Interpolation

A common method for handling high-resolution images is to interpolate the positional encodings of the visual encoder. This approach has been employed in earlier multimodal models trained in a multi-task fashion ([wang2022ofa](#bib.bib20); [yang2022unitab](#bib.bib54); [li2021align](#bib.bib141)) and has since been adopted by many VLMs ([beyer2024paligemma](#bib.bib138); [steiner2024paligemma](#bib.bib139); [arora2023zoology](#bib.bib142)) which require extensive training with high-resolution images during the later stages of development. In addition, several studies propose reducing the visual sequence by merging neighbouring tokens ([bai2023qwen](#bib.bib25); [chen2023minigpt](#bib.bib111)). Visual token compression is discussed in [Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Connecting Visual and Textual Representations in VLMs ‣ 3 Developing Grounding Visual Language Models ‣ Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models"), where it is treated as a function of the multimodal connector component.

##### Handling Arbitrary Resolution Images

Certain approaches address high-resolution inputs by dividing the image into fixed-size sub-images that match the expected dimensions of the visual encoder ([bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [liu2024llavanext](#bib.bib136); [liu2024sphinx](#bib.bib143); [li2024monkey](#bib.bib144); [guo2024llava](#bib.bib145)). Each sub-image is processed independently by the visual backbone, while the original image is downscaled to the same resolution and processed in parallel. The features extracted from all sub-images, together with those from the downscaled whole image, are then concatenated to form a global representation.

### 3.2 Connecting Visual and Textual Representations in VLMs

Two principal strategies have emerged for connecting visual and textual embeddings: directly aligning the dimensionality of the two modalities, and compressing the visual sequence. The former, described in ([mckinzie2024mm1](#bib.bib140); [lin2024preserve](#bib.bib146)), is regarded as a feature-preserving method because it maintains the number of feature maps. In contrast, the latter is considered as a feature-compressing method, as it incorporates a (learnable) component that reduces the number of patch embeddings.

#### 3.2.1 Mapping Visual to Textual Representations

Since the LLM backbones are primarily trained on generic text, an inherent semantic gap arises when processing multi-modal features. Mapping operations
address this gap by transforming the visual embeddings into the dimensionality expected by the language model. This transformation can be implemented as a simple linear projection or a stack of multilayer perceptrons (MLPs).
The resulting embeddings are then concatenated with the text input sequence without any compression.

##### Linear Transformation

The most basic transformation of visual embeddings employs a single linear layer, which was first introduced in ([liu2024visual](#bib.bib100); [pmlr-v202-koh23a](#bib.bib147)). However, few subsequent models have adopted this approach ([ye2024mplug](#bib.bib148)), partially because non-linear transformations provide greater representational capacity.

##### Non-Linear Transformation using MLPs

A natural extension introduces non-linearity into the feature transformation process by employing an MLP. This approach consistently enhances the model’s capabilities across a wide range of multimodal tasks ([liu2023improved](#bib.bib95)), while ensuring that the full visual information is preserved, as no pooling strategy is applied.
Many subsequent VLMs have adopted this idea ([bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [chen2024expanding](#bib.bib59); [li2024llava](#bib.bib130); [marafioti2025smolvlm](#bib.bib135); [liu2024llavanext](#bib.bib136)), as it offers a favourable balance between simplicity of design and performance.

#### 3.2.2 Compressing the Input Sequence

Despite their conceptual simplicity, mapping methods produce long sequences of visual tokens, which reduce the efficiency of both training and inference.
Based on prior works we identify four approaches aimed at compressing the input sequence.

##### Pooling

Pooling is among the most basic approaches for compressing visual embeddings, whereby adjacent patch embeddings are merged through a pooling operation and subsequently projected to match the dimensionality of the language embeddings. Two VLMs ([bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [chen2023minigpt](#bib.bib111)) that adopt this strategy combine four spatially adjacent patch features into a single vector through an MLP before passing them to the large language model.

##### Convolution

CNNs offer a distinct advantage for multimodal learning by preserving local spatial structures and enhancing spatial understanding through their hierarchical feature extraction capabilities. Unlike traditional pooling methods, which may discard important spatial relationships, CNNs retain geometric and positional information that is critical for capturing fine-grained spatial details, particularly in multimodal grounding tasks. Two notable approaches exemplify this idea: C-Abstractor ([cha2024honeybee](#bib.bib149)), which reintroduces two-dimensional (2D) positional embeddings into the visual features, and is subsequently followed by ResNet block ([xie2017aggregated](#bib.bib150)), and the H-Reducer ([hu2024mplug](#bib.bib151)), which employs CNNs to reduce the number of image hidden states by a factor of four.

##### Cross-Attention Module

An alternative approach to compression involves introducing learnable embeddings that cross-attend to the image representations. Since the number of patch embeddings generally exceeds the number of learnable embeddings in the module, this mechanism naturally results in compression. Qwen-VL ([bai2023qwenvlversatilevisionlanguagemodel](#bib.bib114)) adopts this strategy by reducing the number of visual tokens through a single-layer cross-attention module operating between a set of learnable embeddings and the image hidden states.

##### (Multimodal) Resamplers

Similar to the cross-attention module, a resampler component is implemented as a transformer comprising stacked self- and/or cross-attention modules and learnable queries. We identify two notable resamplers proposed in prior work: the Perceiver ([pmlr-v139-jaegle21a](#bib.bib152)) and the Q-former ([li2023blip](#bib.bib153)). The Perceiver has been applied alongside interleaved cross-attention layers on the language model ([alayrac2022flamingo](#bib.bib91); [laurenccon2024matters](#bib.bib99); [awadalla2023openflamingo](#bib.bib154); [li2025otter](#bib.bib155)), wherein the language tokens interact with the compressed visual sequence only through these interleaved cross-attention layers. The Q-former has likewise been adopted in subsequent studies([dai2024instructblip](#bib.bib132); [hu2024bliva](#bib.bib156); [chen2024lion](#bib.bib157)), demonstrating its effectiveness in various settings.

Despite their efficiency, both resamplers have been critiqued in several studies ([lin2024preserve](#bib.bib146); [pantazopoulos-etal-2024-lost](#bib.bib158)), which argue that these components do not necessarily preserve spatial relationships but instead compress the visual embeddings into a bag-of-words-like representation. While feature-preserving approaches offer superior performance, their advantage over feature-compressing connectors diminishes rapidly as image resolution increases.

Moreover, connectors based on CNNs ([cha2024honeybee](#bib.bib149)) consistently outperform attention-based resamplers across all resolutions and task granularities, as they more effectively exploit the two-dimensional structure of images. Finally, some models ([youferret](#bib.bib23); [zhang2024ferret](#bib.bib117)) adopt alternative resampling strategies, such as point-clouds, image segmentation, and clustering. Although these approaches have shown promising results, there is currently little evidence supported by rigorous and fair quantitative evaluation.

### 3.3 Language Model

##### Language Backbones Alternative to Transformers

The vast majority of modern VLMs employ a transformer-based language backbone. Although a few studies have explored Mamba-based models ([zhao2024cobra](#bib.bib127); [qiao2024vl](#bib.bib128)) and reported promising results, these findings do not conclusively demonstrate the effectiveness of a VLM with a Mamba-based language backbone, as the compared models were of similar size but trained under substantially different regimes.

The analysis in ([pantazopoulos-etal-2024-shaking](#bib.bib70)) provides a more detailed examination. However, the models considered are relatively small and not instruction-tuned. Moreover, while earlier work has shown that the quality of language model directly correlates with the overall performance of the VLM ([laurenccon2024matters](#bib.bib99)), the findings in ([pantazopoulos-etal-2024-shaking](#bib.bib70)) indicate that this relationship depends on the downstream task. For example, in grounding and generation tasks, the transformer-based models consistently outperformed their Mamba-based counterparts across all model scales.

##### Language Models without Vision Encoders

Recent approaches have explored the use of language backbones without explicitly generating visual representations through a dedicated vision encoder. The Fuyu model ([fuyu-8b](#bib.bib159)) exemplifies this paradigm by bypassing traditional vision encoders and instead feeding image patches directly into the language model via a simple linear projection to adjust their dimensionality. This architecture offers two key advantages: it operates independently of any pre-trained vision model, and it preserves the complete information from the original image, which can be critical for accurate prompt responses.

However, despite these theoretical benefits, the direct patch approach has not demonstrated superior performance in practice. Fuyu performs significantly worse than similarly-sized contemporary models on standard benchmarks, and PaliGemma ([beyer2024paligemma](#bib.bib138)). Empirical evaluations report substantial performance degradation compared to models that incorporate pre-trained vision encoders. Moreover, processing image representations directly within the language model may impair its effectiveness on text-only tasks, although this hypothesis remains largely untested, as most VLMs are not evaluated on pure textual benchmarks. Finally, the absence of efficient pooling strategies for managing raw pixel data poses scalability challenges in applications that require processing large numbers of visual tokens.

### 3.4 Training Pipeline

The development of a VLM typically begins with unimodal pre-trained backbones, consisting of a language model and a vision encoder. Some earlier works, however, adopt a single-stage training procedure ([alayrac2022flamingo](#bib.bib91); [tsimpoukelli2021multimodal](#bib.bib92); [pmlr-v202-koh23a](#bib.bib147); [awadalla2023openflamingo](#bib.bib154); [li2025otter](#bib.bib155); [gao2023llama](#bib.bib160)).

Most contemporary approaches employ a more complex pipeline involving multiple stages ([bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [chen2024expanding](#bib.bib59); [liu2023improved](#bib.bib95); [laurenccon2024matters](#bib.bib99); [liu2024llavanext](#bib.bib136)) (see ([laurenccon2024building](#bib.bib131)) for a detailed discussion of training stages).
This design is motivated primarily by the limited availability of high-quality data at scale, memory constraints that hinder efficient training, and stability considerations ([laurenccon2024building](#bib.bib131)). During these stages, progressively higher-quality data is introduced, the maximum image resolution is gradually increased, and additional components of the model are unfrozen.

#### 3.4.1 Image-text alignment pretraining

The primary goal of pre-training is to align the backbone models and to train the newly initialised parameters. During this stage, the model is exposed to examples that support the following capabilities: image captioning, handling an arbitrary number of images interleaved with diverse texts, reading comprehension, and grounding capabilities, all of which are essential for downstream applications. Training usually leverages image-text pairs or large-scale web-derived image-text datasets, which are generally constructed by crawling the web, downloading images, and extracting the corresponding textual descriptions from the original HTML files ([schuhmann2022laion](#bib.bib161); [kakaobrain2022coyo-700m](#bib.bib162); [gadre2023datacomp](#bib.bib163)).

Owing to the relative ease of collection, such raw image-text pairs are widely used; however, their effectiveness in establishing strong alignment between images and text varies considerably, as the accompanying alt-texts are often noisy, ungrammatical, or overly brief ([gadre2023datacomp](#bib.bib163)). These issues can introduce challenges during training. Recent approaches have sought to mitigate this by applying synthetic re-captioning ([mckinzie2024mm1](#bib.bib140); [li2023blip](#bib.bib153); [shi2020improving](#bib.bib164); [lai2024veclip](#bib.bib165)), and quality-filtering techniques ([sharifzadeh2024synth](#bib.bib166); [abbas2023semdedup](#bib.bib167)), both of which have demonstrated improved performance.

Training on interleaved image-text documents was first introduced in ([alayrac2022flamingo](#bib.bib91); [laurenccon2024obelics](#bib.bib98)), as it enhances: (i) in-context learning abilities; (ii) the model’s ability to process an arbitrary number of images interleaved with text; and (iii) the model’s exposure to a wider distribution of content beyond standard image-text pairs.
These claims have been validated by other works ([mckinzie2024mm1](#bib.bib140)) and subsequently adopted in follow-up models ([bai2025qwen2](#bib.bib26); [chen2024expanding](#bib.bib59); [ye2024mplug](#bib.bib148); [li2024llava](#bib.bib130); [zhang2024internlm](#bib.bib168); [xue2024xgen](#bib.bib169)).

For reading comprehension tasks, it is common to train on PDF-text pairs ([biten2022ocr](#bib.bib170)) or to employ OCR tools to extract text from images ([zhang2023pmc](#bib.bib171); [yao2024minicpm](#bib.bib172); [textocr-gpt4v](#bib.bib173)). Finally, datasets supporting grounding capabilities require a more complex pipeline, which generates region-level annotations using segmentation, detection, or tagging models.
Two notable works in this direction are GRIT ([peng2023kosmos](#bib.bib6)) and BLIP3-GROUNDING-50M ([xue2024xgen](#bib.bib169)).

GRIT is a collection of image-text pairs constructed via a pipeline that extracts and links text spans, noun phrases, and referring expressions in captions to corresponding image regions. In the first step, the pipeline extracts noun chunks from captions using spaCy ([spacy2](#bib.bib174)) and associates these chunks with bounding boxes via GLIP ([Li\_2022\_CVPR](#bib.bib175)), a pre-trained grounding model. In the second step, spaCy is used to identify dependency relations in the caption, and the noun chunks are expanded into referring expressions by recursively traversing nodes in the dependency tree.
Similarly, in BLIP3-GROUNDING-50M, captions for the associated objects and their locations are obtained from state-of-the-art image tagging ([Zhang\_2024\_CVPR](#bib.bib176)) and detection ([liu2024grounding](#bib.bib177)) models.

#### 3.4.2 Fine-tuning

Fine-tuning VLMs is largely influenced by the training paradigm of LLMs and generally comprises two stages: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by an alignment phase. The former has been well established and constitutes a standard component in the development of most VLMs, whereas the latter remains underexplored, particularly in the context of grounded VLMs.
