(Webpage) Abstract—Building 3D maps of the environment is central to robot navigation, planning, and interaction with objects in a scene. Most existing approaches that integrate semantic concepts with 3D maps largely remain confined to the closed-set setting: they can only reason about a finite set of concepts, pre-defined at training time. Further, these maps can only be queried using class labels, or in more recent work, using text prompts.
We address both these issues with ConceptFusion, a scene representation that is: (i) fundamentally open-set, enabling rea-soning beyond a closed set of concepts (ii) inherently multi-modal, enabling a diverse range of possible queries to the 3D map, from language, to images, to audio, to 3D geometry, all working in concert. ConceptFusion leverages the open-set capabilities of today’s foundation models that have been pre-trained on internet-scale data to reason about concepts across modalities such as natural language, images, and audio. We demonstrate that pixel-aligned open-set features can be fused into 3D maps via traditional SLAM and multi-view fusion approaches.
This enables effective zero-shot spatial reasoning, not needing any additional training or finetuning, and retains long-tailed concepts better than supervised approaches, outperforming them by more than 40% margin on 3D IoU. We extensively evaluate ConceptFusion on a number of real-world datasets, simulated home environments, a real-world tabletop manipulation task, and an autonomous driving platform. We showcase new avenues for blending foundation models with 3D open-set multimodal mapping. We encourage the reader to view the demos on our project page: https://concept-fusion.github.io/ I. INTRODUCTION One of the major catalysts of continued progress in 3D spatial perception [1, 2, 3, 4] has been the advent of deep con-volutional networks trained on large datasets of images. Most of these advancements have relied on a closed-set of concepts, a fixed set of labels available at training time. More recently, however, deep learning is witnessing yet another wave of advancements, this time with the emergence of increasingly larger and multimodal models trained on internet-scale data comprising billions of images, text, and audio [5]. Founda-tion models like CLIP [6], DINO [7], AudioCLIP [8], and their variants have shown impressive performance on open-set scenarios, where the concepts of interest are supplied only at inference time. In this work, we bridge the gap between the rich open-set capabilities enabled by large foundation models and the semantic reasoning abilities expected of futuristic 3D mapping systems.
To be as broadly applicable as possible to a diverse set of robotics tasks, map representations need to be usable zero-shot (i.e. without the need to be retrained each time reasoning capabilities for a new task are desired), and must also posess the following two capabilities: first, 3D maps should be open-set; they should capture a large variety of concepts (orders of magnitude more than existing systems), and at varying levels of detail. For example, the concept “can of soda” could equivalently be “something to drink” or a “<particular brand of soda>” or “a refreshment”. Second, 3D maps should be multimodal; they should be queryable using as many modalities as robots or end-users can leverage. For instance, the search for a particular object in a map should work equally well if the query is a single word (e.g. “soda”), a longer sentence with additional context (e.g. “is there a can of soda on the kitchen table?), an image of a soda can, or just the ‘pop’ sound associated with opening a soda can.
Foundation models possess some of the desired traits needed to achieve open-set, multimodal representations, but are not directly applicable to 3D mapping. This major limitation exists because most foundation models consume images (e.g., CLIP [6], ALIGN [9], AudioCLIP [8]) and produce only a single vector encoding of the entire image in an embedding space. On the other hand, recent approaches trained specifi-cally to align foundation features to 2D pixels forget a large number of concepts during finetuning [10] (see Fig. 4). This does not allow for the level of precise (pixel-level or object-level) reasoning robotic perception systems need across a wide range of concepts, particularly for interaction with the external 3D world (e.g., navigation, manipulation).
To this end, we propose ConceptFusion; an open-set and multimodal 3D mapping technique that blends advances in foundation models for images, language, and audio, with advances in dense 3D reconstruction and simultaneous local-ization and mapping (SLAM). We demonstrate that pixel-level foundation features may be fused into 3D maps by leveraging precisely the same surface fusion techniques as for fusing depth or color information into a 3D map. Crucially, we show that this approach is conceptually simple, principled, and effective even in the zero-shot setting (requiring no additional training or finetuning of foundation model features). In ad-dition, these features can be queried using computationally efficient vector similarity metrics. Our key contributions are the following: • An approach to open-set multimodal 3D mapping that constructs map representations queryable by text, image, audio, and click queries in a zero-shot manner.
• A novel mechanism to compute pixel-aligned (local) features from foundation models that can only gener-ate image-level (global) feature vectors. This is a key prerequisite for 3D mapping, and our approach captures long-tailed concepts significantly better than supervised or finetuned counterparts, outperforming them by a large margin (> 40% mIoU).
• A new RGB-D dataset, UnCoCo, to evaluate open-set multimodal 3D mapping. UnCoCo comprises 78 common household/office objects tagged with more than 500K queries across modalities.
We evaluate ConceptFusion on multiple real-world datasets and tasks, including searching for objects in the real world and simulated home environments, robot manipulation tasks, and autonomous driving.
II. RELATED WORK Foundation models [5] are trained on vast quantities of data in a self-supervised fashion and accomplish a wide array of tasks, without the need for additional re-training or finetuning.
Image-language aligned models like CLIP [6] and ALIGN [9] encode text and images into a shared concept space, and have driven progress in several open-set tasks [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. They have also been extended to other modalities, such as audio [8, 19] and video [20]. In a similar vein, features from image-only foundation models like DINO [7] have been employed as drop-in solutions for reasoning about visual concepts, such as classification, detection, segmentation, keypoint estimation [21, 22].
Models like CLIP only align concepts to text or images as a whole; and not to image pixels or regions [23]. This has led to a series of approaches that extract pixel-aligned features [24, 25, 18, 26, 23]1 that address poor localization quality by training or fine-tuning a pixel-aligned model over a labeled dataset. LSeg [24] leverages pixel-level labels from segmentation datasets, while OpenSeg [18], OVSeg [26], and RegionCLIP [23] use image-caption datasets and employ region-word grounding. However, as we show in Sec. IV-B, while this improves performance over concepts present in the finetuning dataset, these models do poorly at recalling concepts infrequent in the label set used for finetuning. MaskCLIP [27] proposes a zero-shot approach that combines self-attention with engineered 1 × 1 convolution layers for open-set segmentation. However, it struggles with delineating object boundaries, and long-tailed concepts, as we show in Sec IV-B and Sec V-A. Our proposed pixel-aligned features mitigate all of the aforementioned issues by operating over region proposals and by aligning features computed across regions, enabling a variety of spatial reasoning applications.
To fuse our pixel-aligned features into a 3D map, we leverage approaches pioneered by the dense 3D mapping community. Approaches to dense SLAM estimate camera motion, scene geometry, and optionally, color from RGB(-D) images. At the core of nearly all of these methods is the volumetric fusion technique from Curless and Levoy [28], which has been adapted for real-time incremental capture of surface geometry and color [29, 30, 31, 32, 33]. In this work, we extend this line of work to additionally fuse pixel-aligned foundation features to 3D maps in a conceptually simple and computationally efficient manner. Noteworthy research efforts in bridging the gap between online 3D mapping and open-set concept acquisition include [34, 35]. In contrast, our work leverages large foundation features learned offline, over billions of data samples.
Recent approaches exploring foundation models for robotics have demonstrated impressive open-set interaction abilities [36, 37, 38, 39, 40]. While most of these approaches focus on planning and control, we provide a complementary perspective; that of perception systems that build explicit models of scenes and are able to query for concepts. In Sec. VI, we present our outlook for how both of these classes of approaches can augment each other.
III. CONCURRENT WORK Concurrently, multiple approaches are beginning to interface 2D foundation features for 3D scene understanding.
CLIP-Fields encodes a 3D map and pixel (or region)-aligned foundation features (LSeg [24], Detic [41], Sentence-BERT [42]) into a compact neural network [43]. This scene-specific neural network acts as a queryable database which aligns image and language embeddings with 3D scene points, and can be applied to open-set queries specified in language.
A new CLIP-Field is trained per scene; and it remains to be explored whether learned CLIP-Fields could potentially generalize to new scenes, or to changes within a scene.
VLMaps [44], LM-Nav [45], CoWs [46], and NLMap-Saycan [47] leverage the open-set features from pixel-aligned LSeg [24] models for robot navigation based on language com-mands. More recently, OpenScene [48] applied pixel-aligned LSeg [24] and OpenSeg [18] to open-set 3D segmentation; demonstrating that features from these 2D extractors can be distilled into neural networks operating over 3D data. Ding et al. [49] additionally distill features from more complex 2D open-set tasks, such as image captioning, into a model that consumes 3D data. A fundamental point-of-difference with the above set of approaches is that, we demonstrate that it is possible to construct 2D and 3D features zero-shot, alongside the mapping process, and without requiring any finetuning or distillation. This zero-shot capability is also a key enabler in terms of our superior performance on long-tailed concepts and complex queries, and alignment with other modalities.
Another recent approach by Mazur et al. [50] performs real-time fusion of features from foundation models for im-ages, such as DINO [7], into compact 3D neural maps. Our approach, while open-set in this spirit, extends to multiple modalities such as language and audio; presenting a novel method to extract per-pixel features from CLIP.
Perhaps the closest approach to ours is semantic abstrac-tion by Ha and Song [51], which also proposes a zero-shot approach to computing 3D-aligned CLIP features. They explore a different mechanism (attention-explainability [52]) to extract relevant regions corresponding to a text query; and demonstrate a complementary set of capabilities (completion of partly-observed objects, localizing hidden objects from language descriptions). We refer the interested reader to [51] for more details. In this work, we focus on unconditionally assigning CLIP features to image pixels and subsequently to 3D maps; over a wide variety of 3D perception and robotics tasks. A recently proposed approach, 3D-CLR [53], also proposes neural operators for concept learning over 3D scenes. This inspires our design of 3D spatial query modules, however with a significant difference: we lift foundation model features to 3D in a zeroshot manner, preserving the full range of capabilities the models are equipped with; while [53] relies on LSeg [24].

Fusing pixel-aligned foundation features to 3D Map representation: We represent our open-set multimodal 3D map M as an unordered set of points (indexed by k), each with the following attributes: (a) a vertex position vk ∈R3, (b) a normal vector nk ∈R3, (c) a confidence count ¯ ck ∈R, (d) a 3D color vector (optional), and (e) a concept vector fP k enabling open-ended querying.
Frame preprocessing: Each incoming frame It (comprising a color image Ct and a depth image Dt) is preprocessed to compute vertex-normal maps (Vt, Nt) and camera pose estimates Pt [30, 54]. Additionally, as described in Sec. IV-B, we compute the semantic context embedding fP u,v,t ∈fP Xt for each pixel in the input image Xt.
Feature fusion: We fuse fP u,v,t and Xt into the global map following a 3D reconstruction pipeline [30]. First, vertex and normal maps are mapped to the global (map) coordinate frame using the camera pose Pt. We then filter out points with noisy depth values by following the depth map fusion procedure outlined in [30]. The remaining points are fused into the global map M. A key departure from dense mapping approaches is the fusion of concept vectors fP u,v,t in addition to depth (and optionally, color). B. Computing pixel-aligned features Although some approaches have adapted foundation models like CLIP [24, 18, 55], these require additional training on labelled image-text data. This results in pixel-alignment and stronger performance on in-dataset concepts, but we observe (see Fig. 4) that the models struggle with fine-grained concepts absent in the finetuning datasets. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel mechanism to construct pixel-aligned features that combine global (image-level) context encapsulated in models like CLIP, with local (region-level) information.

C. Multimodal querying over 3D feature-fused maps The 3D maps reconstructed by ConceptFusion can be queried using multiple modalities. Given a query qmode, and a map with fused concepts fP k , we compute a per-point score sk ∈[−1, 1] as the cosine similarity defined as sk = ⟨fk, qmode⟩. The computation of qmode changes depending on the modality used for querying.
1) Text query: qtext is computed using the corresponding CLIP text encoder Ftext.
2) Click query: qclick is taken to be the fused feature vector fP k at the clicked point.
3) Image query: qimage is computed as the image-level CLIP embedding of the query image.
4) Audio query: qaudio is the AudioCLIP [8] embedding of the query sound clip.
The similarities can then be post-processed by thresholding based on score, non-maxima suppression, and (optionally) clustering to produce 3D regions of interest.

D. Building complex 3D spatial query modules Unique capabilities unlocked by fusing features into 3D space include the ability to reason about objects that were never co-observed in an image, and the ability to reason about spatial attributes (such as relative positions, orientations, support, containment, etc.) accessible only from 3D represen-tations. To this end, we leverage the computed similarity scores to build a set of 3D spatial comparator (3DSC) modules that may be further composed to recover more complex attributes.
Our set of 3DSCs all take on the relation signature RELATION(QUERYa, QUERYb) and return a scalar or boolean value as appropriate. The complete set of 3DSCs includes (see supplementary material for more details) 1) The HOWFAR(qa, qb) 3DSC returns the distance of objects referenced by queries qa and qb respectively.
2) The boolean 3DSCs ISTOTHERIGHT(qa, qb), ISTOTHELEFT(qa, qb), ONTOPOF(qa, qb), UNDER(qa, qb) return TRUE or FALSE depending on whether or not the object referenced by queries qa and qb satisfy the appropriate spatial relationship (relative to a specified viewing direction).
In Sec. VI, we optionally adopt a large language model [59] for parsing language queries to an appropriate composition of 3DSCs. For instance, the query “what is the distance between the refrigerator and the television?” is parsed into HOWFAR(refrigerator, television). This is depicted in Fig. 5.
However, for all other results presented in this paper— unless otherwise specified—the language queries are directly fed into the CLIP text encoder without any preprocessing.
Implementation details: Our feature fusion algorithm is implemented on top of the ∇SLAM [60] dense SLAM system, as this was one of the few implementations of the PointFusion algorithm [30], and for its convenience of in-terfacing with PyTorch for computing and accessing foun-dation features. For generating class-agnostic (generic) ob-ject masks, we use the Mask2Former [58] or the segment anything (SAM) [57] models for category-agnostic instance segmentation. When using Mask2Former, we generate 100 mask proposals per image. When using SAM, we find that there is significantly lower redundancy in the number of mask proposals – we therefore drop our uniqueness term in Eq. 4.
Our odometry and mapping approaches run at frame-rate (15 Hz). The pixel-aligned feature extraction processes run offline (10–15 seconds / image) on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU.
Real-time inference: To optimize the performance and efficiency of the foundation models employed (SAM [57], DINO [7], and CLIP [6]), we use standard quantization and tracing methods. By applying both quantization and tracing techniques to our models, we are able to achieve significant improvements in their efficiency, without compromising their accuracy. This enables us to deploy our models in real-world scenarios, where memory and runtime efficiency are crucial.
V. CASE STUDIES We design a systematic experimental study to investigate the following questions: 1) How do open-set multimodal 3D maps fare when queried using text, images, clicks, or audio?
2) How do we leverage the rich concept space embedded to 3D for spatial reasoning?
3) How well does ConceptFusion work on real-world robotics tasks?
4) What previously infeasible downstream use-cases can ConceptFusion enable?
Experimental setup: Our experimental benchmark com-prises of sequences from multiple publicly available datasets, and sequences we collect. The benchmark comprises 20 indoor (apartment-scale) scenes from ScanNet [61, 62], Replica [63], and self-captured sequences; 5 outdoor (urban driving) scenes; 20 indoor (tabletop) scenes with common household products (UnCoCo); and 5 synthetic scenes from the ICL [64] and iTHOR benchmarks [65].
Approaches evaluated: Since there is no prior work on con-structing open-set multimodal maps of the kind we build with ConceptFusion, we make a best-effort comparison with con-current work in this space. A. Multimodal queries on the UnCoCo dataset To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing system that supports queries as diverse and in as many modes as Con-ceptFusion; and consequently, there are no publicly available dataset to evaluate such a system on.
UnCoCo: To overcome this gap, we captured our own dataset; which we call UnCoCo, short for Uncommon contexts for Common Concepts. This real-world dataset comprises 3D scans of 78 commonly found household and office objects on a tabletop surface (see Fig. 6). There are 20 RGB-D image sequences in all, comprising a total of 12075 color and depth image pairs. For each image, we provide per-object 2D instance segmentation masks, and for each scene, a corresponding 3D segmentation mask. Importantly, UnCoCo supports a diverse set of query modalities – text, click, image, and audio. For each of these query modalities, we provide a structured and an unstructured set. The structured set comprises carefully curated and vetted queries, whereas the (much larger) unstructured set scrapes query text, and images from web-scale data. Each image in this dataset has 3-5 objects; each object has one structured text query, and 5-40 unstructured text queries (freeform queries, crowdsourced from human annotators); up to 20 structured click queries and up to 100-2000 unstructured click queries; 10 structured image queries and 10-100 unstructured image queries; and 1-5 struc-tured audio queries. With a little over 500000 queries across modalities, UnCoCo is the only dataset to date supporting multimodal 3D query evaluations on commonly found objects.
Text query: We evaluate text-query based object local-ization performance on 3D maps, on the UnCoCo dataset.
This task is extremely challenging due to the versatility of objects present in the dataset, ranging from extremely small objects (e.g., a 4-gram sachet of sugar, whiteboard markers), to thin objects (e.g., face masks, compact discs), to nonconvex geometries (e.g., a whisk, lego block constructions, shells).
We evaluate two state-of-the-art per-pixel CLIP-aligned fea-ture extractors in LSeg [24] and OpenSeg [18], which re-quire additional training over a large labelled dataset; and MaskCLIP [27] – the current state-of-the-art approach for extracting zero-shot per-pixel labels based on a text prompt.
Results are shown in Table I. For each technique evaluated, we report the 3D mean intersection-over-union (IoU) metric, and also detection accuracies at IoU thresholds of 0.15, 0.25, and 0.5. We see that ConceptFusion outperforms all other approaches by a significant margin. We attribute this to two key characteristics of ConceptFusion. First, ConceptFusion operates on the unmodified CLIP feature space, whereas ap-proaches like LSeg and OpenSeg specialize to the datasets they are finetuned on and end up gradually forgetting concepts that are infrequent on the finetuning set. Second, ConceptFusion features efficiently combine global (image-level) features with local (region-level) context; providing a rich pixel-level (and subsequently point-level) grounding. We also observe a similar trend over the unstructured text query set, as reported in Table II. ConceptFusion exhibits more graceful performance degradation to unstructured queries (long sentences).
Image query: In Table III, we report results for the scenario where the query concept is presented in the form of an image.
For instance, the goal of finding a can of soda in a 3D scene is specified by providing a randomly picked image of a soda can from the web. Here, we again observe that ConceptFusion outperforms other finetuned foundation models by a significant margin in terms of both 3D mIoU and detection accuracy.
Interestingly, we note that performances of most approaches across the text and image modalities remain consistent; as evident from the mIoU and detection metrics.
Audio query: A unique capability of our approach is to localize 3D objects based on audio queries. We conduct ex-periments on the UnCoCo dataset, which contains two classes of audio queries. Source-ambiguous queries comprise sounds that are caused due to material properties and geometries of objects and commonly involve object motions including scratching, scraping, rolling, crushing, tearing, etc. Ecolog-ical queries comprise sounds that are unique to an object (or category) – these include sounds like spraying, drilling, stirring, knocking, clicking, etc. To compensate for the lack of open-set sound source localization baselines, we implement a privileged-information baseline by providing AudioCLIP [8] with a set of ground-truth instance boxes per image; and using the computed similarity scores to rank the relevance of each box to the query audio. Results are presented in Table IV.
However, we notice that, using purely local context (as with the AudioCLIP baseline) is not performant enough; and that ConceptFusion features, which fuse global and local contexts, again perform better than purely-local features.
B. Open-Set semantic segmentation on other datasets We also evaluate semantic segmentation performance on existing datasets with well-known concepts (classes either directly or indirectly accessible via COCO Captions [66], a dataset used for finetuning by other pixel-aligned models).
In particular, we provide results on validation subsets of the ScanNet [61], Replica [63], and the SemanticKITTI [68] datasets and present results in Table V (refer to our appendix for further details). Of the approaches presented here, LSeg requires per-pixel CLIP features as labels, OpenSeg leverages per-image captions for labels, and CLIPSeg trains a shallow decoder atop the CLIP image encoder. MaskCLIP is the closest zero-shot baseline; we outperform it by a large margin.
C. Experiments on real robotic systems Our experiments on real robotic systems may also be accessed in a video format on our companion website.
Zero-shot tabletop rearrangement: To evaluate the appli-cability of ConceptFusion to real-world robotic interaction, we conduct experiments on a zero-shot tabletop rearrange-ment task with a UR5e manipulator and an Intel Realsense D415 RGB-D camera. The task involves a workspace (here a tabletop) with a few previously unseen objects in it. In some trials, the object set also includes distractors placed to hamper Fig. 8: Real-world tabletop rearrangement experiments. The robot is provided with rearrangment goals involving novel objects. (shaded area) indicates privileged approaches where off-the-shelf CLIP models are finetuned specifically for seman-tic segmentation. ZS (unshaded area) evaluates zero-shot approaches.
We outperform the closest zero-shot approach, MaskCLIP [27] by a large margin across datasets. Furthermore, ConceptFusion is compet-itive to privileged baselines for this task.

We used a drive-by-wire autonomous vehicle equipped with a calibrated stereo camera and lidar to reconstruct a map of a 320000 square yard (4000 sq. m.) urban area. The 3D map points are used by a lidar odometry algorithm (LeGO-LOAM [70]) for global localization, and the fused features are used for open vocabulary queries to generate global waypoints. Other com-ponents of the autonomy stack include a shortest-path global planner, a Frenet [71] local planner for obstacle avoidance, and a Stanley-Controller [72] for trajectory tracking. This allows us to navigate to open-set goals specified as natural language queries. In our field trials, we evaluated multiple goals, such as garbage bin, roundabout, entrance gate. Results are presented in Table VI. For each approach we indicate the mAcc (mean accuracy) and f-mIoU (frequency-weighted mean intersection-over-union). We see that, each component of the proposed method results in clear, significant improvement in performance. The first baseline (“use global CLIP”) only use the global (image-level) CLIP embedding for each pixel in the image (a trivial baseline). The “Mask2former + Local CLIP” variant takes in mask proposals from Mask2Former (i.e., the exact same proposals used in our full pipeline), but extracts features from each mask independently (i.e., does not apply equations 3 through 6). 3D spatial reasoning abilities: We also evaluate the unique ability of our queryable maps to reason about object spatial re-lationships in 3D. We generate a set of 100 (natural language) spatial reasoning queries over 5 scenes from the ScanRefer validation set. The queries are split into 4 sets (25 queries per set), each designed to evaluate a specific type of 3D spatial relationship – distances, relative positions (e.g., to the left of), support (e.g., on top of), and containment. These queries are chosen such that (a) each query references two objects, and (b) two objects are co-observed in a single image (candidates are proposed using a distance-based threshold; and validated using image segmentation labels) for the distance and relative position query sets. The results are presented in Table VII, and compared against a baseline approach that uses only the pointcloud obtained by backprojecting a single RGB-D image (2.5D). This baseline performs poorly in the distance and relative position queries, where the queries require reasoning about objects that were never co-observed in image space.
In the support and containment queries, the baseline shows better performance, as these are relations that can largely be gleaned from image observations alone. However, this approach still fails for room-level containment queries of type is <OBJ> in <ROOM>); which require additional context.

To demonstrate this, Fig. 10 illustrates two scenarios from the AI2-THOR [65] interactive household simulator. In each scenario, the robot is equipped with the task of finding an object of interest that is not in its map, because it is concealed within a receptacle. We investigate the behavior of an GenericLLM-Agent (a large language model [59]) and a ConceptFusion-Agent (GenericLLM-Agent equipped with a set of rooms and objects queried from our map). As seen in Fig. 10, while the GenericLLM-Agent is able to generate seemingly plausible subgoals to achieve the task, the lack of knowledge of the map inhibits its success. On the other hand, the ConceptFusion-agent successfully achieves both tasks by restricting the generative capabilities of the LLM to scene-specific contexts.
Multilingual abilities: Since ConceptFusion is zero-shot, it is directly applicable to any existing image-level foundation model, without requiring additional finetuning. To demonstrate this, we compute pixel-aligned features from multilingual CLIP models, and this extends the capabilities of our system to interpret and execute queries in several other languages, as illustrated in Fig. 11.

args.summary:
This paper, presented at Robotics: Science and Systems 2023 (Daegu, Republic of Korea, July 10-14, 2023), introduces ConceptFusion, an approach to building open-set multimodal 3D maps. The system fuses pixel-aligned features from foundation models (CLIP, DINO, AudioCLIP, etc.) into 3D maps via SLAM and multi-view fusion techniques, enabling zero-shot querying of maps by text, images, audio, and clicks.

Key contributions include:
- An open-set multimodal 3D mapping approach queryable by text, image, audio, and clicks in a zero-shot manner (no training or finetuning required)
- A novel mechanism to compute pixel-aligned (local) features from foundation models that natively produce only image-level (global) feature vectors
- A new RGB-D dataset called UnCoCo (Uncommon Contexts for Common Concepts) for evaluating open-set multimodal 3D mapping, comprising 78 household/office objects with over 500,000 queries across modalities

Key results:
- ConceptFusion outperforms supervised approaches (LSeg-3D, OpenSeg-3D) and zero-shot baselines (MaskCLIP-3D) by more than 40% margin on 3D IoU
- On text-query object localization, ConceptFusion achieved 0.446 3D mIoU vs 0.289 for OpenSeg-3D and 0.128 for LSeg-3D on the structured UnCoCo subset
- Audio-query accuracy reached 64.29% (source-ambiguous) and 66.67% (ecological) vs 23.81% and 22.22% for AudioCLIP baseline
- For 3D spatial reasoning: 84% success on distance queries, 76% on relative position, 96% on support, 72% on containment (vs random baselines of 24%, 36%, 52%, 44%)
- Outperforms MaskCLIP (closest zero-shot baseline) by a large margin on ScanNet, Replica, and SemanticKITTI semantic segmentation

The authors (from MIT, Université de Montréal, University of Toronto, IIIT Hyderabad, CMU, DEVCOM Army Research Lab, Amazon, and Concordia University) demonstrated ConceptFusion on real-world tasks including zero-shot tabletop rearrangement with a UR5e manipulator and text-driven autonomous navigation on a drive-by-wire vehicle. The approach is built on the ∇SLAM dense SLAM system, uses Mask2Former or SAM for class-agnostic instance segmentation, and runs odometry/mapping at 15Hz.

The paper also discusses integration with large language models (for spatial query parsing and task planning), multilingual capabilities via multilingual CLIP models, and potential synergies with emerging foundation model robotics approaches.

# ConceptFusion: Open-set Multimodal 3D Mapping

## Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2023

[Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula](https://krrish94.github.io)1,  [Alihusein Kuwajerwala](https://www.alihkw.com/)2\*,  [Qiao Gu](https://georgegu1997.github.io/)3\*,   [Mohd Omama](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=jFH3ShsAAAAJ&hl=en)4\*,   [Tao Chen](https://taochenshh.github.io/)1,   [Alaa Maalouf](https://www.csail.mit.edu/person/alaa-maalouf)1   [Shuang Li](https://people.csail.mit.edu/lishuang/)1,   [Ganesh Iyer](https://epiception.github.io/)6†,   [Soroush Saryazdi](https://saryazdi.github.io/)7†,   [Nikhil Keetha](https://nik-v9.github.io/)5,   [Ayush Tewari](https://ayushtewari.com/)1,   [Joshua B. Tenenbaum](http://web.mit.edu/cocosci/josh.html)1,   [Celso Miguel de Melo](https://celsodemelo.net/)8,   [Madhava Krishna](https://robotics.iiit.ac.in/)4,   [Liam Paull](http://liampaull.ca)2,   [Florian Shkurti](http://www.cs.toronto.edu/\~florian/)3,   [Antonio Torralba](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/vision/torralbalab/)1

1MIT, 2Université de Montréal, 3University of Toronto, 4IIIT Hyderabad, 5CMU, 6Amazon, 7Matician, 8DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory

\*Co-second authors †Work done prior to current affiliation

[Paper](assets/pdf/2023-ConceptFusion.pdf)     [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07241)     [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rkXgws8fiDs)     [Code](https://github.com/concept-fusion/concept-fusion)     [Data](#)

![](./static/images/splash.gif)

## ConceptFusion builds open-set 3D maps that can be queried via text, click, image, or audio.

## Video

## Abstract

Building 3D maps of the environment is central to robot navigation, planning, and interaction with objects in a scene. Most existing approaches that integrate semantic concepts with 3D maps largely remain confined to the closed-set setting: they can only reason about a finite set of concepts, pre-defined at training time. Further, these maps can only be queried using class labels, or in recent work, using text prompts.

We address both these issues with ConceptFusion, a scene representation that is: (i) fundamentally open-set, enabling reasoning beyond a closed set of concepts (ii) inherently multi-modal, enabling a diverse range of possible queries to the 3D map, from language, to images, to audio, to 3D geometry, all working in concert. ConceptFusion leverages the open-set capabilities of today’s foundation models pre-trained on internet-scale data to reason about concepts across modalities such as natural language, images, and audio. We demonstrate that pixel-aligned open-set features can be fused into 3D maps via traditional SLAM and multi-view fusion approaches. This enables effective zero-shot spatial reasoning, not needing any additional training or finetuning, and retains long-tailed concepts better than supervised approaches, outperforming them by more than 40% margin on 3D IoU. We extensively evaluate ConceptFusion on a number of real-world datasets, simulated home environments, a real-world tabletop manipulation task, and an autonomous driving platform. We showcase new avenues for blending foundation models with 3D open-set multimodal mapping.

## Approach

### Construct pixel-aligned features

ConceptFusion constructs pixel-aligned features from off-the-shelf foundation models that can only produce a global (image-level) embedding vector. This is achieved by: processing input images to generate generic (class-agnostic) object masks and extracting a local features for each, computing a global feature for the input image as a whole, and fusing the region-specific features with global features using our proposed zero-shot pixel alignment technique.

![](./static/images/pipeline.png)

## Zero-shot pixel alignment

![](./static/images/pixel-aligned-feature-computation.png)

For each image, the global (fG) and local (fL) features are fused to obtain our pixel-aligned features (fP). *Top-left*: We first compute cosine similarities between each local feature (fL) with the global feature (fG). *Top-right*: We compute an inter-feature similarity matrix, and compute the average similarity of each local feature to every other local feature, denoted φ̄i . *Bottom-left*: We combine these similarities to produce weights for fusing fG and fL to obtain pixel-aligned features fP.

## Retaining fine-grained concepts

![](./static/images/pixel-aligned-qualitative.png)

Our approach to computing pixel-aligned features is adept at capturing long-tailed and fine-grained concepts. The plots to the right show the similarity scores between the embeddings of the cropped image regions corresponding to diet coke, lysol, and yogurt and their text embeddings, predicted by the base CLIP model used by LSeg and OpenSeg respectively. This implies that the base CLIP models know these concepts, yet, as can be seen on the tiled plots (center), LSeg and OpenSeg are not able to retrieve these concepts; they forget the concepts when finetuned. On the other hand, our zero-shot pixel-alignment approach does not suffer this drawback, and clearly delineates the corresponding pixels.

## UnCoCo dataset

![](./static/images/uncoco.png)

To evaluate long-tailed reasoning and multimodal reasoning abilities, since there is no existing dataset, we capture a set of 20 RGB-D sequences comprising 78 commonly found objects and annotate them with text, audio, click, and image queries. For each query, we also provide the corresponding ground truth 2D and 3D retrieval results. This image showcases sample tabletop scenes from UnCoCo (left) and the resulting 3D reconstructions and labels (right).

## 3D spatial reasoning

![](./static/images/spatial-query.png)

*What is the distance between the refrigerator from the television?*

A key benefit of lifting foundation features to 3D is the ability to reason about spatial attributes. We implement a set of generic spatial relationship comparators that can be leveraged for querying arbitrary objects. We employ a large language model to parse the queries to generate function calls that can directly be executed. E.g., the query above parses to howFar(refrigirator, television).

## Long-form text queries

ConceptFusion is able to handle long-form text queries and accurately localize objects referenced by the query. In the first two scenarios, OpenSeg is distracted by the presence of several confounding attributes. The third scenario shows a single world query (television) that is part of the COCO Captions dataset used to train OpenSeg, providing it an unfair advantage. ConceptFusion, nonetheless, accurately assigns the highest response to the map points representing the television. In each query, the referenced object is boldfaced.

![](./static/images/scannet-text-query.png)

## Click-queries

Click-queries over a sequence from the ICL dataset. For each clicked point, we compute the cosine similarity of the embedding at that point with that of every other map point and visualize them using a 'jet' colormap. Points in red indicate greatest similarity, while points in blue indicate least similarity. Notice the consistency in semantic concepts. For instance, when we click on a point on the corner lamp (at about 0:45), we also notice that the other corner lamp, as well as lights on top of the ceiling get high similarities assigned.

## Experiments on real robotic systems

### Tabletop rearrangement

![](./static/images/rearrangement.png)

The robot is provided with rearrangment goals involving novel objects. (Top row) push goldfish to the right of the yellow line, where goldfish refers to the brandname of the pack of Cheddar snack. (Bottom row) push baymax to the right of the yellow line, where baymax refers to the plush toy depicting the famous Disney character.

### Autonomous driving

![](./static/images/driving.png)

(Left to right; top to bottom) Autonomous drive-by-wire platform deployed; pointcloud map of the environment with the response to the openset text-query ”football field” (shown in red); path found to the football field (shown in red); car successfully navigates to the destination autonomously. See our anonymized webpage for more results.

## Integrating ConceptFusion with Large Language Models

## Concurrent work

Given the pace of AI research these days, it is extremely challenging to keep up with all of the work around foundation models and open-set perception. We list below a few key approaches that we have come across after beginning work on ConceptFusion. If we may have inadvertently missed out on key concurrent work, please reach out to us over email (or better, open a pull request on [our GitHub page](https://github.com/concept-fusion/concept-fusion.github.io)).

[CLIP-Fields](https://mahis.life/clip-fields/) encodes features from language and vision-language models into a compact, scene-specific neural network trained to predict feature embeddings from 3D point coordinates; to enable open-set visual understanding tasks.

[OpenScene](https://pengsongyou.github.io/openscene) demonstrates that features from pixel-aligned 2D vision-language models can be distilled to 3D, generalize to new scenes, and perform better than their 2D counterparts.

[Deng et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16312) demonstrate interesting ways of learning hierarchical scene abstractions by distilling features from 2D vision-language foundation models, and smart ways of interpreting captions from 2D captioning approaches.

args.summary:
ConceptFusion is an open-source research project (presented at Robotics: Science and Systems, RSS 2023) that builds open-set, multimodal 3D maps of environments. Unlike existing semantic 3D mapping approaches that operate in a "closed-set" setting (limited to a finite set of concepts predefined at training time and queryable only via class labels or text), ConceptFusion is (i) fundamentally open-set, enabling reasoning beyond a closed set of concepts, and (ii) inherently multi-modal, supporting diverse query types including language, images, audio, and 3D geometry, all working together.

The method leverages the open-set capabilities of foundation models pretrained on internet-scale data (e.g., CLIP) to reason across modalities. It constructs pixel-aligned features from off-the-shelf foundation models that typically only produce image-level (global) embeddings via a proposed zero-shot pixel alignment technique: it processes images to generate class-agnostic object masks, extracts local features per region, computes a global image feature, and fuses region-specific (local) and global features. This approach captures long-tailed and fine-grained concepts that supervised methods like LSeg and OpenSeg forget during fine-tuning.

Key technical contributions and findings:
- Achieves effective zero-shot spatial reasoning without any additional training or fine-tuning.
- Outperforms supervised approaches by more than 40% margin on 3D IoU when retaining long-tailed concepts.
- Demonstrates 3D spatial reasoning (e.g., "What is the distance between the refrigerator and the television?") using a large language model to parse queries into executable function calls.
- Handles long-form text queries, click-queries (with cosine similarity retrieval), and audio/image queries.
- Introduces the UnCoCo dataset: 20 RGB-D sequences with 78 commonly found objects, annotated with text, audio, click, and image queries plus ground-truth 2D and 3D retrieval results (created because no existing dataset supported evaluating long-tailed and multimodal reasoning).

The paper evaluates ConceptFusion on real-world datasets, simulated home environments, a real-world tabletop manipulation task (e.g., pushing objects like "goldfish" brand snacks or a "Baymax" plush toy to specified locations), and an autonomous driving platform (successfully navigating to a "football field" based on open-set text query).

Multiple author affiliations include MIT, Université de Montréal, University of Toronto, IIIT Hyderabad, CMU, Amazon, Matician, and DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory. The project also lists concurrent work including CLIP-Fields, OpenScene, LERF, NLMap-SayCan, and 3D-CLR.

## ICRA 2024

[*Qiao Gu*](https://georgegu1997.github.io/) 3\*,   [*Alihusein Kuwajerwala*](https://www.alihkw.com/) 2\*,   [*Sacha Morin*](https://sachamorin.github.io/) 2\*,   [*Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula*](https://krrish94.github.io) 1\*,

1MIT, 2Université de Montréal, 3University of Toronto, 4IIIT Hyderabad, 5JHU APL, 6JHU, 7UMass Amherst, 8DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory

\*Equal contribution

[Paper](assets/pdf/2023-ConceptGraphs.pdf)     [arXiv](http://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16650)     [Video](https://youtu.be/ie9VdL7wieY)     [Tutorial Video](https://youtu.be/56jEFyrqqpo)     [Code](https://github.com/concept-graphs/concept-graphs)

## ConceptGraphs builds open-vocabulary 3D scenegraphs that enable a broad range of perception and task planning capabilities.

## Abstract

For robots to perform a wide variety of tasks, they require a 3D representation of the world that is semantically rich, yet compact and efficient for task-driven perception and planning. Recent approaches have attempted to leverage features from large vision-language models to encode semantics in 3D representations. However, these approaches tend to produce maps with per-point feature vectors, which do not scale well in larger environments, nor do they contain semantic spatial relationships between entities in the environment, which are useful for downstream planning. In this work, we propose ConceptGraphs, an open-vocabulary graph-structured representation for 3D scenes. ConceptGraphs is built by leveraging 2D foundation models and fusing their output to 3D by multi-view association. The resulting representations generalize to novel semantic classes, without the need to collect large 3D datasets or finetune models. We demonstrate the utility of this representation through a number of downstream planning tasks that are specified through abstract (language) prompts and require complex reasoning over spatial and semantic concepts.

## Approach

ConceptGraphs builds an open-vocabulary 3D scene graph from a sequence of posed RGB-D images. We use generic instance segmentation models to segment regions from RGB images, extract semantic feature vectors for each, and project them to a 3D point cloud. These regions are incrementally associated and fused from multiple views, resulting in a set of 3D objects and associated vision (and language) descriptors. Then large vision and language models are used to caption each mapped 3D objects and derive inter-object relations, which generates the edges to connect the set of objects and form a graph. The resulting 3D scene graph provides a structured and comprehensive understanding of the scene and can further be easily translated to a text description, useful for LLM-based task planning.

![](./static/images/pipeline.png)

## Re-localization

We emply ConceptGraphs to localize the robot in a previously mapped environment. Each object encodes a CLIP embedding, which is employed in a landmark-based particle-filter that uses cosine similarity to compute particle weights. Within a few iterations, the robot localizes accurately. In our explainer video, we also demonstrate mapping newly-detected objects that were not present in the original map.

## Text queries via CLIP or GPT-4

We demonstrate the ability of ConceptGraphs to answer open-set text queries. Each object in the scene graphs contains an associated CLIP embedding (fused from multi-view images), as well as a text caption. While the CLIP embeddings work well across a wide range of queries, they fail when the queries reference multiple concepts, involve negation, or complex composition. We may also use LLMs (here, GPT-4) to find objects that address the text query. This approach performs better, especially on complex queries, but requires access to an LLM at inference time (while the CLIP text-query approach is easily deployable on CPUs on-board the robot).

### Queries with both text and image context

We can also handle text queries that include context from an additional image. In this example, we the robot looks at an image of Michael Jordan, and is given a text query "something this guy would play with". It is able to locate the basketball in the scene.

### Traversability puzzle

The Jackal robot solving a traversability challenge. All paths to the goal are obstructed by objects. We query an LLM to identify which objects can be safely pushed or traversed by the robot (green) and which objects would be too heavy or hinder the robot’s movement (red). The LLM relies on the ConceptGraphs node captions to make traversability predictions and we add the non-traversable objects to the Jackal costmap for path planning. The Jackal successfully reaches the goal by going through a curtain and pushing a basketball, while also avoiding contact with bricks, an iron dumbbell, and a flower pot.

## Concurrent work

Given the pace of AI research these days, it is extremely challenging to keep up with all of the work around foundation models and open-set perception. We list below a few key approaches that we have come across after finalizing the ConceptGraphs system. If we may have inadvertently missed out on key concurrent work, please reach out to us over email (or better, open a pull request on [our GitHub page](https://github.com/concept-graphs/concept-graphs.github.io)).

[OVIR-3D](https://openreview.net/forum?id=gVBvtRqU1_) is an open-vocabulary 3D instance-level mapping system that reconstructs an objects from RGB-D images and known poses. Each object is additionally assigned a CLIP embedding for text-query-based retrieval.

[OpenMask3D](https://openmask3d.github.io/) performs 3D instance segmentation (on pointcloud data) based on open-vocabulary queries (specified as text).

[OVSG](https://openreview.net/forum?id=cjEI5qXoT0) reconstructs open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs using OVIR-3D and a graph network encoder.

[SayPlan](https://sayplan.github.io/) demonstrates an efficient planning mechanism using LLMs and 3D Scene Graphs (assumed available).

ConceptGraphs is a research project presented at ICRA 2024 that builds open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs for robot perception and planning. Developed by a multi-institutional team (MIT, Université de Montréal, University of Toronto, IIIT Hyderabad, JHU APL, JHU, UMass Amherst, and DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory), led by corresponding authors Qiao Gu, Alihusein Kuwajerwala, Sacha Morin, and Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula.

The system addresses a key limitation in robotics: existing 3D representations often use per-point feature vectors that don't scale to larger environments and lack semantic spatial relationships between entities. ConceptGraphs constructs graph-structured representations by leveraging 2D foundation models (instance segmentation, vision-language models) and fusing them to 3D via multi-view association from posed RGB-D images. This allows generalization to novel semantic classes without collecting large 3D datasets or fine-tuning models.

Key capabilities demonstrated:
1. Re-localization: Using CLIP embeddings per object in a landmark-based particle filter for robot localization in mapped environments.
2. Open-set text queries: Supporting both CLIP embedding queries (CPU-deployable on-board) and LLM-based queries (e.g., GPT-4) that handle complex queries involving multiple concepts, negation, or composition.
3. Queries with text and image context: E.g., recognizing that "something this guy would play with" referring to Michael Jordan leads to locating a basketball.
4. Traversability puzzle: A Jackal robot uses LLM reasoning over concept-graph node captions to determine which objects can be safely pushed/traversed vs. avoided, successfully navigating to a goal.

The paper includes resources: paper PDF, arXiv (2309.16650), video, tutorial video, and open-source code on GitHub. The work also lists concurrent approaches including OVIR-3D, OpenMask3D, OVSG, and SayPlan. Citation: Gu et al., "Conceptgraphs: Open-vocabulary 3d scene graphs for perception and planning," ICRA 2024, pp. 5021-5028.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Reinforcing Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models with ... ---
URL: https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/d2f2ca2c305e1a9c29bf00a676f0a500-Paper-Conference.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces ViLaSR, a novel approach to enhancing spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) through a "drawing to reason in space" paradigm. Instead of relying solely on text-based reasoning or external perception tools, ViLaSR enables LVLMs to reason by performing elementary drawing operations directly in the visual space—specifically bounding box annotations and auxiliary line drawing—allowing the model to express and analyze spatial relationships through direct visual manipulation.

The paper proposes a three-stage training framework:
1. **Cold-start training** with synthetic data to establish basic drawing abilities.
2. **Reflective rejection sampling** to selectively reinforce reasoning paths that demonstrate both correct answers and self-correction behaviors (e.g., revising visual operations based on intermediate results).
3. **Reinforcement learning** (using GRPO) with rewards balancing answer correctness and reasoning format.

Extensive experiments across five spatial reasoning benchmarks (maze navigation, static spatial reasoning, video-based reasoning, and multi-view reasoning) demonstrate that ViLaSR (based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B) achieves an average improvement of 18.4% over strong baselines. Key results include: 98.2% on MAZE, 63.9% on SpatialEval-Real, 45.4% on VSI-Bench, 37.6% on SPAR-Bench, and 30.2% on MMSI-Bench. The model outperforms significantly larger open-source models (72B) and proprietary models like GPT-4o and Gemini-2.0-Flash on most benchmarks.

Ablation studies reveal that reflective rejection sampling is crucial for self-correction (a 96.5% decrease in reflection behavior when removed), and RL optimization helps consolidate multi-attempt capabilities into strong single-attempt performance while using drawing operations more selectively. The paper is accepted at NeurIPS 2025.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
We propose drawing to reason in space, a novel paradigm that enables LVLMs to reason through elementary drawing operations in the visual space., Our model, named VILASR, consistently outperforms existing methods across diverse spatial reasoning benchmarks... with an average improvement of 18.4%., Reflective rejection sampling significantly enhances the model's self-correction capabilities, with the frequency of reflection behaviors doubling compared to models trained without this intermediate stage., RL optimization effectively consolidates multi-attempt capabilities while maintaining strong single-attempt performance, significantly narrowing the performance gap compared to earlier training stages., Removing this stage leads to a 96.5% decrease in reflection pattern exhibition, fundamentally altering the model's behavior and performance.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Jigsaw-Puzzles: From Seeing to Understanding to Reasoning in ... ---
URL: https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1320.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents Jigsaw-Puzzles, a novel benchmark for evaluating spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). The benchmark consists of 1,100 carefully curated real-world images with high spatial complexity, designed to test VLMs across five tasks that mirror the human cognitive progression from perception to understanding to reasoning: Missing Piece Selection (spatial understanding), Piece Localization, Connection Verification, Anomaly Detection (single-step reasoning), and Order Restoration (multi-step reasoning). The dataset is constructed through a fully automated pipeline, offering advantages in visual complexity, scalability, and automated construction over existing benchmarks.

The authors evaluated 24 state-of-the-art VLMs, including proprietary models (Claude, Gemini, GPT-4o, Grok) and open-source models (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, Kimi-VL, etc.). Key findings include: (1) Even the strongest model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, achieves only 77.14% overall accuracy, far below the 96.36% human performance; (2) A significant gap exists between proprietary and open-source models; (3) VLMs perform particularly poorly on multi-step reasoning (Order Restoration), with Gemini-2.5-Pro reaching only 30.00% accuracy on the open-ended Order Generation task vs. 94.09% for humans; (4) Spatial reasoning capability scales with model size; (5) Reasoning-enhanced models show superior performance, particularly on multi-step tasks, due to self-correction behaviors. The benchmark is released as an open-source resource to advance spatial reasoning research in VLMs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Spatial reasoning is a core component of human cognition, enabling individuals to perceive, comprehend, and interact with the physical world., Even the strongest model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, achieves only 77.14% overall accuracy and performs particularly poorly on the Order Generation task, with only 30.00% accuracy, far below the 90%+ performance achieved by human participants., Our findings expose consistent limitations in current VLMs and provide insights to guide future improvements in spatial reasoning capability., Jigsaw-Puzzles provides a scalable and cognitively grounded benchmark to advance future research on spatial reasoning in VLMs., The persistent gap between humans and VLMs highlights the demanding nature of Jigsaw-Puzzles and affirms its utility as a robust benchmark for spatial reasoning evaluation.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Reinforcing Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models with Interwoven Thinking and Visual Drawing ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.09965v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces ViLaSR, a Vision-Language model for Spatial Reasoning that employs a novel "drawing to reason in space" paradigm. Unlike traditional text-centric multimodal reasoning approaches, ViLaSR enables LVLMs to perform spatial reasoning through elementary visual drawing operations—specifically bounding box annotations and auxiliary line drawing—allowing direct visual manipulation and analysis of spatial relationships.

The authors develop a three-stage training framework:
1. **Cold-start training** with synthetic data to establish basic visual drawing abilities
2. **Reflective rejection sampling** to enhance self-correction behaviors
3. **Reinforcement learning** (using GRPO) to directly optimize for target rewards

Extensive experiments across five spatial reasoning benchmarks (Maze, SpatialEval-Real, VSI-Bench, SPAR-Bench, MMSI-Bench) demonstrate that ViLaSR achieves an average improvement of 18.4% over existing methods. Key results include 98.2% on MAZE, 63.9% on SpatialEval-Real, 45.4% on VSI-Bench, 37.6% on SPAR-Bench, and 30.2% on MMSI-Bench—outperforming both proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini) and open-source models (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA variants).

Ablation studies reveal that reflective rejection sampling doubles the model's self-correction capabilities, and RL optimization effectively consolidates multi-attempt capabilities into strong single-attempt performance. The model is implemented based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and trained on 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

The approach addresses fundamental limitations of existing methods: reliance on black-box perception tools, fragmented reasoning through disconnected tool invocations, and oversimplified reasoning patterns. By enabling models to directly manipulate visual space through elementary operations, ViLaSR bridges the gap between text-centric reasoning and human-like spatial cognition.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents VLTVG, a transformer-based framework for visual grounding—the task of locating an object in an image based on a natural language description. The authors propose three key components:

1. **Visual-Linguistic Verification Module**: Computes fine-grained pixel-wise correlations between visual features and textual embeddings to focus on regions relevant to the language expression while suppressing unrelated areas.

2. **Language-Guided Context Encoder**: Aggregates visual context features (e.g., interaction relations, relative positions) under guidance of textual descriptions to make the target object more distinguishable.

3. **Multi-Stage Cross-Modal Decoder**: Iteratively queries and mulls over visual and linguistic information across N stages (default N=6) to progressively refine the target object's feature representation for accurate localization.

The framework uses a CNN (ResNet-50/101) with transformer encoder layers for visual features and BERT for textual embeddings. Unlike previous methods that rely on pre-generated proposals or anchor boxes, this approach directly retrieves the object's feature representation for localization.

<summary>
# InstructBLIP Model Documentation (Hugging Face Transformers)

## Overview
InstructBLIP is a vision-language model proposed in the paper "InstructBLIP: Towards General-purpose Vision-Language Models with Instruction Tuning" (May 2023) by Wenliang Dai et al. It leverages the BLIP-2 architecture for visual instruction tuning. The model was published on Hugging Face on 2023-05-11 and contributed to Transformers on 2023-06-26.

## Key Features
- Uses the same architecture as BLIP-2 but with a key difference: it also feeds the text prompt (instruction) to the Q-Former (Querying Transformer).
- Introduces instruction-aware visual feature extraction, enabling the model to extract informative features tailored to given instructions.
- Supports FlashAttention and SDPA (Scaled Dot-Product Attention).

## Performance
- Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across all 13 held-out datasets, substantially outperforming BLIP-2 and the larger Flamingo.
- Achieves state-of-the-art performance when fine-tuned on individual downstream tasks (e.g., 90.7% accuracy on ScienceQA IMG).

## Architecture Components
The model consists of three main components:
1. **Vision Encoder** (InstructBlipVisionModel): Processes pixel values (image input) with configurable parameters (hidden_size=1408, 39 layers, 16 attention heads, image_size=224, patch_size=14).
2. **Q-Former** (InstructBlipQFormerModel): Querying Transformer that takes both image features and the instruction text as input (vocab_size=30522, hidden_size=768, 12 layers, 12 attention heads).
3. **Language Model**: Part of the conditional generation pipeline.

## Usage Tips
- BLIP models after release v4.46 require setting `processor.num_query_tokens = model.config.num_query_tokens` and expanding the model embeddings layer to add special `<image>` tokens.
- Typically ~500 tokens per image are needed, so text truncation should be avoided.
- The InstructBlipProcessor wraps an image processor (BlipImageProcessor), a tokenizer (GPT2Tokenizer), and a qformer tokenizer into a single processor.

## Configuration Classes
- **InstructBlipConfig**: Main configuration for the full model (num_query_tokens=32 by default).
- **InstructBlipVisionConfig**: Vision encoder configuration.
- **InstructBlipQFormerConfig**: Q-Former configuration.

## Model Classes
- **InstructBlipModel**: Base model consisting of language model, qformer, and vision encoder.
- **InstructBlipForConditionalGeneration**: Model for generating text given an image and an optional text prompt.
- **InstructBlipVisionModel**: Vision encoder only.
- **InstructBlipQFormerModel**: Q-Former only.

## Key Methodology
The paper conducted a systematic study on vision-language instruction tuning based on pre-trained BLIP-2 models, gathering 26 publicly available datasets transformed into instruction tuning format, categorized into two clusters for held-in instruction tuning and held-out zero-shot evaluation.

<summary>
BLIP-2 is a vision-language pretraining model that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language models (LLMs), using a lightweight Querying Transformer (Q-Former) to bridge the modality gap. It was published in November 2023 by Li et al. from Salesforce.

**Architecture and Pretraining:**
BLIP-2 pretrains in two stages:
1. **Stage 1 (Vision-Language Representation Learning):** Uses a frozen image encoder (ViT from CLIP/EVA-CLIP) and a Q-Former module. The Q-Former has two components: an image Transformer (with 32 learnable query tokens) and a text Transformer. It is pretrained on three tasks: image-text contrastive learning, image-text matching (binary classification), and image-grounded text generation (cross-entropy loss). The image encoder is kept frozen.
2. **Stage 2 (Vision-to-Language Generative Learning):** Connects the Q-Former's image Transformer output via a fully connected layer to a frozen LLM decoder (OPT) or LLM encoder-decoder (Flan-T5). The LLM remains frozen during this stage.

**Performance:**
- BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art results on various vision-language tasks despite having significantly fewer trainable parameters than existing methods.
- It outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer trainable parameters.
- Demonstrates emerging capabilities in zero-shot instructed image-to-text generation.
- On VQA, image captioning (NoCaps, COCO), and image-text retrieval (Flickr), BLIP-2 with ViT-g and Flan-T5 (XXL) achieves best results.

**Limitations:**
- BLIP-2 can produce hallucinations and incorrect outputs due to limitations in the frozen LLM's knowledge (e.g., incorrect quotes, wrong product identification, flawed reasoning about weather/context).

**Data:** Uses 129M images from COCO, Visual Genome, Conceptual Captions (3M and 12M), SBU Captions, and 115M images from the LAION 400M dataset, with synthetic captions generated via bootstrapping.

**Key Takeaway:** BLIP-2 is a computationally efficient vision-language model that leverages frozen components to dramatically reduce trainable parameters while achieving state-of-the-art results, though it inherits knowledge limitations from its frozen LLM.
</summary>

# GLaMM: Pixel Grounding Large Multimodal Model

## Summary

This paper introduces **GLaMM (Grounding Large Multimodal Model)**, the first Large Multimodal Model (LMM) capable of generating natural language responses seamlessly integrated with corresponding object segmentation masks at the pixel level. Unlike prior LMMs that either generate ungrounded text or are limited to single-object grounding, GLaMM can ground objects appearing in conversations and accept both textual and optional visual prompts (e.g., regions of interest) as input.

### Key Contributions:

1. **GLaMM Architecture**: Consists of five core components: Global Image Encoder (ViT-H/14 CLIP), Region Encoder, LLM (Vicuna-7B), Grounding Image Encoder (SAM encoder), and Pixel Decoder (SAM decoder-like). This enables scene-level, region-level, and pixel-level grounding.

2. **Grounded Conversation Generation (GCG)**: A novel task where models produce natural language responses interleaved with object segmentation masks. Evaluation covers caption quality, mask-to-phrase correspondence, mask quality, and region-specific grounding.

3. **GranD Dataset**: A large-scale, densely annotated dataset created via an automated annotation pipeline with 4 hierarchical levels (object localization, relationships, scene graph/dense captioning, extra context). Contains **7.5M unique concepts** grounded in **810M regions** across **11M images**, with 84M referring expressions and 33M grounded captions.

4. **GranDf Dataset**: A high-quality fine-tuning dataset (214K image-grounded text pairs) for GCG, built by repurposing existing datasets (Flickr-30K, RefCOCOg, PSG) using GPT-4, plus manual annotations.

- **GCG**: Outperforms BuboGPT, Kosmos-2, and LISA across all metrics (METEOR, CIDEr, AP50, mIoU, Mask Recall).

- **Region-Level Captioning**: Achieves strong zero-shot and fine-tuned results on Visual Genome and refCOCOg.

- **Conversational QA**: Scores 63.3 on LLaVA-Bench, on par with LLaVA-1.5.

### Training:
- Uses auto-regressive cross-entropy loss for text and binary cross-entropy + DICE loss for segmentation.

Ablation studies confirm that training on all three capabilities is essential, and that incorporating numerical information (distance/location estimation) is particularly important for tasks like TSP. --- SOURCE 12: NLVR2 Bias Analysis ---
URL: https://lil.nlp.cornell.edu/nlvr/NLVR2BiasAnalysis.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This analysis by Alane Suhr and Yoav Artzi from Cornell University examines potential visual bias in the NLVR2 dataset, a binary classification task where models must determine if a natural language statement is true or false about a pair of images.

**Key Findings on Visual Bias:**
- While NLVR2 was designed to be robust to language bias (each sentence appears with both true and false labels), the data collection process allowed workers to choose which image pairs to label as true/false, potentially introducing visual bias.
- Analysis of the training data shows that image pairs appearing multiple times have labels more consistent than expected by chance. For example, of 33,866 pairs appearing twice, 21,267 (62.8%) have the same label in both instances, versus the expected 50%.
- For pairs appearing three times, 128 out of 345 (37.1%) have identical labels across all instances, versus the expected 25%.
- A worst-case model that learns only the visual bias (ignoring language) achieves 83.53% accuracy on the development set.

**New Evaluation Protocol:**
- The authors identify a subset of the evaluation data that is robust to visual bias: image pairs that appear multiple times with different labels (balanced labels).
- They create new evaluation subsets: balanced examples (2,300 out of 6,982 dev examples) and unbalanced examples (3,562 out of 6,982).
- Testing state-of-the-art models (Li et al. 2019 VisualBERT and Tan and Bansal 2019 LXMERT) shows they largely do not take advantage of visual bias, with only small performance drops on balanced sets and small increases on unbalanced sets.

**Conclusion:** The authors propose adding these new evaluation subsets to the NLVR2 evaluation protocol and recommend evaluating models on the original NLVR corpus (synthetic images) as well.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 16: Winoground Benchmark for Visio-Linguistic Reasoning ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/winoground-benchmark

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Winoground Benchmark for Visio-Linguistic Reasoning

The Winoground benchmark is a probing dataset and evaluation protocol designed to test vision-and-language models' ability to perform visio-linguistic compositional reasoning. Its central task presents two images and two captions that share exactly the same set of words—differing only in order (and thus semantics)—requiring the model to correctly match each caption to its corresponding image. Inspired by the Winograd Schema Challenge (Thrush et al., 2022), it reveals critical deficiencies in current multimodal models' handling of nuanced textual orderings and corresponding visual relations.

### Dataset Composition
- 400 primary examples (800 unique images and captions; 1600 image-caption pairs total), balanced with half correct pairings and half deliberately mismatched
- Images licensed from Getty Images and hand-curated by expert annotators
- **Linguistic tags**: object swaps (noun phrase order), relation swaps (verb, adjective, or prepositional reordering), and mixed swaps
- **Visual tags**: "Pragmatics" (nonliteral interpretation), "Symbolic" (stylized/abstract images), and "Series" (images from the same photo series)

### Evaluation Metrics (three scores)
- **Text Score**: Correct caption assigned higher score than incorrect one (chance: 25%)
- **Image Score**: Correct image receives higher score (chance: 25%)
- **Group Score**: Both text and image assignments simultaneously correct (chance: 16.67%)

### Model Performance Gap
- Human annotators vastly outperform models (Text ≈ 89.5%, Image ≈ 88.5%, Group ≈ 85.5%)
- State-of-the-art models (UNITER, CLIP, FLAVA) achieve only 30-35% on text and image scores, with group scores typically below random chance (15%)

### Failure Modes and Model Deficiencies
1. **Compositional Language Understanding is Necessary but Not Sufficient**: Distinguishing semantic minimal pairs doesn't translate to improved Winoground accuracy
2. **Visual Detail Sensitivity**: Failures occur on images with small, blurred, or ambiguous elements (VisuallyDifficult tag)
3. **Ambiguity and Commonsense Reasoning**: Some instances valid under both captions, requiring global/commonsense reasoning
4. **Fusion Bottleneck**: The primary challenge lies in fusing visual and textual representations, not weaknesses of either branch alone

### Model Innovations Catalyzed by Winoground (per Diwan et al., 2022 and related works)
- **ComCLIP (Causal and Entity-Disentangled Matching)**: Breaks images into subject, object, and predicate components for entity-level matching; achieves zero-shot performance gains without additional training
- **CACR (Attention Congruence Regularization)**: Enforces congruence between self-attention patterns in vision and language via matrix KL loss; yields +5.75 points on group score when applied to UNITER
- **DiffusionITM**: Reframes text-to-image generation models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) as discriminative image-text matchers using denoising loss; outperforms CLIP on compositional tasks (image retrieval accuracy ~10-12%)
- **SDS-CLIP**: Fine-tunes CLIP by augmenting contrastive loss with score distillation from diffusion models; yields up to +7% higher group scores with minimal parameter updates
- **SCRAMBLe**: Generates compositional hard negative captions via chain-of-thought LLM prompting, adversarial filtering, and direct preference optimization; improves group accuracy from 49.5% to 54.8%, marking the highest open-weight performance to date (Mishra et al., April 2025)

### Extensions and Applications
- **Winoground-T2I**: Extends the paradigm to 11k contrastive sentence pairs across 20 categories to evaluate text-to-image models' compositional rendering fidelity
- Results transfer modestly to broader vision-language and VQA tasks via preference tuning on synthetic data

### Open Challenges and Future Directions
- Fusion bottlenecks in multi-modal representations
- Performance drops on examples requiring commonsense inference, unusual objects/contexts, or high visual resolution
- Need for more sensitive, reliable, and causally motivated evaluation protocols
- Future work: stronger visual encoders, objectives rewarding compositional matching, hybrid generative-discriminative models, attention regularization, automated data augmentation, and preference learning

The Winoground benchmark and its derivatives are publicly available as diagnostic tools for advancing visio-linguistic compositionality research.
</summary>

**CECE: Caption Expansion with Contradictions and Entailments (ICLR 2025)**

This paper introduces CECE, a method to improve compositional reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by leveraging Natural Language Inference (NLI). The key problem is that VLMs struggle with relating objects, attributes, and spatial relationships, often relying on biased or superficial features.

**Methodology:**
CECE uses an LLM (Llama3.1 70B) to generate lexically diverse entailments (hypotheses that logically follow from a caption) and contradictions (hypotheses incompatible with the caption) from a given text premise. These expansions are then evaluated by a VLM (e.g., LLaVA-1.6) to compute likelihood scores. A two-step balancing mechanism (hyperparameters α1 and α2) integrates scores from entailments, contradictions, and the original caption to produce a final evaluation, preventing semantic drift.

**Key Results:**
- **Winoground:** Achieves 47.5% group score (best prior work: 28.3% with finetuned data), a +19.2% improvement.
- **EqBen:** Achieves 47.9% group score (best prior work: 35.0%), a +12.9% improvement.
- **Human-alignment benchmarks:** Consistently outperforms prior methods across DrawBench, EditBench, COCO-T2I, TIFA160, and Pick-a-Pic without requiring fine-tuning.
- **3D alignment:** Outperforms base models on StanfordT23D.

**Key Contributions:**
1. CECE leverages both entailments and contradictions for richer semantic understanding.
2. It significantly outperforms prior sentence decomposition methods (SDS) and visual programming approaches.
3. It provides lexical diversity (Jaccard similarity of 0.32 vs. 0.53 for SDS) while maintaining semantic meaning.
4. Human validation confirmed entailment accuracy (4.7/5) and contradiction accuracy (1.7/5, indicating correct contradiction).
5. The method is model-agnostic and improves interpretability without fine-tuning.

**Authors:** Paola Cascante-Bonilla, Yu Hou, Yang Trista Cao, Hal Daumé III, Rachel Rudinger (University of Maryland, Stony Brook University, UT Austin)

## Winoground: Probing Vision and Language Models for Visio-Linguistic Compositionality

**Overview:** This paper introduces Winoground, a novel task and dataset for evaluating visio-linguistic compositional reasoning in vision and language (V&L) models. The task involves matching two images to two captions that contain the exact same set of words but in different orders (e.g., "the tree is in the shopping cart" vs. "the shopping cart is in the tree"). The dataset was hand-curated by four expert annotators and contains 400 examples (800 image-caption pairs, 1600 total pairings). It is licensed from Getty Images and available on Hugging Face.

**Key Findings:** All state-of-the-art V&L models tested (UNITER, VILLA, VinVL, VisualBERT, ViLT, LXMERT, ViLBERT, UniT, CLIP, VSE++, VSRN) perform close to or at random chance, with a ~70% performance gap compared to humans on the image score metric. Humans achieve 89.50% text score, 88.50% image score, and 85.50% group score, while the best model (VinVL) achieves only 37.75%, 17.75%, and 14.50% respectively.

**Metrics:** Three evaluation metrics are used:
- **Text score:** Can the model select the correct caption given an image?
- **Image score:** Can the model select the correct image given a caption?
- **Group score:** Both conditions must hold simultaneously.

**Dataset Tags:** Examples are annotated with linguistic tags (Object, Relation, Both swaps) and visual tags (Pragmatics, Symbolic, Series). Models perform worst on the "Series" tag (same photo series), where most achieve 0% group score.

**Analysis Insights:**
- Single-stream models (merged attention) slightly outperform dual-stream models, though CLIP (dual-stream) was trained on an order of magnitude more data.
- Caption length negatively correlates with model performance; models do better on short, less compositional captions.
- There is a significant positive correlation between pretraining dataset size and model scores.
- Models struggle with compositional reasoning, often disregarding adjective information (e.g., treating "brown dog" and "white dog" similarly).

**Conclusion:** The authors conclude that V&L models fall dramatically short of human-level visio-linguistic compositional reasoning. They suggest future work investigate single-stream model strengths, larger pretraining data, improved image encoding, and pretraining objectives emphasizing similar but wrong images.
