--- SOURCE 7: [PDF] Kosmos-1/2 & UnifiedIO v1/2 ---
URL: https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~zk15/teaching/AY2025_cs8803vlm_fall/L11_KosmosUnifiedIO.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This presentation summarizes and compares four major multimodal large language model (MLLM) systems: Kosmos-1/2 and UnifiedIO-1/2, covering their architectures, training approaches, results, and trade-offs.

**KOSMOS-1 (Huang et al., NeurIPS 2023)** is a 1.6B parameter multimodal LLM pretrained from scratch using a standard Transformer-based causal language model architecture. Key architectural innovations include MAGNETO (extra LayerNorm per sublayer for training stability) and Extrapolatable Position Embedding (XPOS), which uses RoPE with per-dimension exponential scaling for better generalization to longer sequences. Training used a mix of text corpora, image-caption pairs (LAION-2B, LAION-400M, COYO-700M, Conceptual Captions), interleaved image-text data (71M Common Crawl web pages), and language-only instruction tuning.

**KOSMOS-2 (Peng et al., ICLR 2024)** adds grounding to the general-purpose MLLM—the ability to link text to specific image regions—using the same architecture and model size (1.6B). Grounding uses Markdown-style links from text spans to location tokens, discretizing images into P×P bins with special tokens. The GRIT dataset was built from LAION-2B and COYO-700M subsets with a two-step pipeline for extracting and linking text spans to image regions. Results showed large improvements in zero-shot grounding performance and strong referring results (even outperforming finetuned SLR on CIDEr), though it lagged non-zero-shot methods on referring expression comprehension and showed a slight drop on VQA vs. KOSMOS-1, suggesting training mix trade-offs. Strengths include elegant token-level grounding; weaknesses include limited architectural novelty and small model size.

**UnifiedIO-1 (Lu et al., 2022, Allen Institute for AI)** is the first single Seq2Seq model for a wide range of AI tasks, trained jointly on 90+ datasets and 95 tasks using a T5-style Transformer encoder-decoder. All inputs/outputs are encoded as tokens in a shared vocabulary (~50k tokens: 32k text, 16k image via VQ-VAE, 1k location). Training used a two-stage pipeline: pretraining (text and image denoising) followed by multi-task joint training with balanced sampling (proportional to √dataset size within groups). Models scaled from 71M to 2.9B parameters. On the GRIT benchmark, it was the first model to support all 7 tasks with the highest average score (64.3 vs 32.0 for GPV-2). Weaknesses include detection struggles in cluttered scenes, image generation capped by VQ-VAE quality, prompt sensitivity, weaker language performance than frontier LLMs, and task imbalance in training.

**UnifiedIO-2** extends the unified architecture to audio, video, and action capabilities with three input encoders (LLaMA for text, ViT for images, Audio Spectrogram Transformer for audio) and thin projection layers, scaling from 1.1 to 6.8B parameters. Gradient stability is achieved through 2D rotary encodings, QK normalization, scaled cosine attention, and Mixture of training with Z-loss. Pretraining used 600 TB of data (33% NLP, 40% image-text pairs, 25% audio/video, 1% 3D embodiment) plus instruction fine-tuning. Training uses a dynamic packing strategy where examples are concatenated up to a 1152-token limit with attention masking, unpacked to maximum 2048 tokens. The presentation notes CoDi (large diffusion layers decoding an aligned latent space) as related work, and observes that CoDi performs better on certain audio/visual generation tasks. The conclusion frames UnifiedIO-2 as the first autoregressive multi-modal model covering vision, text, audio, and action, while posing the question of whether it should be the last.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Kosmos-2: Grounding Multimodal Large Language Models to the World [Quick Review] ---
URL: https://liner.com/review/kosmos2-grounding-multimodal-large-language-models-to-the-world

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Kosmos-2: Grounding Multimodal Large Language Models to the World, by Zhiliang Peng, Wenhui Wang, and collaborators (published June 26, 2023), addresses a major limitation in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): the lack of robust grounding capabilities that enable precise linking of text to the visual world. The proposed method introduces KOSMOS-2, a grounded MLLM that represents referring expressions as Markdown links with location tokens, enabling it to perceive object descriptions and ground text to visual regions. The researchers built a large-scale dataset of grounded image-text pairs called GRIT, linking text spans in captions to spatial locations. KOSMOS-2 converts bounding box coordinates into discrete location tokens integrated with text tokens in a unified input format, and is trained using a Transformer-based causal language model with next-word prediction on an augmented dataset including GRIT.

Experimental results show KOSMOS-2 achieves strong zero-shot performance on phrase grounding, significantly outperforming prior zero-shot models. On Flickr30k Entities test split, it achieved 78.7% R@1 (80.1% R@5 and R@10), versus GRILL's 18.9% R@1. It also surpassed fine-tuned models like VisualBert by 7.4% R@1. However, its accuracy on referring expression comprehension (RefCOCO) is lower than fine-tuned models (52.32% on RefCOCO val vs. OFA's 90.05%), suggesting it struggles with shorter, more specific referring expressions. KOSMOS-2 maintains competitive results on traditional perception-language tasks (image captioning, VQA) and language tasks relative to KOSMOS-1. The paper has 68 references and 830 citations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A significant limitation in existing MLLMs is the absence of robust grounding capabilities, hindering efficient human-AI interaction and limiting the precision of visual answers."

This presentation (given in Vienna, Austria) introduces Kosmos-2, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) that grounds language to the real world by encoding and decoding bounding-box coordinates as location tokens. **Motivation & Objective:** The paper addresses the prohibitive computational cost of end-to-end vision-and-language pre-training. Existing frozen model approaches (like Flamingo) rely mainly on image-to-text generation loss, which insufficiently bridges the vision-language modality gap. **Proposed Method:** BLIP-2 introduces a lightweight Querying Transformer (Q-Former) as a trainable module to bridge frozen image encoders and frozen large language models. The Q-Former is pre-trained in two stages:
- Stage 1: Vision-language representation learning with a frozen image encoder, jointly optimizing Image-Text Contrastive Learning, Image-grounded Text Generation, and Image-Text Matching objectives to ensure queries extract text-relevant visual representations.
- Stage 2: Vision-to-language generative learning with a frozen LLM, using projected query embeddings as soft visual prompts. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on tasks like VQAv2 and image captioning with significantly fewer trainable parameters.

**Experimental Results:** The review addresses six research questions covering zero-shot performance, instructed zero-shot generation, impact of first-stage learning, fine-tuned image captioning, fine-tuned VQA, and image-text retrieval. Key findings include:
- BLIP-2 surpasses existing state-of-the-art models in zero-shot performance, outperforming Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 while using 54 times fewer trainable parameters.
- It shows slightly lower performance on OK-VQA compared to Flamingo80B (which benefits from a larger 70B Chinchilla LLM for open-world knowledge tasks).
- Performance scales positively with stronger frozen components (ViT-g over ViT-L, larger OPT models, or instruction-tuned FlanT5).
- The first-stage vision-language representation learning is crucial; without it, the Q-Former struggles to bridge the modality gap, causing degraded zero-shot performance and potential catastrophic forgetting.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models, a research paper submitted on June 15, 2023, by Junnan Li, Dongxu Li, Silvio Savarese, and Steven Hoi.

**Core Problem:** Traditional vision-and-language pre-training is prohibitively expensive due to end-to-end training of large-scale models.

**Key Innovation:** BLIP-2 introduces a generic and efficient pre-training strategy that bootstraps vision-language pre-training from off-the-shelf frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language models (LLMs). The modality gap is bridged using a lightweight **Querying Transformer (Q-Former)**, which contains only 188 million parameters and serves as the sole trainable component.

**Q-Former Architecture:** The Q-Former uses learnable query embeddings that extract visual information from the frozen image encoder through cross-attention layers and interact with text through self-attention layers, with interaction controlled by attention masks. This design creates an information bottleneck that forces extraction of the most relevant visual features for text generation.

**Two-Stage Pre-Training Strategy:**
- **Stage 1 (Vision-Language Representation Learning):** Connects the Q-Former to a frozen image encoder using three objectives: Image-Text Contrastive Learning (ITC), Image-grounded Text Generation (ITG), and Image-Text Matching (ITM).
- **Stage 2 (Vision-to-Language Generative Learning):** Connects the pre-trained Q-Former to a frozen LLM. The Q-Former's output embeddings are linearly projected to match the LLM's input dimension and serve as "soft visual prompts."

**Performance:** BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks with significantly fewer trainable parameters. Notably, it outperforms Flamingo80B on zero-shot VQAv2 by 8.7% while using 54× fewer trainable parameters.

**Results and Analysis:**
- Demonstrates remarkable zero-shot capabilities in instructed image-to-text generation when connected to powerful LLMs like FlanT5, following natural language instructions for visual reasoning, conversation, and detailed content generation.
- Ablation studies show Stage 1 representation learning is critical—without it, performance drops significantly due to catastrophic forgetting in the LLM, and the ITG objective is particularly important.
- The model supports various image encoders (ViT-L/14, ViT-g/14) and LLMs (OPT family, FlanT5 family), demonstrating generic applicability.

**Limitations:** The authors acknowledge limitations including inaccurate knowledge, incorrect reasoning, and outdated information.

**Significance:** BLIP-2 represents a paradigm shift by demonstrating effective multimodal models can be built through strategic combination of existing components rather than end-to-end training. It is available open-source through Salesforce's LAVIS project.

Method: The paper pre-trains the Q-Former following a two-stage strategy. **Motivation & Objective:** Current multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) lack a visual search mechanism, which impedes their ability to focus on critical visual details in high-resolution or crowded images. The dependency on pre-trained vision encoders, often trained on low-resolution images, leads to information bottlenecks and an inability to proactively seek missing visual information. - SEAL: A novel MLLM meta-architecture incorporating an LLM-guided visual search mechanism for active reasoning and retrieval of visual information in complex tasks.
- V*: An LLM-guided visual search algorithm that leverages LLM common sense knowledge to perform informed searches across varying image resolutions.
- The SEAL framework integrates a VQA LLM with a visual working memory (VWM) to process initial features and dynamically incorporate search results.
- V*Bench: A dedicated benchmark to evaluate MLLMs' detailed visual grounding in high-resolution images.

SEAL achieved 74.78% on attribute recognition and 76.31% on spatial reasoning, versus GPT-4V's 51.30% and 60.52% respectively. Most open-source end-to-end MLLMs scored only in the 30-40% range (near random guessing), exposing the information bottleneck of fixed-resolution pre-trained vision encoders. Even higher-resolution encoders (like LLaVA-1.5 with CLIP-ViT-L-336px) fell significantly short, demonstrating that an active, LLM-guided visual search mechanism is necessary to dynamically focus on relevant visual information.

--- SOURCE 32: V*: Guided Visual Search as a Core Mechanism in Multimodal ... ---
URL: https://vstar-seal.github.io

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage introduces V*, an LLM-guided visual search mechanism for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), created by Penghao Wu (UC San Diego) and Saining Xie (New York University), published December 21, 2023 (arXiv:2312.14135). The work addresses a key limitation of current MLLMs: their dependence on pre-trained vision encoders (e.g., CLIP) that are typically trained on low-resolution images (224×224 or 336×336 pixels), causing them to overlook important details in high-resolution images. Current MLLMs also cannot identify or proactively seek missing visual information—scenarios where even GPT-4V fails.

The proposed integration creates a new MLLM meta-architecture called SEAL (Show, Search, and Tell), composed of a VQA LLM and a visual search model that collaborate through a visual working memory (VWM). The VWM has four blocks: the initial textual question, the initial image, target object crops after search, and coordinates of searched targets. An instantiation uses the LLaVA-7B model.

The V* algorithm works as follows: given an image and a textual target expression, the model first attempts to locate the target directly, obtaining coordinates, confidence scores, and a search cue heatmap. If no object is found (confidence below threshold), it examines the heatmap for target-specific cues. If the cue is prominent, it guides search directly; otherwise, the MLLM uses common sense knowledge and image context to provide a contextual cue about the target's whereabouts. The algorithm then recursively divides the image into 4 non-overlapping equal-sized patches, assigns search priority scores from the heatmap, and processes patches sequentially until the target is found or the patch becomes smaller than a threshold. The V* algorithm is inspired by the A* informed search algorithm, where sub-images are nodes, cost g(n) is a uniform positive constant, and the heuristic h(n) is the negative of the search priority score.

To evaluate the approach, the authors built V*Bench, based on 191 high-resolution images from SAM with average resolution 2246×1582, containing two sub-tasks: attribute recognition (115 samples, e.g., color, material) and spatial relationship reasoning (76 samples). SEAL outperformed other open-source MLLMs and LLM-tool-using systems on this benchmark. The LLM-guided search strategy significantly reduced average search length compared to random and sequential baselines (evaluated on 245 target objects), and both guiding cues (target-specific and contextual) proved helpful. Comparisons with human eye-fixation data from the COCO-Search18 dataset showed V* achieves similar efficiency to human fixations.
</summary>

URL: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026/papers/Tan_UZ3DVG_Unaided_Zero-Shot_3D_Visual_Grounding_with_Generated_Language_Conditions_CVPR_2026_paper.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Summary of UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding with Generated Language Conditions**

This paper, presented at CVPR, introduces UZ3DVG, a novel zero-shot 3D visual grounding (3DVG) framework that localizes target objects in 3D scenes using natural language descriptions. Unlike existing zero-shot methods that rely on additional 2D images or multi-turn interactions with large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) during inference—causing high latency and computational cost—UZ3DVG is the first zero-shot 3DVG model that, during inference, uses only 3D point clouds and text, without 2D imagery or external LLM/VLM interaction.

**Key Components:**
- **MSAG-RC (Multi-Source Spatial Annotation and Reasoning Chain Generator):** Processes RGB-D images to generate 3D spatial pseudo-labels and reasoning chains, bridging the gap between 2D foundation models and 3D labels.
- **RCD (Reasoning Chain Distillation):** Transfers reasoning knowledge from a large teacher network to a lightweight student network, enabling efficient inference.
- **GeoSM (Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling):** Captures both global and local geometric relationships to align textual reasoning with 3D spatial structures.
- **TSVDE (Text-Semantic-Guided Visual Detail Enhancement):** Enriches visual features with fine-grained details from text-relevant regions.

**Key Results:**
- Achieves state-of-the-art on ScanRefer: Acc@0.25/0.5 of 45.42%/41.08% (beats SeeGround by 1.32%/1.68%).
- On the challenging "Multiple" subset of ScanRefer: Acc@0.25/0.5 of 40.49%/36.33% (beats SeeGround by 6.49%/6.33%).
- On NR3D: Overall accuracy of 46.5%, surpassing ZSVG3D by 7.5% and SeeGround by 0.4%.
- Inference speed: 7.69 FPS (approximately 38× faster than SeeGround's 0.2 FPS).

**Training Paradigm:** A VLM is used only during training to generate pseudo-labels and reasoning chains. The lightweight 3DVG model is trained using these generated annotations and does not require any external models during inference.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.10345v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive survey paper on visual grounding in vision-language models (VLMs). Visual grounding refers to the ability of a model to identify regions within visual input that match textual descriptions. The paper covers:

**Definition:** Visual grounding is defined broadly as the capability to precisely localize and identify specific objects, regions, or concepts within a visual context, conditioned on natural language descriptions or instructions.

**Key Research Domains:**
- Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) and Generalized REC (GREC)
- Grounded Visual Question Answering (GVQA)
- Grounded Captioning (GC)
- Agents interacting with Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs)
- Grounded Reasoning

**Representation Methods:**
- Object-centric vs. pixel-level approaches
- Discretized vs. raw coordinate formats
- Set-of-Marks (SOM) method

**VLM Architecture Components:**
- **Vision Encoder:** Typically CLIP-based ViT models (SigLIP shown to slightly outperform CLIP)
- **Connector Module:** Linear projection, MLP, pooling, convolution, cross-attention, or resamplers (Q-former, Perceiver)
- **Language Backbone:** Predominantly transformer-based; Mamba explored but transformers perform significantly better on grounding tasks

**Image Resolution:** High-resolution images reduce hallucinations and improve multimodal understanding. Approaches include positional-encoding interpolation and handling arbitrary resolution via sub-image division.

**Training Pipeline:**
- Image-text alignment pretraining using large-scale web-derived datasets
- Synthetic re-captioning and quality-filtering techniques
- Fine-tuning via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and alignment phase

**Key Findings:** Grounding mitigates hallucinations by encouraging models to commit to specific spatial locations, though some studies show grounding objectives do not exhibit a causal relationship with reductions in object hallucinations. The paper includes a detailed table of VLMs with grounding capabilities (Table 1) listing 25+ models with their architectures and grounding capabilities.

**Challenges:** Modality gap, computational cost of high-resolution processing, reproducibility issues, and inconsistent evaluation protocols.
</summary>

<summary>
SR-3D (Spatial Region 3D) is a 3D-aware vision-language model developed by researchers from UC San Diego, MIT, and NVIDIA. It connects single-view 2D images and multi-view 3D data through a shared visual token space, enabling flexible region prompting via bounding boxes, segmentation masks, or direct 3D annotations without exhaustive multi-frame labeling.

**Key Technical Contributions:**
- Enriches 2D visual features with 3D positional embeddings, allowing the model to leverage strong 2D priors for accurate spatial reasoning across frames
- Introduces a Dynamic Tiling-based Region Extractor that handles high-resolution images and produces robust region embeddings
- Uses a unified architecture where both single-view and multi-view data flow through the same model, with a canonical 3D positional representation

**Training:**
- Single-view VLM initialized from NVILA-Lite-8B, fine-tuned on ~7M samples (instruction tuning + region-prompted datasets)
- Multi-view fine-tuning on ScanQA, SQA3D, Scan2Cap, and EmbodiedScan datasets
- Uses off-the-shelf depth estimation (DepthAnythingV2) for single-view; ground-truth depth for multi-view training

**Key Results:**
- State-of-the-art on 3D QA benchmarks: ScanQA (CIDEr 109.3, EM 30.4), SQA3D (EM 62.2), Scan2Cap (CIDEr 97.9)

- On VSI-Bench (global spatial understanding), outperforms all open-source models and competes with API-based models

**Applications:**
- Works with in-the-wild videos using off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction (e.g., CUT3R, MAST3R) instead of ground-truth depth
- Maintains strong performance with CUT3R-reconstructed point clouds (CIDEr 109.3 vs 109.3 with GT)
- Eliminates need for costly 3D annotations or dense per-frame labeling

**Key Findings:**
- Single-view pre-training significantly enhances multi-view performance
- 3D positional embeddings provide marginal benefit alone but are essential when combined with scaling
- A 2D VLM trained exclusively on single-view data exhibits strong zero-shot spatial reasoning in 3D scenes

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] LL3DA: Visual Interactive Instruction Tuning for Omni-3D Understanding ... ---
URL: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Chen_LL3DA_Visual_Interactive_Instruction_Tuning_for_Omni-3D_Understanding_Reasoning_and_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
LL3DA is a Large Language 3D Assistant (CVPR paper) presented by researchers from Fudan University, Tencent PCG, NUS, and A*STAR that enables a large language model to understand, reason, and plan in complex 3D environments. Unlike prior approaches that project multi-view 2D features into 3D space (which is computationally expensive and ignores geometry/depth information), LL3DA takes point clouds as direct input and responds to both textual instructions and visual interactions (clicks and 3D box annotations). This visual interaction capability helps remove ambiguities inherent in plain text instructions within cluttered 3D scenes.

Architecture: The model uses (1) a frozen masked transformer scene encoder pre-trained on ScanNet detection, (2) a visual prompt encoder that encodes user clicks via 3D Fourier positional embeddings and box annotations via ROI features from a pre-trained 3D detector, and (3) a multi-modal transformer (Q-Former inspired) that aggregates the 3D scene embeddings, visual prompts, and textual instructions into 32 learnable query tokens. These query tokens are projected as a prefix to the textual instructions for a frozen OPT-1.3B LLM backbone. 3D coordinates are converted to plain text tokens (e.g., '<obj>cx, cy, cz, w, h, l</obj>') with values discretized to [0,255] integers, fitting the existing LLM vocabulary without additional learnable tokens.

Key results: LL3DA achieves state-of-the-art performance on 3D Dense Captioning (74.17% C@0.25 and 65.19% C@0.5 on ScanRefer; 51.18% C@0.5 on Nr3D, beating Vote2Cap-DETR by +3.38% and +7.34%) and 3D Question Answering (76.79% CiDEr on ScanQA validation, surpassing 3D-LLM by +7.39%). Adding visual clicks at test time improves ScanQA CiDEr by +6.12%. Ablation studies show early fusion of visual prompts (+3.45% C@0.5), auxiliary "localize" instructions and click prompts improve performance, and textual instructions are beneficial. The model also functions as a generalist across tasks without fine-tuning, with generalist weights serving as strong initialization for fine-tuning.

Datasets: Trained on ScanNet (1,201 train / 312 validation scenes) with annotations from ScanRefer, Nr3D, ScanQA, and the ScanNet subset of 3D-LLM, covering dense captioning, QA, scene description, embodied conversation, and planning. Training requires no more than eight RTX 3090 GPUs within a day.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"LL3DA takes point cloud as the direct input and responds to both text instructions and visual interactions. The additional visual interaction enables LMMs to better comprehend human interactions with the 3D environment and further remove the ambiguities within plain texts."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Language-to-Space Programming for Training-Free 3D Visual Grounding ---
URL: https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.191.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, presented at EMNLP 2025, introduces Language-to-Space Programming (LASP), a training-free method for 3D visual grounding (3DVG). LASP addresses the dual challenges of accuracy and efficiency in 3DVG by using LLM-generated Python code as spatial relation encoders. These encoders compute relation features from object bounding boxes, and an automatic pipeline with test suites evaluates and optimizes the codes across multiple iterations.

Key methodology: (1) LLMs generate Python class-based spatial relation encoders (e.g., "above", "near", "left") that compute pairwise relation features from object geometry; (2) test suites evaluate the codes using test cases from the Nr3D dataset, synthesizing error messages for failed cases; (3) LLMs iteratively optimize codes based on these error messages up to Niter iterations; (4) a semantic parser converts referring utterances into symbolic expressions, and an executor aggregates category and relation features to compute matching scores; (5) a VLM (GPT-4o) module disambiguates candidates using stitched ScanNet images.

Results: LASP achieves 52.9% accuracy on the Nr3D dataset (60.7% easy, 45.3% hard), ranking among the best training-free methods. With ground-truth labels it reaches 67.8% accuracy. It substantially reduces grounding time (7.7s vs. 50.3s for VLM-Grounder) and token costs (3.1k vs. 12k tokens) compared to agent-based methods. On the GRScenes dataset, LASP achieves 90.0% accuracy vs. 15.6% for random baseline, demonstrating cross-dataset generalization. Replacing LLM-generated encoders with human-written functions drops accuracy to 44.0%, highlighting the value of the automated codes.

Ablation studies show the critical importance of optimization, error messages, and in-context examples for generating accurate relation encoders. LASP's codes implicitly learn dataset priors, such as viewpoint assumptions (in 98 of 100 "view-dependent" sentences, the anchor object is the "faced" object). The one-time offline code generation cost is amortized over all test instances.

Limitations include: performance gaps vs. recent supervised methods; symbolic expression struggles with ordinal phrases; limited relation coverage; simplified scene representation (bounding boxes only); test suites only handle atomic relations; and dependence on pre-trained 3D detectors/classifiers. Code is available at https://github.com/InternRobotics/LaSP. Authors are from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. The work is funded by the National Key R&D Program of China.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"LASP introduces LLM-generated codes to analyze 3D spatial relations among objects, along with a pipeline that evaluates and optimizes the codes automatically. Experimental results demonstrate that LASP achieves 52.9% accuracy on the Nr3D benchmark, ranking among the best training-free methods. Moreover, it substantially reduces the grounding time and token costs, offering a balanced trade-off between performance and efficiency."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: LL3DA: Visual Interactive Instruction Tuning for Omni-3D Understanding, Reasoning, and Planning ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2311.18651

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents LL3DA (Large Language 3D Assistant), a novel LMM-based approach for omni-3D understanding, reasoning, and planning. Unlike existing methods that rely on multi-view images projected to 3D (causing computational overhead and performance degradation), LL3DA takes point cloud data as direct input and responds to both textual instructions and visual prompts (user clicks and 3D box annotations).

**Methodology:** The model uses Interactor3D, a multi-modal transformer with a frozen 3D scene encoder (masked transformer pre-trained on ScanNet detection), a visual prompt encoder, and a Q-Former that aggregates information from textual instructions, visual prompts, and 3D scenes into 32 fixed-length learnable querying tokens. These are projected as prefixes to a frozen OPT-1.3B LLM. The Q-Former is initialized only with pre-trained BERT word and position embeddings (full BERT initialization caused repetitive outputs). 3D coordinates are converted to plain text using special tokens (e.g., "«loc»xx, yy, zz<</loc»") with values discretized to unsigned integers [0,255].

**Tasks covered:** 3D Dense Captioning, 3D Question Answering, Scene Description, and Embodied Conversation/Planning. Tasks use "### human:" and "### assistant:" identifiers for multi-turn conversations and distinguish between "describe" vs "describe and localize" (and "answer" vs "answer and localize") instructions.

**Key Results:**
- 3D Dense Captioning: Achieves 65.19% C@0.5 on ScanRefer (+3.38% over Vote2Cap-DETR) and 51.18% C@0.5 on Nr3D (+7.34%), surpassing all prior SOTA methods including multi-task pretrained models (UniT3D, 3DJCG, 3D-VLP) and 3D-VisTA.
- 3D Question Answering: Achieves 76.79% CiDEr on ScanQA validation, 78.16% on test with object, and 70.29% on test without object—surpassing 3D-LLM by +7.39% CiDEr on validation.
- Visual prompts (clicks) during QA evaluation improve results by +6.12% C by removing ambiguities.
- As a generalist (without fine-tuning), LL3DA achieves 62.98% C@0.5 on ScanRefer and 75.67% CiDEr on ScanQA, with fine-tuned weights serving as strong initialization (+2.35% C@0.5 over scratch training on ScanRefer).
- Ablations show unified transformer design (+3.45% C@0.5), auxiliary localization instructions, and click prompts all improve performance.

**Implementation details:** Trained with AdamW optimizer (weight decay 0.1, LR decaying from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶ with cosine annealing, ~100k iterations), batch size 16, ≤8 Nvidia RTX3090 (24G) GPUs within a day. Uses 40k sampled points per scene. Inference uses beam search (beam size 4) or top-k (k=50) + top-p (p=0.95) sampling. Supplementary evaluations show LL3DA significantly outperforms zero-shot frozen LLMs (OPT variants, LLAMA-7B) on scene description, embodied dialogue (best: 260.07 CiDEr with beam search), and embodied planning (best: 196.78 CiDEr with beam search). Codes and pre-trained weights will be fully released.
</summary>

**Architecture and Training:**
- LEO processes egocentric 2D images, 3D point clouds, and texts as input, handling output of both textual responses and embodied action commands via a unified token-sequence architecture
- Uses a decoder-only LLM (Vicuna-7B) with LoRA tuning; 2D images encoded by OpenCLIP ConvNext, 3D objects encoded by PointNet++ followed by a Spatial Transformer
- Employs two-stage learning: (1) 3D VL alignment (LEO-align dataset) and (2) 3D VLA instruction tuning (LEO-instruct dataset)
- Model has ~7B parameters with ~142M tuned parameters; trained via prefix language modeling (GPT-style autoregressive objective)
- Total datasets include object captioning (660K), object referring (354K), scene captioning (20K) for alignment; and 3D captioning (37K), 3D QA (83K), 3D dialogue (11K), task planning (14K), navigation (60K), and manipulation (300K) for instruction tuning

**LLM-Assisted Data Generation:**
- Uses scene-graph-based prompting (from 3DSSG) for richer context compared to box-based prompting
- Proposes object-centric chain of thought (O-CoT) prompting to combat LLM hallucination
- Implements refinement procedures using regular expression matching and scene graph retrieval, achieving 100% accuracy on counting, existence, and non-existence QA tasks (vs. 40-96.8% for baseline methods)

**Key Results:**
- Surpasses state-of-the-art task-specific models on 3D captioning (Scan2Cap: CIDEr 72.4), 3D QA (ScanQA), and embodied reasoning (SQA3D), without task-specific fine-tuning
- Comparable to state-of-the-art on robotic manipulation (CLIPort) and embodied navigation (ObjNav on MP3D/HM3D), with better SPL and zero-shot generalization to novel scenes
- Ablations show: alignment stage provides consistent benefits; generalist-style tuning outperforms specialist training; VLA co-training can slightly harm VL performance; dialogue/planning data reduce hallucination; data balancing mitigates hallucination issues by adding negative samples
- Scaling law analysis shows log-linear loss improvement with data scale, and LLM scaling gives consistent gains (Vicuna-7B > OPT-1.3B, with potential saturation between Vicuna-7B and Vicuna-13B)

**Contributions:** First embodied generalist agent for 3D world; simple framework connecting object-centric 3D representation with LLMs; large-scale comprehensive training datasets; LLM-assisted high-quality 3D VL data generation pipeline; released data, code, and model weights. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper explores transferring pre-trained static 3D point cloud models to the 4D point cloud video domain—the first such exploration. The authors identify that static models capture only spatial information while neglecting temporal dynamics, leading to significant performance gaps when directly transferred. They propose a novel Cross-frame Spatio-temporal Adaptation (CSA) strategy with two key components:
1. Point Tube Adapter: An embedding layer that replaces the static model's embedding layer, grouping points into "point tubes" along both spatial and temporal dimensions (with relative spatio-temporal displacements as features), encoded via an extended lightweight 4D PointNet.
2. Geometric Constraint Temporal Adapter (GCTA): A module that constructs a cross-frame KNN graph based on spatial distance between point tubes, using EdgeConv-style edge features (combining global variation fj−fi with local structural features fi) and max pooling to capture long-term global dynamics.
The pre-trained model's backbone parameters are frozen; only the Point Tube Adapter, GCTA, position encoders (custom MLP-based, per-layer), and task head are fine-tuned.

Experimental results: The method was tested on 3D action recognition (MSR-Action3D) and gesture recognition (SHREC'17), using Point-BERT, Point-MAE, and PointGPT-S as baselines pre-trained on ShapeNet.
- On MSR-Action3D with 24 frames, Point-MAE+CSA achieved 95.12%, outperforming all supervised (best: X4D-SceneFormer at 93.90%) and self-supervised (best: C2P at 94.76%, MaST-Pre at 94.08%) methods across all temporal configurations.
- On SHREC'17, PointGPT-S+CSA reached 96.5%, Point-BERT+CSA achieved 96.2%, and Point-MAE+CSA got 95.2%—outperforming supervised (best: Kinet at 95.2%) and self-supervised (best: PointCMP at 93.3%) approaches.

Ablation studies (with Point-MAE on 12 frames): Baseline frozen model (A0) scored 77.35%; adding Point Tube Adapter (A1) reached 83.97%; adding position encoders (A2) reached 87.11%; Point Tube Adapter + GCTA (A3) reached 94.08%; full model (A4) reached 95.12%. The GCTA's optimal k-neighbors value was k=20 (95.12%), with performance degrading for too few (k=1 or 5) or too many (k=25, 30) neighbors. Using the full video as temporal slice length yielded the best performance (95.12%). The GCTA placed in a "Bypass" configuration produced the best accuracy. CSA outperformed other tuning strategies (valilla adapter, VPT-Deep, IDPT). Attention visualization confirmed the GCTA helps the model focus on key frames where actions occur.

Code is available at https://github.com/LvBaixuan/Point-CSA. The work is supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China grants and other funding agencies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 21: [PDF] CORE-3D: CONTEXT-AWARE OPEN-VOCABULARY - OpenReview ---
URL: https://openreview.net/pdf/9a980b56e8e243213d30d276a3e469eafd2e879e.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces CORE-3D, a training-free pipeline for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding that addresses limitations in existing zero-shot 3D semantic mapping approaches. Current methods assign CLIP embedding vectors to 2D masks generated by vision-language models and project them into 3D, but they suffer from fragmented/incomplete masks (over-segmentation), limited semantic context when applying CLIP directly to isolated masks, and multi-view inconsistencies.

METHOD: The pipeline has three main contributions: (1) Progressive SemanticSAM refinement that incrementally adjusts granularity levels to generate more accurate and complete object-level masks than vanilla SAM, using overlap thresholds to remove redundancy and DBSCAN clustering to separate objects that are adjacent in 2D but separated in 3D; (2) A context-aware CLIP encoding strategy that aggregates five complementary crops per mask (mask crop, bounding box crop, large-context crop at 2.5x scale, huge-context crop at 4x scale, and surroundings crop at 3x scale with the mask blacked out), combined via weighted averaging where the surroundings embedding is subtracted with negative weight to enforce contrastive context; (3) Multi-view 3D mask merging using a symmetric-balanced IoV criterion and geometric heuristics to consolidate overlapping predictions, with averaged unified embeddings.

OBJECT RETRIEVAL: The pipeline extends to natural-language object retrieval in four stages: (1) Query structuring using an LLM to parse free-form queries into structured form Π(q) = (m, R, Ω) (main object, related objects, orientation constraints); (2) Candidate mining via CLIP similarity with top-K matching (avoiding score thresholds) and voxelization for deduplication; (3) View selection with VLM verification of candidates in RGB frames with bounding boxes; (4) Orientation grounding using canonical views at discretized yaw bins resolved by a VLM, followed by final LLM reasoning over verified candidates, referenced objects, and orientation cues.

RESULTS: On the Replica and ScanNet 3D semantic segmentation benchmarks, CORE-3D achieved the best performance across ALL evaluated approaches including training-based (LERF, OpenNeRF, LangSplat, OpenGaussian) and zero-shot methods (ConceptFusion, OpenMask3D, ConceptGraphs, HOV-SG, BBQ-CLIP). On Replica: mAcc 0.38, mIoU 0.29, fmIoU 0.56 (vs. BBQ-CLIP's 0.38/0.27/0.48). On ScanNet: mAcc 0.61, mIoU 0.36, fmIoU 0.46 (vs. BBQ-CLIP's 0.56/0.34/0.36). On the Sr3D+ benchmark (661 sampled instructions), the method achieved grounding accuracy of 41.8 (A@0.1) and 35.6 (A@0.25) overall, substantially outperforming baselines (BBQ: 34.2/22.7, BBQ-CLIP: 14.4/8.8, ConceptGraphs: 13.3/6.2, OpenFusion: 12.6/2.4).

ABLATIONS: Progressive multi-granularity mask generation outperforms vanilla SAM and single-granularity SemanticSAM configurations; context-aware CLIP embeddings strongly outperform the finetuned OvSeg model (same number of parameters as the Large CLIP backbone used, but no finetuning needed); and mask-size-based extension ratios outperform neighbor-coverage-based extension mechanisms.

IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS: Uses EVA02-CLIP (Large) for visual-text alignment, qwen2.5-vl-32b-instruct as the VLM, gpt-5-mini for object extraction, and openai-o4-mini for final decision-making. Experiments run on a single NVIDIA RTX4090 with VLM/LLM components accessed via external APIs. No 3D supervision or task-specific training required.
</summary>

"Existing foundation-model-based approaches still struggle to construct coherent and reliable 3D semantic maps." "We present a training-free pipeline that overcomes these challenges by improving both segmentation and embedding generation through progressive refinement and context-aware encoding." "Our method achieves the best performance across all evaluated approaches—including both training-based and zero-shot methods." "Our method substantially outperforms all baselines across both IoU thresholds and all difficulty subsets." "Our results suggest that leveraging richer 2D segmentation and embedding strategies is a powerful alternative to supervision-heavy pipelines, especially in cluttered, open-world environments."

--- SOURCE 24: ConceptFusion: Open-set Multimodal 3D Mapping ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
ConceptFusion is an open-source research project (presented at Robotics: Science and Systems, RSS 2023) that builds open-set, multimodal 3D maps of environments. Unlike existing semantic 3D mapping approaches that operate in a "closed-set" setting (limited to a finite set of concepts predefined at training time and queryable only via class labels or text), ConceptFusion is (i) fundamentally open-set, enabling reasoning beyond a closed set of concepts, and (ii) inherently multi-modal, supporting diverse query types including language, images, audio, and 3D geometry, all working together.

The method leverages the open-set capabilities of foundation models pretrained on internet-scale data (e.g., CLIP) to reason across modalities. It constructs pixel-aligned features from off-the-shelf foundation models that typically only produce image-level (global) embeddings via a proposed zero-shot pixel alignment technique: it processes images to generate class-agnostic object masks, extracts local features per region, computes a global image feature, and fuses region-specific (local) and global features. This approach captures long-tailed and fine-grained concepts that supervised methods like LSeg and OpenSeg forget during fine-tuning.

Key technical contributions and findings:
- Achieves effective zero-shot spatial reasoning without any additional training or fine-tuning.
- Outperforms supervised approaches by more than 40% margin on 3D IoU when retaining long-tailed concepts.
- Demonstrates 3D spatial reasoning (e.g., "What is the distance between the refrigerator and the television?") using a large language model to parse queries into executable function calls.
- Handles long-form text queries, click-queries (with cosine similarity retrieval), and audio/image queries.
- Introduces the UnCoCo dataset: 20 RGB-D sequences with 78 commonly found objects, annotated with text, audio, click, and image queries plus ground-truth 2D and 3D retrieval results (created because no existing dataset supported evaluating long-tailed and multimodal reasoning).

The paper evaluates ConceptFusion on real-world datasets, simulated home environments, a real-world tabletop manipulation task (e.g., pushing objects like "goldfish" brand snacks or a "Baymax" plush toy to specified locations), and an autonomous driving platform (successfully navigating to a "football field" based on open-set text query).

Multiple author affiliations include MIT, Université de Montréal, University of Toronto, IIIT Hyderabad, CMU, Amazon, Matician, and DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory. The project also lists concurrent work including CLIP-Fields, OpenScene, LERF, NLMap-SayCan, and 3D-CLR.

--- SOURCE 2: Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding from Vision-Language ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.22429

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This arXiv paper (arXiv:2505.22429v1, 28 May 2025) introduces SeeGround, a training-free, zero-shot 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) framework that leverages 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to localize objects in 3D scenes without requiring 3D-specific training or labeled data. The framework bypasses the need for expensive 3D supervision by using a hybrid input format that pairs query-aligned rendered 2D images with spatially enriched textual descriptions derived from a 3D object detector (via an Object Lookup Table, OLT).

**Core Architecture:** SeeGround consists of three main components: (1) a Multimodal 3D Representation module that converts 3D scenes into a hybrid representation combining rendered 2D images with text-based spatial descriptions; (2) a Perspective Adaptation Module (PAM) that dynamically selects optimal viewpoints based on the query (using an anchor object identified by the VLM to orient the virtual camera); and (3) a Fusion Alignment Module (FAM) that uses depth-aware visual prompting to align 2D visual features with 3D spatial semantics, reducing grounding ambiguity in cluttered scenes.

**Key Results:** On ScanRefer, SeeGround achieves 75.7%/68.9% at Acc@0.25/0.5 on the "Unique" split and 34.0%/30.0% on "Multiple", surpassing all zero-shot and weakly supervised baselines (7.7% improvement over prior zero-shot methods) while approaching fully supervised performance. On Nr3D, it achieves 46.1% overall accuracy, a +7.1% improvement over the prior zero-shot state-of-the-art (ZSVG3D), with 54.5% Easy, 38.3% Hard, 42.3% View-Dependent, and 48.2% View-Independent scores. The method uses Qwen2-VL-72b as the VLM and Mask3D for object detection, though it also works with OVIR-3D and improves to 59.5% with ground-truth boxes.

**Ablation findings:** Each component contributes incrementally — 3D positions alone (37.7%), adding layout (39.7%), adding color/texture (39.5%), adding FAM (43.3%), adding PAM (45.0%), and full configuration (46.1%). Query-aligned dynamic viewpoint selection consistently outperforms static strategies (Center2Corner, Edge2Center, Corner2Center, and Bird's Eye View). The method is also robust to incomplete textual descriptions, using visual context to identify targets even when anchor objects are missing from text (which causes LLM-based methods like ZSVG3D to fail).

**Limitations:** Error analysis of 185 sampled cases shows spatial relation errors remain frequent (19%), and the method struggles with complex egocentric references and limited rendering quality from raw point clouds.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/3d-visual-grounding-3dvg

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page provides a comprehensive overview of 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG), the task of localizing objects in 3D scenes (point clouds, meshes, LiDAR sweeps) using free-form natural language descriptions, outputting oriented/axis-aligned 3D bounding boxes or instance masks. 3DVG is fundamental for robotics, embodied AI, AR/VR, and multimodal interaction.

Key task variants include scene input modalities (indoor RGB-D point clouds like ScanNet/ScanRefer, outdoor LiDAR like Talk2Car-3D, implicit representations like 3D Gaussians), supervision regimes (fully supervised, zero-shot, cross-dataset, multi-task), and query richness (from synthetic spatial templates to linguistically diverse prompts with negation, counting, coreference). A generalized real-world formulation takes as input prior scans, current scenes, memory banks of RGB-D views, and natural-language queries.

Major datasets include: ScanRefer/ScanNet (>50K queries over 800 scenes), ReferIt3D (Nr3D/Sr3D), 3RScan/ChangingGrounding (dynamic scenes, 1,482 scans, 478 environments), ViGiL3D (diagnostic benchmark of 350 prompts across 30 linguistic metrics), and outdoor Talk2Car-3D (7,115/998/2,056 splits for autonomous driving). Metrics include Accuracy @ IoU=0.25/0.5, Recall@1, action/motion cost, and dense mask-based F1.

Architectural advances span: two-stage "detect-then-ground" pipelines (PointGroup, VoteNet, Mask3D with cross-modal transformers), single-stage DETR-style end-to-end methods, sparse convolutional backbones with text-guided pruning (TSP3D achieving 12.4 FPS real-time), multi-view modeling (MVT, +11.2% on Nr3D), dense mask prediction (ConcreteNet), phrase-level alignment (3DPAG), and spatial relation modeling (AugRefer's Language-Spatial Adaptive Decoder).

Modality extensions include audio-based grounding (Audio-3DVG, SpeechRefer with ~2-3.6 pp accuracy gains under noise) and memory-driven active agents (Mem-ChangingGrounder for dynamic scenes). Zero-shot/foundation-model approaches leverage 2D VLM transfer (SeeGround, ZSVG3D using Qwen2-VL-72B, CLIP, GPT-4V; SeeGround achieves 44.1%/39.4% Acc@0.25/0.5 on ScanRefer), visual programming, constraint satisfaction (CSVG, +7.0% on ScanRefer, +11.2% on Nr3D), and hybrid representations (S²-MLLM achieving 59.2%/52.7% on ScanRefer).

Current limitations include dataset dependence and poor cross-dataset robustness, language complexity (models lose 20-30 points on negation/ordinal/multi-anchor prompts), lack of real-time/streaming/memory capabilities for pre-reconstructed static scenes, ambiguity in dense clutter, and residual vision-language alignment gaps. Future directions emphasize scalable linguistically rich datasets, self-supervised/continual learning, foundation model adaptation with explicit reasoning, memory/activeness/embodied reasoning, and multi-modal (audio) extensions.
</summary>

URL: https://cvpr.thecvf.com/virtual/2026/poster/40167

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This CVPR 2026 conference page presents the paper "UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding with Generated Language Conditions" by Wenbin Tan, Jiawen Lin, Yuan Xie, Yachao Zhang, and Yanyun Qu. The paper addresses Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding (Zero-Shot 3DVG), which localizes target objects in 3D scenes from natural language descriptions without instance-wise annotation. Existing methods rely on extra 2D images during inference and/or multi-turn LLM/VLM interactions, increasing latency, cost, and deployment complexity. UZ3DVG overcomes these limitations by taking only 3D point clouds and textual descriptions during inference with no dependency on external models. The approach introduces a new training paradigm: a VLM generates object-wise descriptions (pseudo labels) and reasoning chains to train a lightweight 3DVG model with robust spatial reasoning. Key technical components include the Open-Vocabulary Multi-Source Spatial Annotation and Reasoning Chain Generator (which produces spatial pseudo-labels and reasoning chains from RGB-D or 3D-projected 2D images), Reasoning Chain Distillation (transferring reasoning knowledge from a large teacher network to a lightweight student network), and the Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling (GeoSM) module for aligning textual reasoning with 3D spatial structures. Experiments show UZ3DVG achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on ScanRefer and NR3D benchmarks, with inference speeds up to 7.7 FPS — approximately 38 times faster than SOTA methods. The paper was presented as a poster on Fri, Jun 5, 2026, 3:00–5:00 PM PDT at ExHall A & F 221.

--- SOURCE 9: CLIP2Point: Transfer CLIP to Point Cloud Classification ... ---
URL: https://www.cs.cityu.edu.hk/~rynson/papers/iccv23f.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research paper titled "CLIP2Point: Transfer CLIP to Point Cloud Classification with Image-Depth Pre-Training," authored by researchers from Harbin Institute of Technology, Shanghai AI Laboratory, City University of Hong Kong, University of Hong Kong, and Peng Cheng Laboratory.

**Problem & Approach:**
The paper addresses the challenge of transferring vision-language (V-L) pre-trained models (specifically CLIP) to 3D point cloud tasks. The authors note that pre-training across 3D vision and language is limited by insufficient training data (CLIP uses 400M+ image-text pairs, while 3D datasets like ScanNet have only ~100k pairs). They propose CLIP2Point, an image-depth pre-training method using contrastive learning to transfer CLIP knowledge to the 3D domain.

**Key Methodological Contributions:**
1. **Pre-training Data**: Rendered 52,460 pairs of RGB images and depth maps from ShapeNet (55 object categories) using 10 views, with a new depth rendering setting that uses the minimum depth value (rather than weighted summation) with a dilation rate of 2 for better visual effect.
2. **Pre-training Scheme**: Combines intra-modality learning (enhancing invariance of depth aggregation across varying camera distances) and cross-modality learning (aligning depth features with frozen CLIP image features via contrastive losses).
3. **Gated Dual-Path Adapter (GDPA)**: A dual-path structure with global-view aggregators and gated fusion, allowing the ensemble of both CLIP visual encoder and pre-trained depth encoder for efficient downstream adaptation.

**Key Results:**
- Zero-shot classification: ModelNet10 improved from 30.23% (PointCLIP) to 66.63%; ModelNet40 from 20.18% to 49.38%; ScanObjectNN (S-OBJ ONLY) from 15.15% to 35.46%.
- 16-shot classification: Achieved 89.79% accuracy (vs 87.46% without pre-training, and 83.83% for PointCLIP with ViT-B/32).
- Fully-supervised classification on ModelNet40: Achieved 94.2% accuracy (1,024 points, 10 views), outperforming P2P (HorNet-L, 94.0% with 4,096 points, 40 views) and self-supervised methods like Point-MAE (93.8%).
- Ablation studies confirmed intra-modality learning adds 11.09% improvement, and the dual-path structure with gated fusion provides complementary benefits.

**Implementation Details:**
- Used ViT-B/32 vision transformer architecture, LAMB optimizer with learning rate 6×10-3 for pre-training (100 epochs, batch size 256).
- Pre-training data split: 41,943 training and 10,517 validation pairs. RGB image zero-shot accuracy was 54.21% vs 19.98% for depth maps before pre-training.

**Limitations & Future Work:**
The authors note that synthetic pre-training data limits performance on real-world noisy datasets with backgrounds. Future work includes using more realistic data and extending to other 3D tasks (detection, segmentation) and modalities (e.g., near-infrared images). Code is available at https://github.com/tyhuang0428/CLIP2Point.
</summary>

**Dataset & Methodology:**

- The proposed MSR3D baseline model achieves superior performance on both MSQA (54.13% overall) and MSNN (48.4% accuracy).

- Data scaling consistently improves performance across QA, situation, and scene factors.

5. The plan is executed by the goal-conditioned policy within the VNM.

The project includes real-world demonstrations of instruction following and experiments showing the system can disambiguate ambiguous instructions by discovering separate paths to the same goal based on fine-grained instruction modifications. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents ImagineNav, a mapless, open-vocabulary object navigation framework that leverages Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for embodied navigation. The core approach translates complex navigation planning into a best-view image selection problem: the agent uses a Where2Imagine module to predict future 3D navigation waypoints aligned with human navigation habits, generates novel view images at those waypoints using a pretrained diffusion-based Novel View Synthesis (NVS) model, and then uses GPT-4o-mini as a high-level planner to select the most promising exploration direction from the imagined images. Methodology: The Where2Imagine module is a ResNet-18 trained from scratch on human demonstration trajectories from the Habitat-Web project (filtered to angular deviations within ±30° and depth >0.3m), which predicts relative poses (Δx, Δy, θ) for potential waypoints. The NVS model generates new view images at 60° intervals. GPT-4o-mini receives the stitched imagined observations and outputs a JSON with {Reason, Choice} to select the exploration direction. This converts the ObjectNav task into a sequence of point-goal subtasks, requiring no fine-tuning and enabling zero-shot generalization to novel targets.

Results: On the HM3D dataset, ImagineNav achieves a 53.0% success rate and 23.8% SPL, and on HSSD achieves 51.0% and 24.9% respectively, outperforming most prior methods. It even slightly outperforms the best map-based method VLFM (52.5%) in open-vocabulary tasks while being mapless. With oracle (real panoramic) images instead of NVS-synthesized ones, success rates rise to 62.0% on HM3D and 59.0% on HSSD. Ablation studies show future imagination improves success rate from 43.0% to 55.0%, adding Where2Imagine raises it to 64.0%, and the optimal sampling step T is 11. GPT-4o-mini matches GPT-4-Turbo performance while being more cost-effective than LLaVa (44.0%).

Key limitations identified: NVS image quality disparity limits performance, simulator mislabeling of object instances causes false failures, and lack of historical memory can trap the agent in local optima. - Can be shared among multiple robots with different embodiments (e.g., a LoCoBot ground robot vs. a drone) to generate customized obstacle maps on-the-fly based on obstacle categories

This paper introduces SSR3D-LLM (Structured Spatial Reasoning 3D-LLM), a unified 3D-LLM framework for fine-grained 3D object grounding. The core problem addressed: existing unified 3D-LLMs (like Grounded 3D-LLM and Chat-Scene) use single-pointer grounding (QPG), where one pointer selection compresses all query cues (target category, attributes, context objects, spatial relations) into a single decision—this is brittle for fine-grained queries with multiple same-class distractors.

The proposed method, Structured Spatial Grounding (S3G), replaces the single-pointer readout with a sequence of latent spatial reasoning steps. Key components:
- The LLM writes K=4 latent step-marker tokens and M=16 memory tokens from the query over fixed Mask3D object proposals.
- A geometry-aware scorer refines candidate rankings step by step, using a step-length mask (learned length predictor) to freeze updates after useful steps.
- Training uses standard target supervision plus auxiliary referential cues (derived from benchmarks or via an offline Qwen/vLLM annotator for open-form queries) to supervise the latent steps.
- At inference, only the original query and Mask3D proposals are used; latent steps are not decoded as text.
- Grounding-specific updates are confined to lightweight adapters/modules to preserve default language capability.

Results across benchmarks:
- Nr3D: 50.3% accuracy (vs. Grounded 3D-LLM 32.8%, Chat-Scene 25.9%).
- ScanRefer: 58.7/53.9 Acc@0.25/0.50 (vs. Chat-Scene 55.5/50.2, Grounded 3D-LLM 48.6/44.0).
- Multi3DRef: 63.1/57.9 F1@0.25/0.50 (vs. Chat-Scene 57.1/52.4, Grounded 3D-LLM 44.7/40.8).

Language capabilities are preserved (comparable CIDEr/EM scores on dialog, QA, captioning, description without the grounding token). The readout is one-pass and much faster than QPG (e.g., Nr3D latency 0.0363 s/query vs. Grounded 3D-LLM 1.1610) with GPU memory of ~5.8 GB. Ablations show removing step mask and shuffling/reversing steps sharply degrade performance, confirming the ordered latent steps are used.

Limitations: depends on upstream Mask3D proposal quality; fixed step budget K=4 may limit longer relational chains; trained on static ScanNet-style indoor scenes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"3D object grounding localizes referred objects in a 3D scene from natural language. Unified instance-centric 3D-LLMs aim to solve grounding together with dialog, QA, and captioning, yet many rely on a single pointer-style grounding decision that compresses a relational instruction into one selection. This is brittle for fine-grained queries where multiple same-class candidates must be ruled out by context objects and spatial relations."
</key_excerpts>

3DVG-Transformer: Relation Modeling for Visual Grounding on Point Clouds Lichen Zhao∗1, Daigang Cai∗1, Lu Sheng†1, Dong Xu2 1College of Software, Beihang University, China, 2The University of Sydney, Australia {zlc1114, caidaigang, lsheng}@buaa.edu.cn, dong.xu@sydney.edu.au Abstract Visual grounding on 3D point clouds is an emerging vi-sion and language task that benefits various applications in understanding the 3D visual world.
By formulating this task as a grounding-by-detection problem, lots of re-cent works focus on how to exploit more powerful detec-tors and comprehensive language features, but (1) how to model complex relations for generating context-aware ob-ject proposals and (2) how to leverage proposal relations to distinguish the true target object from similar proposals are not fully studied yet. Inspired by the well-known trans-former architecture, we propose a relation-aware visual grounding method on 3D point clouds, named as 3DVG-Transformer, to fully utilize the contextual clues for relation-enhanced proposal generation and cross-modal proposal disambiguation, which are enabled by a newly designed coordinate-guided contextual aggregation (CCA) module in the object proposal generation stage, and a multiplex attention (MA) module in the cross-modal feature fusion stage.
We validate that our 3DVG-Transformer outper-forms the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin, on two point cloud-based visual grounding datasets, ScanRe-fer and Nr3D/Sr3D from ReferIt3D, especially for complex scenarios containing multiple objects of the same category.
1. Introduction As one emerging 3D visual understanding task, visual grounding on point clouds, also called as referring 3D ob-ject localization, aims to locate the desired objects or re-gions in input point cloud from the given textual descrip-tions.
The visual grounding technologies would signif-icantly benefit various real-life applications such as au-tonomous robots, AR/VR, etc. Even though much progress has been made in visual grounding on 2D images [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], it is still a challenging task to design a reliable point-based visual grounding scheme that can well understand the * First two authors contributed equally.
† Corresponding author: Lu Sheng.
relations in complex 3D scenes and distinguish the propos-als of the target object from other similar proposals.
Recently, Chen et al. [6] and Achlioptas et al. [7] pro-posed to tackle visual grounding on 3D point clouds by for-mulating it as a grounding-by-detection problem, together with two newly developed datasets (i.e., ScanRefer [6] and ReferIt3D [7]). To be specific, they first use the state-of-the-art (SOTA) 3D object detector [8] or the ground-truth (GT) bounding boxes to generate object proposals, whose fea-tures are then fused with the language features from the lin-guistic query to predict the most confident proposals. Since then, several variants, such as TGNN [9] and InstanceRe-fer [10], were proposed to leverage instance segmenta-tion [11] and specially designed linguistic features for bet-ter localization and fine-grained matching between the two modalities. However, these methods still suffer from some critical issues: (1) how to model complex relations (e.g. rel-ative spatial locations) within each point cloud, (2) how to exploit various relations among proposals to distinguish the true target object from similar proposals with the aid of tex-tual descriptions. Thus the recent methods [6, 7, 9, 10] usu-ally fail to localize the target object when the input scenes contain multiple objects from the same category. Moreover, due to the relatively small scales of recent visual ground-ing datasets, the existing methods also suffer from the over-fitting problem, which also prevents these methods from learning a generalizable visual grounding model.
To this end, we propose a relation-aware visual ground-ing method on 3D point clouds, named as 3DVG-Transformer.
While our method follows the ground-by-detection strategy from ScanRefer [6], we additionally ex-ploit various relations among proposals at both the object proposal generation stage and the cross-modal fusion stage, based on the powerful relation modeling capability by the well-known transformer architecture [12]. To be specific, in the object proposal generation stage, after producing the cluster centers and features as the initial object proposals, we propose a coordinate-guided contextual aggregation (CCA) module, which stacks a set of coordinate-guided transformer layers to extract multi-level context-aware rep-resentations from both neighboring proposals and the back-2928 ground. Within each transformer layer, we add a new block-wise sparse spatial proximity matrix to the attention ma-trix at each multi-head attention module, so as to explic-itly describe relative spatial locations from proposals in each query proposal’s vicinity. At the cross-modal fusion stage, the word features extracted from the language encod-ing module and the proposal features from the selected pro-posals are fused with a multiplex attention (MA) module.
The multiplex attention module consists of a stack of in-terlaced self-attention and cross-attention blocks, where the self-attention block enhances contextual relationships be-tween proposals and the cross-attention block passes mes-sages from the word features to the proposal features. This module distinguishes the true grounding results from other proposals with the aid of comprehensive contextual knowl-edge within the point cloud and across visual and linguistic domains. The output from the cross-modal fusion module is directly fed into a feed-forward network (FFN) to predict the object confidence score for each proposal. Moreover, we optionally employ a pair of feature augmentation strate-gies for both modalities, (i.e., proposal copy & paste, and word erase), which also benefit the training process.
The contribution of this work is three-fold: (1) A simple and strong visual grounding framework (referred to as 3DVG-Transformer) specifically designed for point clouds, which comprehensively models various relations for relation-enhanced proposal generation and cross-modal proposal disambiguation. (2) A new coordinate-guided con-textual aggregation module for extracting multi-level con-textual features within point clouds, and a multiplex at-tention module for disambiguating the grounding results.
Both modules are inspired by the transformer architec-ture [12]. (3) The state-of-the-art visual grounding perfor-mance on the ScanRefer dataset [6] and Nr3D/Sr3D from the ReferIt3D dataset [7]. Our method significantly outper-forms the baselines [6, 7, 9, 10] on complex scenes with multiple objects from the same category.
2. Related Work Visual Grounding on 2D Images. Visual grounding, or called referring expression comprehension, has been exten-sively studied in various 2D vision and language tasks. It aims to localize a region of interest in an image described by the referring expression [1, 2, 3]. The input textual de-scription can be short phrases [13] or long sentences [14], with the corresponding localization result being specified by a 2D bounding box [13, 15]. The conventional meth-ods are mostly composed of two stages. The first stage is to generate target object proposals by using the pretrained object detectors or the unsupervised objectiveness detector.
And the second stage is to match the most relevant object proposals by identifying the regions of interest, and rank-ing the regions based on their similarities to the query sen-tences [16, 2]. Most of these methods focus on exploit-ing the relationship between objects [16, 17, 18, 19]. For example, Yan et al. [20] also used the graph attention net-works and a modular decomposition method to learn the alignment between relationship and language expression.
In MAttNet [2], Yu et al. proposed the language-based at-tention and visual attention mechanisms to capture multi-modality context information. Although these methods are powerful in dealing with 2D vision and language reasoning tasks, these methods may not work well for visual ground-ing on point clouds where how to handle 3D geometrical relations [6, 7] was less explored yet. Hence, we propose a transformer-based relation modeling scheme that matches the characteristics of point clouds, and is specially tailored to the visual grounding task on this special input data.
Visual Grounding on 3D Point Clouds. Deep learning technologies have been successfully applied to various point cloud based vision tasks, such as classification [21, 22], seg-mentation [23, 22], detection [24, 25], 3D action recogni-tion [26, 22], upsampling [27], and point cloud compres-sion [28]. Visual grounding on 3D point clouds has also received increasing attention from the vision community.
Chen et al. [6] released the ScanRefer dataset and proposed a ground-by-detection framework to learn the grounding model in an end-to-end fashion. ReferIt3D [7] introduced two datasets referred to as Nr3D and Sr3D, which are simi-lar to ScanRefer [6] but based on the ground-truth bounding boxes instead of the predicted ones. Huang et al. [9] pro-posed a Text-guided Graph Neural Network (TGNN) to seg-ment out the target objects in the 3D scenes according to the query sentences. InstanceRefer [10] also exploited a pre-trained panoptic segmentation model, which also relies on the handcrafted language parsing module to select the can-didate bounding boxes. Our 3DVG-Transformer is trained without using any external knowledge, and we pay more at-tention to the relation modeling between object proposals so as to disambiguate similar matches to achieve more robust grounding results.
Transformers in Computer Vision. Inspired by the suc-cess of transformer [12] in natural language processing (NLP), recently researchers also extended the transformer structure for various computer vision tasks like image clas-sification [29], style transfer [30], image captioning [31], video grounding [32] and object detection [33, 34].
In the field of point clouds, Transformer3D-Det [35] used the transformer-based method for 3D object detection, while Pointformer [36] used the so-called Local-Global Trans-former to integrate local features with global features. Dif-ferent from the existing methods, we aim to leverage the transformer architectures to model relationships among the objects and the background of the 3D scenes, for which we and propose a coordinate-guided contextual aggrega-2929 Point Cloud GRU Voting & Grouping Language Classifier Proposal Features Coordinate-guided Contextual Aggregation the floral printed chair is in front of the glass double doors. the floral printed chair is to the left of the grey desk.

The pipeline of our 3DVG-Transformer, which includes an object proposal generation module, a language encoding module, and a cross-modal fusion module. The input of our method is a pair of point cloud and a textual description. The output is the object confidence scores, namely, the bounding box with the highest score will be considered as the final grounding result. The modules marked in yellow are the key components in our framework to enable relation-enhanced visual grounding on point clouds. tion (CCA) module and a multiplex attention (MA) mod-ule to reliably fuse contextual clues to extract the more ro-bust proposal features, and distinguish true grounding re-sults from similar proposals during the cross-modal feature fusion stage.
3. Methodology In this section, we describe the technical details of our 3DVG-Transformer. In Sec. 3.1, we present an overview of our method. In Sec. 3.2 to Sec. 3.3, we elaborate on how to exploit multi-level context clues to enrich the context-awareness of the proposal features, and how to leverage pro-posal relations to disambiguate the grounding results with the aid of word features. In Sec. 3.4, we introduce the ob-jective function of our method, which also includes a pair of feature augmentation strategies for alleviating overfitting.
3.1. Overview As shown in Fig. 1, our 3DVG-Transformer has two in-puts. One is the point cloud P ∈RN×(3+K) that represents the whole 3D scene by 3D coordinates and K-dimensional auxiliary feature (e.g., RGB, normal vectors, or the pre-trained multi-view appearance features [6]). Another in-put is the word embedding W ∈RL×T representing a free-form L-length textual description about a specified tar-get object, which is extracted by using a pretrained GloVE model [37].
The goal of visual grounding on 3D point clouds is to localize the object of interest (i.e., the target ob-ject) in each point cloud, and output an axis-aligned bound-ing box with the center c = [cx, cy, cz]⊤∈R3 in the world coordinate, and the size s = [sx, sy, sz]⊤∈R3.
The overall framework of our 3DVG-Transformer con-sists of three modules at three stages, including the ob-ject proposal generation module, the language encoding module, and the cross-modal fusion module. The object proposal generation module aims to generate the bound-ing boxes from the object proposals B, and simultaneously produce their context-aware proposal features as Fprop ∈ RM×F , where M is the predefined number of proposals, and F is the feature dimension. The language encoding module aims to use the same GRU cell as in ScanRefer [6] to encode the query word embeddings as a set of word fea-tures Fword ∈RL×F , and a global language feature e ∈R ˆ F for the subsequent language classifier to generate the text class [6]. The cross-modal fusion module fuses the pro-posal features Fprop and the word features Fword together to produce the final object confidence scores C = {ci}M i=1 for the generated bounding boxes. Eventually, the bound-ing box with the highest confidence score will be consid-ered as the final grounding result. In this work, we focus on how to reliably model various relationships for the purpose of exploiting rich contextual clues to enhance the proposal features in the object proposal generation module, and at the same time distinguish the true target object from similar proposals in the cross-modal fusion module.
3.2. Relation-enhanced Proposal Generation Similarly as in [6], in the object proposal generation stage, we extract the base features from the given point cloud P with a PointNet++ [38] backbone, then we apply the voting and grouping module [8] to cluster and aggregate them as the initial clusters about all possible object candi-dates. Each initial cluster is represented as {xi, fi}M i=1. xi ∈ R3 and fi ∈RC are each initial cluster’s center and feature, respectively. However, these intermediate outputs only cap-ture local point cloud features that describe the candidate objects, so they are not aware of the relations with other 2930 Coordinate Distance Matrix (a) Initial Cluster Centers Initial Cluster Features Self-Attention Value Query Key FFN Key Value Query FFN Add & Norm Spatial Proximity Calculation Add & Norm Original Cluster Centers Original Cluster Features Output Cluster Centers Output Cluster Features x2 Center Offset Cross-Attention Spatial Proximity Matrix (Output from the Last Layer) (Output from the Last Layer) Spatial Proximity Matrix Spatial Proximity Calculation Intermediate Cluster Features Intermediate Cluster Centers Add & Norm FC FC FC Softmax Query Key Value Attention Matrix(×H) Spatial Proximity Matrix Fused Attention Matrix(×H) FC FC FC Softmax FC FC FC Softmax Concatenation Cross/Self Attention Module (b) FC Figure 2.
