[Shuquan Ye](https://shuquanye.com)1,  [Dongdong Chen](https://www.dongdongchen.bid/)2,  [Songfang Han](http://hansf.me/)3,   [Jing Liao](https://liaojing.github.io/html/)1,

1City University of Hong Kong, 2Microsoft Cloud AI, 3University of California San Diego

  

(Submitted on 15 Dec 2021, accepted on 29 Nov 2022)

[Paper](https://doi.ieeecomputersociety.org/10.1109/TVCG.2022.3225327)     [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.08359v2)     [Code](https://github.com/pleaseconnectwifi/3DQA)     [Dataset](https://github.com/pleaseconnectwifi/3DQA)     [Talk](https://zhidx.com/p/344582.html)

**News**: The dataset and the code have been released! The benchmark and data browser will be available in the future.

![](static/images/fig1.jpg)

  

Illustration of **natural-language, free-form, open-ended** questions collected for 3D scenes via Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT).

Questions in our ScanQA dataset include a comprehensive variety of *appearance and geometry* concepts. For example, Q1 requires information on not only the *appearance* of a single object, but also the *geometry* of that object and a relative *spatial comparison between objects*. Q2 captures the *placement* information from *aggregation* of more than two objects. Q3 requires ability for *navigation to the view-point* as well as *spatial comparison to the average value*.

Tips: You can rotate/move/zoom the scenes, and change point size with '+' or '-'.

## Abstract

Visual Question Answering (VQA) has experienced tremendous progress in recent years. However, most efforts have only focused on 2D image question-answering tasks.

In this paper, we present the first attempt at extending VQA to its 3D counterpart, 3D question answering (3DQA), which can facilitate a machine's perception of 3D real-world scenarios.

Unlike 2D image VQA, 3DQA takes the color point cloud as input and requires both appearance and 3D geometrical comprehension to answer the 3D-related questions. To this end, we propose a novel transformer-based 3DQA framework **"3DQA-TR"**, which consists of two encoders to exploit the appearance and geometry information, respectively. Finally, the multi-modal information about the appearance, geometry, and the linguistic question can attend to each other via a 3D-Linguistic Bert to predict the target answers.

To verify the effectiveness of our proposed 3DQA framework, we further develop the first 3DQA dataset **"ScanQA"**, which builds on the ScanNet dataset and contains over 10K question-answer pairs for 806 scenes. To the best of our knowledge, ScanQA is the first large-scale dataset with natural-language questions and free-form answers in 3D environments that is fully human-annotated. We also use several visualizations and experiments to investigate the astonishing diversity of the collected questions and the significant differences between this task from 2D VQA and 3D captioning.

Extensive experiments on this dataset demonstrate the obvious superiority of our proposed 3DQA framework over existing VQA frameworks, and the effectiveness of our major designs.

## Datset Information

![](static/images/qlength.jpg)![](static/images/qdistrib.jpg)   

It is the first dataset for 3D Question Answering (3DQA) task, which provides **natural-language, free-form, and open-ended** questions and answers in free-perspective 3D scans. In total, the ScanQA dataset provides 10,062 questions (12.48 questions per scene on average) of 1,613 scans from 806 scenes from [ScanNet](http://www.scan-net.org/).

A rich collection of **interesting and diverse** questions with various viewpoints is collected under a carefully designed data collection strategy. To ensure the **quality** of questions and answers, measures such as an online robot checker, manual correction, and syntax check are used. In addition to the answers, the viewpoint, camera setting, and annotators' confidence will be provided.

## 3DQA-TR Framework and Results

![](static/images/fig2.jpg)

  

## Illustration of our pipeline. The 3DQA-TR framework has three jointly trainable parts: appearance encoder (red), geometry encoder (orange), and 3D-L BERT. The geometry encoder provides both structure information of each object and positional and scale information to model spatial relationship between objects. The appearance encoder is used to extract appearance information. Given the encoded appearance and geometry together with question embedding, the 3D-L BERT attends to the intra- and inter- modal interactions and predicts the answer.

![](static/images/fig3.jpg) ![](static/images/fig4.jpg) ![](static/images/fig5.jpg)

  

## Example predictions from 2D VQA baseline and our 3DQA-TR, and human answers in ScanQA.

The annotation webpage is based on [ScanRefer](https://daveredrum.github.io/ScanRefer/). We thank the authors for sharing their codebase. I would like to give my particular thanks to all the annotators, and [Jiaying Lin](https://jiaying.link), for providing the initial idea, and the contribution to the annotation collection webpages and server.

# ScanQA: 3D Question Answering for Spatial Scene Understanding

This is the official repository of our paper [**ScanQA: 3D Question Answering for Spatial Scene Understanding (CVPR 2022)**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10482) by Daichi Azuma, Taiki Miyanishi, Shuhei Kurita, and Motoki Kawanabe.

## Abstract

We propose a new 3D spatial understanding task for 3D question answering (3D-QA). In the 3D-QA task, models receive visual information from the entire 3D scene of a rich RGB-D indoor scan and answer given textual questions about the 3D scene. Unlike the 2D-question answering of visual question answering, the conventional 2D-QA models suffer from problems with spatial understanding of object alignment and directions and fail in object localization from the textual questions in 3D-QA. We propose a baseline model for 3D-QA, called the ScanQA model, which learns a fused descriptor from 3D object proposals and encoded sentence embeddings. This learned descriptor correlates language expressions with the underlying geometric features of the 3D scan and facilitates the regression of 3D bounding boxes to determine the described objects in textual questions. We collected human-edited question-answer pairs with free-form answers grounded in 3D objects in each 3D scene. Our new ScanQA dataset contains over 41k question-answer pairs from 800 indoor scenes obtained from the ScanNet dataset. To the best of our knowledge, ScanQA is the first large-scale effort to perform object-grounded question answering in 3D environments.

# ScanQA: 3D Question Answering for Spatial Scene Understanding

![](https://static.alphaxiv.org/images/organizations/kyoto-university.png)
![](https://static.alphaxiv.org/images/organizations/riken.jpeg)

## Abstract

We propose a new 3D spatial understanding task of 3D Question Answering
(3D-QA). In the 3D-QA task, models receive visual information from the entire
3D scene of the rich RGB-D indoor scan and answer the given textual questions
about the 3D scene. Unlike the 2D-question answering of VQA, the conventional
2D-QA models suffer from problems with spatial understanding of object
alignment and directions and fail the object identification from the textual
questions in 3D-QA. We propose a baseline model for 3D-QA, named ScanQA model,
where the model learns a fused descriptor from 3D object proposals and encoded
sentence embeddings. This learned descriptor correlates the language
expressions with the underlying geometric features of the 3D scan and
facilitates the regression of 3D bounding boxes to determine described objects
in textual questions and outputs correct answers. We collected human-edited
question-answer pairs with free-form answers that are grounded to 3D objects in
each 3D scene. Our new ScanQA dataset contains over 40K question-answer pairs
from the 800 indoor scenes drawn from the ScanNet dataset. To the best of our
knowledge, the proposed 3D-QA task is the first large-scale effort to perform
object-grounded question-answering in 3D environments.

Save

## AI Overview

## Introduction

The development of AI systems that can understand and interact with three-dimensional environments represents a significant challenge in computer vision and natural language processing. While substantial progress has been made in 2D vision-language tasks like Visual Question Answering (VQA), these approaches face fundamental limitations when applied to real-world 3D scenarios. Issues such as occlusion, lack of depth information, and inability to maintain consistent object identification across multiple viewpoints highlight the need for direct 3D approaches to spatial understanding.

![ScanQA Task Examples](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2112.10482v3/img-0.jpeg "ScanQA Task Examples")
*Figure 1: Examples of the ScanQA task showing 3D scans with questions and corresponding answers with 3D bounding box localizations. The model must process complete 3D scene information to answer spatial questions and identify relevant objects.*

![ScanQA Task Examples](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2112.10482v3/img-0.jpeg "ScanQA Task Examples")

This paper introduces ScanQA, which establishes 3D Question Answering (3D-QA) as a distinct task that requires models to process complete visual information from RGB-D indoor scans and answer natural language questions while localizing relevant objects in 3D space. Unlike navigation-based embodied QA approaches, ScanQA focuses on static scene understanding where complete 3D information is available upfront, making it particularly relevant for applications involving pre-captured 3D data.

## Dataset Construction and Characteristics

The ScanQA dataset represents a significant advancement in 3D vision-language resources, built upon the ScanNet dataset's 800 diverse indoor scenes. The dataset creation process involved multiple stages combining automatic generation with extensive human annotation to ensure quality and diversity.

The construction began with automatic question generation using T5-based models to create initial question-answer pairs from ScanRefer referring expressions. However, these automatically generated questions were often inadequate, suffering from issues like being underspecified, not properly grounded in the scene, or too simplistic. To address these limitations, the authors implemented a comprehensive filtering and editing pipeline involving Amazon Mechanical Turk workers who classified questions and rewrote inadequate ones to ensure clarity and scene relevance.

A critical component of the dataset is the custom 3D scene viewer developed for human annotation. This interactive tool allows annotators to rotate, zoom, and explore 3D scenes while accessing object names and IDs, enabling them to provide accurate free-form answers and identify relevant object bounding boxes. The resulting dataset contains 41,363 question-answer pairs with 32,337 unique questions and 16,999 unique answers across 800 scenes, representing an order of magnitude improvement over previous template-based 3D-QA datasets.

![Question Analysis](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2112.10482v3/img-2.jpeg "Question Analysis")
*Figure 2: Hierarchical visualization of question word distributions in the ScanQA dataset, showing the diversity of question types including "What", "Where", "How many", and "What color" questions.*

![Question Analysis](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2112.10482v3/img-2.jpeg "Question Analysis")

The dataset exhibits rich linguistic diversity with questions spanning various types including spatial relationships, object properties, and counting tasks. The human-edited nature ensures natural language variation while maintaining proper grounding in the 3D environment, addressing a key limitation of previous datasets that relied heavily on template-based generation.

## Model Architecture and Methodology

The ScanQA baseline model employs an end-to-end architecture designed to jointly learn object localization and question answering through integrated 3D and language processing. The model consists of three primary layers that progressively transform and fuse visual and linguistic information.

![Model Architecture](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2112.10482v3/img-3.jpeg "Model Architecture")
*Figure 3: The ScanQA model architecture showing the three-layer design: 3D & Language Encoder Layer, 3D & Language Fusion Layer, and Object Localization & QA Layer.*

![Model Architecture](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2112.10482v3/img-3.jpeg "Model Architecture")

The **3D & Language Encoder Layer** processes inputs through parallel pathways. Questions are first embedded using GloVe vectors, then processed by a bidirectional LSTM to produce contextualized word representations. Simultaneously, the 3D point cloud, enriched with coordinates, height, colors, normals, and multiview image features, is fed into VoteNet with a PointNet++ backbone to generate 3D object proposals.

The **3D & Language Fusion Layer** implements transformer-based attention mechanisms inspired by MCAN architecture. A series of transformer encoder layers process the contextualized question representations, while transformer decoder layers process object proposals using the encoded question features as keys and values. This cross-modal attention enables the model to learn relationships between linguistic concepts and spatial objects. A final fusion layer combines these representations into a unified feature vector capturing both 3D scene and question information.

The **Object Localization & QA Layer** produces the task's dual outputs through three specialized modules. The object localization module predicts confidence scores for each object proposal's relevance to the question. The object classification module identifies categories of relevant objects across 18 ScanNet classes, addressing cases where target objects aren't explicitly named. The answer classification module predicts scores for predefined answer candidates using binary cross-entropy loss to accommodate multiple correct answers.

The overall loss function combines contributions from answer classification, object classification, object localization, and VoteNet's object detection loss:

This multi-task learning approach enables synergistic training where improved object localization enhances question answering performance and vice versa.

## Experimental Results and Analysis

The experimental evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the ScanQA approach across multiple metrics and provides insights into the importance of various design choices. The authors evaluated models using both exact match accuracy (EM@1, EM@10) and traditional image captioning metrics (BLEU, ROUGE-L, METEOR, CIDEr, SPICE) to comprehensively assess free-form answer quality.

![Qualitative Results](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2112.10482v3/img-4.jpeg "Qualitative Results")
*Figure 4: Qualitative comparison showing ScanQA's superior performance in object localization and question answering compared to baseline methods. Green boxes indicate correct answers while red crosses show failures.*

![Qualitative Results](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2112.10482v3/img-4.jpeg "Qualitative Results")

The ScanQA model consistently outperformed all baseline approaches across evaluation metrics. Particularly significant was its superiority over 2D-based methods, with the RandomImage+MCAN baseline achieving substantially lower performance, empirically confirming the limitations of 2D approaches for 3D spatial reasoning. The OracleImage+MCAN baseline, which used perfectly centered images of target objects, achieved competitive performance in some cases, indicating that while 2D models can perform well on the QA aspect when given ideal object localization, the challenge lies in robust 3D grounding.

A crucial finding was the importance of end-to-end training. Models that jointly learned object localization and QA significantly outperformed pipeline approaches where these components were trained separately. This validates the hypothesis that synergistic learning between spatial grounding and linguistic reasoning is essential for effective 3D-QA performance.

Human performance established an upper bound with an EM@1 score of 51.6, demonstrating that the task is challenging yet solvable and leaves substantial room for improvement. Ablation studies revealed that both object classification and localization modules were essential, with their removal leading to consistent performance degradation.

The analysis of different input features showed that geometric information (xyz coordinates) provided a strong foundation, while multiview image features and surface normals offered modest improvements. Interestingly, raw RGB values showed inconsistent benefits, suggesting opportunities for better visual feature integration in future work.

## Significance and Future Implications

ScanQA establishes several important contributions to the field of 3D vision-language understanding. First, it formalizes 3D Question Answering as a distinct task that addresses limitations of both 2D VQA approaches and navigation-based embodied QA systems. This task definition fills a critical gap for scenarios involving pre-captured 3D data, such as virtual tours, architectural visualization, and indoor scene analysis.

The creation of a large-scale, human-annotated dataset with free-form questions and explicit 3D object grounding provides an essential resource for the research community. Previous 3D-QA datasets were limited by template-based generation and small scale, while ScanQA offers the diversity and complexity needed to train robust spatial reasoning models.

The baseline model demonstrates that end-to-end learning of object localization and question answering is crucial for effective 3D spatial understanding. This finding has implications for future model development, suggesting that integrated architectures may be more effective than pipeline approaches for complex spatial reasoning tasks.

The work opens several avenues for future research, including development of more sophisticated 3D feature representations, integration of temporal information for dynamic scenes, and extension to outdoor environments. The established benchmark provides a foundation for comparing future approaches and tracking progress in 3D spatial intelligence.

From an applications perspective, ScanQA's capabilities have direct relevance for robotics, augmented reality, smart environments, and accessibility technologies. The ability to answer natural language questions about 3D spaces while grounding responses in specific objects enables more intuitive human-computer interaction in spatial domains and supports the development of embodied AI systems that can truly understand and navigate the physical world.

args.summary:
This paper introduces ScanQA, a new 3D Question Answering (3D-QA) task and baseline model for spatial scene understanding, submitted on May 7, 2022, by researchers affiliated with Kyoto University and RIKEN. The task extends 2D VQA to 3D indoor scenes, requiring models to process complete visual information from RGB-D scans, answer natural language questions, and localize relevant objects in 3D space. Unlike navigation-based embodied QA, ScanQA focuses on static scene understanding with complete 3D information available upfront.

Key contributions include:
- **ScanQA dataset**: Built on 800 indoor scenes from ScanNet, containing 41,363 question-answer pairs, 32,337 unique questions, and 16,999 unique answers. Construction combined T5-based automatic question generation with a comprehensive filtering/editing pipeline involving Amazon Mechanical Turk workers and a custom 3D scene viewer annotation tool. This represents an order of magnitude improvement over previous template-based 3D-QA datasets.
- **ScanQA baseline model**: A three-layer end-to-end architecture including (1) a 3D & Language Encoder Layer using GloVe embeddings with bidirectional LSTM for questions and VoteNet with PointNet++ backbone for 3D object proposals, (2) a 3D & Language Fusion Layer using MCAN-inspired transformer attention, and (3) an Object Localization & QA Layer with separate modules for object localization, object classification (18 ScanNet classes), and answer classification using binary cross-entropy loss.

Experimental results showed the ScanQA model consistently outperformed baselines, particularly 2D-based methods (RandomImage+MCAN), confirming the limitations of 2D approaches for 3D spatial reasoning. A crucial finding was that end-to-end training (joint learning of localization and QA) significantly outperformed pipeline approaches. Human performance established an upper bound with an EM@1 score of 51.6. Ablation studies showed geometric features (xyz coordinates) provided a strong foundation, while RGB values showed inconsistent benefits. The work has applications in robotics, augmented reality, smart environments, and accessibility technologies, with future directions including more sophisticated 3D feature representations and extension to outdoor environments.

This is a Semantic Scholar paper page for "SQA3D: Situated Question Answering in 3D Scenes," an academic paper published on October 14, 2022, at the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). The paper, authored by Xiaojian Ma, Silong Yong, Zilong Zheng, Qing Li, Yitao Liang, Song-Chun Zhu, and Siyuan Huang, has a DOI of 10.48550/arXiv.2210.07474 and Corpus ID 252907411.

The paper introduces SQA3D, a new task designed to benchmark the scene understanding capabilities of embodied agents. The task requires an agent to first understand its situation within a 3D scene, then reason about its surrounding environment, and finally answer a question based on that situated context.

The paper has 16 figures and tables, 369 citations (including 83 background citations, 48 methods citations, and 17 highly influential citations), and 77 references. Its citation count indicates significant impact as a fundamental paper in the field of 3D scene understanding and situated question answering.

Key citing works include:
- EMBOSR: Embodied Spatial Reasoning for Enhanced Situated Question Answering in 3D Scenes (IROS 2024) - fuses foundation models with chain-of-thought methodology
- Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes (NeurIPS 2024) - large-scale multi-modal reasoning dataset.
- Hypo3D: Exploring Hypothetical Reasoning in 3D (ICML 2025)
- Embodied Intelligence for 3D Understanding: A survey on 3D Scene Question Answering (Info Fusion, 2026) - first comprehensive survey of 3D SQA

- Space3D-Bench: Spatial 3D Question Answering Benchmark (ECCV 2024)
- CityEQA: A hierarchical LLM agent on embodied question answering benchmark in city space (EMNLP 2025)

# Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes

Xiongkun Linghu ⋅ Jiangyong Huang ⋅ Xuesong Niu ⋅ Xiaojian (Shawn) Ma ⋅ Baoxiong Jia ⋅ Siyuan Huang

2024 Poster

[Project Page](https://msr3d.github.io/)   [ [Paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/feaeec8ec2d3cb131fe18517ff14ec1f-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.html "Paper")]    [ [Poster](/media/PosterPDFs/NeurIPS%202024/97727.png?t=1731422243.9377327 "Poster")]

### Abstract

Situation awareness is essential for understanding and reasoning about 3D scenes in embodied AI agents. However, existing datasets and benchmarks for situated understanding suffer from severe limitations in data modality, scope, diversity, and scale. To address these limitations, we propose Multi-modal Situated Question Answering (MSQA), a large-scale multi-modal situated reasoning dataset, scalably collected leveraging 3D scene graphs and vision-language models (VLMs) across a diverse range of real-world 3D scenes. MSQA includes 251K situated questionanswering pairs across 9 distinct question categories, covering complex scenarios and object modalities within 3D scenes. We introduce a novel interleaved multimodal input setting in our benchmark to provide both texts, images, and point clouds for situation and question description, aiming to resolve ambiguity in describing situations with single-modality inputs (e.g., texts). Additionally, we devise the Multi-modal Next-step Navigation (MSNN) benchmark to evaluate models’ grounding of actions and transitions between situations. Comprehensive evaluations on reasoning and navigation tasks highlight the limitations of existing vision-language models and underscore the importance of handling multi-modal interleaved inputs and situation modeling. Experiments on data scaling and crossdomain transfer further demonstrate the effectiveness of leveraging MSQA as a pre-training dataset for developing more powerful situated reasoning models, contributing to advancements in 3D scene understanding for embodied AI.

args.summary:
This is the NeurIPS 2024 conference page for the poster "Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes" by Xiongkun Linghu, Jiangyong Huang, Xuesong Niu, Xiaojian (Shawn) Ma, Baoxiong Jia, and Siyuan Huang. 

The research addresses limitations in existing datasets and benchmarks for situated understanding in embodied AI agents, particularly in data modality, scope, diversity, and scale. The authors propose:

- **MSQA (Multi-modal Situated Question Answering)**: A large-scale multi-modal situated reasoning dataset collected via 3D scene graphs and vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse real-world 3D scenes. It contains 251K situated question-answering pairs across 9 question categories, covering complex scenarios and object modalities.
- **Novel interleaved multimodal input setting**: The benchmark provides texts, images, and point clouds for situation and question description, resolving ambiguity in single-modality (e.g., text-only) descriptions.
- **MSNN (Multi-modal Next-step Navigation) benchmark**: Evaluates models' grounding of actions and transitions between situations.

Key findings: Comprehensive evaluations on reasoning and navigation tasks highlight limitations of existing vision-language models and underscore the importance of handling multi-modal interleaved inputs and situation modeling. Experiments on data scaling and cross-domain transfer demonstrate MSQA's effectiveness as a pre-training dataset for developing more powerful situated reasoning models, contributing to advancements in 3D scene understanding for embodied AI.

The page includes links to the project page, paper (published in the NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track), and poster, plus standard NeurIPS website navigation elements.

### Abstract

A unified model for 3D vision-language (3D-VL) understanding is expected to take various scene representations and perform a wide range of tasks in a 3D scene. However, a considerable gap exists between existing methods and such a unified model, due to the independent application of representation and insufficient exploration of 3D multi-task training. In this paper, we introduce PQ3D, a unified model capable of using Promptable Queries to tackle a wide range of 3D-VL tasks, from low-level instance segmentation to high-level reasoning and planning.Tested across ten diverse 3D-VL datasets, This is achieved through three key innovations: (1) unifying various 3D scene representations (i.e., voxels, point clouds, multi-view im- ages) into a shared 3D coordinate space by segment-level grouping, (2) an attention-based query decoder for task-specific information retrieval guided by prompts, and (3) universal output heads for different tasks to support multi-task training. PQ3D demonstrates impressive performance on these tasks, setting new records on most benchmarks. Particularly, PQ3D improves the state- of-the-art on ScanNet200 by 4.9% (AP25), ScanRefer by 5.4% (acc@0.5), Multi3DRefer by 11.7% (F1@0.5), and Scan2Cap by 13.4% (CIDEr@0.5).Moreover, PQ3D supports flexible inference with individual or combined forms of available 3D representations, e.g., solely voxel input

### Install

1. Install conda package

```
conda env create --name envname pip3 install torch==2.0.0 pip3 install torchvision==0.15.1 pip3 install -r requirements.txt 
```

1. install pointnet2

```
cd modules/third_party # PointNet2 cd pointnet2 python setup.py install cd .. 
```

1. Install Minkowski Engine

```
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/MinkowskiEngine.git conda install openblas-devel -c anaconda cd MinkowskiEngine python setup.py install --blas_include_dirs=${CONDA_PREFIX}/include --blas=openblas 
```

### Prepare data

1. download sceneverse data from [scene\_verse\_base](https://github.com/scene-verse/sceneverse?tab=readme-ov-file) and change `data.scene_verse_base` to sceneverse data directory.
2. download segment level data from [scene\_ver\_aux](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1em0G5S4aH4lCIfnjLxyFO3DV3Rwuwnqh?usp=share_link) and change `data.scene_verse_aux` to download data directory.
3. download other data from [scene\_verse\_pred](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/12BjbhXzV7lON4X0tx3e7DdvZHhI1Q1f2?usp=share_link) and change `data.scene_verse_pred` to download data directory.

### Prepare checkpoints

1. download PointNet++ from [pointnet](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1KSu2z9cOMocQg5yYKUTlk0TlDwJZQMKs?usp=share_link) and change `pretrained_weights_dir` to downloaded directory,
2. download checkpoint from [stage1](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1KHayAzF7XlE3R3cz4YUPoHY_1VJkKYpd?usp=share_link), [stage2](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1MDt9yaco_TllGfqqt76UOxMV1JMMVsji?usp=share_link) and change pretrain\_ckpt\_path to certain checkpoint weight.

### Run PQ3D

Stage 1 training for instance segmentation

```
python3 run.py --config-path configs --config-name instseg_sceneverse_gt.yaml 
```

```
python3 run.py --config-path configs --config-name instseg_sceneverse.yaml pretrain_ckpt={ckpt_from_instseg_sceneverser_gt} 
```

Stage 1 evaluation

```
python3 run.py --config-path configs --config-name instseg_sceneverse.yaml mode=test pretrain_ckp_path={pretrain_ckpt_path} 
```

Stage 2 training for vl tasks

```
python3 run.py --config-path configs --config-name unified_tasks_sceneverse.yaml 
```

Stage 2 evaluation

```
python3 run.py --config-path configs --config-name unified_tasks_sceneverse.yaml mode=test pretrain_ckpt_path={pretrain_ckpt_path} 
```

For multi-gpu training usage, we use four GPU in our experiments.

```
python launch.py --mode ${launch_mode} \ --qos=${qos} --partition=${partition} --gpu_per_node=4 --port=29512 --mem_per_gpu=80 \ --config {config} \ 
```

PQ3D is the official GitHub implementation of the ECCV 2024 paper "Unifying 3D Vision-Language Understanding via Promptable Queries" by Ziyu Zhu, Zhuofan Zhang, Xiaojian Ma, Xuesong Niu, Yixin Chen, Baoxiong Jia, Zhidong Deng, Siyuan Huang, and Qing Li (arXiv:2405.11442). The repository has 86 stars, 7 forks, and 7 commits. It includes a public HuggingFace demo.

PQ3D is a unified model that uses Promptable Queries to handle a wide range of 3D vision-language (3D-VL) tasks, from low-level instance segmentation to high-level reasoning and planning. The model achieves this through three key innovations: (1) unifying various 3D scene representations (voxels, point clouds, multi-view images) into a shared 3D coordinate space via segment-level grouping, (2) an attention-based query decoder for task-specific information retrieval guided by prompts, and (3) universal output heads supporting multi-task training. Tested across ten 3D-VL datasets, PQ3D sets new state-of-the-art records on most benchmarks, improving ScanNet200 by 4.9% (AP25), ScanRefer by 5.4% (acc@0.5), Multi3DRefer by 11.7% (F1@0.5), and Scan2Cap by 13.4% (CIDEr@0.5). It also supports flexible inference with individual or combined 3D representations (e.g., solely voxel input).

Repository structure includes directories: common, configs, data, evaluator, model, modules, optim, trainer, along with launch.py, run.py, requirements.txt, and a MIT LICENSE.

Timeline: July 2024 — HuggingFace demo released and model codes released; August 2024 — training and evaluation released.

Installation involves setting up conda, PointNet2 (modules/third_party), and MinkowskiEngine (NVIDIA). Data preparation requires downloading sceneverse base data (from scene-verse GitHub), segment-level data (scene_verse_aux), and other data (scene_verse_pred). Checkpoints for PointNet++ and stage1/stage2 models are available via Google Drive links.

Training/evaluation steps include Stage 1 (instance segmentation, via instseg_sceneverse_gt.yaml and instseg_sceneverse.yaml configs) and Stage 2 (VL tasks via unified_tasks_sceneverse.yaml). Multi-GPU training uses run via launch.py with 4 GPUs. The authors acknowledge open-source contributions from Vil3dref, Mask3d, Openscene, Xdecoder, and 3D-VisTA.

## Abstract

Recent advancements in 3D Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for 3D scene understanding. However, previous methods exhibit deficiencies in general referencing and grounding capabilities for intricate scene comprehension. In this paper, we introduce the use of object identifiers and object-centric representations to interact with scenes at the object level. Specifically, we decompose the input 3D scene into a set of object proposals, each assigned a unique identifier token, which enables efficient object referencing and grounding during user-assistant interactions. Given the scarcity of scene-language data, we model the scene embeddings as a sequence of explicit object-level embeddings, derived from semantic-rich 2D or 3D representations. By employing object identifiers, we transform diverse 3D scene-language tasks into a unified question-answering format, facilitating joint training without the need for additional task-specific heads. With minimal fine-tuning on all downstream tasks, our model significantly outperforms existing methods on benchmarks including ScanRefer, Multi3DRefer, Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and SQA3D.

## AI Overview

## Introduction

Chat-Scene represents a significant advancement in bridging 3D scene understanding with Large Language Models (LLMs), addressing fundamental limitations in current Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) when applied to 3D environments. While existing 2D MLLMs have achieved remarkable success in visual understanding and interaction, their extension to 3D scenes has been hindered by challenges in object referencing, grounding, and the scarcity of high-quality 3D scene-language paired datasets.

![Chat-Scene Architecture](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2312.08168v4/img-0.jpeg "Chat-Scene Architecture")

![Chat-Scene Architecture](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2312.08168v4/img-0.jpeg "Chat-Scene Architecture")

The paper introduces a unified framework that enables precise object-level interaction within 3D scenes through two key innovations: object identifiers for unambiguous referencing and object-centric representations that leverage pre-trained foundation models. This approach transforms diverse 3D scene understanding tasks into a single question-answering format, eliminating the need for specialized architectures while achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.

## Core Methodology

Chat-Scene's methodology centers on decomposing 3D scenes into individual object proposals and establishing direct correspondences between these objects and the language model through learnable identifier tokens. This object-centric approach addresses the fundamental challenge of precise spatial reasoning in 3D environments.

The system begins by using Mask3D, a pre-trained 3D instance segmentation model, to decompose input point clouds into distinct object proposals. Each detected object is assigned a unique identifier token (e.g., `<OBJ013>`) that becomes part of the LLM's extended vocabulary. These identifiers enable unambiguous object referencing, avoiding the ambiguities inherent in natural language descriptions like "the chair on the left."

`<OBJ013>`

The architecture extracts multi-modal features for each object through parallel encoding pipelines. A 3D encoder (Uni3D) processes the point cloud representation of each object to capture geometric and spatial properties. Simultaneously, a 2D encoder (DINOv2) extracts semantic features by projecting object point clouds onto multi-view images and processing the resulting masked regions. This dual-modality approach compensates for the limitations of 3D-only representations while leveraging the rich semantic understanding available in well-trained 2D foundation models.

The extracted 3D and 2D features are mapped into the LLM's token embedding space through separate visual-language projectors - three-layer MLPs that transform the high-dimensional visual features into representations compatible with the language model. The final scene representation consists of sequences of object-level embeddings, where each object is represented by its identifier token, 3D features, and 2D features.

## Task Unification and Training

A crucial contribution of Chat-Scene is the unification of diverse 3D scene-language tasks under a single conversational framework. Traditional approaches require task-specific architectures and heads for different objectives like visual grounding, dense captioning, and visual question answering. Chat-Scene transforms all these tasks into a unified question-answering format where object identifiers serve as the bridge between natural language and 3D objects.

The training process employs a single-stage approach using only cross-entropy loss on the language model's output. This contrasts with traditional two-stage methods that require separate alignment and fine-tuning phases. The model jointly optimizes the visual-language projectors and the LLM (using LoRA for efficiency) on aggregated data from five benchmarks: ScanRefer, Multi3DRef, Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and SQA3D.

The prompt template design enables natural interaction where users can reference specific objects using identifiers in their queries, and the assistant responds by including relevant object identifiers in its answers. For example, a user might ask "Find the closest trash bin to `<OBJ013>`" and receive a response like "The closest trash bin is `<OBJ023>`."

## Experimental Results and Performance Analysis

Chat-Scene demonstrates substantial improvements across all evaluated benchmarks, establishing new state-of-the-art results in multiple 3D scene understanding tasks. On visual grounding tasks, the model achieves 50.2% [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection) on ScanRefer and 52.4% [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection) on Multi3DRefer, representing improvements of 3.7% and 14.0% respectively over previous best methods.

For dense captioning on Scan2Cap, Chat-Scene scores 77.1% [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection), an 8.7% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art. The model also excels on visual question answering tasks, achieving 87.7% CIDEr on ScanQA and 54.6% EM on SQA3D, consistently outperforming existing LLM-based approaches.

The ablation studies reveal important insights about the methodology's components. The learnable object identifiers prove superior to both plain text descriptions and fixed embeddings, while also being more token-efficient (3N tokens versus 6N for plain text with N objects). The multi-modal object-centric representations show that 2D features alone often outperform 3D-only features, highlighting the value of semantic information from well-trained 2D foundation models. The combination of both modalities consistently yields the best performance.

## Video Input Capabilities

Chat-Scene extends beyond static 3D point clouds to handle 2D video input without depth information. Using DEVA, a tracking-based video detector, the system extracts object proposals from video frames and applies the same object-centric representation learning approach. Results show competitive performance on video-based grounding and VQA tasks, with [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection) of 22.8% for video grounding and comparable VQA performance to 3D input methods.

![Video Input Results](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2312.08168v4/img-2.jpeg "Video Input Results")

![Video Input Results](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2312.08168v4/img-2.jpeg "Video Input Results")

This capability demonstrates the flexibility of the object-centric approach and its potential for broader applications where 3D sensors may not be available.

## Limitations and Future Directions

Despite its strong performance, Chat-Scene exhibits certain limitations that point to important future research directions. The model struggles with accurate counting of large numbers of objects, particularly when individual object detection is imperfect. It also shows deficiencies in understanding structural elements like walls and floors, likely due to their exclusion from typical object-focused training annotations.

Fine-grained attribute distinctions, such as identifying objects by subtle color differences when multiple similar items are present, remain challenging. Additionally, ambiguous dataset annotations where descriptions could match multiple objects complicate evaluation and highlight the need for more precise annotation practices.

The qualitative analysis reveals that while Chat-Scene excels at basic spatial reasoning and object identification, it requires further development in contextual understanding of complex indoor environments and handling of ambiguous natural language descriptions.

## Significance and Impact

Chat-Scene represents a paradigm shift in 3D scene understanding by enabling object-level interaction within a unified conversational framework. The approach's significance extends beyond performance improvements to fundamental advances in how AI systems can understand and interact with 3D environments.

The methodology's ability to mitigate 3D data scarcity through pre-trained foundation models offers a practical solution to a persistent challenge in the field. By leveraging existing 2D and 3D knowledge rather than requiring vast amounts of paired 3D scene-language data, the approach makes high-quality 3D MLLMs more feasible to develop and deploy.

The unified task framework has broader implications for reducing architectural complexity and promoting more general-purpose AI systems. Rather than developing specialized models for each 3D understanding task, the single conversational interface supports diverse applications while maintaining strong performance across all evaluated benchmarks.

These advances have immediate practical applications in robotics, where precise object referencing is crucial for task execution, and in augmented reality systems that require natural language interfaces for 3D interaction. The work also opens pathways for more sophisticated AI assistants capable of understanding and manipulating complex real-world environments through natural conversation.

Chat-Scene (submitted September 28, 2024) is a research paper by authors from Zhejiang University and associated institutions (including Yilun Chen, Zehan Wang, Rongjie Huang, Runsen Xu, Tai Wang, Luping Liu, Xize Cheng, Jiangmiao Pang, and Zhou Zhao) that presents a unified framework for bridging 3D scene understanding with Large Language Models (LLMs).

Chat-Scene introduces two key innovations: (1) object identifiers (unique tokens like <OBJ013>) assigned to each object proposal for unambiguous referencing, and (2) object-centric representations leveraging pre-trained foundation models. The system uses Mask3D for 3D instance segmentation to decompose point clouds into object proposals, then extracts multi-modal features through parallel encoders - Uni3D (3D geometric features) and DINOv2 (2D semantic features from multi-view projection). These features are mapped into the LLM's embedding space via three-layer MLP projectors. The model transforms diverse 3D scene-language tasks (visual grounding, dense captioning, VQA) into a unified question-answering format without task-specific heads, training with a single-stage approach using cross-entropy loss and LoRA for efficiency on data from five benchmarks.

Two-dimensional features alone often outperform 3D-only features, with the combination yielding the best results. The model also extends to 2D video input via DEVA tracking, achieving 22.8% Acc@0.5 for video grounding.

LIMITATIONS: The model struggles with counting large numbers of objects, understanding structural elements (walls, floors), fine-grained attribute distinctions (e.g., subtle color differences), and ambiguous dataset annotations.

SIGNIFICANCE: The approach mitigates 3D data scarcity by leveraging pre-trained 2D/3D foundation models, reduces architectural complexity through a unified conversational framework, and has practical applications in robotics and augmented reality requiring object-level interaction with 3D environments.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Summary of UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding with Generated Language Conditions**

This paper, presented at CVPR, introduces UZ3DVG, a novel zero-shot 3D visual grounding (3DVG) framework that localizes target objects in 3D scenes using natural language descriptions. Unlike existing zero-shot methods that rely on additional 2D images or multi-turn interactions with large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) during inference—causing high latency and computational cost—UZ3DVG is the first zero-shot 3DVG model that, during inference, uses only 3D point clouds and text, without 2D imagery or external LLM/VLM interaction.

**Key Components:**
- **MSAG-RC (Multi-Source Spatial Annotation and Reasoning Chain Generator):** Processes RGB-D images to generate 3D spatial pseudo-labels and reasoning chains, bridging the gap between 2D foundation models and 3D labels.
- **RCD (Reasoning Chain Distillation):** Transfers reasoning knowledge from a large teacher network to a lightweight student network, enabling efficient inference.
- **GeoSM (Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling):** Captures both global and local geometric relationships to align textual reasoning with 3D spatial structures.
- **TSVDE (Text-Semantic-Guided Visual Detail Enhancement):** Enriches visual features with fine-grained details from text-relevant regions.

**Key Results:**
- Achieves state-of-the-art on ScanRefer: Acc@0.25/0.5 of 45.42%/41.08% (beats SeeGround by 1.32%/1.68%).
- On the challenging "Multiple" subset of ScanRefer: Acc@0.25/0.5 of 40.49%/36.33% (beats SeeGround by 6.49%/6.33%).
- On NR3D: Overall accuracy of 46.5%, surpassing ZSVG3D by 7.5% and SeeGround by 0.4%.
- Inference speed: 7.69 FPS (approximately 38× faster than SeeGround's 0.2 FPS).

**Training Paradigm:** A VLM is used only during training to generate pseudo-labels and reasoning chains. The lightweight 3DVG model is trained using these generated annotations and does not require any external models during inference.
</summary>

<summary>
This is a comprehensive survey paper on visual grounding in vision-language models (VLMs). Visual grounding refers to the ability of a model to identify regions within visual input that match textual descriptions. The paper covers:

**Definition:** Visual grounding is defined broadly as the capability to precisely localize and identify specific objects, regions, or concepts within a visual context, conditioned on natural language descriptions or instructions.

**Key Research Domains:**

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] LL3DA: Visual Interactive Instruction Tuning for Omni-3D Understanding ... ---
URL: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Chen_LL3DA_Visual_Interactive_Instruction_Tuning_for_Omni-3D_Understanding_Reasoning_and_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
LL3DA is a Large Language 3D Assistant (CVPR paper) presented by researchers from Fudan University, Tencent PCG, NUS, and A*STAR that enables a large language model to understand, reason, and plan in complex 3D environments. Unlike prior approaches that project multi-view 2D features into 3D space (which is computationally expensive and ignores geometry/depth information), LL3DA takes point clouds as direct input and responds to both textual instructions and visual interactions (clicks and 3D box annotations). This visual interaction capability helps remove ambiguities inherent in plain text instructions within cluttered 3D scenes.

Architecture: The model uses (1) a frozen masked transformer scene encoder pre-trained on ScanNet detection, (2) a visual prompt encoder that encodes user clicks via 3D Fourier positional embeddings and box annotations via ROI features from a pre-trained 3D detector, and (3) a multi-modal transformer (Q-Former inspired) that aggregates the 3D scene embeddings, visual prompts, and textual instructions into 32 learnable query tokens. These query tokens are projected as a prefix to the textual instructions for a frozen OPT-1.3B LLM backbone. 3D coordinates are converted to plain text tokens (e.g., '<obj>cx, cy, cz, w, h, l</obj>') with values discretized to [0,255] integers, fitting the existing LLM vocabulary without additional learnable tokens.

Key results: LL3DA achieves state-of-the-art performance on 3D Dense Captioning (74.17% C@0.25 and 65.19% C@0.5 on ScanRefer; 51.18% C@0.5 on Nr3D, beating Vote2Cap-DETR by +3.38% and +7.34%) and 3D Question Answering (76.79% CiDEr on ScanQA validation, surpassing 3D-LLM by +7.39%). Adding visual clicks at test time improves ScanQA CiDEr by +6.12%. Ablation studies show early fusion of visual prompts (+3.45% C@0.5), auxiliary "localize" instructions and click prompts improve performance, and textual instructions are beneficial. The model also functions as a generalist across tasks without fine-tuning, with generalist weights serving as strong initialization for fine-tuning.

Datasets: Trained on ScanNet (1,201 train / 312 validation scenes) with annotations from ScanRefer, Nr3D, ScanQA, and the ScanNet subset of 3D-LLM, covering dense captioning, QA, scene description, embodied conversation, and planning. Training requires no more than eight RTX 3090 GPUs within a day.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"LL3DA takes point cloud as the direct input and responds to both text instructions and visual interactions. The additional visual interaction enables LMMs to better comprehend human interactions with the 3D environment and further remove the ambiguities within plain texts."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Language-to-Space Programming for Training-Free 3D Visual Grounding ---
URL: https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.191.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, presented at EMNLP 2025, introduces Language-to-Space Programming (LASP), a training-free method for 3D visual grounding (3DVG). LASP addresses the dual challenges of accuracy and efficiency in 3DVG by using LLM-generated Python code as spatial relation encoders. These encoders compute relation features from object bounding boxes, and an automatic pipeline with test suites evaluates and optimizes the codes across multiple iterations.

Key methodology: (1) LLMs generate Python class-based spatial relation encoders (e.g., "above", "near", "left") that compute pairwise relation features from object geometry; (2) test suites evaluate the codes using test cases from the Nr3D dataset, synthesizing error messages for failed cases; (3) LLMs iteratively optimize codes based on these error messages up to Niter iterations; (4) a semantic parser converts referring utterances into symbolic expressions, and an executor aggregates category and relation features to compute matching scores; (5) a VLM (GPT-4o) module disambiguates candidates using stitched ScanNet images.

Results: LASP achieves 52.9% accuracy on the Nr3D dataset (60.7% easy, 45.3% hard), ranking among the best training-free methods. With ground-truth labels it reaches 67.8% accuracy. It substantially reduces grounding time (7.7s vs. 50.3s for VLM-Grounder) and token costs (3.1k vs. 12k tokens) compared to agent-based methods. On the GRScenes dataset, LASP achieves 90.0% accuracy vs. 15.6% for random baseline, demonstrating cross-dataset generalization. Replacing LLM-generated encoders with human-written functions drops accuracy to 44.0%, highlighting the value of the automated codes.

Ablation studies show the critical importance of optimization, error messages, and in-context examples for generating accurate relation encoders. LASP's codes implicitly learn dataset priors, such as viewpoint assumptions (in 98 of 100 "view-dependent" sentences, the anchor object is the "faced" object). The one-time offline code generation cost is amortized over all test instances.

Limitations include: performance gaps vs. recent supervised methods; symbolic expression struggles with ordinal phrases; limited relation coverage; simplified scene representation (bounding boxes only); test suites only handle atomic relations; and dependence on pre-trained 3D detectors/classifiers. Code is available at https://github.com/InternRobotics/LaSP. Authors are from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. The work is funded by the National Key R&D Program of China.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"LASP introduces LLM-generated codes to analyze 3D spatial relations among objects, along with a pipeline that evaluates and optimizes the codes automatically. Experimental results demonstrate that LASP achieves 52.9% accuracy on the Nr3D benchmark, ranking among the best training-free methods. Moreover, it substantially reduces the grounding time and token costs, offering a balanced trade-off between performance and efficiency."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: LL3DA: Visual Interactive Instruction Tuning for Omni-3D Understanding, Reasoning, and Planning ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2311.18651

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents LL3DA (Large Language 3D Assistant), a novel LMM-based approach for omni-3D understanding, reasoning, and planning. Unlike existing methods that rely on multi-view images projected to 3D (causing computational overhead and performance degradation), LL3DA takes point cloud data as direct input and responds to both textual instructions and visual prompts (user clicks and 3D box annotations).

**Methodology:** The model uses Interactor3D, a multi-modal transformer with a frozen 3D scene encoder (masked transformer pre-trained on ScanNet detection), a visual prompt encoder, and a Q-Former that aggregates information from textual instructions, visual prompts, and 3D scenes into 32 fixed-length learnable querying tokens. These are projected as prefixes to a frozen OPT-1.3B LLM. The Q-Former is initialized only with pre-trained BERT word and position embeddings (full BERT initialization caused repetitive outputs). 3D coordinates are converted to plain text using special tokens (e.g., "«loc»xx, yy, zz<</loc»") with values discretized to unsigned integers [0,255].

**Tasks covered:** 3D Dense Captioning, 3D Question Answering, Scene Description, and Embodied Conversation/Planning. Tasks use "### human:" and "### assistant:" identifiers for multi-turn conversations and distinguish between "describe" vs "describe and localize" (and "answer" vs "answer and localize") instructions.

**Key Results:**
- 3D Dense Captioning: Achieves 65.19% C@0.5 on ScanRefer (+3.38% over Vote2Cap-DETR) and 51.18% C@0.5 on Nr3D (+7.34%), surpassing all prior SOTA methods including multi-task pretrained models (UniT3D, 3DJCG, 3D-VLP) and 3D-VisTA.
- 3D Question Answering: Achieves 76.79% CiDEr on ScanQA validation, 78.16% on test with object, and 70.29% on test without object—surpassing 3D-LLM by +7.39% CiDEr on validation.
- Visual prompts (clicks) during QA evaluation improve results by +6.12% C by removing ambiguities.
- As a generalist (without fine-tuning), LL3DA achieves 62.98% C@0.5 on ScanRefer and 75.67% CiDEr on ScanQA, with fine-tuned weights serving as strong initialization (+2.35% C@0.5 over scratch training on ScanRefer).
- Ablations show unified transformer design (+3.45% C@0.5), auxiliary localization instructions, and click prompts all improve performance.

**Implementation details:** Trained with AdamW optimizer (weight decay 0.1, LR decaying from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶ with cosine annealing, ~100k iterations), batch size 16, ≤8 Nvidia RTX3090 (24G) GPUs within a day. Uses 40k sampled points per scene. Inference uses beam search (beam size 4) or top-k (k=50) + top-p (p=0.95) sampling. Supplementary evaluations show LL3DA significantly outperforms zero-shot frozen LLMs (OPT variants, LLAMA-7B) on scene description, embodied dialogue (best: 260.07 CiDEr with beam search), and embodied planning (best: 196.78 CiDEr with beam search). Codes and pre-trained weights will be fully released.
</summary>

This paper presents 3D-VisTA, a pre-trained Transformer model for 3D Vision and Text Alignment, designed to connect the 3D physical world with natural language for embodied intelligence. **Core Contributions:**
1. **3D-VisTA Architecture**: A simple, unified Transformer that uses vanilla self-attention layers for both single-modal modeling and multi-modal fusion, without sophisticated task-specific designs, auxiliary losses, or optimization tricks. 2. **ScanScribe Dataset**: The first large-scale 3D scene-text pairs dataset for 3D-VL pre-training, containing 278K 3D scene-text pairs for 2,995 RGB-D scans of 1,185 unique indoor scenes (from ScanNet and 3R-Scan), with 56.1K unique object instances. Text was sourced from existing datasets (ScanQA, ScanRefer, ReferIt3D), templates, and GPT-3 generation from scene graphs. Object diversity was increased by replacing 10% of objects with Objaverse 3D objects.

3. **Self-supervised Pre-training**: Uses three objectives - Masked Language Modeling (MLM), Masked Object Modeling (MOM), and Scene-Text Matching (STM) - to learn 3D point cloud and text alignment.

**Results (State-of-the-Art):**
- ScanRefer: improved by 8.1% (acc@0.5)
- Sr3D: improved by 3.6%
- Scan2Cap: improved by 10.1% (C@0.25) and 19.2% (C@0.5)
- ScanQA: improved by 3.5%/2.1% (EM@1)

- Ablation studies show 4-layer transformer depth is optimal, all three pre-training objectives are beneficial, and using all data sources (ScanNet, 3R-Scan, Objaverse) yields best performance

- Uses scene-graph-based prompting (from 3DSSG) for richer context compared to box-based prompting
- Proposes object-centric chain of thought (O-CoT) prompting to combat LLM hallucination
- Implements refinement procedures using regular expression matching and scene graph retrieval, achieving 100% accuracy on counting, existence, and non-existence QA tasks (vs. 40-96.8% for baseline methods)

- Surpasses state-of-the-art task-specific models on 3D captioning (Scan2Cap: CIDEr 72.4), 3D QA (ScanQA), and embodied reasoning (SQA3D), without task-specific fine-tuning

Geometric Constraint Temporal Adapter (GCTA): A module that constructs a cross-frame KNN graph based on spatial distance between point tubes, using EdgeConv-style edge features (combining global variation fj−fi with local structural features fi) and max pooling to capture long-term global dynamics.
The pre-trained model's backbone parameters are frozen; only the Point Tube Adapter, GCTA, position encoders (custom MLP-based, per-layer), and task head are fine-tuned.

Experimental results: The method was tested on 3D action recognition (MSR-Action3D) and gesture recognition (SHREC'17), using Point-BERT, Point-MAE, and PointGPT-S as baselines pre-trained on ShapeNet.
- On MSR-Action3D with 24 frames, Point-MAE+CSA achieved 95.12%, outperforming all supervised (best: X4D-SceneFormer at 93.90%) and self-supervised (best: C2P at 94.76%, MaST-Pre at 94.08%) methods across all temporal configurations.
- On SHREC'17, PointGPT-S+CSA reached 96.5%, Point-BERT+CSA achieved 96.2%, and Point-MAE+CSA got 95.2%—outperforming supervised (best: Kinet at 95.2%) and self-supervised (best: PointCMP at 93.3%) approaches.

Ablation studies (with Point-MAE on 12 frames): Baseline frozen model (A0) scored 77.35%; adding Point Tube Adapter (A1) reached 83.97%; adding position encoders (A2) reached 87.11%; Point Tube Adapter + GCTA (A3) reached 94.08%; full model (A4) reached 95.12%. The GCTA's optimal k-neighbors value was k=20 (95.12%), with performance degrading for too few (k=1 or 5) or too many (k=25, 30) neighbors. Using the full video as temporal slice length yielded the best performance (95.12%). The GCTA placed in a "Bypass" configuration produced the best accuracy. CSA outperformed other tuning strategies (valilla adapter, VPT-Deep, IDPT). Attention visualization confirmed the GCTA helps the model focus on key frames where actions occur.

Code is available at https://github.com/LvBaixuan/Point-CSA. The work is supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China grants and other funding agencies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"To address this, we propose a novel Cross-frame Spatio-temporal Adaptation (CSA) strategy by introducing the Point Tube Adapter as the embedding layer and the Geometric Constraint Temporal Adapter (GCTA) to enforce temporal consistency across frames."

--- SOURCE 21: [PDF] CORE-3D: CONTEXT-AWARE OPEN-VOCABULARY - OpenReview ---
URL: https://openreview.net/pdf/9a980b56e8e243213d30d276a3e469eafd2e879e.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces CORE-3D, a training-free pipeline for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding that addresses limitations in existing zero-shot 3D semantic mapping approaches. Current methods assign CLIP embedding vectors to 2D masks generated by vision-language models and project them into 3D, but they suffer from fragmented/incomplete masks (over-segmentation), limited semantic context when applying CLIP directly to isolated masks, and multi-view inconsistencies.

METHOD: The pipeline has three main contributions: (1) Progressive SemanticSAM refinement that incrementally adjusts granularity levels to generate more accurate and complete object-level masks than vanilla SAM, using overlap thresholds to remove redundancy and DBSCAN clustering to separate objects that are adjacent in 2D but separated in 3D; (2) A context-aware CLIP encoding strategy that aggregates five complementary crops per mask (mask crop, bounding box crop, large-context crop at 2.5x scale, huge-context crop at 4x scale, and surroundings crop at 3x scale with the mask blacked out), combined via weighted averaging where the surroundings embedding is subtracted with negative weight to enforce contrastive context; (3) Multi-view 3D mask merging using a symmetric-balanced IoV criterion and geometric heuristics to consolidate overlapping predictions, with averaged unified embeddings.

OBJECT RETRIEVAL: The pipeline extends to natural-language object retrieval in four stages: (1) Query structuring using an LLM to parse free-form queries into structured form Π(q) = (m, R, Ω) (main object, related objects, orientation constraints); (2) Candidate mining via CLIP similarity with top-K matching (avoiding score thresholds) and voxelization for deduplication; (3) View selection with VLM verification of candidates in RGB frames with bounding boxes; (4) Orientation grounding using canonical views at discretized yaw bins resolved by a VLM, followed by final LLM reasoning over verified candidates, referenced objects, and orientation cues.

RESULTS: On the Replica and ScanNet 3D semantic segmentation benchmarks, CORE-3D achieved the best performance across ALL evaluated approaches including training-based (LERF, OpenNeRF, LangSplat, OpenGaussian) and zero-shot methods (ConceptFusion, OpenMask3D, ConceptGraphs, HOV-SG, BBQ-CLIP). On Replica: mAcc 0.38, mIoU 0.29, fmIoU 0.56 (vs. BBQ-CLIP's 0.38/0.27/0.48). On ScanNet: mAcc 0.61, mIoU 0.36, fmIoU 0.46 (vs. BBQ-CLIP's 0.56/0.34/0.36). On the Sr3D+ benchmark (661 sampled instructions), the method achieved grounding accuracy of 41.8 (A@0.1) and 35.6 (A@0.25) overall, substantially outperforming baselines (BBQ: 34.2/22.7, BBQ-CLIP: 14.4/8.8, ConceptGraphs: 13.3/6.2, OpenFusion: 12.6/2.4).

ABLATIONS: Progressive multi-granularity mask generation outperforms vanilla SAM and single-granularity SemanticSAM configurations; context-aware CLIP embeddings strongly outperform the finetuned OvSeg model (same number of parameters as the Large CLIP backbone used, but no finetuning needed); and mask-size-based extension ratios outperform neighbor-coverage-based extension mechanisms.

IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS: Uses EVA02-CLIP (Large) for visual-text alignment, qwen2.5-vl-32b-instruct as the VLM, gpt-5-mini for object extraction, and openai-o4-mini for final decision-making. Experiments run on a single NVIDIA RTX4090 with VLM/LLM components accessed via external APIs. No 3D supervision or task-specific training required.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Existing foundation-model-based approaches still struggle to construct coherent and reliable 3D semantic maps." "We present a training-free pipeline that overcomes these challenges by improving both segmentation and embedding generation through progressive refinement and context-aware encoding." "Our method achieves the best performance across all evaluated approaches—including both training-based and zero-shot methods." "Our method substantially outperforms all baselines across both IoU thresholds and all difficulty subsets." "Our results suggest that leveraging richer 2D segmentation and embedding strategies is a powerful alternative to supervision-heavy pipelines, especially in cluttered, open-world environments."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 24: ConceptFusion: Open-set Multimodal 3D Mapping ---
URL: https://concept-fusion.github.io

SUMMARY:
<summary>
ConceptFusion is an open-source research project (presented at Robotics: Science and Systems, RSS 2023) that builds open-set, multimodal 3D maps of environments. Unlike existing semantic 3D mapping approaches that operate in a "closed-set" setting (limited to a finite set of concepts predefined at training time and queryable only via class labels or text), ConceptFusion is (i) fundamentally open-set, enabling reasoning beyond a closed set of concepts, and (ii) inherently multi-modal, supporting diverse query types including language, images, audio, and 3D geometry, all working together.

The method leverages the open-set capabilities of foundation models pretrained on internet-scale data (e.g., CLIP) to reason across modalities. It constructs pixel-aligned features from off-the-shelf foundation models that typically only produce image-level (global) embeddings via a proposed zero-shot pixel alignment technique: it processes images to generate class-agnostic object masks, extracts local features per region, computes a global image feature, and fuses region-specific (local) and global features. This approach captures long-tailed and fine-grained concepts that supervised methods like LSeg and OpenSeg forget during fine-tuning.

Key technical contributions and findings:
- Achieves effective zero-shot spatial reasoning without any additional training or fine-tuning.
- Outperforms supervised approaches by more than 40% margin on 3D IoU when retaining long-tailed concepts.
- Demonstrates 3D spatial reasoning (e.g., "What is the distance between the refrigerator and the television?") using a large language model to parse queries into executable function calls.
- Handles long-form text queries, click-queries (with cosine similarity retrieval), and audio/image queries.
- Introduces the UnCoCo dataset: 20 RGB-D sequences with 78 commonly found objects, annotated with text, audio, click, and image queries plus ground-truth 2D and 3D retrieval results (created because no existing dataset supported evaluating long-tailed and multimodal reasoning).

The paper evaluates ConceptFusion on real-world datasets, simulated home environments, a real-world tabletop manipulation task (e.g., pushing objects like "goldfish" brand snacks or a "Baymax" plush toy to specified locations), and an autonomous driving platform (successfully navigating to a "football field" based on open-set text query).

Multiple author affiliations include MIT, Université de Montréal, University of Toronto, IIIT Hyderabad, CMU, Amazon, Matician, and DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory. The project also lists concurrent work including CLIP-Fields, OpenScene, LERF, NLMap-SayCan, and 3D-CLR.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding from Vision-Language ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.22429

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This arXiv paper (arXiv:2505.22429v1, 28 May 2025) introduces SeeGround, a training-free, zero-shot 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) framework that leverages 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to localize objects in 3D scenes without requiring 3D-specific training or labeled data. The framework bypasses the need for expensive 3D supervision by using a hybrid input format that pairs query-aligned rendered 2D images with spatially enriched textual descriptions derived from a 3D object detector (via an Object Lookup Table, OLT).

**Core Architecture:** SeeGround consists of three main components: (1) a Multimodal 3D Representation module that converts 3D scenes into a hybrid representation combining rendered 2D images with text-based spatial descriptions; (2) a Perspective Adaptation Module (PAM) that dynamically selects optimal viewpoints based on the query (using an anchor object identified by the VLM to orient the virtual camera); and (3) a Fusion Alignment Module (FAM) that uses depth-aware visual prompting to align 2D visual features with 3D spatial semantics, reducing grounding ambiguity in cluttered scenes.

**Key Results:** On ScanRefer, SeeGround achieves 75.7%/68.9% at Acc@0.25/0.5 on the "Unique" split and 34.0%/30.0% on "Multiple", surpassing all zero-shot and weakly supervised baselines (7.7% improvement over prior zero-shot methods) while approaching fully supervised performance. On Nr3D, it achieves 46.1% overall accuracy, a +7.1% improvement over the prior zero-shot state-of-the-art (ZSVG3D), with 54.5% Easy, 38.3% Hard, 42.3% View-Dependent, and 48.2% View-Independent scores. The method uses Qwen2-VL-72b as the VLM and Mask3D for object detection, though it also works with OVIR-3D and improves to 59.5% with ground-truth boxes.

**Ablation findings:** Each component contributes incrementally — 3D positions alone (37.7%), adding layout (39.7%), adding color/texture (39.5%), adding FAM (43.3%), adding PAM (45.0%), and full configuration (46.1%). Query-aligned dynamic viewpoint selection consistently outperforms static strategies (Center2Corner, Edge2Center, Corner2Center, and Bird's Eye View). The method is also robust to incomplete textual descriptions, using visual context to identify targets even when anchor objects are missing from text (which causes LLM-based methods like ZSVG3D to fail).

**Limitations:** Error analysis of 185 sampled cases shows spatial relation errors remain frequent (19%), and the method struggles with complex egocentric references and limited rendering quality from raw point clouds.
</summary>

"We present SeeGround, a zero-shot 3DVG framework that leverages 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to bypass the need for 3D-specific training."

--- SOURCE 4: 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/3d-visual-grounding-3dvg

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page provides a comprehensive overview of 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG), the task of localizing objects in 3D scenes (point clouds, meshes, LiDAR sweeps) using free-form natural language descriptions, outputting oriented/axis-aligned 3D bounding boxes or instance masks. 3DVG is fundamental for robotics, embodied AI, AR/VR, and multimodal interaction.

Key task variants include scene input modalities (indoor RGB-D point clouds like ScanNet/ScanRefer, outdoor LiDAR like Talk2Car-3D, implicit representations like 3D Gaussians), supervision regimes (fully supervised, zero-shot, cross-dataset, multi-task), and query richness (from synthetic spatial templates to linguistically diverse prompts with negation, counting, coreference). A generalized real-world formulation takes as input prior scans, current scenes, memory banks of RGB-D views, and natural-language queries.

Major datasets include: ScanRefer/ScanNet (>50K queries over 800 scenes), ReferIt3D (Nr3D/Sr3D), 3RScan/ChangingGrounding (dynamic scenes, 1,482 scans, 478 environments), ViGiL3D (diagnostic benchmark of 350 prompts across 30 linguistic metrics), and outdoor Talk2Car-3D (7,115/998/2,056 splits for autonomous driving). Metrics include Accuracy @ IoU=0.25/0.5, Recall@1, action/motion cost, and dense mask-based F1.

<summary>
This is a research paper titled "CLIP2Point: Transfer CLIP to Point Cloud Classification with Image-Depth Pre-Training," authored by researchers from Harbin Institute of Technology, Shanghai AI Laboratory, City University of Hong Kong, University of Hong Kong, and Peng Cheng Laboratory.

**Problem & Approach:**
The paper addresses the challenge of transferring vision-language (V-L) pre-trained models (specifically CLIP) to 3D point cloud tasks. The authors note that pre-training across 3D vision and language is limited by insufficient training data (CLIP uses 400M+ image-text pairs, while 3D datasets like ScanNet have only ~100k pairs). They propose CLIP2Point, an image-depth pre-training method using contrastive learning to transfer CLIP knowledge to the 3D domain.

**Key Methodological Contributions:**
1. **Pre-training Data**: Rendered 52,460 pairs of RGB images and depth maps from ShapeNet (55 object categories) using 10 views, with a new depth rendering setting that uses the minimum depth value (rather than weighted summation) with a dilation rate of 2 for better visual effect.
2. **Pre-training Scheme**: Combines intra-modality learning (enhancing invariance of depth aggregation across varying camera distances) and cross-modality learning (aligning depth features with frozen CLIP image features via contrastive losses).
3. **Gated Dual-Path Adapter (GDPA)**: A dual-path structure with global-view aggregators and gated fusion, allowing the ensemble of both CLIP visual encoder and pre-trained depth encoder for efficient downstream adaptation.

**Key Results:**
- Zero-shot classification: ModelNet10 improved from 30.23% (PointCLIP) to 66.63%; ModelNet40 from 20.18% to 49.38%; ScanObjectNN (S-OBJ ONLY) from 15.15% to 35.46%.
- 16-shot classification: Achieved 89.79% accuracy (vs 87.46% without pre-training, and 83.83% for PointCLIP with ViT-B/32).
- Fully-supervised classification on ModelNet40: Achieved 94.2% accuracy (1,024 points, 10 views), outperforming P2P (HorNet-L, 94.0% with 4,096 points, 40 views) and self-supervised methods like Point-MAE (93.8%).
- Ablation studies confirmed intra-modality learning adds 11.09% improvement, and the dual-path structure with gated fusion provides complementary benefits.

**Implementation Details:**
- Used ViT-B/32 vision transformer architecture, LAMB optimizer with learning rate 6×10-3 for pre-training (100 epochs, batch size 256).
- Pre-training data split: 41,943 training and 10,517 validation pairs. RGB image zero-shot accuracy was 54.21% vs 19.98% for depth maps before pre-training.

**Limitations & Future Work:**
The authors note that synthetic pre-training data limits performance on real-world noisy datasets with backgrounds. Future work includes using more realistic data and extending to other 3D tasks (detection, segmentation) and modalities (e.g., near-infrared images). Code is available at https://github.com/tyhuang0428/CLIP2Point.

This paper presents ImagineNav, a mapless, open-vocabulary object navigation framework that leverages Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for embodied navigation. This converts the ObjectNav task into a sequence of point-goal subtasks, requiring no fine-tuning and enabling zero-shot generalization to novel targets.

URL: https://siyuanhuang.com/files/3DLLM_CVPR_v2.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This presentation by Siyuan Huang (BIGAI) addresses whether current approaches to 3D Large Language Models (LLMs) are on the right path. It discusses the challenges of 3D scene understanding compared to 2D images (more objects, spatial relations, occlusion, clutter), and notes that 2D MLLMs significantly underperform humans on 3D scene understanding benchmarks like VSI-Bench (CVPR 2025).

The talk reviews key 3D-VL datasets (ScanRefer, ReferIt3D, SceneVerse, Multi3DRefer, ScanQA, SQA3D, 3D-GRAND, MSR3D) and models (3D-LLM, LEO, Chat-Scene, LL3DA, 3D-VisTA, LLM-Grounder), but argues that existing 3D-LLMs fail to generalize well despite benchmark improvements.

The presenter identifies three key pitfalls in 3D-VL evaluation, introducing their Beacon3D benchmark (CVPR 2025):
1. **Flawed test data** — blind LLMs achieve good results on SQA3D (visual ignorance), showing models can perform tasks without visual input
2. **Insufficient evaluation metrics** — models are susceptible to language variations (weak language robustness); rephrasing texts elicits different results
3. **Isolation of grounding and QA tasks** — probing (PQ3D) reveals poor grounding-QA coherence

Beacon3D offers high-quality test data (800+ objects across ScanNet, 3RScan, MultiScan; diverse knowledge types), object-centric evaluation metrics, and Grounding-QA Chains with Chain-of-Analysis. Key findings: object-centric metrics show significant performance drops (particularly in QA); grounding-QA coherence is weak (both correct ≤ 20%); half of QA failures stem from bad answering skills, and half of QA successes stem from shortcuts or overfitting.

Regarding LLM integration: incorporating LLMs weakens grounding and does not fundamentally enhance QA (w/o LLM ≈ LLM-based), because current 3D QA tasks only involve basic language modeling — the bottleneck lies in perception and VL alignment.

The presentation proposes two improvement paths:
1. **Perception (LEO-VL)**: bridging 2D-3D perception with efficient representation, reducing tokens to 33% while achieving SOTA performance and higher efficiency
2. **Reasoning (SceneCOT)**: eliciting chain-of-thought reasoning in 3D scenes via explicit visual grounding, region recognition, entity grounding, symbolic engines, and grounded reasoning — demonstrating SOTA performance in situated reasoning (SQA3D, MSQA) and object-centric reasoning (Beacon3D), particularly in counting and spatial relations

The summary of the "right path": Evaluation needs Beacon3D-style rigorous metrics, Perception should use efficient 2D-3D bridging (LEO-VL), and Reasoning should leverage CoT (SceneCOT). The presenter emphasizes that aligned VL representation and unleashing LLM reasoning capability are the most promising paths, and post-training remains underexplored but promising for reliable models.
</summary>
