URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.28490v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces SSR3D-LLM (Structured Spatial Reasoning 3D-LLM), a unified 3D-LLM framework for fine-grained 3D object grounding. The core problem addressed: existing unified 3D-LLMs (like Grounded 3D-LLM and Chat-Scene) use single-pointer grounding (QPG), where one pointer selection compresses all query cues (target category, attributes, context objects, spatial relations) into a single decision—this is brittle for fine-grained queries with multiple same-class distractors.

The proposed method, Structured Spatial Grounding (S3G), replaces the single-pointer readout with a sequence of latent spatial reasoning steps. Key components:
- The LLM writes K=4 latent step-marker tokens and M=16 memory tokens from the query over fixed Mask3D object proposals.
- A geometry-aware scorer refines candidate rankings step by step, using a step-length mask (learned length predictor) to freeze updates after useful steps.
- Training uses standard target supervision plus auxiliary referential cues (derived from benchmarks or via an offline Qwen/vLLM annotator for open-form queries) to supervise the latent steps.
- At inference, only the original query and Mask3D proposals are used; latent steps are not decoded as text.
- Grounding-specific updates are confined to lightweight adapters/modules to preserve default language capability.

Results across benchmarks:
- Nr3D: 50.3% accuracy (vs. Grounded 3D-LLM 32.8%, Chat-Scene 25.9%).
- ScanRefer: 58.7/53.9 Acc@0.25/0.50 (vs. Chat-Scene 55.5/50.2, Grounded 3D-LLM 48.6/44.0).
- Multi3DRef: 63.1/57.9 F1@0.25/0.50 (vs. Chat-Scene 57.1/52.4, Grounded 3D-LLM 44.7/40.8).

Language capabilities are preserved (comparable CIDEr/EM scores on dialog, QA, captioning, description without the grounding token). The readout is one-pass and much faster than QPG (e.g., Nr3D latency 0.0363 s/query vs. Grounded 3D-LLM 1.1610) with GPU memory of ~5.8 GB. Ablations show removing step mask and shuffling/reversing steps sharply degrade performance, confirming the ordered latent steps are used.

Limitations: depends on upstream Mask3D proposal quality; fixed step budget K=4 may limit longer relational chains; trained on static ScanNet-style indoor scenes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"3D object grounding localizes referred objects in a 3D scene from natural language. Unified instance-centric 3D-LLMs aim to solve grounding together with dialog, QA, and captioning, yet many rely on a single pointer-style grounding decision that compresses a relational instruction into one selection. This is brittle for fine-grained queries where multiple same-class candidates must be ruled out by context objects and spatial relations."

--- SOURCE 1: 3DVG-Transformer: Relation Modeling for Visual Grounding on Point Clouds ---
URL: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2021/papers/Zhao_3DVG-Transformer_Relation_Modeling_for_Visual_Grounding_on_Point_Clouds_ICCV_2021_paper.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents 3DVG-Transformer, a novel relation-aware visual grounding method for 3D point clouds presented by researchers from Beihang University (Lichen Zhao, Daigang Cai, Lu Sheng) and the University of Sydney (Dong Xu). The method formulates visual grounding as a grounding-by-detection problem and addresses two key limitations of prior work: (1) modeling complex relations for generating context-aware object proposals, and (2) leveraging proposal relations to distinguish true target objects from similar proposals.

The framework consists of three modules. The object proposal generation module uses a newly designed coordinate-guided contextual aggregation (CCA) module, which stacks coordinate-guided transformer layers that add a block-wise sparse spatial proximity matrix to the attention matrix to explicitly model relative spatial locations between proposals (with k1=20 neighbors for self-attention and k2=5 for cross-attention). The language encoding module uses a GRU cell with GloVE word embeddings. The cross-modal fusion module uses a multiplex attention (MA) module with interlaced self-attention and cross-attention blocks to disambiguate grounding results. Two optional feature augmentation strategies address overfitting: proposal copy & paste and word erase.

Key experimental results: On ScanRefer validation set (2D+3D), the method achieves Acc@0.25 of 47.57% and Acc@0.5 of 34.67% (overall), significantly outperforming baselines. On the "multiple" subset it achieves 39.30% Acc@0.25 and 28.42% Acc@0.5, with gains exceeding 6.5% and 5.2% over prior SOTA. On the ScanRefer online test set it achieves 49.76% Acc@0.25 and 35.12% Acc@0.5 overall. On Nr3D and Sr3D datasets it achieves overall accuracies of 40.8% and 51.4%, outperforming InstanceRefer by 2.0% and 3.4% respectively, particularly excelling on the challenging "hard" and "view-indep." subsets.

The ablation study confirms each component contributes to performance: removing both CCA and MA drops accuracy from 47.57% to 41.45% Acc@0.25, and the additive approach for fusing the spatial proximity matrix ("Add SPM") outperforms multiplication or omitting it entirely. The method shows particular strength in complex scenarios containing multiple objects of the same category and with long textual descriptions. The work was supported by the National Key Research and Development Project of China (No. 2018AAA0101900) and NSF of China (No. 61906012).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We propose a relation-aware visual grounding method on 3D point clouds, named as 3DVG-Transformer, to fully utilize the contextual clues for relation-enhanced proposal generation and cross-modal proposal disambiguation, which are enabled by a newly designed coordinate-guided contextual aggregation (CCA) module in the object proposal generation stage, and a multiplex attention (MA) module in the cross-modal feature fusion stage."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: [PDF] Point Transformer - CVF Open Access ---
URL: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2021/papers/Zhao_Point_Transformer_ICCV_2021_paper.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents the Point Transformer, a self-attention network architecture designed for 3D point cloud processing. The authors, from University of Oxford, HKU, CUHK, and Intel Labs, argue that transformers are naturally suited for point clouds since self-attention is fundamentally a set operator (invariant to permutation and cardinality), making it appropriate for point sets embedded in metric space.

**Methodology:** The core contribution is the Point Transformer layer, which applies vector self-attention locally on k-nearest-neighbor neighborhoods (k=16) around each point. The layer incorporates a trainable, parameterized relative position encoding that is added to both the attention generation branch and the feature transformation branch. The network architecture uses a U-net design with five encoder stages (downsampling rates [1,4,4,4,4]), transition-down modules (using farthest point sampling and kNN-based max pooling), transition-up modules (using trilinear interpolation), and is built entirely from self-attention layers, pointwise transformations, and pooling—no convolutions are used for preprocessing or auxiliary branches.

**Key Results:** The Point Transformer sets new state-of-the-art results across three benchmarks:
- S3DIS semantic segmentation (Area 5): 70.4% mIoU, 76.5% mAcc, 90.8% OA—first model to cross the 70% mIoU threshold, improving on prior state-of-the-art by 3.3 percentage points; 73.5% mIoU with 6-fold cross-validation. The model has only 4.9M parameters vs. 14.9M (KPConv) and 30.1M (SparseConv)
- ModelNet40 shape classification: 93.7% overall accuracy and 90.6% mAcc
- ShapeNetPart object part segmentation: 86.6% instance mIoU, 83.7% category mIoU

**Ablation Studies (on S3DIS Area 5):** k=16 neighbors is optimal. Relative position encoding outperforms absolute or no encoding, and adding it to both branches is important. Vector attention (70.4% mIoU) significantly outperforms scalar attention (64.6%), MLP+pooling (63.7%), and plain MLP (61.7%), demonstrating that channel-wise adaptive attention is highly beneficial for 3D data. Softmax normalization is essential (70.4% vs 66.5% mIoU without).

**Implementation:** Built in PyTorch using SGD optimizer (momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0001), 40K iterations with learning rate 0.5 (dropped by 10x at steps 24K and 32K) for S3DIS; 200 epochs with initial learning rate 0.05 (dropped at epochs 120 and 160) for ModelNet40 and ShapeNetPart.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Self-attention networks have revolutionized natural language processing... [The] self-attention operator, which is at the core of transformer networks, is in essence a set operator: it is invariant to permutation and cardinality of the input elements. The application of self-attention to 3D point clouds is therefore quite natural, since point clouds are essentially sets embedded in 3D space."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Point2Real: Bridging the Gap between Point Cloud and ... ---
URL: https://rpwang.net/publications/Point2Real_Bridging%20the%20Gap%20between%20Point%20Cloud%20and%20Realistic%20Image%20for%20Open-World%203D%20Recognition_AAAI2024.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents Point2Real, a training-free framework for open-world 3D point cloud recognition that bridges the domain gap between discrete 3D point clouds and the 2D Vision-Language domain (e.g., CLIP). The authors (Hanxuan Li, Bin Fu, Ruiping Wang, Xilin Chen from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) identify three primary sources of the domain gap: shape (discrete vs. continuous geometry), texture (point clouds lack texture information), and view (an extra dimension requiring discriminative viewpoint selection).

Point2Real consists of three modules:
1. **Shape Recovery Module**: Converts discrete point clouds into meshes using an iterative ball-pivoting algorithm (with holes filling and smoothing) to approximate real-world continuous geometry.
2. **Texture Rendering Module**: Uses ray tracing-based rendering with a texture candidate list (beige, metallic green, leather red, pink, brown, dark grey), selecting the most suitable texture via CLIP classification confidence.
3. **Multi-view Adapter**: A heuristic algorithm using depth surface area as an indicator of viewpoint discriminability, generating weights for feature aggregation across multiple views.

**Key Results:**
- Zero-shot classification (Table 1): Achieves state-of-the-art results on ModelNet10 (79.5%), ModelNet40 (65.8%), and ScanObjectNN (57.7% OBJ ONLY, 53.0% OBJ BG, 38.1% PB T50 RS), surpassing all training-free methods and most training-based methods. It exceeds PointCLIP V2 by +6.4% on ModelNet10, +1.6% on ModelNet40, and +7.6%, +12.2%, +2.7% on the three ScanObjectNN splits respectively.
- Few-shot classification (Table 5): Consistently outperforms PointCLIP and PointCLIP+RSP across 1, 2, 4, 8, 16-shot settings on ModelNet40 (67.5% vs 52.6% at one-shot; 86.3% vs 86.3% at 16-shot), with the greatest advantage in data-limited settings.
- Ablation studies confirm that texture information yields substantial improvements (CLIP is texture-sensitive), iterative ball-pivoting outperforms single iteration and Poisson reconstruction, and the Multi-view Adapter adds value especially in real-world scenarios where viewpoint recognizability cannot be assumed.

**Implementation details:** 5 iterations of ball-pivoting with radii (5,4,3,2,1), rendering via Blender Python API with Cycles engine, 10 viewpoints, ViT-B/16 backbone, 1024 input points. Blender-based Point2Real completes inference within ~3 seconds (2.936s), with a faster PyTorch3D version at 0.0397s. Code is publicly available at github.com/HanXuan-Li/Point2Real. The framework extends to few-shot tasks via a dual-path network that fuses rendered image and depth map features with a three-layer MLP with residual connections.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Point2Real leverages a shape recovery module that devises an iterative ball-pivoting algorithm to convert point clouds into meshes, narrowing the gap in shape at first. To simulate photo-realistic images, a set of refined textures as candidates is applied for rendering, where the CLIP confidence is utilized to select the suitable one."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: PointCLIP: Point Cloud Understanding by CLIP [Quick Review] ---
URL: https://liner.com/review/pointclip-point-cloud-understanding-by-clip

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a detailed review of the research paper "PointCLIP: Point Cloud Understanding by CLIP" by Renrui Zhang and Ziyu Guo et al., published December 4, 2021, with 71 references and 485 citations. The paper addresses the challenge of transferring CLIP's 2D pre-trained knowledge to 3D point cloud recognition, enabling zero-shot classification of "unseen" 3D objects without costly retraining.

**Proposed Method:** PointCLIP projects point clouds onto multi-view depth maps (without rendering) and aggregates view-wise zero-shot predictions using CLIP's 2D pre-trained encoders. Key components include:
- A learnable inter-view adapter that extracts compact global features from concatenated multi-view features via residual connections, fine-tuned with few-shot 3D data while freezing CLIP's encoders.
- The framework can also serve as a multi-knowledge ensembling module, boosting fully-trained 3D networks by combining complementary 2D contrastive knowledge.

**Key Experimental Results:**
- Zero-shot classification achieved 30.23% accuracy on ModelNet10, 20.18% on ModelNet40, and 15.38% on ScanObjectNN (which faces increased category counts and real-world noise).
- Performance is highly sensitive to projection settings (projection distance and depth map side length), with optimal settings varying across datasets.
- Prompt design significantly impacts accuracy; "point cloud depth map of a [CLASS]." yielded the best results (20.18% on ModelNet40).
- Increasing projected views improves performance initially, but more than 6 views introduces redundancy and decay. The right view is often most informative, while top and bottom views contribute less.
- Visual encoder choice matters; larger models like RN50 x 16 achieved 23.78% on ModelNet40, but simply increasing depth does not guarantee improved accuracy.

The review outlines 8 research questions covering zero-shot performance, projection settings, prompt design, few-shot classification via inter-view adapter, ensembling capabilities, adapter architecture, fusion ratio optimization, and full training-set fine-tuning.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
PointCLIP demonstrates promising zero-shot classification capabilities on 3D point cloud datasets, effectively transferring 2D pre-trained knowledge without any 3D training. It achieves 30.23% accuracy on ModelNet10, but performance decreases on more complex datasets like ModelNet40 (20.18%) and ScanObjectNN (15.38%).

--- SOURCE 11: ScanQA: 3D Question Answering for Spatial Scene Understanding [Quick Review] ---
URL: https://liner.com/review/scanqa-3d-question-answering-for-spatial-scene-understanding

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (Dec 20, 2021, by Daich Azuma, Taiki Miyanishi, and others; 54 references, 237 citations) presents ScanQA, a novel 3D Question Answering (3D-QA) framework for spatial scene understanding. The motivation is that existing 2D-QA models struggle with spatial understanding of object alignment, directions, and localization in 3D scenes, while current 3D datasets are constrained by size and template-based question variety. The proposed ScanQA baseline model processes textual questions and entire 3D scene visual information (point clouds and RGB frames) to predict answers and corresponding 3D bounding boxes for referenced objects. It integrates three layers: a 3D & language encoder (transforming questions into contextualized word representations and point clouds into object proposals), a 3D & language fusion layer (combining 3D object features with language using transformer-based encoder/decoder layers), and an object localization & QA layer that estimates target object boxes and predicts answers, enabling synergistic learning between localization and QA.

Key experimental results: ScanQA significantly outperforms all 2D-based and 3D-based baselines across all evaluation metrics (EM@1, EM@10, BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, CIDEr, SPICE) and data splits. On the 'Test w/ objects' split, ScanQA achieves EM@1 of 23.45 versus 22.31 for the best 2D baseline (RandomImage+MCAN) and 20.56 for the best 3D baseline (ScanRefer+MCAN e2e). End-to-end training with 3D and language information is crucial, and jointly optimizing object localization and QA yields a more coherent scene-language understanding. While oracle-enhanced 2D baselines can be competitive, ScanQA outperforms them without relying on impractical oracle settings. Human performance on ScanQA is EM@1 of 51.6, indicating significant room for improvement. The research explored five questions: comparison to baselines (RQ1), impact of localization/classification modules (RQ2), different 3D feature representations (RQ3), model parameter variations like layers and hidden size (RQ4), and performance across different question types (RQ5).
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces ScanQA, a new 3D Question Answering (3D-QA) task and baseline model for spatial scene understanding, submitted on May 7, 2022, by researchers affiliated with Kyoto University and RIKEN. The task extends 2D VQA to 3D indoor scenes, requiring models to process complete visual information from RGB-D scans, answer natural language questions, and localize relevant objects in 3D space. Unlike navigation-based embodied QA, ScanQA focuses on static scene understanding with complete 3D information available upfront.

Key contributions include:
- **ScanQA dataset**: Built on 800 indoor scenes from ScanNet, containing 41,363 question-answer pairs, 32,337 unique questions, and 16,999 unique answers. Experimental results showed the ScanQA model consistently outperformed baselines, particularly 2D-based methods (RandomImage+MCAN), confirming the limitations of 2D approaches for 3D spatial reasoning. A crucial finding was that end-to-end training (joint learning of localization and QA) significantly outperformed pipeline approaches. Human performance established an upper bound with an EM@1 score of 51.6. Ablation studies showed geometric features (xyz coordinates) provided a strong foundation, while RGB values showed inconsistent benefits. The work has applications in robotics, augmented reality, smart environments, and accessibility technologies, with future directions including more sophisticated 3D feature representations and extension to outdoor environments.

This presentation by Siyuan Huang (BIGAI) addresses whether current approaches to 3D Large Language Models (LLMs) are on the right path. The talk reviews key 3D-VL datasets (ScanRefer, ReferIt3D, SceneVerse, Multi3DRefer, ScanQA, SQA3D, 3D-GRAND, MSR3D) and models (3D-LLM, LEO, Chat-Scene, LL3DA, 3D-VisTA, LLM-Grounder), but argues that existing 3D-LLMs fail to generalize well despite benchmark improvements.

The presenter identifies three key pitfalls in 3D-VL evaluation, introducing their Beacon3D benchmark (CVPR 2025):
1. **Flawed test data** — blind LLMs achieve good results on SQA3D (visual ignorance), showing models can perform tasks without visual input
2. **Insufficient evaluation metrics** — models are susceptible to language variations (weak language robustness); rephrasing texts elicits different results
3. **Isolation of grounding and QA tasks** — probing (PQ3D) reveals poor grounding-QA coherence

Beacon3D offers high-quality test data (800+ objects across ScanNet, 3RScan, MultiScan; diverse knowledge types), object-centric evaluation metrics, and Grounding-QA Chains with Chain-of-Analysis. Key findings: object-centric metrics show significant performance drops (particularly in QA); grounding-QA coherence is weak (both correct ≤ 20%); half of QA failures stem from bad answering skills, and half of QA successes stem from shortcuts or overfitting.

Regarding LLM integration: incorporating LLMs weakens grounding and does not fundamentally enhance QA (w/o LLM ≈ LLM-based), because current 3D QA tasks only involve basic language modeling — the bottleneck lies in perception and VL alignment.

The presentation proposes two improvement paths:
1. **Perception (LEO-VL)**: bridging 2D-3D perception with efficient representation, reducing tokens to 33% while achieving SOTA performance and higher efficiency
2. **Reasoning (SceneCOT)**: eliciting chain-of-thought reasoning in 3D scenes via explicit visual grounding, region recognition, entity grounding, symbolic engines, and grounded reasoning — demonstrating SOTA performance in situated reasoning (SQA3D, MSQA) and object-centric reasoning (Beacon3D), particularly in counting and spatial relations

The summary of the "right path": Evaluation needs Beacon3D-style rigorous metrics, Perception should use efficient 2D-3D bridging (LEO-VL), and Reasoning should leverage CoT (SceneCOT). The presenter emphasizes that aligned VL representation and unleashing LLM reasoning capability are the most promising paths, and post-training remains underexplored but promising for reliable models.

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

**Surveys and overviews**

1. **Awesome-Visual-Grounding survey (TPAMI 2025)** [1]: A comprehensive survey on visual grounding accepted by TPAMI in 2025, maintained by Linhui Xiao et al. It covers the past decade of visual grounding research, including main tasks (Referring Expression Comprehension, Phrase Grounding), settings (fully supervised, weakly supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, zero-shot, multi-task, generalized visual grounding), method categories (traditional CNN-based, Transformer-based, VLP-based, grounding-oriented pre-training, and Grounding Multimodal LLMs), and applications including 3D visual grounding, video object grounding, and robotic/multimodal agent applications. The survey claims it is "the first survey in the past five years to systematically track and summarize the development of visual grounding over the last decade" and "currently the most comprehensive review in the field of visual grounding." Related works include OneRef (NeurIPS 2024), HiVG (ACM MM 2024), and CLIP-VG (TMM 2023).

2. **Visual Grounding in 2D and 3D survey (Information Fusion, Vol. 126, Feb 2026)** [2]: Claims to be the first comprehensive survey to systematically integrate research across both 2D Visual Grounding (2DVG) and 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG). It categorizes core methodologies, focusing on the evolution from two-stage paradigms (generating candidate regions then matching with text queries) to one-stage paradigms (end-to-end efficiency via direct regression or set prediction). Emerging trends include integration of LLMs for enhanced semantic reasoning, cross-dimensional knowledge transfer between 2D and 3D VG, and monocular 3DVG. It covers benchmark datasets (RefCOCO/+/g for 2D, ScanRefer for 3D), evaluation metrics, and performance benchmarks, and identifies key challenges and future research directions. The article has 254 references and has been cited 17 times; publication volume in VG shows a clear upward trend across CVPR, ICCV, NeurIPS, and AAAI.

3. **"Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models" (arXiv:2509.10345 — note: arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed venues)** [3]: A survey defining visual grounding as "the ability of a model to identify a region within some visual input that matches a textual description." Key research domains: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) and Generalized REC (GREC), Grounded Visual Question Answering (GVQA), Grounded Captioning (GC), GUI agents, and grounded reasoning. Representation methods: object-centric vs. pixel-level approaches, discretized vs. raw coordinate formats, and the Set-of-Marks (SOM) method. Architecture components: vision encoder (typically CLIP-based ViT; SigLIP shown to slightly outperform CLIP), connector module (linear projection, MLP, pooling, convolution, cross-attention, or resamplers like Q-former/Perceiver), and language backbone (predominantly transformer-based; Mamba explored but transformers perform significantly better on grounding tasks). High-resolution images reduce hallucinations and improve multimodal understanding. Training pipeline: image-text alignment pretraining, synthetic re-captioning and quality-filtering, then SFT and alignment. Key findings: grounding mitigates hallucinations by encouraging commitment to specific spatial locations, though some studies show grounding objectives do not exhibit a causal relationship with reductions in object hallucinations. Includes Table 1 listing 25+ VLMs with grounding capabilities. Challenges: modality gap, computational cost of high-resolution processing, reproducibility, inconsistent evaluation.

4. **Awesome-LLM-3D (ActiveVisionLab, GitHub)** [4]: A curated list of 150+ papers on "3D-Related Tasks empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs)" and other foundation models (CLIP, SAM), covering 3D understanding, reasoning, generation, embodied agents, and benchmarks. Categories include: 3D Unified Understanding and Generation via LLM, 3D Understanding via LLM, 3D Understanding via other Foundation Models, 3D Reasoning, 3D Generation, 3D Embodied Agent, and 3D Benchmarks (2.3k stars). The associated survey is "When LLMs Step into the 3D World: A Survey and Meta-Analysis of 3D Tasks via Multi-modal Large Language Models" (arXiv:2405.10255), with a second version updated to July 2025 literature. The Real-3DQA benchmark paper was accepted at ICLR 2026.

5. **"A Survey on Text-guided 3D Visual Grounding" (arXiv:2406.05785 — preprint; companion version published in TNNLS 2025)** [5]: Presents a comprehensive taxonomy of text-guided 3D visual grounding (T-3DVG), which "aims to locate a specific object that semantically corresponds to a language query from a complicated 3D scene."

6. **Awesome-3D-Visual-Grounding (GitHub, associated with TNNLS 2025 survey)** [6]: Up-to-date curated list of text-guided 3D visual grounding papers, associated with "A Survey on Text-guided 3D Visual Grounding: Elements, Recent Advances, and Future Directions" by Daizong Liu, Yang Liu, Wencan Huang, and Wei Hu, published in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems (2025). Categories and representative papers:
   - **Fully-Supervised Two-Stage (proposal-then-selection):** ScanRefer (ECCV 2020, TUM/Simon Fraser), ReferIt3D (ECCV 2020, Stanford/KAUST), AugRefer (AAAI 2025), DSM (2025), AS3D (2025), Ges3ViG (CVPR 2025, gesture-based), Audio-3DVG (2025). Approaches include graph neural networks, spatial embeddings, multi-view inputs, pre-training, segmentation, and Chain-of-Thoughts reasoning.
   - **Fully-Supervised One-Stage (unified detection-interaction):** 3DVG-Transformer (ICCV 2021), 3D-SPS (CVPR 2022), EDA (CVPR 2023), G3-LQ (CVPR 2024), ProxyTransformation (2025), TSP3D (CVPR 2025, sparse voxel pruning).
   - **Weakly-Supervised:** Distilling coarse-to-fine semantic matching knowledge (ICCV 2023), visual linguistic alignment (2023), 3DWG via category/instance-level alignment (ICRA 2025).
   - **Semi-Supervised:** Cross-task knowledge transfer for joint grounding/captioning (ACMMM 2024), Bayesian self-training (ECCV 2024).
   - **Other-Modality (no point cloud input):** Refer-it-in-RGBD (CVPR 2021), Mono3DVG (AAAI 2024, monocular images), EmbodiedScan (CVPR 2024), WildRefer (2023), and recent RGB/Depth/monocular works.
   - **LLMs-based:** ViewRefer (GPT-based), LAMM (NeurIPS 2023), LLM-Grounder (2023), COT3DREF (ICLR 2024), Visual Programming for zero-shot (CVPR 2024), 3DMIT, SCENEVERSE (large-scale dataset), Robin3D, VLM-Grounder (CoRL 2024), Lexicon3D, and numerous 2025 VLM/MLLM/LLM zero-shot grounding and spatial reasoning works.

**Evaluation and critique of 3D-VL models**

7. **Beacon3D (CVPR 2025 poster page)** [7]: "Unveiling the Mist over 3D Vision-Language Understanding: Object-centric Evaluation with Chain-of-Analysis" by Jiangyong Huang, Baoxiong Jia, Yan Wang, Ziyu Zhu, Xiongkun Linghu, Qing Li, Song-Chun Zhu, and Siyuan Huang. Identifies three limitations in existing 3D-VL benchmarks: (1) flawed test data with ambiguous referential text, (2) oversimplified metrics vulnerable to language variations, and (3) isolation of grounding and QA tasks. Beacon3D provides (i) high-quality test data with precise and natural language, (ii) object-centric evaluation with multiple tests per object, and (iii) a novel chain-of-analysis paradigm. Key findings: object-centric evaluation reveals true model performance and weak generalization in QA; grounding-QA coherence remains fragile; and "incorporating large language models (LLMs) to 3D-VL models, though commonly viewed as a practical technique, hinders grounding capabilities and has yet to elevate QA capabilities."

8. **Siyuan Huang's CVPR talk "3D Large Language Models: Are We on the Right Path?" (slides)** [8]: Notes that 2D MLLMs significantly underperform humans on 3D scene understanding benchmarks like VSI-Bench (CVPR 2025), especially in spatial reasoning (distance, direction, counting). Reviews key 3D-VL datasets (ScanRefer, ReferIt3D, SceneVerse, Multi3DRefer, ScanQA, SQA3D, 3D-GRAND, MSR3D) and models (3D-LLM, LEO, Chat-Scene, LL3DA, 3D-VisTA, LLM-Grounder). Three pitfalls of 3D-VL evaluation: (1) flawed test data — blind LLMs achieve good results on SQA3D (visual ignorance); (2) insufficient evaluation metrics — models are susceptible to language variations (weak language robustness); (3) isolation of grounding and QA — probing (PQ3D) reveals poor grounding-QA coherence. Beacon3D findings: object-centric metrics show significant performance drops (particularly QA); grounding-QA coherence is weak (both correct ≤ 20%); half of QA failures stem from bad answering skills, and half of QA successes stem from shortcuts or overfitting. LLM integration weakens grounding and does not fundamentally enhance QA (w/o LLM ≈ LLM-based), since current 3D QA tasks only involve basic language modeling — the bottleneck lies in perception and VL alignment. Proposed improvements: perception via LEO-VL (bridging 2D-3D perception, reducing tokens to 33% while achieving SOTA) and reasoning via SceneCOT (chain-of-thought reasoning with explicit visual grounding, region recognition, entity grounding, symbolic engines, and grounded reasoning; SOTA on SQA3D, MSQA, Beacon3D, particularly counting and spatial relations).

**Foundational 3D scene–language datasets and tasks**

9. **ScanRefer (ECCV 2020) — paper PDF** [9]: Introduces "3D object localization in RGB-D scans using natural language descriptions." The ScanRefer architecture takes a 3D point cloud scene and a free-form natural language description, and predicts the 3D bounding box of the target object. Architecture: detection & encoding modules based on PointNet++ and VoteNet, plus a fusion & localization module integrating 3D geometric features with language embeddings (GRU with GloVE) to match object proposals to descriptions. The ScanRefer dataset is "the first large-scale effort to perform object localization via natural language expression directly in 3D," containing 51,583 descriptions of 11,046 objects from 800 ScanNet scenes; descriptions average 20.27 words and include spatial relations (98.7%), color (74.7%), shape (64.9%), comparatives, superlatives, and ordinals; collected via a two-stage AMT pipeline. Results: 41.19% Acc@0.25IoU and 27.40% Acc@0.5IoU on validation, outperforming 2D methods back-projected to 3D (e.g., One-stage + backproj: 20.38% and 9.04%) and VoteNet with random category matching (10.00% and 5.28%). Key excerpt: "We show that our end-to-end method outperforms the best 2D visual grounding method that simply backprojects its 2D predictions to 3D by a significant margin (9.04 Acc@0.5IoU vs. 22.39 Acc@0.5IoU)." Multiview image features, normals, and a language-to-object classifier loss all contribute to performance.

10. **ScanRefer Benchmark (leaderboard)** [10]: Two leaderboards. **ScanRefer Localization (visual grounding)**, ranked by Acc@0.25/0.5 with "Unique," "Multiple," and "Overall" splits: top performers are UniVLG (0.8895 acc@0.25, 0.8236 acc@0.5 overall), Chat-Scene (0.8887/0.8005), and ConcreteNet (0.8607/0.7923). Other notable methods: Cus3d, D-LISA, M3DRef variants, PointCLIP, CORE-3DVG, and 3DInsVG; many are linked to publications at NeurIPS, ECCV, CVPR, ICCV, and AAAI. The ScanRefer baseline (ECCV 2020) achieves Overall acc@0.25IoU = 0.4244, acc@0.5IoU = 0.2603. **Scan2Cap Dense Captioning** leaderboard: Chat-Scene-thres0.5 leads CIDEr@0.5IoU (0.3456); Vote2Cap-DETR++ leads BLEU-4@0.5IoU (0.1908), DCmAP (0.1864), and mAP@0.5 (0.5090); other methods include TMP, CFM, CM3D-Trans+, D3Net, 3DJCG, and the original Scan2Cap baseline.

11. **ScanRefer GitHub** [11]: ECCV 2020 paper by Dave Zhenyu Chen, Angel X. Chang, and Matthias Nießner (TUM and Simon Fraser University). Code for training, evaluation, visualization; supports RGB, normals, multiview features, language classification. A Benchmark Challenge is available on a hidden test set; annotated viewpoints were released January 2023. Best overall performance reported: 42.27% Acc@0.25IoU and 26.9% Acc@0.5IoU (xyz+multiview+normals, no language classification). Requires PyTorch 1.6, CUDA 10.2, PointNet++ CUDA modules. Licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0.

12. **Refer-it-in-RGBD (CVPR 2021)** [12]: "A Bottom-Up Approach for 3D Visual Grounding in RGBD Images" — presents a novel task of 3D visual grounding in single-view RGBD images where referred objects are often only partially scanned due to occlusion. Method: fuses language and visual features at the voxel level to generate a heatmap coarsely localizing relevant regions, then conducts adaptive feature learning based on the heatmap and object-level matching with another visio-linguistic fusion; uses weighted farthest point sampling (FPS) guided by the heatmap. Contributions: novel task; content-aware bottom-up approach; SUNRefer dataset with 7,699 RGBD images and 38,495 referring expression annotations on 7,699 objects (built on SUNRGBD). Results: outperforms previous methods by 11.2% and 15.6% Acc@0.5 on SUNRefer and ScanRefer respectively; on SUNRefer achieves 35.9% Acc@0.5, 49.6% Acc@0.25, 52.9% R@5; on ScanRefer (single-RGBD) 31.5% Acc@0.5, 56.5% Acc@0.25, 49.3% R@5; processes streaming RGBD at 10 fps.

13. **ScanQA (CVPR 2022) — Liner review** [13]: By Daich Azuma, Taiki Miyanishi, and others. Proposes a 3D Question Answering (3D-QA) framework for spatial scene understanding. The ScanQA baseline processes textual questions and entire 3D scenes (point clouds and RGB frames) to predict answers and 3D bounding boxes for referenced objects. Architecture: (1) 3D & Language Encoder (questions into contextualized word representations; point clouds into object proposals), (2) 3D & Language Fusion Layer (transformer encoder/decoder combining 3D object features with language), (3) Object Localization & QA Layer (joint estimation of target object boxes and answers). Results: on 'Test w/ objects' split, EM@1 of 23.45 vs. 22.31 for the best 2D baseline (RandomImage+MCAN) and 20.56 for the best 3D baseline (ScanRefer+MCAN e2e). End-to-end training is crucial. Human performance on ScanQA is EM@1 of 51.6.

14. **ScanQA GitHub** [13a]: Official repository for the CVPR 2022 paper by Daichi Azuma, Taiki Miyanishi, Shuhei Kurita, and Motoki Kawanabe (ATR-DBI lab). "We propose a new 3D spatial understanding task for 3D question answering (3D-QA). In the 3D-QA task, models receive visual information from the entire 3D scene of a rich RGB-D indoor scan and answer given textual questions about the 3D scene." The ScanQA dataset contains over 41,000 question-answer pairs from 800 indoor scenes derived from ScanNet, described as "the first large-scale effort to perform object-grounded question-answering in 3D environments." Benchmark hosted on EvalAI. Acknowledges facebookresearch/votenet and daveredrum/ScanRefer.

15. **ScanQA (alphaXiv description)** [14]: Submitted May 7, 2022, by researchers affiliated with Kyoto University and RIKEN. The ScanQA dataset contains 41,363 question-answer pairs with 32,337 unique questions and 16,999 unique answers across 800 scenes built on ScanNet, combining T5-based automatic question generation with a comprehensive filtering/editing pipeline involving AMT workers and a custom 3D scene viewer annotation tool — "an order of magnitude improvement over previous template-based 3D-QA datasets." Baseline: three-layer end-to-end architecture with GloVe + bidirectional LSTM for questions and VoteNet with PointNet++ for 3D object proposals, MCAN-inspired transformer attention fusion, and separate modules for object localization, object classification (18 ScanNet classes), and answer classification. Key finding: joint end-to-end learning of localization and QA significantly outperforms pipeline approaches; geometric features provide a strong foundation while RGB values show inconsistent benefits. Human upper bound EM@1 = 51.6. Applications in robotics, AR, smart environments, accessibility.

16. **ScanQA (arXiv listing)** [14b]: Accepted at CVPR 2022; the first three authors contributed equally; project page and code at https://github.com/ATR-DBI/ScanQA.

17. **3D Question Answering (IEEE Transactions on Visualization & Computer Graphics)** [15]: By Shuquan Ye, Dongdong Chen, Songfang Han, and Jing Liao (City University of Hong Kong, Microsoft Cloud AI, UCSD). Submitted 15 Dec 2021, accepted 29 Nov 2022. Presents the first attempt to extend VQA from 2D images to 3D environments; takes color point clouds as input and requires appearance plus 3D geometrical comprehension. The 3DQA-TR framework has two encoders — an appearance encoder and a geometry encoder (providing structure, positional, and scale information to model spatial relationships) — plus a 3D-Linguistic BERT for multi-modal attention to predict answers. The ScanQA dataset (first large-scale, fully human-annotated 3DQA dataset on ScanNet) contains 10,062 question-answer pairs (12.48 questions per scene on average) across 1,613 scans from 806 scenes; questions are natural-language, free-form, open-ended, collected via AMT with an online robot checker, manual correction, and syntax check; viewpoint, camera settings, and annotator confidence are provided.

18. **SQA3D (Hugging Face paper page)** [16]: "Situated Question Answering in 3D Scenes" is a benchmark requiring the agent to first understand its situation (position, orientation, etc.) in a 3D scene as described by text, then reason about its surrounding environment and answer a question under that situation. Based on 650 ScanNet scenes: 6.8k unique situations, 20.4k descriptions, and 33.4k diverse reasoning questions covering spatial relation comprehension, commonsense understanding, navigation, and multi-hop reasoning. "The best state-of-the-art approach achieves only 47.20% overall score, while amateur human participants reach 90.06%."

19. **SQA3D (ICLR 2023 slides)** [17]: Presented at ICLR 2023 by researchers from BIGAI, UCLA, Tsinghua University, and Peking University (Xiaojian Ma, Silong Yong, Zilong Zheng, Qing Li, Yitao Liang, Song-Chun Zhu, Siyuan Huang). Data collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk with a multi-staged strategy. Findings: adding situation text and an auxiliary location prediction task improved model performance; 3D scans are a better scene representation than egocentric videos and BEV pictures; zero-shot large models (GPT-3, Unified QA) show potential in commonsense reasoning and spatial language understanding but are bottlenecked by 3D captions; significant gap remains between machine (47.2%) and human (90.06%) performance; models attending to relevant objects are more likely to answer correctly.

20. **SQA3D (arXiv listing)** [18]: ICLR 2023; first two authors contributed equally; project website https://sqa3d.github.io. Subjects: cs.CV, cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG.

21. **SQA3D (Semantic Scholar record)** [19]: Published at ICLR (Oct 14, 2022). 369 citations. Key citing works: EMBOSR: Embodied Spatial Reasoning for Enhanced Situated Question Answering in 3D Scenes (IROS 2024), Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes (NeurIPS 2024), Hypo3D: Exploring Hypothetical Reasoning in 3D (ICML 2025), Embodied Intelligence for 3D Understanding: A survey on 3D Scene Question Answering (Information Fusion 2026), SceneCOT, SIG3D: Situational Awareness Matters in 3D Vision Language Reasoning (CVPR 2024), Space3D-Bench: Spatial 3D Question Answering Benchmark (ECCV 2024), CityEQA (EMNLP 2025). Foundational references include ScanQA (CVPR 2022), Embodied Question Answering (CVPR 2018), 3D Question Answering (2024), Embodied QA in Photorealistic Environments with Point Cloud Perception (CVPR 2019), STAR (NeurIPS 2021), EgoTaskQA (NeurIPS 2022), Episodic Memory QA (CVPR 2022), Visual7W (CVPR 2016), ALFWorld (ICLR 2021), OK-VQA (CVPR 2019).

22. **MSQA: Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes (NeurIPS 2024, Datasets and Benchmarks Track)** [20]: By Xiongkun Linghu, Jiangyong Huang, Xuesong Niu, Xiaojian (Shawn) Ma, Baoxiong Jia, and Siyuan Huang. Proposes MSQA, a large-scale multi-modal situated reasoning dataset collected via 3D scene graphs and vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse real-world 3D scenes, containing 251K situated question-answering pairs across 9 question categories covering complex scenarios and object modalities. Introduces a novel interleaved multimodal input setting providing texts, images, and point clouds for situation and question description, resolving ambiguity in single-modality descriptions. Also proposes MSNN (Multi-modal Next-step Navigation), which evaluates models' grounding of actions and transitions between situations. Evaluations highlight limitations of existing VLMs and the importance of handling multi-modal interleaved inputs and situation modeling; MSQA proves effective as a pre-training dataset for situated reasoning models.

23. **SceneVerse (project page)** [21]: From the Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence (BIGAI): the first million-scale 3D vision-language dataset for grounded scene understanding, with approximately 68K 3D indoor scenes and 2.5M vision-language pairs, derived from human annotations and a scalable scene-graph-based generation approach using 3D scene graphs and LLMs. Scenes curated from ARKitScene, ScanNet, MultiScan, and 3RScan. Introduces Grounded Pre-training for Scenes (GPS), a transformer-based model trained with multi-level contrastive losses aligning 3D scenes and texts at object-level, referral-object-level, and scene-level. State-of-the-art on all existing 3D visual grounding benchmarks; demonstrates scaling effects in pre-train/fine-tune and zero-shot settings. Published at ECCV 2024; paper arXiv:2401.09340.

24. **SceneVerse (ECCV 2024 poster page)** [22]: By Baoxiong Jia, Yixin Chen, Huangyue Yu, Yan Wang, Xuesong Niu, Tengyu Liu, Qing Li, and Siyuan Huang. Addresses scarcity of paired 3D vision-language data and the lack of a unified learning framework. Achieves SOTA on 3D visual grounding and question-answering benchmarks; data scale-up is generally beneficial for 3D models on tasks like semantic segmentation; zero-shot transfer experiments demonstrate potential in challenging 3D-VL tasks.

**3D visual grounding models**

25. **3DVG-Transformer (ICCV 2021) — paper PDF** [23]: By Lichen Zhao, Daigang Cai, Lu Sheng (Beihang University), and Dong Xu (University of Sydney). A relation-aware visual grounding method on 3D point clouds, formulating grounding as grounding-by-detection. Three modules: (1) object proposal generation with a coordinate-guided contextual aggregation (CCA) module that stacks coordinate-guided transformer layers adding a block-wise sparse spatial proximity matrix to the attention matrix to explicitly model relative spatial locations between proposals (k1=20 neighbors for self-attention, k2=5 for cross-attention); (2) language encoding via a GRU cell with GloVE word embeddings; (3) cross-modal fusion with a multiplex attention (MA) module using interlaced self-attention and cross-attention blocks. Optional feature augmentation: proposal copy & paste and word erase. Results on ScanRefer validation (2D+3D): Acc@0.25 of 47.57% and Acc@0.5 of 34.67% (overall); on the "multiple" subset 39.30% and 28.42%, gains exceeding 6.5% and 5.2% over prior SOTA. Online test: 49.76% Acc@0.25 and 35.12% Acc@0.5. On Nr3D and Sr3D: 40.8% and 51.4% overall, outperforming InstanceRefer by 2.0% and 3.4%. Ablations: removing both CCA and MA drops accuracy to 41.45% Acc@0.25; additive fusion of the spatial proximity matrix ("Add SPM") outperforms multiplication or omission.

26. **3DVG-Transformer (ICCV 2021) — proceedings HTML** [24]: Citation: Zhao, Lichen and Cai, Daigang and Sheng, Lu and Xu, Dong, "3DVG-Transformer: Relation Modeling for Visual Grounding on Point Clouds," Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), 2021, pp. 2928–2937.

27/28. **3DVG-Transformer GitHub** [25][26]: Achieved 1st place on the ScanRefer benchmark (2021/3–2021/11) and won the CVPR 2021 1st Workshop on Language for 3D Scenes challenge; results comparable to CVPR 2022 publications. "3DVG-Transformer+" validation results (2D+3D): 83.25 Acc@0.25 (Unique), 41.20 Acc@0.25 (Multiple), 49.36 (Overall); online benchmark: 51.24 overall Acc@0.25 and 37.04 overall Acc@0.5. Built on the initial ScanRefer codebase; requires ScanRefer dataset, GloVe embeddings (~990MB), ScanNetV2, optional ENet multiview features (~36GB); tested on Ubuntu 16.04/18.04, PyTorch 1.2.0, CUDA 10.0; MIT License.

29. **UZ3DVG (CVPR 2026)** [27]: "UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding with Generated Language Conditions." The first zero-shot 3DVG model that, during inference, uses only 3D point cloud inputs without 2D imagery or external LLMs/VLMs. Components: MSAG-RC (Multi-Source Spatial Annotation and Reasoning Chain Generator) processes RGB-D images to generate 3D spatial pseudo-labels and reasoning chains; RCD (Reasoning Chain Distillation) transfers reasoning knowledge from a large teacher network to a lightweight student network; GeoSM (Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling) captures global and local geometric relationships to align textual reasoning with 3D spatial structures; TSVDE (Text-Semantic-Guided Visual Detail Enhancement) enriches visual features with fine-grained details from text-relevant regions. Results: ScanRefer Acc@0.25/0.5 of 45.42%/41.08% (beats SeeGround by 1.32%/1.68%); on the "Multiple" subset 40.49%/36.33% (beats SeeGround by 6.49%/6.33%); NR3D overall 46.5% (surpassing ZSVG3D by 7.5% and SeeGround by 0.4%); inference speed 7.69 FPS (~38× faster than SeeGround's 0.2 FPS). A second configuration obtains 43.13% and 35.05% on Acc@0.25/0.50, surpassing ZSVG3D by 23.13%/17.45%, at 9.43 FPS vs 0.21 FPS (~45× speedup). A VLM is used only during training to generate pseudo-labels and reasoning chains. Code: https://github.com/tanwb/UZ3DVG. (Note: venue year is CVPR 2026, outside the 2022–2025 window.)

38. **3D-VisTA (ICCV 2023) — paper PDF** [35]: By researchers from Tsinghua University and the National Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence, BIGAI. Pre-training objectives: Masked Language Modeling (MLM), Masked Object Modeling (MOM), Scene-Text Matching (STM). Results (improvements over SOTA): ScanRefer +8.1% (acc@0.5), Sr3D +3.6%, Scan2Cap +10.1% (C@0.25) and +19.2% (C@0.5), ScanQA +3.5%/2.1% (EM@1), SQA3D +1.9%. Key references: Image2Point, Tip-Adapter, CLIP-Adapter, PointPillars.

58. **PointCLIP (GitHub)** [55]: Official CVPR 2022 implementation — the first method to apply CLIP for point cloud recognition. Projects point clouds onto multi-view depth maps (without rendering) and aggregates view-wise zero-shot predictions using CLIP's 2D encoders; features an inter-view adapter for few-shot performance and supports multi-knowledge ensemble. A pre-trained 16-shot checkpoint produces 86.71% on ModelNet40 (87%+ with post-search). PointCLIP V2 with stronger zero-shot performance is available in a separate repo.

59. **PointCLIP (Liner review)** [56]: Zero-shot classification: 30.23% on ModelNet10, 20.18% on ModelNet40, 15.38% on ScanObjectNN. Performance is highly sensitive to projection settings; the prompt "point cloud depth map of a [CLASS]." yields the best results (20.18% on ModelNet40); more than 6 projected views introduces redundancy; the right view is most informative; RN50×16 achieved 23.78% on ModelNet40. The inter-view adapter extracts compact global features via residual connections, fine-tuned with few-shot data while freezing CLIP encoders; also serves as a multi-knowledge ensembling module.

60. **PointCLIP (arXiv listing)** [57]: arXiv:2112.02413; subjects cs.CV, cs.AI, cs.RO; open sourced with code and model available.

61. **Point2Real (AAAI 2024)** [58]: "Point2Real: Bridging the Gap between Point Cloud and Realistic Image for Open-World 3D Recognition" by Hanxuan Li, Bin Fu, Ruiping Wang, Xilin Chen (Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences). A training-free framework for open-world 3D point cloud recognition addressing three sources of domain gap — shape (discrete vs continuous geometry), texture (point clouds lack texture), and view. Modules: (1) Shape Recovery Module — iterative ball-pivoting algorithm (with holes filling and smoothing) converting point clouds to meshes; (2) Texture Rendering Module — ray tracing-based rendering with a texture candidate list (beige, metallic green, leather red, pink, brown, dark grey), selecting the most suitable texture via CLIP classification confidence; (3) Multi-view Adapter — heuristic algorithm using depth surface area as a viewpoint discriminability indicator, generating weights for feature aggregation. Results: zero-shot classification on ModelNet10 79.5%, ModelNet40 65.8%, ScanObjectNN 57.7% (OBJ ONLY), 53.0% (OBJ BG), 38.1% (PB T50 RS) — surpassing all training-free methods and most training-based methods; exceeds PointCLIP V2 by +6.4% on ModelNet10, +1.6% on ModelNet40, and +7.6%, +12.2%, +2.7% on the three ScanObjectNN splits. Few-shot: consistently outperforms PointCLIP and PointCLIP+RSP across 1/2/4/8/16-shot (67.5% vs 52.6% at one-shot; 86.3% at 16-shot). Ablations confirm texture yields substantial improvements, iterative ball-pivoting beats single iteration and Poisson reconstruction, and the Multi-view Adapter helps in real-world scenarios. Implementation: 5 iterations (radii 5,4,3,2,1), Blender Python API cycles, 10 viewpoints, ViT-B/16, 1024 points; inference ~3s (Blender) or 0.0397s (PyTorch3D). Code: github.com/HanXuan-Li/Point2Real.

62. **Point-BERT (CVPR 2022) — ResearchGate** [59]: "Point-BERT: Pre-training 3D Point Cloud Transformers with Masked Point Modeling." Conference paper, June 2022, DOI: 10.1109/CVPR52688.2022.01871.

63. **Point-BERT (GitHub)** [60]: By Xumin Yu, Lulu Tang, Yongming Rao, Tiejun Huang, Jie Zhou, and Jiwen Lu. "Point-BERT is a new paradigm for learning Transformers to generalize the concept of BERT onto 3D point cloud. Inspired by BERT, we devise a Masked Point Modeling (MPM) task to pre-train point cloud Transformers." Method: divides point clouds into local patches; uses a discrete Variational AutoEncoder (dVAE) as a point cloud Tokenizer to generate discrete point tokens; randomly masks patches and feeds them into a backbone Transformer; pre-training objective is to recover original point tokens at masked locations under Tokenizer supervision. Fine-tuned results on ModelNet40: 92.67% Acc (1024 pts), 92.91% (4096), 93.19% (8192); with voting up to 93.76%; ScanObjectNN: 88.12% (objectonly), 87.43% (objectbg), 83.07% (hardest). Pre-trained dVAE and Point-BERT models trained on ShapeNet; 695 stars; MIT license.

64. **Point-BERT (arXiv listing)** [61]: Accepted to CVPR 2022; arXiv:2111.14819; project page https://point-bert.ivg-research.xyz; subjects cs.CV, cs.AI, cs.LG.

65. **Point-In-Context (NeurIPS 2023)** [62]: "Explore In-Context Learning for 3D Point Cloud Understanding" by Zhongbin Fang, Xiangtai Li, Xia Li, Joachim M. Buhmann, Chen Change Loy, and Mengyuan Liu (Sun Yat-sen University, NTU, ETH Zurich, Peking University). The first general framework for 3D visual prompting; treats multiple 3D point cloud tasks as task-aware prompting. Creates the first benchmark for 3D in-context learning based on ShapeNet and ShapeNetPart, comprising 217,454 samples across four tasks: point cloud reconstruction, denoising, registration, and part segmentation. Proposes the Joint Sampling (JS) module to solve information leakage in Masked Point Modeling. Variants PIC-Sep and PIC-Cat use a standard transformer encoder-decoder with ℓ2 Chamfer Distance loss. Results: PIC-Cat avg reconstruction CD 4.3, denoising 5.3, registration 14.1, mIOU 78.95; PIC-Sep 4.7, 7.6, 10.3, 74.95 — SOTA among multitask models on all four tasks. Task-specific models (PointNet, DGCNN, PCT, ACT) still outperform PIC on most individual tasks, but PIC excels at generalization to out-of-distribution data (ModelNet40 registration) and unseen tasks. JS module is critical. Ablations: Farthest Point Sampling better for reconstruction; ℓ2 loss best; 70% mask ratio generally best; CD-aware prompt selection significantly improves results (registration CD drops from 10.3 to 4.1 for PIC-Sep). Limitation: struggles to reconstruct detailed parts of complex point clouds. Code: github.com/fanglaosi/Point-In-Context.

66. **Point-CSA (CVPR 2025)** [63]: "Adapting Pre-trained 3D Models for Point Cloud Video Understanding via Cross-frame Spatio-temporal Adaptation" — the first exploration of transferring pre-trained static 3D point cloud models to 4D point cloud video. Proposes Cross-frame Spatio-temporal Adaptation (CSA) with: (1) Point Tube Adapter — an embedding layer grouping points into "point tubes" along spatial and temporal dimensions (with relative spatio-temporal displacements as features), encoded via an extended lightweight 4D PointNet; (2) Geometric Constraint Temporal Adapter (GCTA) — constructs a cross-frame KNN graph based on spatial distance between point tubes, using EdgeConv-style edge features (combining global variation fj−fi with local structural features fi) and max pooling. Backbone parameters are frozen; only adapters, position encoders, and task head are fine-tuned. Results: MSR-Action3D (24 frames): Point-MAE+CSA 95.12%, outperforming all supervised (best X4D-SceneFormer 93.90%) and self-supervised (best C2P 94.76%, MaST-Pre 94.08%) methods; SHREC'17: PointGPT-S+CSA 96.5%, Point-BERT+CSA 96.2%, Point-MAE+CSA 95.2% (supervised best Kinet 95.2%, self-supervised best PointCMP 93.3%). Ablations on 12 frames with Point-MAE: baseline frozen 77.35%; +Point Tube Adapter 83.97%; +position encoders 87.11%; +GCTA 94.08%; full model 95.12%. Optimal GCTA k=20; "Bypass" placement best; full video as temporal slice best. Code: github.com/LvBaixuan/Point-CSA. Supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China.

67. **Point Transformer (ICCV 2021)** [64]: By researchers from University of Oxford, HKU, CUHK, and Intel Labs. "Self-attention networks have revolutionized natural language processing... The application of self-attention to 3D point clouds is therefore quite natural, since point clouds are essentially sets embedded in 3D space." Core: Point Transformer layer applying vector self-attention locally on kNN neighborhoods (k=16), with a trainable, parameterized relative position encoding added to both the attention generation and feature transformation branches. U-net design with five encoder stages, transition-down (farthest point sampling + kNN max-pooling) and transition-up (trilinear interpolation); no convolutions. Results: S3DIS Area 5 semantic segmentation 70.4% mIoU, 76.5% mAcc, 90.8% OA — first model to cross 70% mIoU, +3.3 pp over prior SOTA; 73.5% mIoU with 6-fold cross-validation; only 4.9M parameters vs 14.9M (KPConv) and 30.1M (SparseConv). ModelNet40: 93.7% OA, 90.6% mAcc. ShapeNetPart: 86.6% instance mIoU, 83.7% category mIoU. Ablations: k=16 optimal; relative position encoding outperforms absolute/none and adding to both branches important; vector attention (70.4%) significantly outperforms scalar attention (64.6%), MLP+pooling (63.7%), and plain MLP (61.7%); softmax normalization essential (70.4% vs 66.5%).

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Reinforcing Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models with ... ---
URL: https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/d2f2ca2c305e1a9c29bf00a676f0a500-Paper-Conference.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces ViLaSR, a novel approach to enhancing spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) through a "drawing to reason in space" paradigm. Instead of relying solely on text-based reasoning or external perception tools, ViLaSR enables LVLMs to reason by performing elementary drawing operations directly in the visual space—specifically bounding box annotations and auxiliary line drawing—allowing the model to express and analyze spatial relationships through direct visual manipulation.

The paper proposes a three-stage training framework:
1. **Cold-start training** with synthetic data to establish basic drawing abilities.
2. **Reflective rejection sampling** to selectively reinforce reasoning paths that demonstrate both correct answers and self-correction behaviors (e.g., revising visual operations based on intermediate results).
3. **Reinforcement learning** (using GRPO) with rewards balancing answer correctness and reasoning format.

Extensive experiments across five spatial reasoning benchmarks (maze navigation, static spatial reasoning, video-based reasoning, and multi-view reasoning) demonstrate that ViLaSR (based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B) achieves an average improvement of 18.4% over strong baselines. Key results include: 98.2% on MAZE, 63.9% on SpatialEval-Real, 45.4% on VSI-Bench, 37.6% on SPAR-Bench, and 30.2% on MMSI-Bench. The model outperforms significantly larger open-source models (72B) and proprietary models like GPT-4o and Gemini-2.0-Flash on most benchmarks.

Ablation studies reveal that reflective rejection sampling is crucial for self-correction (a 96.5% decrease in reflection behavior when removed), and RL optimization helps consolidate multi-attempt capabilities into strong single-attempt performance while using drawing operations more selectively. The paper is accepted at NeurIPS 2025.
</summary>

This paper presents Jigsaw-Puzzles, a novel benchmark for evaluating spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). # InstructBLIP Model Documentation (Hugging Face Transformers)

## Overview
InstructBLIP is a vision-language model proposed in the paper "InstructBLIP: Towards General-purpose Vision-Language Models with Instruction Tuning" (May 2023) by Wenliang Dai et al. It leverages the BLIP-2 architecture for visual instruction tuning. The model was published on Hugging Face on 2023-05-11 and contributed to Transformers on 2023-06-26.

## Key Features
- Uses the same architecture as BLIP-2 but with a key difference: it also feeds the text prompt (instruction) to the Q-Former (Querying Transformer).
- Introduces instruction-aware visual feature extraction, enabling the model to extract informative features tailored to given instructions.
- Supports FlashAttention and SDPA (Scaled Dot-Product Attention).

## Performance
- Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across all 13 held-out datasets, substantially outperforming BLIP-2 and the larger Flamingo.
- Achieves state-of-the-art performance when fine-tuned on individual downstream tasks (e.g., 90.7% accuracy on ScienceQA IMG).

## Architecture Components
The model consists of three main components:
1. **Vision Encoder** (InstructBlipVisionModel): Processes pixel values (image input) with configurable parameters (hidden_size=1408, 39 layers, 16 attention heads, image_size=224, patch_size=14).
2. **Q-Former** (InstructBlipQFormerModel): Querying Transformer that takes both image features and the instruction text as input (vocab_size=30522, hidden_size=768, 12 layers, 12 attention heads).
3. **Language Model**: Part of the conditional generation pipeline.

## Usage Tips
- BLIP models after release v4.46 require setting `processor.num_query_tokens = model.config.num_query_tokens` and expanding the model embeddings layer to add special `<image>` tokens.
- Typically ~500 tokens per image are needed, so text truncation should be avoided.
- The InstructBlipProcessor wraps an image processor (BlipImageProcessor), a tokenizer (GPT2Tokenizer), and a qformer tokenizer into a single processor.

## Configuration Classes
- **InstructBlipConfig**: Main configuration for the full model (num_query_tokens=32 by default).
- **InstructBlipVisionConfig**: Vision encoder configuration.
- **InstructBlipQFormerConfig**: Q-Former configuration.

## Model Classes
- **InstructBlipModel**: Base model consisting of language model, qformer, and vision encoder.
- **InstructBlipForConditionalGeneration**: Model for generating text given an image and an optional text prompt.
- **InstructBlipVisionModel**: Vision encoder only.
- **InstructBlipQFormerModel**: Q-Former only.

## Key Methodology
The paper conducted a systematic study on vision-language instruction tuning based on pre-trained BLIP-2 models, gathering 26 publicly available datasets transformed into instruction tuning format, categorized into two clusters for held-in instruction tuning and held-out zero-shot evaluation.

<summary>
BLIP-2 is a vision-language pretraining model that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language models (LLMs), using a lightweight Querying Transformer (Q-Former) to bridge the modality gap. It was published in November 2023 by Li et al. from Salesforce.

**Architecture and Pretraining:**
BLIP-2 pretrains in two stages:
1. **Stage 1 (Vision-Language Representation Learning):** Uses a frozen image encoder (ViT from CLIP/EVA-CLIP) and a Q-Former module. The Q-Former has two components: an image Transformer (with 32 learnable query tokens) and a text Transformer. It is pretrained on three tasks: image-text contrastive learning, image-text matching (binary classification), and image-grounded text generation (cross-entropy loss). The image encoder is kept frozen.
2. **Stage 2 (Vision-to-Language Generative Learning):** Connects the Q-Former's image Transformer output via a fully connected layer to a frozen LLM decoder (OPT) or LLM encoder-decoder (Flan-T5). The LLM remains frozen during this stage.

**Performance:**
- BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art results on various vision-language tasks despite having significantly fewer trainable parameters than existing methods.
- It outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer trainable parameters.
- Demonstrates emerging capabilities in zero-shot instructed image-to-text generation.
- On VQA, image captioning (NoCaps, COCO), and image-text retrieval (Flickr), BLIP-2 with ViT-g and Flan-T5 (XXL) achieves best results.

**Limitations:**
- BLIP-2 can produce hallucinations and incorrect outputs due to limitations in the frozen LLM's knowledge (e.g., incorrect quotes, wrong product identification, flawed reasoning about weather/context).

**Data:** Uses 129M images from COCO, Visual Genome, Conceptual Captions (3M and 12M), SBU Captions, and 115M images from the LAION 400M dataset, with synthetic captions generated via bootstrapping.

**Key Takeaway:** BLIP-2 is a computationally efficient vision-language model that leverages frozen components to dramatically reduce trainable parameters while achieving state-of-the-art results, though it inherits knowledge limitations from its frozen LLM.

1. **Mask Referring Modeling (MRefM):** A novel paradigm comprising Referring-aware Mask Image Modeling (Referring MIM) and Referring-aware Mask Language Modeling (Referring MLM). SUMMARY:
<summary>
Shikra is an open-source Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) project on GitHub designed to enable "referential dialogue" — spatial coordinate inputs/outputs in natural language — without needing additional vocabularies, position encoders, pre-/post-detection, or external plug-in models. The project was first released on June 28, 2023, with the paper "Shikra: Unleashing Multimodal LLM's Referential Dialogue Magic" (arXiv:2306.15195). Code, data, and the shikra-7b checkpoint were released on July 3, 2023, and an online demo launched on July 16, 2023.

Key details:
- The repository has 816 stars and 48 forks, with 12 commits.
- Two checkpoints are maintained: shikra-7b-delta-v1 (used for paper evaluations) and a frequently updated ckpt (shikra7b-delta-v1-0708, continuously updated with new features).
- Weights are released as delta weights to comply with the LLaMA model license; users must apply the delta to original LLaMA-7b weights via the provided apply_delta.py scripts.
- Installation: conda environment with Python 3.10 and requirements.txt, plus accelerate config.
- Demos: A Gradio web demo (requires GPU with at least 16GB memory for torch.float16, or can use 8-bit quantization with some performance loss) and a server-client demo.
- Training and inference use accelerate launch with mmengine-style config arguments and HuggingFace Trainer arguments (e.g., --num_train_epochs, --output_dir, --per_device_eval_batch_size). Prediction results are saved as JSONL files.
- The project builds upon LLaVA, Vicuna, ChatGLM-Efficient-Tuning, and GLIGEN. Citation: Chen, Keqin et al., arXiv:2306.15195, 2023.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This presentation summarizes and compares four major multimodal large language model (MLLM) systems: Kosmos-1/2 and UnifiedIO-1/2, covering their architectures, training approaches, results, and trade-offs.

**KOSMOS-1 (Huang et al., NeurIPS 2023)** is a 1.6B parameter multimodal LLM pretrained from scratch using a standard Transformer-based causal language model architecture. Key architectural innovations include MAGNETO (extra LayerNorm per sublayer for training stability) and Extrapolatable Position Embedding (XPOS), which uses RoPE with per-dimension exponential scaling for better generalization to longer sequences. Training used a mix of text corpora, image-caption pairs (LAION-2B, LAION-400M, COYO-700M, Conceptual Captions), interleaved image-text data (71M Common Crawl web pages), and language-only instruction tuning.

**KOSMOS-2 (Peng et al., ICLR 2024)** adds grounding to the general-purpose MLLM—the ability to link text to specific image regions—using the same architecture and model size (1.6B). Grounding uses Markdown-style links from text spans to location tokens, discretizing images into P×P bins with special tokens. The GRIT dataset was built from LAION-2B and COYO-700M subsets with a two-step pipeline for extracting and linking text spans to image regions. Results showed large improvements in zero-shot grounding performance and strong referring results (even outperforming finetuned SLR on CIDEr), though it lagged non-zero-shot methods on referring expression comprehension and showed a slight drop on VQA vs. KOSMOS-1, suggesting training mix trade-offs. Strengths include elegant token-level grounding; weaknesses include limited architectural novelty and small model size.

**UnifiedIO-1 (Lu et al., 2022, Allen Institute for AI)** is the first single Seq2Seq model for a wide range of AI tasks, trained jointly on 90+ datasets and 95 tasks using a T5-style Transformer encoder-decoder. All inputs/outputs are encoded as tokens in a shared vocabulary (~50k tokens: 32k text, 16k image via VQ-VAE, 1k location). Training used a two-stage pipeline: pretraining (text and image denoising) followed by multi-task joint training with balanced sampling (proportional to √dataset size within groups). Models scaled from 71M to 2.9B parameters. On the GRIT benchmark, it was the first model to support all 7 tasks with the highest average score (64.3 vs 32.0 for GPV-2). Weaknesses include detection struggles in cluttered scenes, image generation capped by VQ-VAE quality, prompt sensitivity, weaker language performance than frontier LLMs, and task imbalance in training.

**UnifiedIO-2** extends the unified architecture to audio, video, and action capabilities with three input encoders (LLaMA for text, ViT for images, Audio Spectrogram Transformer for audio) and thin projection layers, scaling from 1.1 to 6.8B parameters. Gradient stability is achieved through 2D rotary encodings, QK normalization, scaled cosine attention, and Mixture of training with Z-loss. Pretraining used 600 TB of data (33% NLP, 40% image-text pairs, 25% audio/video, 1% 3D embodiment) plus instruction fine-tuning. Training uses a dynamic packing strategy where examples are concatenated up to a 1152-token limit with attention masking, unpacked to maximum 2048 tokens. The presentation notes CoDi (large diffusion layers decoding an aligned latent space) as related work, and observes that CoDi performs better on certain audio/visual generation tasks. The conclusion frames UnifiedIO-2 as the first autoregressive multi-modal model covering vision, text, audio, and action, while posing the question of whether it should be the last.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This presentation (given in Vienna, Austria) introduces Kosmos-2, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) that grounds language to the real world by encoding and decoding bounding-box coordinates as location tokens. The model treats LLMs as general-purpose interfaces, pairing text with visual elements such as "a campfire" referenced with location tokens like (<loc4> <loc1007>). Key capabilities include: 1) language and vision-language mastery, 2) multimodal grounding and referring (linking referring expressions to image regions and vice versa), and 3) potential for downstream applications. Training uses text corpora, interleaved image-text data, and grounded image-text data. Grounded data is constructed through a two-step process: first preparing noun chunk—bounding box pairs (via detection and post-processing of noun chunks like "a dog: [290,371,605,750]" and "a field: [0,264,919,921]"), and second preparing referring expression—bounding box pairs using sentence dependency relations, dropping substring expressions (e.g., keeping "a dog in a field of flowers" while dropping "a field of flowers" and "flowers"). This resulted in a dataset of 90M images and 137M objects. Example applications shown include referring expression comprehension, VQA counting, text recognition, image captioning, and driving/robotic instruction tasks (e.g., "go through the intersection and turn right"). The model is also demonstrated with reasoning examples such as unusual animal identification (turtle faster than rabbit). Resources include an HF Space demo, Nvidia hosted demo, paper, and official code.

**Motivation & Objective:** The paper addresses the prohibitive computational cost of end-to-end vision-and-language pre-training. - BLIP-2 surpasses existing state-of-the-art models in zero-shot performance, outperforming Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 while using 54 times fewer trainable parameters.

- Performance scales positively with stronger frozen components (ViT-g over ViT-L, larger OPT models, or instruction-tuned FlanT5).

**Core Problem:** Traditional vision-and-language pre-training is prohibitively expensive due to end-to-end training of large-scale models.

**Key Innovation:** BLIP-2 introduces a generic and efficient pre-training strategy that bootstraps vision-language pre-training from off-the-shelf frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language models (LLMs). The modality gap is bridged using a lightweight **Querying Transformer (Q-Former)**, which contains only 188 million parameters and serves as the sole trainable component.

**Q-Former Architecture:** The Q-Former uses learnable query embeddings that extract visual information from the frozen image encoder through cross-attention layers and interact with text through self-attention layers, with interaction controlled by attention masks. This design creates an information bottleneck that forces extraction of the most relevant visual features for text generation.

**Two-Stage Pre-Training Strategy:**
- **Stage 1 (Vision-Language Representation Learning):** Connects the Q-Former to a frozen image encoder using three objectives: Image-Text Contrastive Learning (ITC), Image-grounded Text Generation (ITG), and Image-Text Matching (ITM).
- **Stage 2 (Vision-to-Language Generative Learning):** Connects the pre-trained Q-Former to a frozen LLM. The Q-Former's output embeddings are linearly projected to match the LLM's input dimension and serve as "soft visual prompts."

**Performance:** BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks with significantly fewer trainable parameters. Notably, it outperforms Flamingo80B on zero-shot VQAv2 by 8.7% while using 54× fewer trainable parameters.

**Results and Analysis:**
- Demonstrates remarkable zero-shot capabilities in instructed image-to-text generation when connected to powerful LLMs like FlanT5, following natural language instructions for visual reasoning, conversation, and detailed content generation.
- Ablation studies show Stage 1 representation learning is critical—without it, performance drops significantly due to catastrophic forgetting in the LLM, and the ITG objective is particularly important.
- The model supports various image encoders (ViT-L/14, ViT-g/14) and LLMs (OPT family, FlanT5 family), demonstrating generic applicability.

**Limitations:** The authors acknowledge limitations including inaccurate knowledge, incorrect reasoning, and outdated information.

**Significance:** BLIP-2 represents a paradigm shift by demonstrating effective multimodal models can be built through strategic combination of existing components rather than end-to-end training. It is available open-source through Salesforce's LAVIS project.

Key findings: (1) Speed—smaller depths are faster when computation isn't saturated, but differences become negligible with full GPU utilization; (2) Accuracy—depth, head dimension, and MLP ratio have little impact on performance at the same parameter count.

1. **Vision-Language Contrastive Training**: Aligns InternViT-6B with multilingual LLaMA-7B on noisy web-scale image-text pairs (LAION-en, LAION-multi, LAION-COCO, COYO, Wukong). The original 6.03 billion image-text pairs were cleaned to 4.98 billion.

--- SOURCE 32: V*: Guided Visual Search as a Core Mechanism in Multimodal ... ---
URL: https://vstar-seal.github.io

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage introduces V*, an LLM-guided visual search mechanism for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), created by Penghao Wu (UC San Diego) and Saining Xie (New York University), published December 21, 2023 (arXiv:2312.14135). The work addresses a key limitation of current MLLMs: their dependence on pre-trained vision encoders (e.g., CLIP) that are typically trained on low-resolution images (224×224 or 336×336 pixels), causing them to overlook important details in high-resolution images. Current MLLMs also cannot identify or proactively seek missing visual information—scenarios where even GPT-4V fails.

The proposed integration creates a new MLLM meta-architecture called SEAL (Show, Search, and Tell), composed of a VQA LLM and a visual search model that collaborate through a visual working memory (VWM). The VWM has four blocks: the initial textual question, the initial image, target object crops after search, and coordinates of searched targets. An instantiation uses the LLaVA-7B model.

The V* algorithm works as follows: given an image and a textual target expression, the model first attempts to locate the target directly, obtaining coordinates, confidence scores, and a search cue heatmap. If no object is found (confidence below threshold), it examines the heatmap for target-specific cues. If the cue is prominent, it guides search directly; otherwise, the MLLM uses common sense knowledge and image context to provide a contextual cue about the target's whereabouts. The algorithm then recursively divides the image into 4 non-overlapping equal-sized patches, assigns search priority scores from the heatmap, and processes patches sequentially until the target is found or the patch becomes smaller than a threshold. The V* algorithm is inspired by the A* informed search algorithm, where sub-images are nodes, cost g(n) is a uniform positive constant, and the heuristic h(n) is the negative of the search priority score.

To evaluate the approach, the authors built V*Bench, based on 191 high-resolution images from SAM with average resolution 2246×1582, containing two sub-tasks: attribute recognition (115 samples, e.g., color, material) and spatial relationship reasoning (76 samples). SEAL outperformed other open-source MLLMs and LLM-tool-using systems on this benchmark. The LLM-guided search strategy significantly reduced average search length compared to random and sequential baselines (evaluated on 245 target objects), and both guiding cues (target-specific and contextual) proved helpful. Comparisons with human eye-fixation data from the COCO-Search18 dataset showed V* achieves similar efficiency to human fixations.
</summary>
