**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

*Tavily search #1 (3 parallel queries):*
- "3D visual grounding vision-language models top conference 2022 2023 2024 2025"
- "3D-LLM 3D vision language model NeurIPS CVPR 2023 2024"
- "ScanRefer ReferIt3D 3D captioning grounding conference paper"

*Tavily search #2 (5 parallel queries):*
- "LL3DA 3D vision language model visual grounding conference paper"
- "3D-VisTA vision transformer 3D scene understanding conference paper"
- "LEO embodied agent 3D language model CVPR NeurIPS ICLR"
- "PointCLIP Point-BERT 3D point cloud understanding conference paper"
- "ConceptFusion 3D scene representation language open-vocabulary"

*Tavily search #3 (6 parallel queries):*
- "3DVG-Transformer direct 3D visual grounding language ICCV 2021 citation"
- "PointCLIP point cloud understanding CLIP AAAI 2022 citation"
- "ScanQA 3D question answering ScanNet ICCV 2021 citation SQA3D situated question answering ECCV 2022"
- "Chat-Scene SceneVerse PQ3D 3D vision language ICLR 2025 ECCV 2024"
- "embodied navigation vision language models LM-Nav VLMaps ECCV ICRA CVPR top venue"
- "Grounded 3D-LLM with referential tokens ICLR 2025 SpatialRGPT CVPR 2025"

*Tavily search #4 (6 parallel queries):*
- "3DVG-Transformer point cloud visual grounding ICCV 2021 authors Zhao 3D-SPS"
- "PointCLIP: point cloud understanding CLIP projection AAAI 2022 Zhang"
- "ScanQA: 3D question answering ICCV 2021 Azuma 3D captioning"
- "SQA3D situated question answering embodied agents ECCV 2022 Ma"
- "SceneVerse million-scale 3D vision-language ECCV 2024 PQ3D promptable queries 3D vision language"
- "Chat-Scene bridging 3D scene large language models ICLR 2025 grounding"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

**Surveys and overviews**

1. **Awesome-Visual-Grounding survey (TPAMI 2025)** [1]: A comprehensive survey on visual grounding accepted by TPAMI in 2025, maintained by Linhui Xiao et al. It covers the past decade of visual grounding research, including main tasks (Referring Expression Comprehension, Phrase Grounding), settings (fully supervised, weakly supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, zero-shot, multi-task, generalized visual grounding), method categories (traditional CNN-based, Transformer-based, VLP-based, grounding-oriented pre-training, and Grounding Multimodal LLMs), and applications including 3D visual grounding, video object grounding, and robotic/multimodal agent applications. The survey claims it is "the first survey in the past five years to systematically track and summarize the development of visual grounding over the last decade" and "currently the most comprehensive review in the field of visual grounding." Related works include OneRef (NeurIPS 2024), HiVG (ACM MM 2024), and CLIP-VG (TMM 2023).

2. **Visual Grounding in 2D and 3D survey (Information Fusion, Vol. 126, Feb 2026)** [2]: Claims to be the first comprehensive survey to systematically integrate research across both 2D Visual Grounding (2DVG) and 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG). It categorizes core methodologies, focusing on the evolution from two-stage paradigms (generating candidate regions then matching with text queries) to one-stage paradigms (end-to-end efficiency via direct regression or set prediction). Emerging trends include integration of LLMs for enhanced semantic reasoning, cross-dimensional knowledge transfer between 2D and 3D VG, and monocular 3DVG. It covers benchmark datasets (RefCOCO/+/g for 2D, ScanRefer for 3D), evaluation metrics, and performance benchmarks, and identifies key challenges and future research directions. The article has 254 references and has been cited 17 times; publication volume in VG shows a clear upward trend across CVPR, ICCV, NeurIPS, and AAAI.

3. **"Towards Understanding Visual Grounding in Vision-Language Models" (arXiv:2509.10345 — note: arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed venues)** [3]: A survey defining visual grounding as "the ability of a model to identify a region within some visual input that matches a textual description." Key research domains: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) and Generalized REC (GREC), Grounded Visual Question Answering (GVQA), Grounded Captioning (GC), GUI agents, and grounded reasoning. Representation methods: object-centric vs. pixel-level approaches, discretized vs. raw coordinate formats, and the Set-of-Marks (SOM) method. Architecture components: vision encoder (typically CLIP-based ViT; SigLIP shown to slightly outperform CLIP), connector module (linear projection, MLP, pooling, convolution, cross-attention, or resamplers like Q-former/Perceiver), and language backbone (predominantly transformer-based; Mamba explored but transformers perform significantly better on grounding tasks). High-resolution images reduce hallucinations and improve multimodal understanding. Training pipeline: image-text alignment pretraining, synthetic re-captioning and quality-filtering, then SFT and alignment. Key findings: grounding mitigates hallucinations by encouraging commitment to specific spatial locations, though some studies show grounding objectives do not exhibit a causal relationship with reductions in object hallucinations. Includes Table 1 listing 25+ VLMs with grounding capabilities. Challenges: modality gap, computational cost of high-resolution processing, reproducibility, inconsistent evaluation.

4. **Awesome-LLM-3D (ActiveVisionLab, GitHub)** [4]: A curated list of 150+ papers on "3D-Related Tasks empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs)" and other foundation models (CLIP, SAM), covering 3D understanding, reasoning, generation, embodied agents, and benchmarks. Categories include: 3D Unified Understanding and Generation via LLM, 3D Understanding via LLM, 3D Understanding via other Foundation Models, 3D Reasoning, 3D Generation, 3D Embodied Agent, and 3D Benchmarks (2.3k stars). The associated survey is "When LLMs Step into the 3D World: A Survey and Meta-Analysis of 3D Tasks via Multi-modal Large Language Models" (arXiv:2405.10255), with a second version updated to July 2025 literature. The Real-3DQA benchmark paper was accepted at ICLR 2026.

5. **"A Survey on Text-guided 3D Visual Grounding" (arXiv:2406.05785 — preprint; companion version published in TNNLS 2025)** [5]: Presents a comprehensive taxonomy of text-guided 3D visual grounding (T-3DVG), which "aims to locate a specific object that semantically corresponds to a language query from a complicated 3D scene."

6. **Awesome-3D-Visual-Grounding (GitHub, associated with TNNLS 2025 survey)** [6]: Up-to-date curated list of text-guided 3D visual grounding papers, associated with "A Survey on Text-guided 3D Visual Grounding: Elements, Recent Advances, and Future Directions" by Daizong Liu, Yang Liu, Wencan Huang, and Wei Hu, published in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems (2025). Categories and representative papers:
   - **Fully-Supervised Two-Stage (proposal-then-selection):** ScanRefer (ECCV 2020, TUM/Simon Fraser), ReferIt3D (ECCV 2020, Stanford/KAUST), AugRefer (AAAI 2025), DSM (2025), AS3D (2025), Ges3ViG (CVPR 2025, gesture-based), Audio-3DVG (2025). Approaches include graph neural networks, spatial embeddings, multi-view inputs, pre-training, segmentation, and Chain-of-Thoughts reasoning.
   - **Fully-Supervised One-Stage (unified detection-interaction):** 3DVG-Transformer (ICCV 2021), 3D-SPS (CVPR 2022), EDA (CVPR 2023), G3-LQ (CVPR 2024), ProxyTransformation (2025), TSP3D (CVPR 2025, sparse voxel pruning).
   - **Weakly-Supervised:** Distilling coarse-to-fine semantic matching knowledge (ICCV 2023), visual linguistic alignment (2023), 3DWG via category/instance-level alignment (ICRA 2025).
   - **Semi-Supervised:** Cross-task knowledge transfer for joint grounding/captioning (ACMMM 2024), Bayesian self-training (ECCV 2024).
   - **Other-Modality (no point cloud input):** Refer-it-in-RGBD (CVPR 2021), Mono3DVG (AAAI 2024, monocular images), EmbodiedScan (CVPR 2024), WildRefer (2023), and recent RGB/Depth/monocular works.
   - **LLMs-based:** ViewRefer (GPT-based), LAMM (NeurIPS 2023), LLM-Grounder (2023), COT3DREF (ICLR 2024), Visual Programming for zero-shot (CVPR 2024), 3DMIT, SCENEVERSE (large-scale dataset), Robin3D, VLM-Grounder (CoRL 2024), Lexicon3D, and numerous 2025 VLM/MLLM/LLM zero-shot grounding and spatial reasoning works.

**Evaluation and critique of 3D-VL models**

7. **Beacon3D (CVPR 2025 poster page)** [7]: "Unveiling the Mist over 3D Vision-Language Understanding: Object-centric Evaluation with Chain-of-Analysis" by Jiangyong Huang, Baoxiong Jia, Yan Wang, Ziyu Zhu, Xiongkun Linghu, Qing Li, Song-Chun Zhu, and Siyuan Huang. Identifies three limitations in existing 3D-VL benchmarks: (1) flawed test data with ambiguous referential text, (2) oversimplified metrics vulnerable to language variations, and (3) isolation of grounding and QA tasks. Beacon3D provides (i) high-quality test data with precise and natural language, (ii) object-centric evaluation with multiple tests per object, and (iii) a novel chain-of-analysis paradigm. Key findings: object-centric evaluation reveals true model performance and weak generalization in QA; grounding-QA coherence remains fragile; and "incorporating large language models (LLMs) to 3D-VL models, though commonly viewed as a practical technique, hinders grounding capabilities and has yet to elevate QA capabilities."

8. **Siyuan Huang's CVPR talk "3D Large Language Models: Are We on the Right Path?" (slides)** [8]: Notes that 2D MLLMs significantly underperform humans on 3D scene understanding benchmarks like VSI-Bench (CVPR 2025), especially in spatial reasoning (distance, direction, counting). Reviews key 3D-VL datasets (ScanRefer, ReferIt3D, SceneVerse, Multi3DRefer, ScanQA, SQA3D, 3D-GRAND, MSR3D) and models (3D-LLM, LEO, Chat-Scene, LL3DA, 3D-VisTA, LLM-Grounder). Three pitfalls of 3D-VL evaluation: (1) flawed test data — blind LLMs achieve good results on SQA3D (visual ignorance); (2) insufficient evaluation metrics — models are susceptible to language variations (weak language robustness); (3) isolation of grounding and QA — probing (PQ3D) reveals poor grounding-QA coherence. Beacon3D findings: object-centric metrics show significant performance drops (particularly QA); grounding-QA coherence is weak (both correct ≤ 20%); half of QA failures stem from bad answering skills, and half of QA successes stem from shortcuts or overfitting. LLM integration weakens grounding and does not fundamentally enhance QA (w/o LLM ≈ LLM-based), since current 3D QA tasks only involve basic language modeling — the bottleneck lies in perception and VL alignment. Proposed improvements: perception via LEO-VL (bridging 2D-3D perception, reducing tokens to 33% while achieving SOTA) and reasoning via SceneCOT (chain-of-thought reasoning with explicit visual grounding, region recognition, entity grounding, symbolic engines, and grounded reasoning; SOTA on SQA3D, MSQA, Beacon3D, particularly counting and spatial relations).

**Foundational 3D scene–language datasets and tasks**

9. **ScanRefer (ECCV 2020) — paper PDF** [9]: Introduces "3D object localization in RGB-D scans using natural language descriptions." The ScanRefer architecture takes a 3D point cloud scene and a free-form natural language description, and predicts the 3D bounding box of the target object. Architecture: detection & encoding modules based on PointNet++ and VoteNet, plus a fusion & localization module integrating 3D geometric features with language embeddings (GRU with GloVE) to match object proposals to descriptions. The ScanRefer dataset is "the first large-scale effort to perform object localization via natural language expression directly in 3D," containing 51,583 descriptions of 11,046 objects from 800 ScanNet scenes; descriptions average 20.27 words and include spatial relations (98.7%), color (74.7%), shape (64.9%), comparatives, superlatives, and ordinals; collected via a two-stage AMT pipeline. Results: 41.19% Acc@0.25IoU and 27.40% Acc@0.5IoU on validation, outperforming 2D methods back-projected to 3D (e.g., One-stage + backproj: 20.38% and 9.04%) and VoteNet with random category matching (10.00% and 5.28%). Key excerpt: "We show that our end-to-end method outperforms the best 2D visual grounding method that simply backprojects its 2D predictions to 3D by a significant margin (9.04 Acc@0.5IoU vs. 22.39 Acc@0.5IoU)." Multiview image features, normals, and a language-to-object classifier loss all contribute to performance.

10. **ScanRefer Benchmark (leaderboard)** [10]: Two leaderboards. **ScanRefer Localization (visual grounding)**, ranked by Acc@0.25/0.5 with "Unique," "Multiple," and "Overall" splits: top performers are UniVLG (0.8895 acc@0.25, 0.8236 acc@0.5 overall), Chat-Scene (0.8887/0.8005), and ConcreteNet (0.8607/0.7923). Other notable methods: Cus3d, D-LISA, M3DRef variants, PointCLIP, CORE-3DVG, and 3DInsVG; many are linked to publications at NeurIPS, ECCV, CVPR, ICCV, and AAAI. The ScanRefer baseline (ECCV 2020) achieves Overall acc@0.25IoU = 0.4244, acc@0.5IoU = 0.2603. **Scan2Cap Dense Captioning** leaderboard: Chat-Scene-thres0.5 leads CIDEr@0.5IoU (0.3456); Vote2Cap-DETR++ leads BLEU-4@0.5IoU (0.1908), DCmAP (0.1864), and mAP@0.5 (0.5090); other methods include TMP, CFM, CM3D-Trans+, D3Net, 3DJCG, and the original Scan2Cap baseline.

11. **ScanRefer GitHub** [11]: ECCV 2020 paper by Dave Zhenyu Chen, Angel X. Chang, and Matthias Nießner (TUM and Simon Fraser University). Code for training, evaluation, visualization; supports RGB, normals, multiview features, language classification. A Benchmark Challenge is available on a hidden test set; annotated viewpoints were released January 2023. Best overall performance reported: 42.27% Acc@0.25IoU and 26.9% Acc@0.5IoU (xyz+multiview+normals, no language classification). Requires PyTorch 1.6, CUDA 10.2, PointNet++ CUDA modules. Licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0.

12. **Refer-it-in-RGBD (CVPR 2021)** [12]: "A Bottom-Up Approach for 3D Visual Grounding in RGBD Images" — presents a novel task of 3D visual grounding in single-view RGBD images where referred objects are often only partially scanned due to occlusion. Method: fuses language and visual features at the voxel level to generate a heatmap coarsely localizing relevant regions, then conducts adaptive feature learning based on the heatmap and object-level matching with another visio-linguistic fusion; uses weighted farthest point sampling (FPS) guided by the heatmap. Contributions: novel task; content-aware bottom-up approach; SUNRefer dataset with 7,699 RGBD images and 38,495 referring expression annotations on 7,699 objects (built on SUNRGBD). Results: outperforms previous methods by 11.2% and 15.6% Acc@0.5 on SUNRefer and ScanRefer respectively; on SUNRefer achieves 35.9% Acc@0.5, 49.6% Acc@0.25, 52.9% R@5; on ScanRefer (single-RGBD) 31.5% Acc@0.5, 56.5% Acc@0.25, 49.3% R@5; processes streaming RGBD at 10 fps.

13. **ScanQA (CVPR 2022) — Liner review** [13]: By Daich Azuma, Taiki Miyanishi, and others. Proposes a 3D Question Answering (3D-QA) framework for spatial scene understanding. The ScanQA baseline processes textual questions and entire 3D scenes (point clouds and RGB frames) to predict answers and 3D bounding boxes for referenced objects. Architecture: (1) 3D & Language Encoder (questions into contextualized word representations; point clouds into object proposals), (2) 3D & Language Fusion Layer (transformer encoder/decoder combining 3D object features with language), (3) Object Localization & QA Layer (joint estimation of target object boxes and answers). Results: on 'Test w/ objects' split, EM@1 of 23.45 vs. 22.31 for the best 2D baseline (RandomImage+MCAN) and 20.56 for the best 3D baseline (ScanRefer+MCAN e2e). End-to-end training is crucial. Human performance on ScanQA is EM@1 of 51.6.

14. **ScanQA GitHub** [13a]: Official repository for the CVPR 2022 paper by Daichi Azuma, Taiki Miyanishi, Shuhei Kurita, and Motoki Kawanabe (ATR-DBI lab). "We propose a new 3D spatial understanding task for 3D question answering (3D-QA). In the 3D-QA task, models receive visual information from the entire 3D scene of a rich RGB-D indoor scan and answer given textual questions about the 3D scene." The ScanQA dataset contains over 41,000 question-answer pairs from 800 indoor scenes derived from ScanNet, described as "the first large-scale effort to perform object-grounded question-answering in 3D environments." Benchmark hosted on EvalAI. Acknowledges facebookresearch/votenet and daveredrum/ScanRefer.

15. **ScanQA (alphaXiv description)** [14]: Submitted May 7, 2022, by researchers affiliated with Kyoto University and RIKEN. The ScanQA dataset contains 41,363 question-answer pairs with 32,337 unique questions and 16,999 unique answers across 800 scenes built on ScanNet, combining T5-based automatic question generation with a comprehensive filtering/editing pipeline involving AMT workers and a custom 3D scene viewer annotation tool — "an order of magnitude improvement over previous template-based 3D-QA datasets." Baseline: three-layer end-to-end architecture with GloVe + bidirectional LSTM for questions and VoteNet with PointNet++ for 3D object proposals, MCAN-inspired transformer attention fusion, and separate modules for object localization, object classification (18 ScanNet classes), and answer classification. Key finding: joint end-to-end learning of localization and QA significantly outperforms pipeline approaches; geometric features provide a strong foundation while RGB values show inconsistent benefits. Human upper bound EM@1 = 51.6. Applications in robotics, AR, smart environments, accessibility.

16. **ScanQA (arXiv listing)** [14b]: Accepted at CVPR 2022; the first three authors contributed equally; project page and code at https://github.com/ATR-DBI/ScanQA.

17. **3D Question Answering (IEEE Transactions on Visualization & Computer Graphics)** [15]: By Shuquan Ye, Dongdong Chen, Songfang Han, and Jing Liao (City University of Hong Kong, Microsoft Cloud AI, UCSD). Submitted 15 Dec 2021, accepted 29 Nov 2022. Presents the first attempt to extend VQA from 2D images to 3D environments; takes color point clouds as input and requires appearance plus 3D geometrical comprehension. The 3DQA-TR framework has two encoders — an appearance encoder and a geometry encoder (providing structure, positional, and scale information to model spatial relationships) — plus a 3D-Linguistic BERT for multi-modal attention to predict answers. The ScanQA dataset (first large-scale, fully human-annotated 3DQA dataset on ScanNet) contains 10,062 question-answer pairs (12.48 questions per scene on average) across 1,613 scans from 806 scenes; questions are natural-language, free-form, open-ended, collected via AMT with an online robot checker, manual correction, and syntax check; viewpoint, camera settings, and annotator confidence are provided.

18. **SQA3D (Hugging Face paper page)** [16]: "Situated Question Answering in 3D Scenes" is a benchmark requiring the agent to first understand its situation (position, orientation, etc.) in a 3D scene as described by text, then reason about its surrounding environment and answer a question under that situation. Based on 650 ScanNet scenes: 6.8k unique situations, 20.4k descriptions, and 33.4k diverse reasoning questions covering spatial relation comprehension, commonsense understanding, navigation, and multi-hop reasoning. "The best state-of-the-art approach achieves only 47.20% overall score, while amateur human participants reach 90.06%."

19. **SQA3D (ICLR 2023 slides)** [17]: Presented at ICLR 2023 by researchers from BIGAI, UCLA, Tsinghua University, and Peking University (Xiaojian Ma, Silong Yong, Zilong Zheng, Qing Li, Yitao Liang, Song-Chun Zhu, Siyuan Huang). Data collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk with a multi-staged strategy. Findings: adding situation text and an auxiliary location prediction task improved model performance; 3D scans are a better scene representation than egocentric videos and BEV pictures; zero-shot large models (GPT-3, Unified QA) show potential in commonsense reasoning and spatial language understanding but are bottlenecked by 3D captions; significant gap remains between machine (47.2%) and human (90.06%) performance; models attending to relevant objects are more likely to answer correctly.

20. **SQA3D (arXiv listing)** [18]: ICLR 2023; first two authors contributed equally; project website https://sqa3d.github.io. Subjects: cs.CV, cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG.

21. **SQA3D (Semantic Scholar record)** [19]: Published at ICLR (Oct 14, 2022). 369 citations. Key citing works: EMBOSR: Embodied Spatial Reasoning for Enhanced Situated Question Answering in 3D Scenes (IROS 2024), Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes (NeurIPS 2024), Hypo3D: Exploring Hypothetical Reasoning in 3D (ICML 2025), Embodied Intelligence for 3D Understanding: A survey on 3D Scene Question Answering (Information Fusion 2026), SceneCOT, SIG3D: Situational Awareness Matters in 3D Vision Language Reasoning (CVPR 2024), Space3D-Bench: Spatial 3D Question Answering Benchmark (ECCV 2024), CityEQA (EMNLP 2025). Foundational references include ScanQA (CVPR 2022), Embodied Question Answering (CVPR 2018), 3D Question Answering (2024), Embodied QA in Photorealistic Environments with Point Cloud Perception (CVPR 2019), STAR (NeurIPS 2021), EgoTaskQA (NeurIPS 2022), Episodic Memory QA (CVPR 2022), Visual7W (CVPR 2016), ALFWorld (ICLR 2021), OK-VQA (CVPR 2019).

22. **MSQA: Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes (NeurIPS 2024, Datasets and Benchmarks Track)** [20]: By Xiongkun Linghu, Jiangyong Huang, Xuesong Niu, Xiaojian (Shawn) Ma, Baoxiong Jia, and Siyuan Huang. Proposes MSQA, a large-scale multi-modal situated reasoning dataset collected via 3D scene graphs and vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse real-world 3D scenes, containing 251K situated question-answering pairs across 9 question categories covering complex scenarios and object modalities. Introduces a novel interleaved multimodal input setting providing texts, images, and point clouds for situation and question description, resolving ambiguity in single-modality descriptions. Also proposes MSNN (Multi-modal Next-step Navigation), which evaluates models' grounding of actions and transitions between situations. Evaluations highlight limitations of existing VLMs and the importance of handling multi-modal interleaved inputs and situation modeling; MSQA proves effective as a pre-training dataset for situated reasoning models.

23. **SceneVerse (project page)** [21]: From the Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence (BIGAI): the first million-scale 3D vision-language dataset for grounded scene understanding, with approximately 68K 3D indoor scenes and 2.5M vision-language pairs, derived from human annotations and a scalable scene-graph-based generation approach using 3D scene graphs and LLMs. Scenes curated from ARKitScene, ScanNet, MultiScan, and 3RScan. Introduces Grounded Pre-training for Scenes (GPS), a transformer-based model trained with multi-level contrastive losses aligning 3D scenes and texts at object-level, referral-object-level, and scene-level. State-of-the-art on all existing 3D visual grounding benchmarks; demonstrates scaling effects in pre-train/fine-tune and zero-shot settings. Published at ECCV 2024; paper arXiv:2401.09340.

24. **SceneVerse (ECCV 2024 poster page)** [22]: By Baoxiong Jia, Yixin Chen, Huangyue Yu, Yan Wang, Xuesong Niu, Tengyu Liu, Qing Li, and Siyuan Huang. Addresses scarcity of paired 3D vision-language data and the lack of a unified learning framework. Achieves SOTA on 3D visual grounding and question-answering benchmarks; data scale-up is generally beneficial for 3D models on tasks like semantic segmentation; zero-shot transfer experiments demonstrate potential in challenging 3D-VL tasks.

**3D visual grounding models**

25. **3DVG-Transformer (ICCV 2021) — paper PDF** [23]: By Lichen Zhao, Daigang Cai, Lu Sheng (Beihang University), and Dong Xu (University of Sydney). A relation-aware visual grounding method on 3D point clouds, formulating grounding as grounding-by-detection. Three modules: (1) object proposal generation with a coordinate-guided contextual aggregation (CCA) module that stacks coordinate-guided transformer layers adding a block-wise sparse spatial proximity matrix to the attention matrix to explicitly model relative spatial locations between proposals (k1=20 neighbors for self-attention, k2=5 for cross-attention); (2) language encoding via a GRU cell with GloVE word embeddings; (3) cross-modal fusion with a multiplex attention (MA) module using interlaced self-attention and cross-attention blocks. Optional feature augmentation: proposal copy & paste and word erase. Results on ScanRefer validation (2D+3D): Acc@0.25 of 47.57% and Acc@0.5 of 34.67% (overall); on the "multiple" subset 39.30% and 28.42%, gains exceeding 6.5% and 5.2% over prior SOTA. Online test: 49.76% Acc@0.25 and 35.12% Acc@0.5. On Nr3D and Sr3D: 40.8% and 51.4% overall, outperforming InstanceRefer by 2.0% and 3.4%. Ablations: removing both CCA and MA drops accuracy to 41.45% Acc@0.25; additive fusion of the spatial proximity matrix ("Add SPM") outperforms multiplication or omission.

26. **3DVG-Transformer (ICCV 2021) — proceedings HTML** [24]: Citation: Zhao, Lichen and Cai, Daigang and Sheng, Lu and Xu, Dong, "3DVG-Transformer: Relation Modeling for Visual Grounding on Point Clouds," Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), 2021, pp. 2928–2937.

27/28. **3DVG-Transformer GitHub** [25][26]: Achieved 1st place on the ScanRefer benchmark (2021/3–2021/11) and won the CVPR 2021 1st Workshop on Language for 3D Scenes challenge; results comparable to CVPR 2022 publications. "3DVG-Transformer+" validation results (2D+3D): 83.25 Acc@0.25 (Unique), 41.20 Acc@0.25 (Multiple), 49.36 (Overall); online benchmark: 51.24 overall Acc@0.25 and 37.04 overall Acc@0.5. Built on the initial ScanRefer codebase; requires ScanRefer dataset, GloVe embeddings (~990MB), ScanNetV2, optional ENet multiview features (~36GB); tested on Ubuntu 16.04/18.04, PyTorch 1.2.0, CUDA 10.0; MIT License.

29. **UZ3DVG (CVPR 2026)** [27]: "UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding with Generated Language Conditions." The first zero-shot 3DVG model that, during inference, uses only 3D point cloud inputs without 2D imagery or external LLMs/VLMs. Components: MSAG-RC (Multi-Source Spatial Annotation and Reasoning Chain Generator) processes RGB-D images to generate 3D spatial pseudo-labels and reasoning chains; RCD (Reasoning Chain Distillation) transfers reasoning knowledge from a large teacher network to a lightweight student network; GeoSM (Geometry-Aware Spatial Modeling) captures global and local geometric relationships to align textual reasoning with 3D spatial structures; TSVDE (Text-Semantic-Guided Visual Detail Enhancement) enriches visual features with fine-grained details from text-relevant regions. Results: ScanRefer Acc@0.25/0.5 of 45.42%/41.08% (beats SeeGround by 1.32%/1.68%); on the "Multiple" subset 40.49%/36.33% (beats SeeGround by 6.49%/6.33%); NR3D overall 46.5% (surpassing ZSVG3D by 7.5% and SeeGround by 0.4%); inference speed 7.69 FPS (~38× faster than SeeGround's 0.2 FPS). A second configuration obtains 43.13% and 35.05% on Acc@0.25/0.50, surpassing ZSVG3D by 23.13%/17.45%, at 9.43 FPS vs 0.21 FPS (~45× speedup). A VLM is used only during training to generate pseudo-labels and reasoning chains. Code: https://github.com/tanwb/UZ3DVG. (Note: venue year is CVPR 2026, outside the 2022–2025 window.)

30. **LASP: Language-to-Space Programming for Training-Free 3D Visual Grounding (EMNLP 2025)** [28]: By researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. Introduces LLM-generated Python code as spatial relation encoders that compute relation features from object bounding boxes, with an automatic pipeline using test suites to evaluate and optimize codes across multiple iterations. A VLM (GPT-4o) module disambiguates candidates using stitched ScanNet images. Results: 52.9% accuracy on Nr3D (60.7% easy, 45.3% hard), among the best training-free methods; with ground-truth labels reaches 67.8%. Substantially reduces grounding time (7.7s vs 50.3s for VLM-Grounder) and token costs (3.1k vs 12k tokens). On GRScenes, 90.0% accuracy vs. 15.6% for a random baseline. Replacing LLM-generated encoders with human-written functions drops accuracy to 44.0%. Ablation shows the critical importance of optimization, error messages, and in-context examples; codes implicitly learn dataset priors (in 98 of 100 "view-dependent" sentences, the anchor object is the "faced" object). Limitations: performance gaps vs. recent supervised methods; symbolic expressions struggle with ordinal phrases; limited relation coverage; simplified bounding-box-only scene representation; dependence on pre-trained 3D detectors/classifiers. Code: https://github.com/InternRobotics/LaSP. Funded by the National Key R&D Program of China.

31. **PQ3D (ECCV 2024) — GitHub** [29]: "Unifying 3D Vision-Language Understanding via Promptable Queries" by Ziyu Zhu, Zhuofan Zhang, Xiaojian Ma, Xuesong Niu, Yixin Chen, Baoxiong Jia, Zhidong Deng, Siyuan Huang, and Qing Li. A unified model using Promptable Queries to tackle a wide range of 3D-VL tasks, from low-level instance segmentation to high-level reasoning and planning, via three innovations: (1) unifying various 3D scene representations (voxels, point clouds, multi-view images) into a shared 3D coordinate space by segment-level grouping; (2) an attention-based query decoder for task-specific information retrieval guided by prompts; (3) universal output heads supporting multi-task training. Tested across ten 3D-VL datasets: "PQ3D improves the state-of-the-art on ScanNet200 by 4.9% (AP25), ScanRefer by 5.4% (acc@0.5), Multi3DRefer by 11.7% (F1@0.5), and Scan2Cap by 13.4% (CIDEr@0.5)." Supports flexible inference with individual or combined forms of 3D representations (e.g., solely voxel input). Training: Stage 1 instance segmentation, Stage 2 VL tasks; uses sceneverse base data; MIT license.

32. **PQ3D (project page)** [30]: "PQ3D, a unified model for 3D vision-language understanding, capable of taking various prompts and representations to perform a wide range of tasks in a 3D Scene."

33. **Chat-Scene (NeurIPS 2024) — alphaXiv description** [31]: By Zhejiang University researchers (Yilun Chen, Zehan Wang, Rongjie Huang, Runsen Xu, Tai Wang, Luping Liu, Xize Cheng, Jiangmiao Pang, Zhou Zhao). A unified framework bridging 3D scene understanding with LLMs. Introduces object identifiers (unique tokens like `<OBJ013>`) assigned to each object proposal for unambiguous referencing, and object-centric representations leveraging pre-trained foundation models. Uses Mask3D for 3D instance segmentation; extracts multi-modal features via parallel encoders — Uni3D (3D geometric) and DINOv2 (2D semantic from multi-view projection) — mapped into the LLM embedding space via three-layer MLP projectors. Transforms diverse 3D scene-language tasks (visual grounding, dense captioning, VQA) into a unified QA format without task-specific heads; single-stage training with cross-entropy loss and LoRA on data from five benchmarks. Results: 50.2% Acc@0.5 on ScanRefer (+3.7%), 52.4% Acc@0.5 on Multi3DRefer (+14.0%), 77.1% CIDEr@0.5 on Scan2Cap (+8.7%), 87.7% CIDEr on ScanQA, 54.6% EM on SQA3D. Learnable object identifiers outperform plain text and fixed embeddings while being more token-efficient (3N vs 6N tokens). Two-dimensional features alone often outperform 3D-only features, with combination best. Extends to 2D video input via DEVA tracking, achieving 22.8% Acc@0.5 for video grounding. Limitations: counting large numbers of objects, structural elements, fine-grained attribute distinctions, ambiguous dataset annotations.

34. **Chat-Scene (NeurIPS 2024 poster page)** [32]: Authors: Haifeng Huang, Yilun Chen, Zehan Wang, Rongjie Huang, Runsen Xu, Tai Wang, Luping Liu, Xize Cheng, Yang Zhao, Jiangmiao Pang, Zhou Zhao. "we decompose the input 3D scene into a set of object proposals, each assigned a unique identifier token, which enables efficient object referencing and grounding during user-assistant interactions"; "we transform diverse 3D scene-language tasks into a unified question-answering format, facilitating joint training without the need for additional task-specific heads." With minimal fine-tuning, significantly outperforms existing methods on ScanRefer, Multi3DRefer, Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and SQA3D.

35/36. **Chat-Scene GitHub and OpenReview** [33][33a]: GitHub: "[NeurIPS 2024 & TPAMI 2026]" multi-modal LLM for 3D scene understanding, excelling in 3D grounding, captioning, and question answering. OpenReview (cited by 197): "we introduce the use of object identifiers and object-centric representations to interact with scenes at the object level."

37. **CORE-3D (OpenReview PDF — venue unclear, appears to be a preprint)** [34]: A training-free pipeline for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding. Contributions: (1) Progressive SemanticSAM refinement for more accurate and complete object-level masks (uses overlap thresholds and DBSCAN clustering); (2) context-aware CLIP encoding aggregating five complementary crops per mask (mask crop, bounding box crop, large-context crop at 2.5×, huge-context crop at 4×, surroundings crop at 3× with mask blacked out, combined via weighted averaging with the surroundings embedding subtracted with negative weight); (3) multi-view 3D mask merging via symmetric-balanced IoV criterion and geometric heuristics. Object retrieval: LLM query structuring into Π(q) = (m, R, Ω); candidate mining via CLIP similarity with top-K matching and voxelization deduplication; view selection with VLM verification; orientation grounding using canonical views at discretized yaw bins; final LLM reasoning. Results: on Replica — mAcc 0.38, mIoU 0.29, fmIoU 0.56; on ScanNet — mAcc 0.61, mIoU 0.36, fmIoU 0.46; best across all evaluated approaches including training-based (LERF, OpenNeRF, LangSplat, OpenGaussian) and zero-shot methods (ConceptFusion, OpenMask3D, ConceptGraphs, HOV-SG, BBQ-CLIP). On Sr3D+ (661 sampled instructions): 41.8 A@0.1 and 35.6 A@0.25 overall, substantially outperforming baselines (BBQ: 34.2/22.7, BBQ-CLIP: 14.4/8.8, ConceptGraphs: 13.3/6.2, OpenFusion: 12.6/2.4). Uses EVA02-CLIP (Large), qwen2.5-vl-32b-instruct, gpt-5-mini for object extraction, and openai-o4-mini for final decision-making; runs on a single RTX4090.

**3D vision–language pre-trained models and LLM-based assistants**

38. **3D-VisTA (ICCV 2023) — paper PDF** [35]: By researchers from Tsinghua University and the National Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence, BIGAI. A simple, unified Transformer using vanilla self-attention layers for both single-modal modeling and multi-modal fusion, without task-specific designs, auxiliary losses, or optimization tricks. Components: text encoding module (initialized with BERT's first four layers), scene encoding module (PointNet++ on object point clouds), and multi-modal fusion module; spatial relations between objects are explicitly encoded into self-attention weights. **ScanScribe dataset**: first large-scale 3D scene-text pairs dataset for 3D-VL pre-training — 278K 3D scene-text pairs for 2,995 RGB-D scans of 1,185 unique indoor scenes (from ScanNet and 3R-Scan), with 56.1K unique object instances; text from existing datasets (ScanQA, ScanRefer, ReferIt3D), templates, and GPT-3 generation from scene graphs; 10% of objects replaced with Objaverse objects. Pre-training objectives: Masked Language Modeling (MLM), Masked Object Modeling (MOM), Scene-Text Matching (STM). Results (improvements over SOTA): ScanRefer +8.1% (acc@0.5), Sr3D +3.6%, Scan2Cap +10.1% (C@0.25) and +19.2% (C@0.5), ScanQA +3.5%/2.1% (EM@1), SQA3D +1.9%. Pre-training gains: 6.7%/6.8% on Nr3D/Sr3D, 4.7%/4.3% on ScanRefer, 1.8%/2.6% EM@1 on ScanQA, 4.2% C@0.25 on Scan2Cap, 1.8% average on SQA3D. Data efficiency: with only 30% of annotations, pre-trained 3D-VisTA outperforms scratch-trained models with full data. Ablations: 4-layer transformer depth optimal; all three pre-training objectives beneficial; all data sources best. Future work: offline 3D object detection is a bottleneck; scaling up ScanScribe and model size promising.

39. **3D-VisTA (Semantic Scholar)** [36]: 3D-VisTA achieves SOTA results on 3D-VL tasks ranging from visual grounding and dense captioning to question answering and situated reasoning. Related works listed: UniVLG (unified 2D/3D vision-language architecture), PanoGrounder (multi-modal panoramic representation with pretrained 2D VLMs; SOTA on ScanRefer and Nr3D), SeeGround (zero-shot 3DVG leveraging 2D VLMs), SceneVerse GPS, LEO-VL (efficient scene representation), SAT (2D semantics-assisted training), SemAbs (open-world 3D scene understanding from 2D VLMs), 3D-SPS, Multi-View Transformer (MVT).

40. **3D-VisTA (GitHub)** [37]: Official implementation; 217 stars. Supports tasks: scanrefer, scanqa, sr3d, nr3d, sqa, scan2cap. Citation: Zhu, Ziyu and Ma, Xiaojian and Chen, Yixin and Deng, Zhidong and Huang, Siyuan and Li, Qing, journal={ICCV}, year={2023}.

41. **3D-VisTA (Liner quick review)** [38]: Confirms SOTA on six diverse 3D-VL tasks (visual grounding, dense captioning, QA, situated reasoning) with superior data efficiency; even when trained from scratch, competitive with SOTA. Pre-training improves alignment of long text queries with 3D scenes (larger improvements for longer sentences on ScanRefer).

42. **3D-LLM (NeurIPS 2023) — paper PDF** [39]: "Injecting the 3D World into Large Language Models" — introduces a new family of 3D-based Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) that take 3D point clouds and their features as input and perform a diverse set of 3D-related tasks: captioning, dense captioning, 3D question answering, task decomposition, 3D grounding, 3D-assisted dialog, navigation. **Data generation**: three prompting pipelines (Boxes-Demonstration-Instruction, ChatCaptioner-based, Revision-based) using ChatGPT to generate ~1M 3D-language data pairs covering multiple tasks from 3D assets (Objaverse, ScanNet, Habitat-Matterport). **Architecture**: uses 2D pretrained VLMs (Flamingo 9B, BLIP-2) as backbones with a 3D feature extractor that constructs 3D features from rendered multi-view images via three methods (Direct Reconstruction, Feature Fusion, Neural Field); a novel 3D localization mechanism adds position embeddings and location tokens to capture spatial information. **Results**: outperforms SOTA on ScanQA (BLEU-1 by 9%, CIDER by 10%), SQA3D, and 3DMV-VQA; outperforms 2D VLMs on held-in tasks (3D captioning, 3D-assisted dialog, task decomposition). **Limitation**: the 3D feature extractor relies on 2D multi-view images, requiring an additional rendering process for all 3D scenes. Published at NeurIPS 2023; project page: https://vis-www.cs.umass.edu/3dllm/.

43. **3D-LLM (NeurIPS 2023 Spotlight poster page)** [40]: By Yining Hong, Haoyu Zhen, Peihao Chen, Shuhong Zheng, Yilun Du, Zhenfang Chen, and Chuang Gan. "Using three types of prompting mechanisms that we design, we are able to collect over 300k 3D-language data covering these tasks." (Note: poster says over 300k; the paper PDF reports ~1M.)

44. **3D-LLM (NeurIPS proceedings abstract page)** [41]: Same paper; "Experiments on ScanQA show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a large margin (e.g., the BLEU-1 score surpasses state-of-the-art score by 9%)." Qualitative examples demonstrate capabilities beyond existing LLMs and VLMs.

45. **LL3DA (CVPR 2024) — paper PDF** [42]: "LL3DA: Visual Interactive Instruction Tuning for Omni-3D Understanding, Reasoning, and Planning" by researchers from Fudan University, Tencent PCG, NUS, and A*STAR. "LL3DA takes point cloud as the direct input and responds to both text instructions and visual interactions. The additional visual interaction enables LMMs to better comprehend human interactions with the 3D environment and further remove the ambiguities within plain texts." Architecture: (1) a frozen masked transformer scene encoder pre-trained on ScanNet detection; (2) a visual prompt encoder encoding user clicks via 3D Fourier positional embeddings and box annotations via ROI features from a pre-trained 3D detector; (3) a multi-modal transformer (Q-Former inspired) aggregating 3D scene embeddings, visual prompts, and textual instructions into 32 learnable query tokens, projected as a prefix to a frozen OPT-1.3B LLM. 3D coordinates are converted to plain text tokens (e.g., `<obj>cx, cy, cz, w, h, l</obj>`) with values discretized to [0,255] integers, fitting the existing LLM vocabulary without additional learnable tokens. Results: 3D Dense Captioning 74.17% C@0.25 and 65.19% C@0.5 on ScanRefer; 51.18% C@0.5 on Nr3D, beating Vote2Cap-DETR by +3.38% and +7.34%; 3DQA 76.79% CIDEr on ScanQA validation, surpassing 3D-LLM by +7.39%. Adding visual clicks at test time improves ScanQA CIDEr by +6.12%. Ablations show early fusion of visual prompts (+3.45% C@0.5), auxiliary "localize" instructions, and click prompts improve performance. Works as a generalist across tasks without fine-tuning; training requires no more than eight RTX 3090 GPUs within a day. Datasets: ScanNet (1,201 train / 312 validation scenes) with annotations from ScanRefer, Nr3D, ScanQA, and the ScanNet subset of 3D-LLM, covering dense captioning, QA, scene description, embodied conversation, and planning.

46. **LL3DA (arXiv full text)** [43]: Additional details: the Interactor3D multi-modal transformer is initialized only with pre-trained BERT word and position embeddings (full BERT initialization caused repetitive outputs); coordinates use special tokens like `«loc»xx, yy, zz<</loc»` with unsigned integer values [0,255]. Tasks distinguished by "describe" vs "describe and localize" and "answer" vs "answer and localize" instructions, using "### human:" and "### assistant:" identifiers. ScanQA test results: 78.16% CIDEr (test with object) and 70.29% (test without object). As a generalist (without fine-tuning): 62.98% C@0.5 on ScanRefer and 75.67% CIDEr on ScanQA; fine-tuned weights serve as strong initialization (+2.35% C@0.5 over scratch). Training: AdamW, weight decay 0.1, LR 10⁻⁴→10⁻⁶ cosine annealing, ~100k iterations, batch size 16, ≤8 Nvidia RTX3090 within a day, 40k sampled points per scene; inference with beam search (size 4) or top-k (k=50)+top-p (p=0.95). Supplementary: significantly outperforms zero-shot frozen LLMs (OPT variants, LLAMA-7B) on scene description, embodied dialogue (best 260.07 CIDEr with beam search), and embodied planning (best 196.78 CIDEr with beam search).

47. **LL3DA (Semantic Scholar record)** [44]: Full author list: Sijin Chen, Xin Chen, Xiaoyan Zhang, Mingsheng Li, Gang Yu, Hao Fei, Hongyuan Zhu, Jiayuan Fan, Tao Chen. CVPR 2024, pp. 26418–26428, DOI: 10.1109/CVPR52733.2024.02496. 268 citations. Notable citing works: 3D-LLaVA (Omni Superpoint Transformer), Ross3d (Reconstructive Visual Instruction Tuning with 3D-Awareness), LSceneLLM, PQ3D, VLM-3R, SplatTalk (3D VQA with Gaussian Splatting), Inst3D-LMM, Spatial 3D-LLM, ViewMind3D, LayoutVLM. 75 references including M3DBench, 3D-LLM (NeurIPS 2023), CLIP-Guided Vision-Language Pretraining, Multi-CLIP, 3D-VisTA, 3D-CLR, LEO, GPT4RoI, StableLLaVA, SQA3D.

48. **SR-3D: "3D Aware Region Prompted Vision Language Model" (arXiv:2509.13317 — arXiv preprint)** [45]: By researchers from UC San Diego, MIT, and NVIDIA. SR-3D (Spatial Region 3D) connects single-view 2D images and multi-view 3D data through a shared visual token space, enabling flexible region prompting via bounding boxes, segmentation masks, or direct 3D annotations without exhaustive multi-frame labeling. Enriches 2D visual features with 3D positional embeddings; introduces a Dynamic Tiling-based Region Extractor for high-resolution images; unified architecture where single-view and multi-view data flow through the same model with a canonical 3D positional representation. Training: single-view VLM initialized from NVILA-Lite-8B, fine-tuned on ~7M samples (instruction tuning + region-prompted datasets); multi-view fine-tuning on ScanQA, SQA3D, Scan2Cap, and EmbodiedScan; uses off-the-shelf depth (DepthAnythingV2) for single-view, ground-truth depth for multi-view. Results: ScanQA CIDEr 109.3, EM 30.4; SQA3D EM 62.2; Scan2Cap CIDEr 97.9; 2D VLM region-level mAP 78.0, Acc 88.6% on COCO; SR-3D-Bench qualitative 79.5% and quantitative 83.3%; outperforms all open-source models on VSI-Bench and competes with API-based models. Works with in-the-wild videos via off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction (CUT3R, MAST3R), maintaining CIDEr 109.3 with CUT3R-reconstructed point clouds. Key findings: single-view pre-training significantly enhances multi-view performance; 3D positional embeddings provide marginal benefit alone but are essential with scaling; a 2D VLM trained exclusively on single-view data exhibits strong zero-shot spatial reasoning in 3D scenes.

**Embodied generalist agents and open-set 3D mapping**

49. **LEO (ICML 2024) — project page** [46]: "An Embodied Generalist Agent in 3D World" — an embodied multi-modal and multi-task generalist agent for the 3D world, by researchers from Peking University, BIGAI Beijing, Carnegie Mellon University, and Tsinghua University (Jiangyong Huang, Silong Yong, Xiaojian Ma, Xiongkun Linghu, et al., equal contribution among first four). "We introduce an embodied multi-modal and multi-task generalist agent that excels in perceiving, grounding, reasoning, planning, and acting in the 3D world." Scene representation: point clouds partitioned into object-centric point clouds (ground truth or predicted proposals), processed by a 3D encoder for object-centric features, with an optional 2D branch for ego-view observations; unified LLM-based sequence including a system message, 2D image tokens, 3D object tokens, an instruction, and a final response, trained with a simple auto-regressive loss. Trained in two stages: (i) 3D vision-language alignment and (ii) 3D vision-language-action instruction tuning. Curated datasets LEO-align and LEO-instruct cover object-level and scene-level multi-modal tasks. Demonstrates proficiency across 3D captioning, question answering, embodied reasoning, embodied navigation, and robotic manipulation. Published in Proceedings of ICML 2024.

50. **LEO (arXiv full text)** [47]: Architecture: decoder-only LLM (Vicuna-7B) with LoRA; 2D images encoded by OpenCLIP ConvNext; 3D objects encoded by PointNet++ followed by a Spatial Transformer; ~7B parameters with ~142M tuned; prefix language modeling objective. Data: LEO-align — object captioning (Objaverse, 660K), object referring (ScanNet + 3RScan, 354K generated), scene captioning (3RScan, 20K generated); LEO-instruct — 3D captioning (ScanNet, 37K), 3D QA (ScanNet + 3RScan, 83K generated), 3D dialogue (3RScan, 11K generated), task planning (3RScan, 14K generated), navigation (MP3D, 60K), manipulation (CLIPort, 300K). LLM-assisted generation: scene-graph-based prompting (3DSSG), object-centric chain of thought (O-CoT) prompting to combat LLM hallucination, refinement via regular expression matching and scene graph retrieval achieving 100% accuracy on counting/existence/non-existence QA (vs 40–96.8% for baselines). Results: surpasses SOTA task-specific models on 3D captioning (Scan2Cap CIDEr 72.4), 3D QA (ScanQA), and embodied reasoning (SQA3D) without task-specific fine-tuning; comparable to SOTA on robotic manipulation (CLIPort) and embodied navigation (ObjNav on MP3D/HM3D) with better SPL and zero-shot generalization. Ablations: alignment stage consistently beneficial; generalist-style tuning outperforms specialist training; VLA co-training can slightly harm VL performance; dialogue/planning data reduce hallucination; data balancing with negative samples mitigates hallucination. Scaling law: log-linear loss improvement with data scale; Vicuna-7B > OPT-1.3B, with potential saturation between Vicuna-7B and Vicuna-13B. Limitations: generalization to novel scenes; gap between VL learning and embodied action control. Supported by National Science and Technology Major Project (2022ZD0114900).

51. **LEO (GitHub)** [48]: ICML 2024; 488 stars, MIT license. Team: Jiangyong Huang, Silong Yong, Xiaojian Ma, Xiongkun Linghu, Puhao Li, Yan Wang, Qing Li, Song-Chun Zhu, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang. LLM: Vicuna-7B (v1.1); point cloud backbones: PointNet++, PointBERT (PointNext optional). Checkpoints: align.pth (LoRA-trained alignment stage) and sft_noact.pth (instruction tuning without embodied acting tasks). Data on HuggingFace (huangjy-pku/LEO_data). Training on NVIDIA A100-80GB/A800-80GB. Milestones: 2024.01 HuggingFace demo; 2024.03 code and data; 2024.04 inference/scaling scripts, weights, EAI training code; 2024.05 accepted by ICML 2024; 2024.07 EAI data examples.

52. **LEO (Synced article)** [49]: Introduced by BIGAI, Peking University, CMU, Tsinghua. Contributions: first generalist agent capable of perceiving, grounding, reasoning, planning, and acting in 3D; demonstration that fine-tuning LLMs with object-centric multi-modal representations and embodied action sequences yields a generalist agent; large dataset with quality-enhancing techniques; extensive evaluation showing proficiency in embodied navigation and robotic manipulation with consistent gains as data scales; release of data, code, weights. Published November 26, 2023.

53. **ConceptFusion (RSS 2023) — paper PDF** [50]: "ConceptFusion: Open-set Multimodal 3D Mapping" — builds open-set multimodal 3D maps by fusing pixel-aligned features from foundation models (CLIP, DINO, AudioCLIP, etc.) into 3D maps via SLAM and multi-view fusion techniques, enabling zero-shot querying of maps by text, images, audio, and clicks. Contributions: open-set multimodal 3D mapping queryable by text/image/audio/clicks with no training or finetuning; a novel mechanism to compute pixel-aligned (local) features from foundation models that natively produce image-level (global) features; a new RGB-D dataset UnCoCo (Uncommon Contexts for Common Concepts) with 78 household/office objects and over 500,000 queries across modalities. Results: outperforms supervised approaches (LSeg-3D, OpenSeg-3D) and zero-shot baselines (MaskCLIP-3D) by more than 40% margin on 3D IoU; text-query object localization 0.446 3D mIoU vs 0.289 for OpenSeg-3D and 0.128 for LSeg-3D on the structured UnCoCo subset; audio-query accuracy 64.29% (source-ambiguous) and 66.67% (ecological) vs 23.81% and 22.22% for AudioCLIP baseline. 3D spatial reasoning: 84% success on distance queries, 76% on relative position, 96% on support, 72% on containment (vs random baselines 24%, 36%, 52%, 44%). Outperforms MaskCLIP on ScanNet, Replica, and SemanticKITTI semantic segmentation. Built on ∇SLAM dense SLAM; uses Mask2Former or SAM for class-agnostic instance segmentation; odometry/mapping at 15Hz. Demonstrated on real-world zero-shot tabletop rearrangement with a UR5e manipulator and text-driven autonomous navigation on a drive-by-wire vehicle. Authors from MIT, Université de Montréal, University of Toronto, IIIT Hyderabad, CMU, DEVCOM Army Research Lab, Amazon, Concordia University. RSS 2023, Daegu, Republic of Korea, July 10–14, 2023. (Note: RSS is not among the user's listed venues, but the model was explicitly named in the research topic.) Integrates with LLMs for spatial query parsing and task planning; supports multilingual CLIP models.

54. **ConceptFusion (project page)** [51]: "ConceptFusion builds open-set 3D maps that can be queried via text, click, image, or audio." Leverages open-set capabilities of foundation models pre-trained on internet-scale data to reason across modalities (natural language, images, audio, 3D geometry). Zero-shot pixel alignment technique: processes images to generate class-agnostic object masks, extracts local features per region, computes a global image feature, and fuses region-specific (local) and global features — capturing long-tailed and fine-grained concepts that supervised methods like LSeg and OpenSeg forget during fine-tuning. Spatial reasoning (e.g., "What is the distance between the refrigerator and the television?") via an LLM parsing queries into executable function calls. UnCoCo dataset: 20 RGB-D sequences with 78 commonly found objects annotated with text, audio, click, and image queries plus ground-truth 2D/3D retrieval results. Evaluated on real-world datasets, simulated home environments, tabletop manipulation (e.g., pushing "goldfish" brand snacks or a "Baymax" plush toy), and an autonomous driving platform (navigating to a "football field" via open-set text query). Concurrent work: CLIP-Fields, OpenScene, LERF, NLMap-SayCan, 3D-CLR.

55. **ConceptGraphs (ICRA 2024)** [52]: "Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graphs for Perception and Planning" — builds graph-structured open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs from posed RGB-D images using generic instance segmentation models, extracting semantic feature vectors per region and projecting them to a 3D point cloud; generalizes to novel semantic classes without collecting large 3D datasets or fine-tuning. Capabilities: (1) re-localization via CLIP embeddings per object in a landmark-based particle filter; (2) open-set text queries with both CLIP embeddings (CPU-deployable on-board) and LLM-based queries (e.g., GPT-4) handling multiple concepts, negation, or composition; (3) queries with text and image context (e.g., "something this guy would play with" referencing Michael Jordan → basketball); (4) traversability puzzle: a Jackal robot uses LLM reasoning over concept-graph node captions. Multi-institutional team (MIT, Université de Montréal, University of Toronto, IIIT Hyderabad, JHU APL, JHU, UMass Amherst, DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory; corresponding authors Qiao Gu, Alihusein Kuwajerwala, Sacha Morin, Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula). Citation: Gu et al., ICRA 2024, pp. 5021–5028. Concurrent approaches: OVIR-3D, OpenMask3D, OVSG, SayPlan. (Note: ICRA is not among the user's listed venues.)

56. **Open-Fusion (ICRA 2024 Oral)** [53]: "Open-Fusion: Real-time Open-Vocabulary 3D Mapping and Queryable Scene Representation" — from University of Arkansas, West Virginia University, and University of Liverpool (Kashu Yamazaki, Taisei Hanyu, Khoa Vo, Thang Pham, Minh Tran, Gianfranco Doretto, Anh Nguyen, Ngan Le). "Open-Fusion builds open-vocabulary 3D queryable scene that bridges the 3D perception and language models for robotics in real-time." Harnesses a pre-trained vision-language foundation model (VLFM) for open-set semantic comprehension and the Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) for 3D reconstruction; integrates region-based embeddings and confidence maps with 3D knowledge via an enhanced Hungarian-based feature-matching mechanism. Two modules: Real-time Semantic TSDF 3D Scene Reconstruction Module and Open-Vocabulary Query and Scene Understanding Module. Delivers annotation-free 3D segmentation for open-vocabulary queries without additional 3D training; benchmark tests on ScanNet show superiority over leading zero-shot methods; supports object queries and semantic queries (ScanNetV2 20 classes). Concurrent works: NLMap, VLMaps, CLIP-Fields, LERF, ConceptFusion. arXiv preprint 2310.03923. (Note: ICRA is not among the user's listed venues.)

**Point cloud encoders and CLIP-based 3D understanding**

57. **PointCLIP (CVPR 2022) — Semantic Scholar record** [54]: "PointCLIP: Point Cloud Understanding by CLIP" by Renrui Zhang, Ziyu Guo, Wei Zhang, Kunchang Li, Xupeng Miao, Bin Cui, Yu Jiao Qiao, Peng Gao, and Hongsheng Li. CVPR 2022, pp. 8542–8552; DOI: 10.1109/CVPR52688.2022.00836; posted Dec 4, 2021; 689 citations. Investigates whether CLIP, pre-trained by large-scale image-text pairs in 2D, can be generalized to 3D recognition — proposing PointCLIP, which conducts alignment between 3D point cloud data and CLIP's pre-trained 2D vision-language knowledge. Key citing works: CLIP2Scene, CLIP2Point, PointCLIP V2 (ICCV 2023, collaborates CLIP and GPT for unified 3D open-world learning), CLIP2, P2P (NeurIPS 2022, Point-to-Pixel prompting, 89.3% on ScanObjectNN), CLIPoint3D. Key references: Image2Point, Tip-Adapter, CLIP-Adapter, PointPillars.

58. **PointCLIP (GitHub)** [55]: Official CVPR 2022 implementation — the first method to apply CLIP for point cloud recognition. Projects point clouds onto multi-view depth maps (without rendering) and aggregates view-wise zero-shot predictions using CLIP's 2D encoders; features an inter-view adapter for few-shot performance and supports multi-knowledge ensemble. A pre-trained 16-shot checkpoint produces 86.71% on ModelNet40 (87%+ with post-search). PointCLIP V2 with stronger zero-shot performance is available in a separate repo.

59. **PointCLIP (Liner review)** [56]: Zero-shot classification: 30.23% on ModelNet10, 20.18% on ModelNet40, 15.38% on ScanObjectNN. Performance is highly sensitive to projection settings; the prompt "point cloud depth map of a [CLASS]." yields the best results (20.18% on ModelNet40); more than 6 projected views introduces redundancy; the right view is most informative; RN50×16 achieved 23.78% on ModelNet40. The inter-view adapter extracts compact global features via residual connections, fine-tuned with few-shot data while freezing CLIP encoders; also serves as a multi-knowledge ensembling module.

60. **PointCLIP (arXiv listing)** [57]: arXiv:2112.02413; subjects cs.CV, cs.AI, cs.RO; open sourced with code and model available.

61. **Point2Real (AAAI 2024)** [58]: "Point2Real: Bridging the Gap between Point Cloud and Realistic Image for Open-World 3D Recognition" by Hanxuan Li, Bin Fu, Ruiping Wang, Xilin Chen (Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences). A training-free framework for open-world 3D point cloud recognition addressing three sources of domain gap — shape (discrete vs continuous geometry), texture (point clouds lack texture), and view. Modules: (1) Shape Recovery Module — iterative ball-pivoting algorithm (with holes filling and smoothing) converting point clouds to meshes; (2) Texture Rendering Module — ray tracing-based rendering with a texture candidate list (beige, metallic green, leather red, pink, brown, dark grey), selecting the most suitable texture via CLIP classification confidence; (3) Multi-view Adapter — heuristic algorithm using depth surface area as a viewpoint discriminability indicator, generating weights for feature aggregation. Results: zero-shot classification on ModelNet10 79.5%, ModelNet40 65.8%, ScanObjectNN 57.7% (OBJ ONLY), 53.0% (OBJ BG), 38.1% (PB T50 RS) — surpassing all training-free methods and most training-based methods; exceeds PointCLIP V2 by +6.4% on ModelNet10, +1.6% on ModelNet40, and +7.6%, +12.2%, +2.7% on the three ScanObjectNN splits. Few-shot: consistently outperforms PointCLIP and PointCLIP+RSP across 1/2/4/8/16-shot (67.5% vs 52.6% at one-shot; 86.3% at 16-shot). Ablations confirm texture yields substantial improvements, iterative ball-pivoting beats single iteration and Poisson reconstruction, and the Multi-view Adapter helps in real-world scenarios. Implementation: 5 iterations (radii 5,4,3,2,1), Blender Python API cycles, 10 viewpoints, ViT-B/16, 1024 points; inference ~3s (Blender) or 0.0397s (PyTorch3D). Code: github.com/HanXuan-Li/Point2Real.

62. **Point-BERT (CVPR 2022) — ResearchGate** [59]: "Point-BERT: Pre-training 3D Point Cloud Transformers with Masked Point Modeling." Conference paper, June 2022, DOI: 10.1109/CVPR52688.2022.01871.

63. **Point-BERT (GitHub)** [60]: By Xumin Yu, Lulu Tang, Yongming Rao, Tiejun Huang, Jie Zhou, and Jiwen Lu. "Point-BERT is a new paradigm for learning Transformers to generalize the concept of BERT onto 3D point cloud. Inspired by BERT, we devise a Masked Point Modeling (MPM) task to pre-train point cloud Transformers." Method: divides point clouds into local patches; uses a discrete Variational AutoEncoder (dVAE) as a point cloud Tokenizer to generate discrete point tokens; randomly masks patches and feeds them into a backbone Transformer; pre-training objective is to recover original point tokens at masked locations under Tokenizer supervision. Fine-tuned results on ModelNet40: 92.67% Acc (1024 pts), 92.91% (4096), 93.19% (8192); with voting up to 93.76%; ScanObjectNN: 88.12% (objectonly), 87.43% (objectbg), 83.07% (hardest). Pre-trained dVAE and Point-BERT models trained on ShapeNet; 695 stars; MIT license.

64. **Point-BERT (arXiv listing)** [61]: Accepted to CVPR 2022; arXiv:2111.14819; project page https://point-bert.ivg-research.xyz; subjects cs.CV, cs.AI, cs.LG.

65. **Point-In-Context (NeurIPS 2023)** [62]: "Explore In-Context Learning for 3D Point Cloud Understanding" by Zhongbin Fang, Xiangtai Li, Xia Li, Joachim M. Buhmann, Chen Change Loy, and Mengyuan Liu (Sun Yat-sen University, NTU, ETH Zurich, Peking University). The first general framework for 3D visual prompting; treats multiple 3D point cloud tasks as task-aware prompting. Creates the first benchmark for 3D in-context learning based on ShapeNet and ShapeNetPart, comprising 217,454 samples across four tasks: point cloud reconstruction, denoising, registration, and part segmentation. Proposes the Joint Sampling (JS) module to solve information leakage in Masked Point Modeling. Variants PIC-Sep and PIC-Cat use a standard transformer encoder-decoder with ℓ2 Chamfer Distance loss. Results: PIC-Cat avg reconstruction CD 4.3, denoising 5.3, registration 14.1, mIOU 78.95; PIC-Sep 4.7, 7.6, 10.3, 74.95 — SOTA among multitask models on all four tasks. Task-specific models (PointNet, DGCNN, PCT, ACT) still outperform PIC on most individual tasks, but PIC excels at generalization to out-of-distribution data (ModelNet40 registration) and unseen tasks. JS module is critical. Ablations: Farthest Point Sampling better for reconstruction; ℓ2 loss best; 70% mask ratio generally best; CD-aware prompt selection significantly improves results (registration CD drops from 10.3 to 4.1 for PIC-Sep). Limitation: struggles to reconstruct detailed parts of complex point clouds. Code: github.com/fanglaosi/Point-In-Context.

66. **Point-CSA (CVPR 2025)** [63]: "Adapting Pre-trained 3D Models for Point Cloud Video Understanding via Cross-frame Spatio-temporal Adaptation" — the first exploration of transferring pre-trained static 3D point cloud models to 4D point cloud video. Proposes Cross-frame Spatio-temporal Adaptation (CSA) with: (1) Point Tube Adapter — an embedding layer grouping points into "point tubes" along spatial and temporal dimensions (with relative spatio-temporal displacements as features), encoded via an extended lightweight 4D PointNet; (2) Geometric Constraint Temporal Adapter (GCTA) — constructs a cross-frame KNN graph based on spatial distance between point tubes, using EdgeConv-style edge features (combining global variation fj−fi with local structural features fi) and max pooling. Backbone parameters are frozen; only adapters, position encoders, and task head are fine-tuned. Results: MSR-Action3D (24 frames): Point-MAE+CSA 95.12%, outperforming all supervised (best X4D-SceneFormer 93.90%) and self-supervised (best C2P 94.76%, MaST-Pre 94.08%) methods; SHREC'17: PointGPT-S+CSA 96.5%, Point-BERT+CSA 96.2%, Point-MAE+CSA 95.2% (supervised best Kinet 95.2%, self-supervised best PointCMP 93.3%). Ablations on 12 frames with Point-MAE: baseline frozen 77.35%; +Point Tube Adapter 83.97%; +position encoders 87.11%; +GCTA 94.08%; full model 95.12%. Optimal GCTA k=20; "Bypass" placement best; full video as temporal slice best. Code: github.com/LvBaixuan/Point-CSA. Supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China.

67. **Point Transformer (ICCV 2021)** [64]: By researchers from University of Oxford, HKU, CUHK, and Intel Labs. "Self-attention networks have revolutionized natural language processing... The application of self-attention to 3D point clouds is therefore quite natural, since point clouds are essentially sets embedded in 3D space." Core: Point Transformer layer applying vector self-attention locally on kNN neighborhoods (k=16), with a trainable, parameterized relative position encoding added to both the attention generation and feature transformation branches. U-net design with five encoder stages, transition-down (farthest point sampling + kNN max-pooling) and transition-up (trilinear interpolation); no convolutions. Results: S3DIS Area 5 semantic segmentation 70.4% mIoU, 76.5% mAcc, 90.8% OA — first model to cross 70% mIoU, +3.3 pp over prior SOTA; 73.5% mIoU with 6-fold cross-validation; only 4.9M parameters vs 14.9M (KPConv) and 30.1M (SparseConv). ModelNet40: 93.7% OA, 90.6% mAcc. ShapeNetPart: 86.6% instance mIoU, 83.7% category mIoU. Ablations: k=16 optimal; relative position encoding outperforms absolute/none and adding to both branches important; vector attention (70.4%) significantly outperforms scalar attention (64.6%), MLP+pooling (63.7%), and plain MLP (61.7%); softmax normalization essential (70.4% vs 66.5%).

**Researcher context**

68. **Zhengyuan Yang (personal academic homepage)** [65]: Member of Technical Staff at Microsoft AI Superintelligence; Ph.D. from University of Rochester (advised by Prof. Jiebo Luo); B.S. from USTC. Research focused on multimodal foundation models and post-training for long-horizon tasks. Awards: ACM SIGMM Award for Outstanding Ph.D. Thesis (2022; thesis "Visual Grounding: Building Cross-Modal Visual-Text Alignment"), Twitch Research Fellowship, ICPR 2018 Best Industry Related Paper Award, and Winner of CVPR 2021 TextCaps and ReferIt3D Challenges. Notable publications including MM-REACT, GPT-4V in Wonderland, The Dawn of LMMs, MM-Vet, survey book "Multimodal Foundation Models: From Specialists to General-Purpose Assistants." Recent highlights: 2026 H1 MAI-Code-1-Flash (5B-active token-efficient coding model, 71.6 SWE-Bench Verified, 51.2 SWE-Bench Pro, up to 60% fewer tokens); 2025 H1 works on multimodal reasoning and agentic models (ViCrit, ThinkLite-VL, Point-RFT, Vision Value Model, ImageGen-CoT, RAGEN, VAGEN, benchmarks ViCrit-Bench, EMMA, SITE, V-MAGE, MMWorld); five papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025, two to EMNLP 2025, three to ICCV 2025, two to ICML 2025 (one Oral), two to CVPR 2025, five to ICLR 2025; 2024 papers at NeurIPS, ECCV, ICML, CVPR, ACL, COLM, ACMMM. Service: Area Chair (ICLR, ACMMM, EMNLP, NAACL), SPC for AAAI (2023–25), Exhibits and Demos Chair ICME 2024, Associate Editor TCSVT.

69. **Qing Li (personal news page)** [66]: Highlights: ICCV 2023 paper on 3D-VisTA; CVPR 2024 paper on CLOVA (tool-based visual assistants); ICML 2024 papers on LEO (3D embodied generalist agent) and INSIGHT (neural-symbolic RL, Spotlight, top 3.5%); ECCV 2024 papers on PQ3D, SceneVerse (first million-scale 3D vision-language dataset), and VideoAgent; three NeurIPS 2024 papers (FIRE, UltraEdit, OmniJARVIS); tutorial on multimodal generalist agents; organized the 1st workshop on Open-World Agents (NeurIPS 2024); Top Reviewer of NeurIPS 2024; ICLR 2025 papers on Multimodal Knowledge Editing and Multimodal Agent Tuning (Spotlight); two CVPR 2025 papers; two ICCV 2025 papers (MTU3D, receiving perfect review scores, and Embodied VideoAgent); Area Chair for NeurIPS 2025; three NeurIPS 2025 papers (SPORT Agent, Anywhere3D, NEP). Emphasis on multimodal/embodied agents, 3D vision-language understanding, dataset creation (UltraEdit ~4M images, SceneVerse million-scale), and vision-language-action models.

---

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

The following tool calls were made during research, using the `tavily_search` tool (batches) and `think_tool`:

1. `think_tool` – initial reflection on research scope.
2. `tavily_search` batch 1:
   - "spatial understanding vision-language models benchmarks top conference 2022 2023 2024 2025"
   - "VSR Visual Spatial Reasoning benchmark NeurIPS CVPR"
   - "3D spatial reasoning benchmarks vision-language models ScanRefer ReferIt3D conference"
3. `think_tool` – reflection on organizing follow-up searches.
4. `tavily_search` batch 2:
   - "GQA dataset visual reasoning NeurIPS 2019 publication"
   - "CLEVR diagnostic dataset CVPR 2017"
   - "NLVR2 natural language visual reasoning benchmark ACL 2019"
   - "Winoground visio-linguistic compositional reasoning ICLR 2022"
   - "VALSE benchmark linguistic phenomena vision language ACL 2022"
5. `think_tool` – closing reflection on remaining benchmarks to verify.

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Overview

The research covered benchmarks, datasets, and evaluation methodologies for measuring spatial understanding and reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs), with sources spanning 2017–2025 (ICCV/NeurIPS/CVPR 2025 and ICLR 2025 papers were verified). Findings are organized into 2D spatial benchmarks, 3D spatial benchmarks, spatial-reasoning-specific evaluation findings, recent diagnostic benchmarks and enhancement methods, and resource repositories. Venue verification was performed per source; several benchmarks requested by the user (e.g., RefCOCO series, ScanRefer, R2R, NDH) were only mentioned in passing within the sources gathered, and their venue details could not be independently confirmed by the researcher; those are flagged as "mentioned in [source]" rather than given fabricated citations.

---

## 2. 2D Spatial Benchmarks

### 2.1 GQA — Real-World Visual Reasoning and Compositional QA

**Full citation (as verified):** Hudson, Drew A. and Manning, Christopher D., "GQA: A New Dataset for Real-World Visual Reasoning and Compositional Question Answering," CVPR 2019 (oral presentation); arXiv:1902.09506 [cs.CL].

- GQA is a visual question answering dataset designed for real-world visual reasoning, containing **22 million multi-step, compositional questions** paired with images from COCO and Flickr, each with **scene graphs of objects and relations** ([4][5]).
- The dataset is "balanced to reduce answer distribution biases and mitigate language priors," includes "structured semantic representations for strong supervision," and introduces "new metrics to evaluate accuracy, consistency, validity, and plausibility" ([5]).
- It "supports detailed diagnosis based on question type, difficulty, and reasoning steps" ([5]).
- Usage in spatial evaluation: GQA questions include relations and spatial predicates; the dataset has been used to evaluate pretrained V&L models (e.g., LXMERT, VisualBERT in NLVR2 follow-ups) and in ProTo (NeurIPS 2021 program-guided transformer), which "outperforms Meta Module Networks (MMN) on complex visual reasoning tasks" and achieves 98.1% validation accuracy on its program synthesis model ([17]).
- The GQA-spatial subset (1,451 images isolating spatial reasoning) is used in the What's Up? benchmark (see Section 2.4) ([1]).

### 2.2 CLEVR — Compositional Language and Elementary Visual Reasoning

**Full citation (as verified):** Johnson, Justin; Hariharan, Bharath; van der Maaten, Laurens; Fei-Fei, Li; Zitnick, C. Lawrence; and Girshick, Ross B., "CLEVR: A Diagnostic Dataset for Compositional Language and Elementary Visual Reasoning," CVPR 2017 ([6][7][8]).

- CLEVR is "a diagnostic dataset that tests a range of visual reasoning abilities," designed "to test visual reasoning abilities with minimal biases," with detailed annotations describing "the kind of reasoning each question requires" ([6][7]).
- Dataset composition: **70,000 training images (699,989 questions), 15,000 validation images (149,991 questions), and 15,000 test images (14,988 questions)**, with answers, scene graph annotations, and functional program representations for all train/val images ([7]).
- The **Compositional Generalization Test (CoGenT)** "tests generalization to novel attribute combinations across two conditions (A and B) with different color-shape assignments" ([7]).
- Questions test "various aspects of visual reasoning including attribute identification, counting, comparison, spatial relationships, and logical operations"; each question is represented "both in natural language and as a functional program," where the functional program "allows for precise determination of the reasoning skills required to answer each question" ([7]).
- Evaluation status: describes how the dataset "has been used extensively to evaluate and diagnose weaknesses in VQA models, including neural module networks, transformer-based models like LXMERT, and large multimodal models like GPT-4V"; "state-of-the-art models struggle with compositionality, spatial relationships, and relational reasoning despite strong quantitative results" ([6]).
- Derivative works include "CLEVR-Analogy (analogical reasoning), QLEVR (quantificational language), and compositional reasoning analyses of VLMs" ([6]), as well as **CLEVR-Dialog** (NAACL-HLT 2019), a diagnostic dataset for multi-round visual dialog, containing "5 instances of 10-round dialogs for about 85k CLEVR images, totaling to 4.25M question-answer pairs" — with results: Random 3.4%, Random-Q 33.4%, CorefNMN 68.0% (best) ([9]).

### 2.3 NLVR / NLVR2 — Natural Language for Visual Reasoning

**Full citation (as verified):** Suhr, Alane; Zhou, Stephanie; Zhang, Ally; Zhang, Iris; Bai, Huajun; and Artzi, Yoav, "A Corpus for Reasoning About Natural Language Grounded in Photographs," ACL 2019 (Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the ACL, Florence, Italy) ([11][12]).

- NLVR2 contains **107,292 examples** where each example pairs a natural language caption (29,680 unique sentences) with **two photographs** (127,502 unique images), and the task is "to determine whether a natural language caption is true about a pair of photographs" ([11][12]).
- NLVR contains 92,244 pairs of English sentences grounded in synthetic images ([10]).
- The dataset covers "a wide range of linguistic phenomena including numerical expressions, quantifiers, coreference, and negation," with spatial relations occurring in 49% of the analyzed sentences ([11][12]).
- Inter-annotator agreement: 0.912 α and 0.889 κ; vocabulary 7,457 word types (NLVR: 252); mean sentence length 14.8 tokens (NLVR: 11.2) ([12]).
- Human performance: 96.1% (96.2% dev); state-of-the-art visual reasoning methods perform poorly — best system (MAXENT) achieved 54.8% on Test-P, FiLM reached 52.1%; "all generalize poorly" ([11][12]).
- NLVR2 leaderboard (no longer updated): #1 UNITER 78.4% Dev / 80.4% Test-U; #2 LXMERT 74.9% / 76.2%; #3 VisualBERT 67.4% / 67.3% ([10]).
- **NLVR2 bias analysis:** "some amount of visual bias likely exists" — of 33,866 image pairs appearing twice, 62.8% have the same label (vs. expected 50%); a worst-case model exploiting only visual bias achieves 83.53% accuracy on the dev set. New evaluation subsets (balanced: 2,300 of 6,982 dev examples; unbalanced: 3,562) were proposed and added to the official protocol ([13]).
- Both hidden test sets were publicly released on August 18, 2022 ([10]).

### 2.4 Winoground — Visio-Linguistic Compositionality

**Full citation (as verified):** Thrush, Tristan; Jiang, Ryan; Bartolo, Max; Singh, Aman; Williams, Adina; Menon, Douwe; Lee, Kenton; Kiela, Douwe; ... "Winoground: Probing Vision and Language Models for Visio-Linguistic Compositionality," CVPR 2022 ([15][16][17]).

- "A novel task and dataset for evaluating the ability of vision and language models to conduct visio-linguistic compositional reasoning. Given two images and two captions, the goal is to match them correctly — but crucially, both captions contain a completely identical set of words, only in a different order" ([15]).
- Dataset: **400 examples** (800 image-caption pairs, 1,600 total pairings), hand-curated by four expert annotators, images licensed from Getty Images; balanced with half correct pairings and half deliberately mismatched ([15][16][18]).
- **Three evaluation scores:** Text score (correct caption selected given image, chance 25%), Image score (correct image selected given caption, chance 25%), Group score (both simultaneously correct, chance 16.67%) ([15][16]).
- **Key result:** "All state-of-the-art V&L models tested (UNITER, VILLA, VinVL, VisualBERT, ViLT, LXMERT, ViLBERT, UniT, CLIP, VSE++, VSRN) perform close to or at random chance, with a ~70% performance gap compared to humans on the image score metric. Humans achieve 89.50% text score, 88.50% image score, and 85.50% group score, while the best model (VinVL) achieves only 37.75%, 17.75%, and 14.50% respectively" ([15][16]).
- Dataset tags: linguistic (Object, Relation, Both swaps) and visual (Pragmatics, Symbolic, Series); "models perform worst on the 'Series' tag, where most achieve 0% group score" ([15]).
- Analysis findings: single-stream models slightly outperform dual-stream; caption length negatively correlates with performance; "significant positive correlation between pretraining dataset size and model scores"; models "struggle with compositional reasoning, often disregarding adjective information (e.g., treating 'brown dog' and 'white dog' similarly)" ([15]). The primary challenge "may lie in the fusion of visual and textual representations, rather than in weaknesses of either branch alone" ([18]).
- Winoground-T2I extends the paradigm to 11k contrastive sentence pairs across 20 categories to evaluate text-to-image compositional rendering. Methods catalyzed by Winoground include ComCLIP, CACR (+5.75 group score), DiffusionITM, SDS-CLIP, and SCRAMBLe (improving group accuracy from 49.5% to 54.8%) ([18]).

### 2.5 VALSE — Vision And Language Structured Evaluation

**Full citation (as verified):** Parcalabescu, Letitia; Cafagna, Michele; Muradjan, Lilit; Frank, Anette; ... "VALSE: A Task-Independent Benchmark for Vision and Language Models for Grounded Language Understanding," ACL 2022 (Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the ACL, pages 8253–8280, Dublin, Ireland) ([19][20]).

- "A task-independent benchmark for testing general-purpose pretrained vision and language (V&L) models on their visio-linguistic grounding capabilities across specific linguistic phenomena" ([19]).
- **Six "pieces" (tests):** (1) Existence (505 examples, existential quantifiers, Visual7W); (2) Plurality (851 examples, semantic number, MSCOCO); (3) Counting (868 balanced, 691 adversarial, 900 small numbers, Visual7W); (4) **Spatial relations (535 examples, preposition understanding, MSCOCO with SpanBERT-generated foils)**; (5) Actions (648 action replacement + 949 actant swap, SWiG); (6) Coreference (708 standard + 104 clean, VisDial v1.0) ([19]).
- **Methodology (foiling):** "correct captions are minimally edited to create invalid foils"; balancing word frequency distributions between captions and foils to prevent statistical bias; language models (BERT, SpanBERT) for plausible foil generation; GRUEN grammaticality filtering; NLI (ALBERT) to filter entailed foils; human validation on AMT (87.7% of instances validated by at least 2/3 annotators, 73.6% unanimous) ([19]).
- Models benchmarked zero-shot: CLIP, LXMERT, ViLBERT, ViLBERT 12-in-1, VisualBERT, plus unimodal text-only GPT-1 and GPT-2. "ViLBERT 12-in-1 performed best overall, nearly solving existence (95.6% accr, 96.3% AUROC)," but "all models struggled with plurality, counting, spatial relations, actions, and coreference. VisualBERT performed below random baseline (48.8% accuracy)" ([19]).
- Conclusion: "current V&L models can identify named objects and their presence in images but struggle to ground interdependencies and relationships in visual scenes when constrained by linguistic indicators" ([19]).
